IL1: Congenital heart disease (CHD) comprises a variety of cardiovascular malformations, which, collectively, affects approximately 2% of newborns. Over the past few decades, there has been stunning progress in devising effective interventions for CHD. Despite that, CHD remains the leading cause of newborn deaths due to birth defects, and survivors continue to suffer from co-morbidities such as neurodevelopmental delays as well as early mortality. Elaborating the genetic causes of CHD, believed to account for the majority of its etiology, is of importance, both for devising prevention and therapeutic strategies. For this invited lecture, the genetic epidemiology of CHD as well as ongoing efforts, principally through the use of next generation sequencing-based approaches, to elaborate the genetic architecture of CHD as a complex genetic trait will be reviewed. In addition, the implications of these findings as they related to outcomes for CHD survivors will be discussed. Finally, opportunities ahead to explain the missing heritability of CHD will be described.
IL2: Genome function is regulated temporally and tissue-specifically through the coordinated interplay between genomic features and the factors that interact with them. Such interactions are modulated by epigenetic modifications which can be both dynamic and stable within somatic lineages. In the germline and upon fertilization in mammals, however, epigenetic modifications are erased and then reconstructed. In early development, this epigenetic reprogramming initiates a hierarchy of epigenetic states that contribute to chromatin architecture, gene regulation and the management of transposable elements regulating genome function and normal development. Despite this post-fertilisation epigenetic erasure and reconstruction, an epigenetic process such as genomic imprinting is transmitted from parent to offspring resulting in epigenetic inheritance. Here we discuss imprinting and the management of transposable elements as models for understanding epigenetic inheritance, epigenetic hierarchies and the influence of these on the regulation of the genome.
IL3: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a genetically complex neurodegenerative disorder in which common variants may influence disease susceptibility, severity, and therapeutic response. Large-scale GWAS study in UK has shown that genetic variants associated with higher blood total cholesterol levels play a causal role in sporadic ALS. Using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) motor neurons, we identified ropinirole as an ALS therapeutic candidate and conducted the investigator-initiated phase 1/2a ROPALS trial. Ropinirole was well tolerated and showed signals of clinical benefit, including slower ALSFRS- R decline during extended treatment. Mechanistically, ropinirole suppressed the SREBP2-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis pathway in ALS iPSC-derived motor neurons. Integration of cellular phenotypes with human genetic data further linked cholesterol metabolism to disease heterogeneity. The polygenic risk score (PRS) for blood total cholesterol was associated with ALS severity and the degree of clinical improvement following ropinirole treatment. A higher cholesterol PRS was also associated with increased cholesterol biosynthesis in motor neurons and greater in vitro responsiveness to ropinirole. These findings illustrate how integrating human genetics with iPSC-based disease modeling can identify pathogenic pathways, stratify patients, and guide mechanism-based drug development for sporadic ALS. A pivotal Phase 3 trial of ropinirole is in preparation.
IL4: Since the completion of the Human Genome Project in 2000 and the publication of the full sequence comprising approximately 3 billion base pairs in 2003, sequencing technology has advanced dramatically, rapidly ushering in an era where clinical application is feasible. The genome serves as an individual's biological blueprint and provides crucial information for disease diagnosis and treatment; however, as it is also considered the ultimate form of personal data requiring appropriate protection and handling, nations worldwide are advancing various initiatives related to genomic medicine and research as national projects. In Japan, Biobank Japan was launched in 2003. Implementation of genomic medicine was discussed at the Council for the Promotion of Genomic Medicine in 2015, followed by the formulation of the Action Plan for Whole Genome Analysis (First Edition) in 2019 and a revised edition in 2022. In 2023, the Genomic Medicine Promotion Act was enacted, and the Basic Plan for Genomic Medicine was established in 2025. Subsequently, March 30, 2026, the Genomic Medicine Japan (GeMJ) was launched. GeMJ is founded on the principles of being patient-initiated and ensuring that benefits are returned to patients. It inherits data from AMED research groups such as the Kokudo group and aims to establish close collaborations to continuously collect and centrally manage clinical, genomic, and other omics data. The ultimate goal is to make this data available to researchers in academia and industry to facilitate drug discovery and related advancements. Although GeMJ currently operates out of a space within the National Cancer Center, plans for its future expansion and development are actively underway.
IL5: Post-transcriptional modifications of RNA are highly diverse, with over 170 types identified to date. These modifications regulate multiple layers of gene expression, including RNA localization, stability, and translation. Accordingly, genetic variants that impair RNA modification cause human diseases; examples include the type 2 diabetes risk gene CDKAL1, which modifies cytosolic tRNA-Lys, and pathogenic mitochondrial tRNA mutations in MELAS and MERRF, which abolish taurine modification at the wobble position. Although functional analyses of RNA modifications have advanced considerably, most studies have focused on their intracellular roles, leaving the metabolic fate of modified nucleosides released upon RNA degradation and turnover largely unclear. Recently, we reported that modified nucleosides, the metabolites of these RNA modifications, are present in diverse forms and high abundance in extracellular fluids such as blood, urine, and aqueous humor. Furthermore, certain modified nucleosides, such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A), trigger immune responses through specific receptor signaling (Mol Cell 2021, Nat Commun 2024). We also found that some modified nucleosides are inherently toxic and that intrinsic detoxification mechanisms protect cells from this toxicity; impairment of these mechanisms may contribute to the pathogenesis of human metabolic diseases (Cell 2025). In this talk, I will outline our work and the latest findings on modified nucleosides as a novel class of RNA-derived humoral factors.
EL: Recent advances in genome editing techniques have expanded opportunities in life sciences and biomedical research. At the same time, their application to human embryos and germ cells has raised scientific, ethical, and social concerns. Because genetic modifications introduced into germ cells or embryos may be inherited by future generations, many countries have adopted a cautious approach to heritable human genome editing (hereinafter referred to as “HHGE”). In Japan, the use of genome editing techniques in human embryos had previously been addressed through administrative guidelines and self-regulatory measures. However, these approaches lacked legal enforceability. Following international discussions on HHGE, the need for a statutory framework became evident. As a result, the Act on the Regulation of the Handling of Human Genome- Edited Embryos and Germ Cells was in 2026. The Act establishes a comprehensive regulatory framework covering not only genome-edited human embryos but also genome-edited human germ cells and embryos derived from such germ cells. The term “genome-edited” under the Act covers not only genome-editing techniques such as CRISPR-Cas9 but also related techniques, including transcriptomic and epigenomic editing. The Act principally prohibits the transfer of human genome-edited embryos and germ cells into a human or Animal uterus. In addition, it establishes requirements for their handling, including notification obligations, compliance with ministerial guidelines, and regulatory oversight measures. The Act is relevant to researchers and healthcare professionals in human genetics and reproductive medicine. This presentation will outline the legislative background, key concepts, and regulatory framework of the Act and provide an update on subordinate legislation and other implementation measures.
S1-1: Background: Extranodal natural killer T-cell lymphoma (NKTCL) is an aggressive malignancy. Methods: We performed a genome-wide association study in East Asian populations (1,417 cases and 20,402 controls overall). Findings: Two novel susceptibility loci were identified: IL18RAP at 2q12.1 and HLA-DRB1 at 6p21.3. IL18RAP functional analyses supported a regulatory effect, and knockdown inhibited NKTCL cell proliferation. Interpretation: The findings implicate inflammation, IL18-IL18RAP signaling and antigen presentation in NKTCL development.
S1-2: Marked heterogeneity in the genetic architecture of complex diseases across East Asian populations poses a challenge for precision medicine, yet its evolutionary origins remain poorly understood. This study investigated how population history and environmental adaptation have shaped disease-related genetic variation across East Asia. We analyzed a spatiotemporally resolved ancient genomic dataset using genome-wide selection scans, genotype-environment association analyses, and functional predictions. We further integrated newly sequenced and previously published present-day genomes to characterize major ancestral components and their contributions to disease-related genetic variation. We identified widespread adaptive signals. Hypoxia-related selection on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau reflected adaptation to physical environments, while immune-related selection, particularly in the HLA region, was consistent with long-term host-pathogen interactions. Subsistence transitions and dietary change left metabolic signatures at loci involved in lipid metabolism and alcohol processing. Ancestry-aware analyses further revealed structured differences in genetic architecture across immune, cardiometabolic, and hematological traits, contributing to a geographically heterogeneous landscape of disease-related genetic variation within East Asia. Together, these findings place present-day disease-related genetic heterogeneity in East Asia within a deep evolutionary context and underscore the importance of incorporating population history and ancestral diversity into precision genomic research.
S1-3: Background: Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative disorders. Despite advances in genetic diagnosis, clinical presentation and disease progression vary substantially even among patients with the same genetic subtype, limiting genotype-based prediction of disease course. Objective(s): To characterize the genetic and clinical spectrum, delineate genotype-specific longitudinal motor trajectories, and identify clinically distinct phenotypic subgroups in a large single-center HSP cohort. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 235 genetically confirmed HSP patients from Seoul National University Hospital. Motor disability was serially assessed using the Four-Stage Scale of Motor Disability (4SMD). Hierarchical clustering incorporating age at onset, baseline 4SMD stage, annualized 4SMD change, and complex HSP was performed using Gower distance. Genotype-specific progression rates were assessed using generalized estimating equation models. Results: SPAST was the most frequently implicated gene (133 patients, 56.6%), followed by ATL1 (13.6%) and KIF1A (8.5%). Compared with SPAST, patients with SPG11 showed more rapid progression, with a greater annualized 4SMD change (β = 0.11; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.04–0.17; p = 0.001), whereas REEP1 showed slower progression (β = -0.04; 95% CI, -0.05 to -0.03; p < 0.001). Phenotype-based clustering identified four subgroups of HSP: early-onset severe group (17.9%), late-onset rapidly progressive group enriched for SPG11 (5.8%), and two slowly progressive groups distinguished by age at onset, enriched for ATL1/KIF1A (42.2%) and SPAST (34.1%), respectively. Conclusion(s): Disease progression in HSP varied substantially by genotype, and phenotype-based clustering provided clinically meaningful stratification beyond genotype, identifying distinct patterns of disease onset, severity, and progression.
S1-4: Purpose: Intragenic duplications are typically interpreted according to exon-level copy-number changes, assuming that duplications involving the same exons have similar functional consequences. We investigated whether long-read sequencing (LRS) could improve the clinical interpretation of intragenic DMD duplications by resolving their genomic architecture. Methods: Nine unrelated individuals with intragenic DMD duplications identified by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) underwent PacBio LRS. Structural findings were integrated with clinical and familial segregation data. Results: LRS resolved the genomic architecture of all duplications, revealing tandem duplications, an inverted duplication, and a complex rearrangement involving insertional translocation. Despite similar exon-level copy-number changes, duplications differed in their structural context and predicted transcriptional consequences. In one family, segregation analysis identified multiple clinically unaffected hemizygous male carriers of a duplication initially considered pathogenic, prompting structural re-evaluation. LRS demonstrated that the rearrangement was structurally compatible with preserved gene function, illustrating that identical exon-level duplications can have distinct functional consequences. Conclusion: Exon-level copy-number analysis alone is insufficient to predict the functional consequences of intragenic duplications. Structural characterization by LRS improves variant interpretation and may reduce misclassification while supporting more accurate reproductive and diagnostic decision-making.
S1-5: Epidemiology seeks to understand the determinants and patterns of health and disease at the population level. Peripheral blood harbors two layers of genomic information: inherited germline variation between individuals and acquired somatic variation within individuals. Germline pathogenic variants can confer susceptibility to multiple cancers, yet the associated risks may vary substantially with environmental factors. Evaluating gene-environment interactions can clarify this heterogeneity and inform the assessment and management of inherited cancer risk. Somatic variation, exemplified by clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), provides a complementary perspective. CHIP can be viewed both as a consequence of genetic, environmental, and age-related influences and as a potential contributor to disease risk. Evaluating CHIP within a framework that considers both mediation and interaction helps clarify its role in the relationship between environmental factors and clinical outcomes. Together, these perspectives extend gene-environment frameworks to incorporate somatic variation and provide insights into disease mechanisms that may not be apparent when each factor is examined in isolation. This presentation discusses how epidemiological approaches can integrate genomic variation between and within individuals to advance our understanding of disease risk and inform risk assessment and prevention.
S1-6: Genetic effects on human complex traits vary with age, sex, and lifestyle. Characterizing gene–environment (G×E) interactions can therefore reveal how environmental contexts shape genetic architecture and its biological consequences. We developed a scalable framework for systematic G×E analysis across multiple environmental factors and applied it to Japanese and European biobanks with extensive replication (total N = 980,004). We identified 94 genome-wide significant G×E interactions and characterized their environmental specificity, providing a cross-population atlas of context-dependent genetic effects. Genome-wide analyses revealed contributions to missing heritability and environmental modulation of relationships between traits. To incorporate these effects into phenotype prediction, we developed a two-dimensional polygenic score model combining marginal genetic and G×E effects, improving prediction accuracy for body mass index by 17%. Integrating genetic signals with single-cell transcriptomic data revealed an age-dependent shift in pulse pressure genetics, from smooth muscle contraction to endothelial senescence. Metabolome-wide analyses of 325 metabolites (N = 242,450) identified 39 G×E loci, including lipid metabolism genes with opposite genetic effects between sexes. These findings connect environmental modulation of genetic effects to cellular and molecular processes and highlight its relevance to genetic prediction and drug development. This lecture will discuss how G×E analyses advance our understanding of the dynamic genetic basis of complex traits.
S2-1: Long-read sequencing (LRS) is transforming neurogenetics by revealing genomic features that are difficult to resolve using short-read sequencing. LRS enable direct characterization of repeat expansions and structural variants, long-range haplotype phasing, and analysis of epigenetic features. Repeat expansion disorders are an important application of LRS. In RFC1-associated Cerebellar Ataxia, Neuropathy, and Vestibular Areflexia Syndrome (CANVAS), accurate genotyping requires determination not only of repeat length but also of repeat motif. Analyses using Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms demonstrate the value of directly reading expanded alleles, while also revealing platform-dependent challenges in repeat genotyping. LRS also enables disease-associated variants to be placed on extended haplotypes. Analysis of the SCA36 repeat expansion and surrounding regions has provided insights into shared and divergent haplotypes among affected populations, offering clues to the origins and spread of disease alleles. Long-read sequencing can also provide epigenetic information, including DNA methylation, in addition to primary DNA sequence. Emerging approaches may further extend these analyses to other layers of genome regulation, while continued advances in sequencing and analytical methods are improving our ability to explore complex genomic variation. Together, these developments are expanding the scope of LRS from variant detection toward a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular architecture of neurogenetic disease.
S2-2: Repeat expansion disorders are common among neurological and muscular diseases. Advances in whole-genome sequencing and long-read sequencing technologies have accelerated the discovery of pathogenic repeat expansions. These advances have not only provided further insights into the characteristic features of repeat expansion disorders but have also revealed new aspects of their pathogenesis. In many repeat expansion disorders, longer repeat expansions are associated with more severe phenotypes. Further expansion of repeats in successive generations can lead to genetic anticipation. However, recent studies have shown that repeat length alone does not determine disease onset and severity; the sequence composition within the repeat tract and epigenomic features, such as DNA methylation, can also play important roles. Another characteristic is the variability and unpredictability of clinical phenotypes. For example, C9orf72 repeat expansions can cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and substantial phenotypic variability is not uncommon even within the same family. A third characteristic is the frequent presence of founder effects, resulting in marked geographic differences in disease prevalence. Finally, somatic instability of repeat expansions has recently attracted increasing attention, particularly in Huntington’s disease. In this symposium, I will provide an overview of these characteristic features of repeat expansion disorders, incorporating recent advances and emerging concepts in the field.
S2-3: Repeat expansion disorders are classically inherited, but repeat instability acquired during life may contribute to sporadic neurodegeneration. In Huntington disease, somatic expansion of the HTT CAG tract in striatal projection neurons is a key determinant of dysfunction and onset. A reported de novo somatic C9orf72 expansion in sporadic frontotemporal dementia suggests that pathogenic alleles can arise within vulnerable tissues. We investigated this paradigm in multiple system atrophy (MSA), a sporadic α-synucleinopathy defined by glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes. Long-read sequencing of a familial proband identified an unstable AGG repeat expansion in intron 1 of BIN1. Expansions >80 repeats were enriched in pathologically confirmed MSA (9/67, 13.4%) versus brain controls (0/65) (P=0.003), but not significantly in blood-based cohorts. In one patient, a 91-repeat allele was detected only in cerebellum; shorter expanded signals in frontal lobe and spinal cord but not blood supported somatic, region-specific instability. BIN1 accumulated in phosphorylated alpha-synuclein-positive oligodendroglial inclusions, and insoluble BIN1 was increased in MSA brain. These findings support a model in which tissue-specific repeat expansion and BIN1 aggregation contribute to MSA.
S2-4: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibits marked heterogeneity regarding age, site of onset, pattern of progression, non-motor manifestations, and survival time. Although 5–10% of patients with ALS are classified as having familial ALS, the remaining 90–95% have sporadic ALS. Pathogenic variants in ALS-causing genes, such as SOD1 and FUS, influence the clinical phenotype of ALS. For example, patients with SOD1-ALS often present with lower limb onset, whereas those with FUS-ALS have an earlier age at onset and a more aggressive disease course. Moreover, genetic modifiers contribute to the phenotypic heterogeneity of ALS. Intermediate-length CAG repeat expansions in ATXN2 and common variants in UNC13A are known modifiers of survival in patients with ALS. Elucidating these genetic factors is essential for understanding disease mechanisms and developing precision medicine approaches for ALS. Phenotype-specific genome-wide association studies (GWAS) were performed using data from the Japanese Consortium for ALS Research (JaCALS). In the survival GWAS, three loci showed genome-wide significance for survival; FGF1, THSD7A, and LRP1. Furthermore, FGF1 and THSD7A variants reduce in vitro survival of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons in patients with ALS. In the GWAS for age at onset, the GPM6A locus was associated with onset 4.4-year earlier (rs113161727, p=1.08 × 10−9), with a larger effect of 10.2 years in SOD1-ALS. The risk allele was correlated with higher GPM6A expression in iPSC-derived motor neurons of patients. The findings demonstrate that genetic modifiers shape the clinically relevant aspects of ALS heterogeneity. Defining the genetic architecture of the disease onset and progression may facilitate patient stratification and advance precision medicine for ALS.
S2-5: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a refractory neurological disease that causes progressive motor neuron degeneration, and no fundamental cure exists. Currently, riluzole, edaravone, and high-dose intramuscular mecobalamin injections are the only disease-modifying treatments. Approximately 5–10% of ALS cases are familial, and more than 30 related genes have been identified. In 2023, toferersen was first approved as an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy for SOD1-ALS. With genotype-based targeted therapies now emerging for ALS, the field is at a therapeutic turning point. ASO development targets include SOD1, which accounts for around 30% of Japanese familial cases; the RNA-binding proteins FUS and TARDBP; and the C9orf72 gene with hexanucleotide repeat expansion, which is common in Europe and the US. Since 1991, our laboratory has collected familial ALS cases to elucidate their genetic and clinical features. To support future precision medicine for ALS, we have collaborated with five domestic institutions to establish and operate the Japan Familial ALS Trial-ready registry (J-FAST). We screen for SOD1, FUS, TARDBP, and C9orf72 in familial ALS and sporadic cases with onset before age 40, and add comprehensive analyses as needed. We also record each case's natural history in an electronic system. Through ongoing registry enrollment, we identify clinical trial candidates and gather data to evaluate the efficacy of new treatments. We also validate biological samples and imaging biomarkers to advance the search for surrogate pathogenic markers.
S3-1: Human embryo implantation is a critical transition in establishing pregnancy. During this period, extensive metabolic and epigenetic remodeling accompanies transitions between pluripotent states and the acquisition of competence for subsequent lineage differentiation. Understanding how these processes are coordinated offers a molecular perspective on the relationship between maternal and environmental factors, including nutrition, and early development. Human pluripotent stem cell models have provided insights into metabolic transitions and changes in DNA methylation and chromatin regulation associated with peri-implantation development. These studies suggest that metabolic rewiring contributes to epigenetic regulation by modulating the availability of substrates and cofactors involved in DNA methylation. In this symposium, I will discuss metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic dynamics around human embryo implantation, drawing on human developmental models. Particular emphasis will be placed on the interplay between central carbon metabolism, DNA methylation, and histone modifications during pluripotency transitions. I will also briefly discuss the extensive DNA methylation reprogramming that occurs during human primordial germ cell development, highlighting a distinct context of epigenetic resetting. Together, these perspectives will illuminate how epigenetic plasticity supports early human development and provide a basis for considering its sensitivity to the nutritional environment.
S3-2: Low birth weight (LBW) is associated with various health risks across the life course. However, its impact on subsequent reproductive and pregnancy outcomes remains incompletely understood. This presentation reviews current evidence on the associations between being born with LBW and subsequent infertility and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Regarding infertility, many studies have shown no clear association between LBW and infertility in women, whereas several reports suggest an increased risk in men. In our cohort of 1,063 pregnant women at the National Center for Child Health and Development (NCCHD), participants’ own birth weight was not significantly associated with conception by assisted reproductive technology. In contrast, epidemiological studies have suggested that women born with LBW are at increased risk of pregnancy complications. Our analysis of approximately 46,000 women in the JPHC-NEXT study showed increased risks of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and gestational diabetes among women born with LBW. In a separate NCCHD cohort, women born with LBW were also at increased risk of preterm birth and of delivering LBW or small-for-gestational-age infants, suggesting an intergenerational association. These associations may involve multiple pathways, including genetic factors, maternal adult phenotype, and the intrauterine environment. Overall, although current evidence does not indicate a clear increase in infertility risk among women born with LBW, their risks of several adverse pregnancy outcomes appear to be increased. A woman’s own birth history may therefore provide valuable information for preconception risk assessment and counseling.
S3-3: Maternal diet is a key modifiable factor for adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs). In the Nurses' Health Study II, healthier pre-pregnancy dietary patterns were inversely associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and/or hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), while an insulinemic dietary pattern increased GDM risk. A composite healthy lifestyle score (BMI, diet, activity, smoking, alcohol, multivitamin use) was also inversely associated with APOs, driven largely by GDM, HDP, and low birthweight; similar findings were replicated in the Japan Environment and Children's Study. In contrast, diet quality was not consistently associated with miscarriage, though a processed dietary pattern was linked to increased miscarriage risk in a recent meta-analysis, highlighting food processing as a dimension distinct from diet quality. This talk also reviews genetics of dietary behavior: heritability of food preference is moderate but single-gene effects are weak; salt-sensitivity genes relevant to HDP show inconsistent associations; and sugar-sweetened beverages amplify, while healthy dietary patterns attenuate, genetic risk of obesity. Notably, gene-diet/lifestyle interactions have been directly demonstrated in GDM, where women with high genetic risk benefit most from Mediterranean diet adherence or lifestyle intervention, with effects persisting at 5 years postpartum. These findings suggest dietary modification can attenuate genetic susceptibility, underscoring the importance of diet and lifestyle guidance as a core component of preconception care.
S3-4: Vitamin D plays an important role in immune development and has also been implicated in alveolar and airway epithelial development, but the life stage at which vitamin D status most strongly influences childhood asthma susceptibility remains unclear. In our Japanese birth cohort, cord blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentrations were inversely associated with asthma at age 5 years, whereas maternal and postnatal 25(OH)D concentrations showed no clear associations. These findings suggest that fetal vitamin D status may represent a particularly relevant window and may not be fully captured by maternal circulating 25(OH)D concentrations alone. Fetal vitamin D availability is influenced by placental uptake, transport, and metabolism of maternal vitamin D. Previous studies suggest that genetic variation in vitamin D metabolism and signaling pathways may influence circulating vitamin D status and biological response, while distinct vitamin D metabolite profiles may provide additional information on maternal-fetal vitamin D physiology. Epigenetic regulation of placental vitamin D-related pathways may add another layer of interindividual variation at the maternal-fetal interface. Integrating longitudinal birth cohort data with placental, metabolic, genetic, and epigenetic perspectives may help clarify the biological determinants of fetal vitamin D status and how these determinants contribute to childhood asthma susceptibility. This framework may also inform preconception and pregnancy nutrition strategies aimed at optimizing long-term respiratory health.
S3-5: Introduction Maternal low birth weight (LBW) has been associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and placenta-mediated pregnancy complications (PMPCs). However, studies examining HDP and GDM according to gestational age at onset are limited. In addition, few studies have examined the association between a woman’s intrauterine environment, including in utero exposure to HDP, and PMPCs. Methods We used data from the Japan Environment and Children’s Study (JECS) and the Tohoku Medical Megabank Three-Generation Cohort Study (TMM BirThree Cohort Study). In the JECS (n=77,345), associations of MBW with early-, preterm late-, and term late-onset HDP, as well as early- and late GDM, were examined using multinomial logistic regression models. In the TMM BirThree Cohort Study (n=6,364), associations of combinations of MBW, gestational age, and in utero exposure to HDP with PMPCs were examined using modified Poisson regression models. Results In the JECS, among women with LBW, adjusted odds ratios (95% CI) for early-, preterm late-, and term late-onset HDP were 1.05 (0.67– 1.66), 1.75 (1.22–2.50), and 1.50 (1.15–1.94), respectively. The corresponding odds ratios for early- and late GDM were 1.35 (0.91– 1.98) and 1.66 (1.30–2.12), respectively. In the TMM BirThree Cohort Study, women born at term with LBW and without in utero exposure to HDP had a higher risk of PMPCs (adjusted risk ratio, 2.12 [1.56–2.86]). Among women with in utero exposure to HDP, the adjusted risk ratios for PMPCs were 1.41 (1.08–1.83) in those born at term with normal birth weight and 2.65 (1.01–6.98) in those born preterm with LBW. Discussion Information on a woman’s intrauterine environment, including her birth weight and in utero exposure to HDP, may be useful for assessing her risk of pregnancy complications later in life.
S3-6: Folic acid (FA) supplementation is recommended for all women of child-bearing age and those who are pregnant to prevent neural tube defects in offspring. Meanwhile, several studies have shown that maternal FA fortification also reduces the incidence of congenital heart disease, particularly outflow tract (OFT) malformations, although the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unknown. Using Tbx1 hypomorphic mice (Tbx1neo/neo), a model of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, we recently demonstrated that maternal FA supplementation ameliorates the OFT malformation phenotype. In the control group, Tbx1neo/neo embryos developed complete persistent truncus arteriosus, in which the aorta and pulmonary artery fail to septate, resulting in a single great vessel lacking a main pulmonary artery. In contrast, in 60% of Tbx1neo/neo embryos in the maternal FA-supplemented group (the FA group), partial formation of the main pulmonary artery was observed. Neural crest cells (NCCs), which migrate from the neural tube into the OFT and give rise to the aortopulmonary septum, showed improved migration into the OFT and pharyngeal arch arteries in the FA group, with increased NCC numbers in the OFT and reduced ectopic neuronal differentiation. Single-cell RNA sequencing and immunohistochemistry revealed activation of the Notch and Midkine signaling pathways in NCCs in the FA group. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the reduction of congenital heart defects observed with FA supplementation and suggest its potential as a simple, minimally invasive preventive intervention.
S4-1: Inherited dyslipidemias provide a unique opportunity to connect genotype with phenotype through clinical laboratory testing. Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), the most common inherited disorder of lipoprotein metabolism, causes lifelong elevation of LDL cholesterol and markedly increases the risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Clinical diagnosis remains essential, but genetic testing can confirm the molecular basis and facilitate cascade screening. Genotype alone does not fully explain phenotypic heterogeneity, emphasizing the value of integrating LDL-C, lipoprotein(a), apolipoproteins, imaging, and other biomarkers. The Japanese Research Group on Primary Dyslipidemias addresses homozygous FH and rare disorders including LCAT deficiency, sitosterolemia, Tangier disease, primary chylomicronemia, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, abetalipoproteinemia, and homozygous familial hypobetalipoproteinemia. These diseases show how lipid profiles, apolipoproteins, sterols, enzyme activities, and organ-specific manifestations can guide targeted genetic testing. This presentation reviews the laboratory and genetic features of major primary dyslipidemias, with particular emphasis on FH, and discusses how biochemical and molecular testing can bridge genotype and phenotype. Recognizing characteristic laboratory patterns is critical for early diagnosis, treatment, family screening, and disease awareness. Collaboration among clinicians, laboratory professionals, genetic specialists, and patients can help identify affected patients before preventable complications occur.
S4-2: HbA1c is widely used for the diagnosis and management of diabetes mellitus as a marker of average blood glucose levels over the preceding 1–2 months. In 1910, James B. Herrick reported sickle-shaped red blood cells. In 1949, Linus Pauling and colleagues demonstrated that hemoglobin from patients with sickle cell anemia had a different electrophoretic mobility from normal hemoglobin, providing evidence of a molecular abnormality. This finding stimulated the discovery of hemoglobin variants. Meanwhile, electrophoretic studies of patients with diabetes revealed a hemoglobin fraction markedly increased compared with that in individuals without diabetes. This fraction was subsequently identified as HbA1c. As HbA1c became established in diabetes care, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) enabled accurate HbA1c measurement while also separating hemoglobin fractions and visualizing chromatographic patterns. Routine HbA1c testing can unexpectedly reveal asymptomatic hemoglobin variants. A discrepancy between blood glucose and HbA1c levels or an abnormal chromatographic peak may provide an important clue. Further hemoglobin analysis and molecular genetic testing of globin genes, including HBB, HBA1, and HBA2, can establish the genotype. Conversely, hemoglobin variants may affect HbA1c results depending on the variant and analytical method, potentially leading to inaccurate assessment of glycemic status. This presentation will review the history of HbA1c measurement and abnormal hemoglobins, focusing on how an unexpected laboratory finding can lead from phenotype to genotype, and how genotype can subsequently explain the laboratory and clinical phenotype.
S4-3: Hereditary gastrointestinal tumor syndromes show distinct endoscopic phenotypes associated with germline pathogenic variants. Gastrointestinal endoscopy plays an important role in translating genotype-based cancer risk into early detection and prevention. In Lynch syndrome, colorectal neoplasms frequently arise in the proximal colon and may be flat or subtle. Image-enhanced endoscopy and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted detection are expected to improve surveillance; however, recent randomized trials have shown limited additional benefit of AI over high-quality colonoscopy. In familial adenomatous polyposis, cold snare polypectomy and intensive endoscopic downstaging polypectomy can reduce colorectal polyp burden and may postpone colectomy. Endoscopic treatment is also increasingly applied to duodenal adenomas. In hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, minute signet ring cell carcinoma foci are difficult to detect. High-definition endoscopy, narrow-band imaging and magnifying endoscopy may help identify subtle lesions, although systematic biopsies remain essential. Hamartomatous polyposis syndromes also demonstrate genotype-specific phenotypes. In Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, capsule endoscopy and balloon-assisted enteroscopy enable detection and treatment of small-bowel polyps, while juvenile polyposis syndrome and PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome show characteristic gastrointestinal findings. This presentation reviews how advanced imaging, AI and endoscopic treatment can bridge genotype and phenotype and contribute to precision cancer prevention.
S4-4: In the era of genomic medicine, cardiovascular genetics relies heavily on clinical examinations to bridge the gap between genotype and phenotype. While genetic testing has become more accessible, clinical physiological and imaging tests remain indispensable for diagnosis, risk stratification, and family screening. In inherited arrhythmias, the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is essential. Furthermore, exercise stress tests are vital for risk stratification; in conditions such as Long QT Syndrome (LQTS), evaluating stress test results is often essential both for deciding whether genetic testing is warranted and for interpreting the resulting genetic findings. For cardiomyopathies, imaging modalities are crucial for diagnosis. A significant challenge in cardiovascular genetics is phenotypic heterogeneity; even within the same family sharing the identical genotype, individuals may present with different phenotypes, such as hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy. Thus, clinical testing is vital for pedigree analysis and for the clinical interpretation of genetic variants. In familial hypercholesterolemia, beyond blood lipid profiles, physical findings such as Achilles tendon thickness, along with follow-up carotid ultrasonography, are essential for comprehensive management. For heritable connective tissue disorders, preventing sudden death is the primary goal. Monitoring vascular diameters through echocardiography is indispensable for determining the optimal timing for surgical intervention. In conclusion, genetic testing alone is insufficient for the diagnosis and management of hereditary cardiovascular diseases. Due to incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity, clinical examinations remain an essential pillar for accurate diagnosis, risk assessment, and family screening.
S5-2: Genome sequencing has transformed rare disease diagnostics, yet many individuals remain undiagnosed and variants of uncertain significance (VUS) are a growing challenge. Pathogenicity scores rely on molecular data, while the phenotype, often the most informative clue, is assessed subjectively. AI-driven phenomics aims to make the phenotype as quantifiable as the genotype. In this lecture, I will present PhenoScore, an open-source AI framework combining facial image analysis with Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-based clinical features to quantify phenotypic similarity. PhenoScore recognises distinct phenotypes for most syndromes tested and enables genotype-phenotype studies, such as identifying phenotypic subgroups within a gene. Validated against functional data for ANKRD11 missense variants, PhenoScore outperformed REVEL and complemented AlphaMissense, providing objective phenotypic evidence for VUS interpretation (ACMG PP4). Phenotyping itself remains a bottleneck: translating clinical notes into HPO terms is slow, and clinical text often cannot leave the hospital. I will show how large language models can learn expert-level, source-grounded phenotype annotation and be distilled into small models that run locally, making deep phenotyping scalable while keeping patient data in the hospital. Together, these approaches move us towards precision diagnosis in which genotype and phenotype are interpreted jointly.
S5-3: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI built on transformer-based large language models, has advanced remarkably in recent years, and initiatives utilising it now span many fields, including medicine and healthcare. For rare diseases, however, the conditions themselves are rare, so securing large data volumes is difficult, and AI, which typically requires substantial data sets, has at times been unsuitable. Nevertheless, successful applications are emerging, such as the use of highly accurate symptom data, while AI-assisted diagnosis using genomic variants, for which large volumes of data are now being accumulated, is also progressing (approximately 80% of rare diseases are estimated to be genetically caused). In this lecture, I shall introduce two AI initiatives for rare disease diagnosis in which the presenter is involved. One is a diagnostic support programme that lists candidate diagnoses based on a patient's symptoms. The other estimates the effects of missense variants on protein three-dimensional structure. Both are already in practical use, streamlining rare disease diagnosis. AI is thus advancing even in rare diseases, long considered unsuitable for it. Beyond the two diagnostic programmes introduced here, many imaging programmes (X-ray, CT, MRI, electroencephalography ets.) have been developed. It is hoped that these will be refined and updated according to their respective characteristics, enabling faster diagnosis of individual rare diseases and paving the way for the next steps.
S6-1: Vertebrates, including humans, possess paired appendages (locomotor organs) known as limbs and paired fins. Although adult mammals cannot regenerate amputated limbs at all, mice are capable of regenerating digit tips during the early fetal stage. This suggests that we do not completely lack the ability to regenerate appendages, but rather that this capacity rapidly declines during development. Among vertebrates, some animals (such as urodele amphibians) retain the ability to regenerate appendages throughout their lives, while others (such as anuran amphibians and bony fishes) show a decline in regenerative capacity during the larval stage. Understanding how these animals regenerate their appendages and identifying the causes behind the decline of this capacity will provide significant insights toward achieving limb regeneration in mammals. In this presentation, I will outline research on appendage regeneration in several vertebrate model organisms and discuss the possibilities of applying these findings to mammals and humans.
S6-2: Pathogenic genetic variants contribute to a broad spectrum of vascular diseases, ranging from germline disorders such as Marfan syndrome and RASopathies including Noonan syndrome, to vascular malformations caused by somatic mosaic variants, such as brain arteriovenous malformations and Sturge–Weber syndrome (SWS). Understanding these diseases requires determining how causal variants alter endothelial phenotypes and responses to flow. However, static in vitro culture systems cannot adequately recapitulate this physiological flow environment. In this talk, I will introduce isogenic human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) disease models generated by genome editing and their differentiation into vascular endothelial cells. I will then present two platforms for reconstructing vascular flow: a vessel-on-a-chip system for generating three-dimensional vascular networks and an orbital shaker-based flow system. These platforms enable morphological and functional analyses of vascular structures, including endothelial barrier integrity. Combining these systems with multi-omics analyses allows identification of molecular pathways underlying vascular disease phenotypes. Using a cellular model of SWS, we found that disease-associated endothelial cells exhibit dysregulated responses to flow, accompanied by altered endothelial identity and transcriptional regulation. Finally, I will discuss therapeutic target identification and drug discovery based on these disease models, highlighting the potential of integrating human iPSCs, genome editing, flow-based modeling, and multi-omics to understand and treat vascular diseases.
S6-3: Disruption of methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD) proteins causes neurodevelopmental disorders, including MECP2-related Rett syndrome (RTT) and MBD5-associated neurodevelopmental disorder (MAND). How chromatin dysregulation produces disease phenotypes remains incompletely understood. We previously showed that MeCP2 organizes a silent-chromatin loop at the imprinted DLX5-DLX6 locus. In Mecp2-null brain, the loop is lost and Dlx5/Dlx6 expression increases; DLX5 also showed loss of imprinting in RTT lymphoblastoid cells, implicating altered GABAergic regulation. More recently, we identified LBX1, a scoliosis-associated transcription factor, as a direct MeCP2 target. MECP2 disruption reduced LBX1 expression, and GABRB1 and P2RX7 were identified as LBX1-dependent downstream genes, suggesting a link between MeCP2 dysfunction and scoliosis in RTT. We next examined MBD5 haploinsufficiency, with MBD6 haploinsufficiency as a related MBD-family comparison, in SH-SY5Y cells. Both showed shared downregulation of mitochondrial genes, including COX17, COX4I2, MCUB, and PDK1. Public ChIP-seq data indicated co-localization of MBD5, MBD6, and BAP1-complex components at the COX17 promoter. Haploinsufficient cells showed reduced basal and ATP-linked respiration, impaired growth in galactose, and a glycolytic shift. Together, these studies extend MBD biology from chromatin architecture to neuronal gene networks and mitochondrial function, linking epigenetic dysregulation to RTT and MAND.
S6-4: Full-length gene-humanized mice, generated by replacing endogenous mouse loci with corresponding human genomic regions, including noncoding and regulatory sequences, provide a physiologically relevant in vivo platform for investigating human biology and disease. However, reliable humanization of large genomic regions remains technically challenging. Here, we describe a streamlined strategy based on two sequential CRISPR-assisted homologous recombination steps in mouse embryonic stem cells, enabling targeted integration of human genomic regions exceeding 200 kbp at diverse loci. The resulting humanized alleles recapitulate human-like splicing patterns and organ-specific gene expression while retaining essential biological functions. Moreover, introducing pathogenic human variants into the humanized CYBB locus reproduced impaired reactive oxygen species production, a hallmark of chronic granulomatous disease. Beyond inherited disorders, targeted integration of full-length human genes encoding species-specific factors, such as pathogen receptors absent from mice, could overcome species barriers and expand the utility of mice for infectious disease research. By linking human genomic variation to organism-level phenotypes, this versatile approach provides a foundation for elucidating disease mechanisms and developing physiologically relevant models suitable for preclinical evaluation of targeted therapies, including gene therapy.
S6-5: “Genomically” humanized animal models are powerful tools for understanding the pathogenesis of human genetic diseases and developing novel therapeutic strategies. However, conventional transgenic technologies have limitations in faithfully reproducing diseases involving large genes, complex genomic regions, or chromosome-level abnormalities. To overcome these limitations, we have developed transchromosomic (Tc) technologies using human chromosome fragments, human artificial chromosomes (HACs), and mouse artificial chromosomes (MACs). These chromosome-based technologies enable the stable introduction of Mb-sized human genomic regions while preserving their genomic context and regulatory elements. In this symposium, I will introduce disease models for Down syndrome, facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) developed using HAC/MAC technology, and discuss how these models can contribute to understanding disease mechanisms and developing and evaluating therapeutic approaches. I will also introduce fully human antibody-producing animals carrying human immunoglobulin loci, and mice and rats carrying human drug-metabolism gene clusters as examples of genomically humanized models for biomedical and pharmaceutical research. Furthermore, I will present a novel method for direct chromosome transfer from human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with a rapid approach for cloning large human genomic regions into HACs/MACs. Taken together, these chromosome engineering technologies provide a unique platform for generating genomically humanized animal models and will facilitate disease research and the development of novel therapies.
S7-1: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) may extend precision oncology beyond targeted genomic profiling, but whether its additional findings translate into additional patient benefit remains to be established. Tumor-normal WGS can provide a more comprehensive assessment of structural rearrangements, copy-number alterations, and mutational signatures, while also enabling the assessment of selected germline findings. These capabilities can complement gene panel testing, refine diagnosis, and identify additional therapeutic opportunities. Translating this potential into patient benefit requires timely return of clinically relevant findings and sustainable systems that connect genomic analysis with clinical care. Japan's Action Plan for Whole Genome Sequencing 2022 provides the policy framework for this transition, building on research supported by the Japan Agency for Medical Research and Development (AMED). Genomic Medicine Japan (GeMJ) was established in March 2026 to support the return of genomic findings, advance personalized medicine, and promote research and drug discovery. In collaboration with research groups and clinical institutions, GeMJ aims to standardize analysis and reporting, strengthen quality assurance, and build infrastructure linking genomic and longitudinal clinical data, with secure access and appropriate governance for secondary use. This presentation reviews policy progress and GeMJ's priorities for national implementation, focusing on the practical requirements for timely reporting, clinical follow-up, and sustainable data use. Clear responsibilities, patient and public involvement, and evaluation of the added clinical value of WGS are essential to translating these efforts into measurable benefits for current and future patients.
S7-2: Background: MGPT primarily aims to diagnose hereditary cancer syndromes through germline analysis, whereas tumor-normal paired whole-genome sequencing (TN-WGS) primarily aims to identify tumor genomic alterations and therapeutic targets. Although not its primary purpose, TN-WGS can also reveal germline findings (GF), creating new challenges in their interpretation and disclosure. Methods: We analyzed 1,693 TN-WGS datasets through May 2026. Germline pathogenic variants (GPVs) associated with hereditary cancer syndromes (HCS) and other genetic disorders were evaluated. Since its establishment in February 2022, the Germline Findings Board (GFB), a multidisciplinary expert panel, has sequentially reviewed cases requiring detailed assessment for appropriate disclosure. Results: GPVs associated with HCS were identified in 86 patients (5.1%), with approximately half found in tumor types not previously associated with the causative genes. GPVs related to non-cancerous hereditary diseases were also identified. Of 868 consecutive cases reviewed by the GFB, only 7 (0.8%) were considered eligible for disclosure, including variants in LDLR, MYBPC3, and TTN in patients with relevant phenotypes. Conclusion: TN-WGS can uncover GF beyond conventional hereditary cancer testing, although identifying hereditary cancer is not its primary purpose. Clinical implementation requires a framework linking genomic findings with clinical and phenotypic assessment and appropriate communication. Genetic counseling is essential to support patients and families while maximizing the clinical value of TN- WGS.
S7-3: With the establishment of Genomic Medicine Japan (GeMJ) and ongoing efforts to implement whole-genome sequencing (WGS) in clinical practice, germline findings are expected to become increasingly common. Similar challenges are already encountered in multigene panel testing (MGPT) and comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP). For high-penetrance cancer susceptibility genes such as BRCA1/2 and mismatch repair genes, evidence supporting risk management and treatment selection is well established. In contrast, evidence remains limited for pathogenic variants in moderate-penetrance genes such as ATM, RAD51C, and RAD51D. A recent statement from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) defined reduced-penetrance pathogenic variants (RPPVs) as variants associated with lower penetrance than typical pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in the same gene, while still conferring clinically meaningful risk. This distinction is critical because pathogenicity does not directly determine the magnitude of cancer risk. In this presentation, "moderate-penetrance variants" encompasses both pathogenic variants in moderate-penetrance genes and RPPVs. From the dual perspectives of clinical genetics and medical oncology, I will discuss their implications for risk assessment, medical management, and treatment selection.
S7-4: Cancer predisposition syndromes (CPS) are increasingly recognized as important in pediatric oncology. Germline pathogenic variants in cancer predisposition genes are identified in approximately 10% and more of children with cancer, while conventional approaches based on tumor type, clinical features, and family history may fail to identify affected patients. Multi-gene panel testing has expanded access to germline analysis; however, some cancer-predisposing variants, including structural and non-coding variants, may remain undetected. Whole-genome sequencing may overcome limitations of targeted approaches and enable more comprehensive germline profiling. Integrating germline and tumor genomic data may further aid variant interpretation. Early identification of CPS is particularly important because its clinical impact can extend throughout a patient's lifetime. A germline diagnosis may influence treatment, enable surveillance for subsequent malignancies, and facilitate cascade testing and surveillance for relatives. Li-Fraumeni syndrome exemplifies these benefits: surveillance can include whole-body MRI. Prospective studies in Japan are evaluating the feasibility and effectiveness of such surveillance. As germline analysis becomes more comprehensive, interpretive challenges remain, including variants of uncertain significance, mosaicism, and clonal hematopoiesis. In this presentation, I will discuss practical considerations for germline profiling in pediatric oncology and its contributions to lifelong cancer risk management for patients and their families.
S7-5: The transition from targeted panels to whole-genome sequencing (WGS) in oncology creates opportunities to identify medically actionable germline secondary findings (SFs) beyond cancer predisposition. The ACMG recommends actively evaluating selected SFs in clinical exome and genome sequencing. Its SF v3.3 list includes genes associated with cardiomyopathies, inherited arrhythmias, aortopathies, and familial hypercholesterolemia, reflecting opportunities for prevention and early intervention. Yet a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant does not, by itself, establish disease or predict an individual's clinical outcome. Incomplete and age-dependent penetrance, gene- and variant-specific mechanisms, and uncertain risk estimates in unselected populations complicate interpretation, particularly in patients without cardiovascular symptoms or family history. For oncology teams, challenges extend beyond deciding which findings to return: who should evaluate them, when should patients be referred, and how should families be followed? This presentation will address variant interpretation, phenotype assessment, risk stratification, and referral to cardiovascular genetics services. We will discuss the respective roles of oncology, clinical genetics, and cardiology in disclosure, counseling, surveillance, and cascade testing. As cancer WGS moves toward broader clinical implementation in Japan, coordinated referral pathways will be essential to translate findings into appropriate, proportionate care.
S8-1: Preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M) in Japan has been performed for serious genetic disorders. Severity has been assessed case by case, considering natural history, prognosis, age at onset, phenotype, penetrance, treatment options, family history, and individual circumstances. Recent advances in genomic medicine, however, have made such assessment increasingly complex. First, novel therapies, including gene therapies, are becoming available for genetic disorders previously considered untreatable, altering their natural history and prognosis. How these advances should be incorporated into severity assessment remains challenging. Second, expanded newborn screening may identify novel variants in families without an affected proband. In such cases, limited phenotypic information within the family and evidence on genotype–phenotype correlations make prediction of disease onset and severity difficult. Third, applications for hereditary tumour syndromes, which typically have adult onset, variable penetrance, and options for surveillance and preventive intervention, have emerged, reflecting autonomous decision-making by individuals at genetic risk informed by the availability of PGT-M overseas. These developments raise challenges in integrating changing natural history, uncertainty in phenotype prediction, presymptomatic genetic information, and autonomous decision-making into severity assessment. This presentation discusses these challenges emerging from PGT-M review in Japan and considers future approaches to assessing severity.
S8-2: In 1983, in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer (IVF-ET) was first performed in Japan. Initial purpose of IVF-ET was to treat infertile couples. Moreover, it enabled technologies beyond mere infertility treatment. Preimplantation genetic testing is one of them. A certain university hospital submitted an application to the Japan Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology (JSOG), requesting approval for the implementation and a ruling of its appropriateness. Submitted case was Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The Committee of JSOG reached the conclusion of rejection for the case after full discussion. Through this discussion, the Committee released the statement as follows: JSOG permits preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD: former word for PGT-M) only for serious hereditary disease carrier families. Besides, preimplantation genetic screening (PGS: former word for PGT-A) was prohibited during the discussion. The significant issue in this statement was the criteria for seriousness. Through the screening of several new applications in the JSOG Committee, the criteria for seriousness became established. Serious hereditary disease which meets the criteria for PGD was considered to be the disease symptoms of which appear prior to adulthood causing severe impairment to daily life or leading to death. This concept was developed based on several submitted cases of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Considering various hereditary diseases other than Duchenne muscular dystrophy, criteria for seriousness are subject to change as a matter of course.
S8-3: The assessment of disease severity in Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Monogenic Disorders (PGT-M) has traditionally relied on factors such as age of onset, clinical prognosis, and the availability of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs). In neurological practice, however, patients and their families often experience profound psychological distress, ethical dilemmas, and multidimensional life disruptions experienced by patients and their families—aspects that cannot be fully captured by physical survival rates or age of onset alone. Furthermore, recently DMTs are improving outcomes in some conditions, but predicting onset and severity from genetic information remains challenging. Adult onset does not necessarily indicate low severity. Assessment must consider the lifelong course, including natural history, cognitive and behavioral effects, survival, and treatment options. Individuals with adult-onset hereditary neurological or neuromuscular disorders who wish to undergo PGT-M may be asymptomatic or may already be experiencing symptoms. Alongside genetic risks to their children, they must navigate life choices amid uncertainty about their own disease onset or progression and their future lives. Even when PGT-M enables individuals to have children who do not inherit the condition, challenges related to their own disease and family life continue. This presentation aims to reconsider how disease severity and the limits of genetic prediction should be taken into account when assessing eligibility for PGT-M in adult-onset hereditary neurological and neuromuscular disorders. It also considers how multidisciplinary care can support informed and autonomous decision-making within this regulatory framework, while providing continuity of care before disease onset and after reproductive decisions.
S8-4: Cancer is common, affecting more than half of people during their lifetime. In hereditary tumors, a detected variant cannot always be identified as the direct cause of an individual's cancer. Many hereditary tumor genes lack established founder pathogenic variants, making it difficult to evaluate seriousness from a pathogenic variant alone. However, a strong genotype-phenotype relationship may be suspected when a variant confers high cancer risk in childhood or young adulthood, or when multiple cancers, a strong family history, or familial clustering suggest high penetrance. In my view, the seriousness of hereditary tumors should be considered case by case, based on age at onset, cancer risk, features, prevention, early detection and treatment options, and genotype-phenotype consistency in the individual and family. Otherwise, embryos may be selected based on a variant whose association with disease is insufficiently supported. Genetic counseling that explains the value and limitations of genomic information and supports decisions consistent with each client's values and life plans is particularly important when considering the seriousness of a genetic condition. Nationwide access should enable clients who still strongly desire PGT-M after thorough counseling to choose it. Given the potentially large number of candidates and time-sensitive concerns about age and fertility, sustainable, timely review is needed without compromising careful case assessment. Greater collaboration among genetics-related societies and healthcare professionals will be needed to sustain this system.
S8-5: What counts as “severity” in PGT-M is not self-evident. This presentation discusses five questions from pediatric and bioethical perspectives. First, is severity inherent in the condition, or shaped by social conditions such as limited support and social barriers? Second, from whose perspective is severity judged: that of the future child, people living with the condition, families, clinicians, or experts? Third, what does a judgment of severity justify? A medical assessment that a condition is severe is not equivalent to the normative judgment that it warrants embryo selection, nor can such a judgment be reduced to the future child’s “best interests” or anticipated suffering. Fourth, does each judgment end with the individual case? Even when each decision is made autonomously and case by case, the accumulation of such choices may reshape social norms. Fifth, who bears—and who lives with—the consequences over time? Couples must decide now, while institutional norms and social meanings emerge more slowly and affect those who did not participate, including future generations. Severity in PGT-M is therefore not only about where to draw a clinical boundary, but also about what such judgments justify, what norms and social meanings they create, and how we remain accountable for them over time. Having chosen to incorporate selection into medical practice, we must be prepared to live with the uncertainty, tension, and responsibility that follow—rather than treating each decision as if it ends with the individual case.
S9-1: SRY gene testing is being reintroduced internationally to determine eligibility for competition in the female category. World Athletics (WA) announced its policy in 2025, followed by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) in 2026, with testing planned for the Olympic Games from 2028. Unlike genetic testing for diagnosis, treatment, or health management, this testing is performed outside the medical framework to determine eligibility. However, it may reveal previously unknown genetic information related to differences of sex development and lead to genetic healthcare. IOC implementation may expand the sports and athletes subject to testing and lower the age at testing, including young athletes aspiring to compete at the highest level. Thus, genetic testing initiated outside medicine may increasingly enter clinical genetics through testing requests or result management. This issue concerns not gender identity itself, but the use of genetic information related to biological sex as a criterion for competition categories. Questions include the meaning of SRY testing within the biological diversity of sex, its implementation in sports, and ethical and social issues such as fairness, dignity, and privacy. This symposium will examine the medical meaning of SRY testing, ethical and social issues, and result disclosure and genetic counseling. Rather than reaching a conclusion for or against testing, we will focus on athletes who may learn unexpected genetic information and discuss how genetics professionals can communicate results and support medical and psychosocial needs.
S9-2: Sex differentiation is a biological process that forms the two sex phenotypes, male and female, by operating across a three tiered hierarchy, i.e., chromosomes, gonads, and the body, including the formation of male or female typical internal and external genitalia. Its ultimate functional goal is the acquisition of the functions required for sexual reproduction. In mammals, this differentiation is driven by SRY, a SOX transcription factor located on the Y chromosome. In the presence of SRY, undifferentiated embryonic gonads develop into testes, whereas in its absence, they develop into ovaries. Subsequently, the sexual characteristics of the body - centered on the internal and external reproductive organs - are shaped by hormones, primarily testosterone secreted by the testes. DSDs arise when prenatal developmental processes associated with sex follow an atypical trajectory. This concept is entirely distinct from gender defined sexual minorities. Many of the underlying phenomena in DSD can be described biologically, and understanding the mechanisms of DSD helps illuminate the broader issues surrounding sex and potentially gender. In this lecture, I will discuss the mechanisms of DSD from a clinical perspective, which will deepen our understanding of sex.
S9-3: Ahead of Tokyo 2025 World Athletics Championships, World Athletics (WA) required female entrants to submit results of one-time SRY testing, sparking debate. This was not unprecedented: at Atlanta 1996, eight of 3,387 female athletes tested SRY-positive, yet all were allowed to compete. The IOC ended universal sex testing in 1999. After Caster Semenya's 2009 world title, eligibility for athletes with differences of sex development (DSD) became a major issue. Testosterone-based rules followed in 2011 and were progressively tightened. In 2025, WA returned to genetic screening, citing limitations of testosterone suppression in eliminating androgen-related performance advantages. As the only clinical geneticist on the Japan Association of Athletics Federations (JAAF) Medical Committee, and a certified sports physician involved in DSD issues for over 20 years, I played a central role in implementing blood-based FISH testing for Tokyo 2025. I provided pre-test explanations and obtained informed consent; results were disclosed to athletes with support from certified genetic counselors. Eligibility testing may reveal unexpected genetic findings and prompt evaluation for DSD, affecting health, identity and psychological well-being. SRY positivity alone establishes neither a DSD diagnosis nor performance advantage. This talk reviews post-Atlanta eligibility rules and JAAF's implementation, examining how clinical genetics and sports medicine can protect athletes' dignity, privacy and informed choice within a mandatory eligibility process.
S9-4: Genetic knowledge and testing technologies developed for research and medicine are now applied to sex-segregated sport for non-medical purposes. The IOC policy announced on March 26, 2026, states that genetic testing targeting SRY (SRY testing) will be used for eligibility confirmation. National sports organizations sending athletes to the Olympic Games must address this new testing system, although its normative and procedural frameworks remain insufficiently defined. Athletes may need to come to terms with genetic information concerning their sexuality, including their bodies and identity, and their lives and close relationships. The choices they face include “self-determined choices” regarding additional testing, medical care, and information sharing, and “choices imposed by the system,” such as appeals, category changes, and whether to continue competing. Sex verification testing in sport was discontinued after 2000, while genetics has advanced understanding of human genetic diversity and sex development, along with standards for responsible genetic testing. Therefore, SRY testing for female athletes, including minors, requires examination not only of accuracy and procedures, but also of responsibility sharing between sport and genetic medicine in system design. It is also necessary to consider how non-medical use of genetic testing in sport may influence the future positioning of genetic information. Furthermore, the appropriateness of uniformly applying SRY testing across all sports, regardless of sport characteristics, must be reconsidered. This presentation discusses these issues through dialogue with genetics and genetic medicine.
S9-5: SRY gene testing has recently been reintroduced to determine eligibility for female athletes in major international competitions. Although not performed for medical purposes, detection of SRY may reveal previously unknown medical and genetic information concerning sex chromosomes and sex development. Further evaluation may identify a difference of sex development (DSD), raising issues beyond eligibility, including health management, reproductive health, family communication, self-concept, body image, and privacy. Previous reports on sex verification in sports have described psychosocial and confidentiality concerns associated with unexpected identification of DSD. Literature on disclosure of a DSD diagnosis also emphasizes gradual, ongoing information provision tailored to the individual’s understanding and needs, together with psychosocial support and interprofessional collaboration. However, there is no direct evidence regarding approaches to, or the effectiveness of, genetic counseling specifically for athletes undergoing SRY testing. Obtaining information required under current eligibility rules and deciding how much one wishes to know about one’s own genetic and medical information are, in principle, distinct decisions. It is therefore important to distinguish screening for competition eligibility from testing for medical diagnosis. Based on existing literature, this presentation will consider how genetics professionals may communicate the implications of unexpected genetic findings to athletes, support decision-making regarding further medical evaluation, and address subsequent psychosocial issues.
S10-1: Epigenome information defines cellular identity, and heterogeneity in epigenome states may underlie phenotypic diversity. However, how such diversity arises during the establishment and maintenance of an epigenome state remains poorly understood. We have previously explored epigenome heterogeneity among different human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines by profiling various histone modifications. Most of the heterogeneity was observed in regions of low transcriptional activity or non-coding regions, such as repressed promoters, intergenic regions, or repeat elements, with little effect on transcriptional profiles. We also found that these epigenetic states are associated with differential kinetics of epigenetic reprogramming during in vitro germ cell fate induction, indicating that such heterogeneity affects future cell fate. Notably, we observed epigenetic heterogeneity at evolutionarily young transposable elements (TEs) across iPSC lines; however, detailed locus-specific discussions have been technically challenging due to their repetitive nature. To explore this further, we performed long-read whole-genome sequencing of eight human iPSC lines and conducted in-depth comparative analyses. DNA methylation profiling revealed that a substantial fraction of evolutionarily young TEs, such as L1HS, carry hypomethylated promoter regions, with variation across lines. In addition, by integrating multiple variant-calling tools, we further identified non-reference TE insertions and found line-specific insertion events, a fraction of which retain the full-length form. Together, these data suggest that TEs may contribute to generating not only genetic but also epigenetic heterogeneity among human iPSC lines.
S10-2: We have pursued blastocyst complementation, in which pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) are injected into preimplantation embryos designed to lack a target organ as a potential solution to the shortage of transplantable organs. In mouse–rat chimeras, we demonstrated the generation of various organs from donor PSCs, more recently achieved the birth of human-to-mouse chimeras. However, organ-complementing human-to-animal chimeras have yet to be achieved due to the low chimerism of human cells and commitment to the cardiovascular lineages. We therefore investigate when and how “developmental compatibility” breaks down in interspecies chimeras. One of the barrier arises shortly after implantation: human cells are excluded from the host preimplantation epiblast. This was recapitulated in interspecies PSC coculture, where mouse and rat cells intermixed, whereas human and mouse cells underwent sorting out. In contrast, human and chimpanzee cells intermixed. Consistently, human and mouse cells failed to form a chimeric epiblast in embryo model, whereas human and chimpanzee cells did. These findings suggest that the capacity for systemic chimera formation may correlate with evolutionary distance. We are now investigating the molecular basis of “xeno-barriers” by combining 2D coculture, embryo models, and in vivo chimeras. In addition to sorting out, we observed other abnormalities in interspecies chimeras. These phenotypes provide an opportunity to uncover fundamental mechanisms that invisible in intraspecies chimeras. Understanding and overcoming these xeno-barriers may advance organ regeneration while establishing interspecies chimeras as versatile tools for developmental and cell biology.
S10-3: Limb bud progenitor cells (LPCs) originate from the lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) and possess unique multipotency and patterning capacity to generate the major tissues of mature limbs. Previously, using the mouse as a primary model, we identified reprogramming factors capable of conferring LPC-like identity on non-limb fibroblasts. Forced co-expression of the transcriptional regulators Prdm16, Zbtb16, Lin28a, and Lin41 (PZLL) induced fibroblasts to acquire gene expression profiles and differentiation potential closely resembling those of LPCs.
