Discussion and Conclusions: Our results demonstrate for the first time that ART-conceived individuals exhibit genome-wide methylation abnormalities affecting both parental alleles, suggesting that these abnormalities may arise from ART procedures rather than parental infertility.
O1-05: Telomeres serve to protect the ends of chromosomes. The length of the telomeric DNA that constitutes telomeres shortens with each cell division and eventually becomes too short to perform its protective function. Preimplantation embryonic development is an exception in which telomere DNA length increases. In particular, rapid elongation of telomere DNA length is believed to occur during the early stages of embryo development. In this study, we used bovine fertilized ova to investigate the effects of drugs that improve mitochondrial function on telomere length in preimplantation embryos. We analyzed the temporal changes in telomere length in bovine oocytes, two-cell-stage embryos, morulae, and blastocysts using qPCR. Next, we cultured bovine embryos in medium supplemented with C14H22N4O2 2HCl (BGP-15) (10 μM), a drug developed for the treatment of insulin resistance. We measured the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of the resulting morulae and analyzed the telomere length and mitochondrial (mt) DNA copy number of the morulae and blastocysts using qPCR. Telomere DNA length was calculated as the relative copy number relative to β-actin using qPCR. Telomere length in bovine embryos initially shortened at the two-cell stage and then lengthened as the embryos developed into morulae and blastocysts. BGP-15 increased mtDNA copy number and OCR in morulae (p < 0.01). However, BGP-15 had no effect on the telomere length of the fertilized ova. BGP-15 improved mitochondrial function and mitochondrial DNA copy number in bovine morulae, but no effect on telomere length was observed.
O1-06: <Objective> Female reproductive aging is associated with a decline in fertility, largely through deterioration in oocyte quality. However, the effects of aging on the reproductive tract microbiota and the peri-implantation microenvironment are unclear. This study aimed to investigate age-associated alterations in the reproductive tract microbiota and to evaluate their correlation with in vitro fertilization (IVF) outcomes. <Methods> A total of 38 participants was enrolled, comprising 22 in the successful pregnancy (S-) group (35.0 ± 3.8 years) and 28 in the unsuccessful (U-) group (36.5 ± 2.9 years). Vaginal and intrauterine samples were collected in IVF and frozen embryo transfer cycles. Extracted microbial genomic DNA was sequenced by next-generation sequencing and analyzed by QIIME2 at genus and species levels. <Results> Vaginal microbiota changed across the menstrual cycle and showed greater diversity and higher Lactobacillus species abundance than intrauterine samples. Overall Lactobacillus abundance was not significantly associated with IVF outcomes. In women aged ≥35 years (n = 38), microbiota profiles clustered closely together, whereas in women aged 30~34 years (n = 12), two distinct clusters emerged. Longitudinal analysis of participants sampled before and after pregnancy (n = 4) revealed marked shifts in vaginal microbial diversity. <Conclusion> Female reproductive aging is associated with changes in reproductive tract microbial composition and diversity. These alterations may influence the peri-implantation microenvironment and contribute to IVF outcomes.
O2-01: By comprehensive analysis of human gene expression, we identified URST1 (up-regulated in solid tumor 1) as a new prognostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target for lung cancer. URST1 mRNA and its gene product were highly expressed in most lung cancer cell lines and clinical tissues but barely detectable in normal lung epithelial cells and tissues as detected by real-time qPCR, western blotting, and immunocytochemistry. Immunohistochemical analysis using tissue microarray showed that URST1 expression was observed in 231 (64.5%) of 358 non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC). Strong URST1 expression was significantly associated with poor prognosis for NSCLC patients (P = 0.0003). Knockdown of URST1 expression using URST1-specific siRNAs significantly inhibited the growth of lung cancer cells probably by induction of G2/M arrest and subsequent apoptosis through the activation of several proteins associated with apoptosis. Treating lung cancer cells with small-molecule inhibitors against URST1 suppressed cell growth, partly by inducing G2/M arrest. Microarray analysis and gene knock-down assays using lung cancer cells by siRNAs for URST1 suggested various URST1-related cancer-related signaling pathways. These data suggest that URST1 could be a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for lung cancer.
O2-02: Large-scale cancer genome sequencing has advanced driver gene discovery, yet low-frequency functional drivers remain difficult to identify. Because protein function depends on three-dimensional structure, mutations distant in the primary sequence may converge spatially and affect common functional regions. We therefore applied a structure-based framework to detect spatial clustering of somatic mutations as a signal of driver gene candidates. We mapped somatic mutations from 15,305 tumors across 27 cancer types provided by the US National Cancer Institute onto AlphaFold2-predicted protein structures and evaluated inter-mutation distances of 18,966 genes. This identified 441 genes with significant spatial clustering in pan-cancer analysis and 296 genes in cancer-type-specific analyses, including known drivers such as TP53, KRAS, PTEN, and BRAF. We then characterized these clusters using Pfam domains. Tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) showed the lowest fraction of mutations within annotated domains, whereas oncogenes showed the highest, suggesting distinct mutation patterns between loss-of-function and gain-of-function drivers. We further validated 16 candidates in lung cancer cell lines. Knockdown of several genes suppressed proliferation. Among them, GeneX overexpression promoted cell growth, and its mutation enhanced proliferation compared with wild-type. Patients with somatic GeneX mutations also showed poorer survival. Together, these results suggest that structure-based mutational clustering is useful for prioritizing functionally relevant cancer driver gene candidates.
O2-03: Acquired resistance to targeted therapy is a major cause of cancer relapse. Although alternative splicing has the potential to reconfigure oncogenic signaling, its involvement in resistance to RAS/MAPK pathway inhibitors remains unclear. We analyzed RNA-seq data from 473 CCLE cell lines with matched DepMap drug response data. JuncBASE analysis showed that splicing variations in RAS/MAPK-related genes were linked to drug response, independent of total gene expression. PCA and k-means clustering separated cells into two splicing-defined groups. Cluster 2 was more sensitive to osimertinib (EGFRi) and RMC-6236 (pan-RASi), whereas cluster 1 was less sensitive. KRAS, YAP1, and SCRIB exons showed distinct usage patterns between clusters. Differential expression analysis identified an RNA-binding and splicing regulator as a candidate driver of the phenotype. Long-read RNA-seq data from 8 CCLE cell lines further suggested that expression change in this splicing regulator was correlated with target isoform usage and drug sensitivity. We generated knockout models using EGFR-mutant (PC-9, HCC4006) and KRAS-mutant (H358) lung cancer cells. Loss of the splicing regulator altered key splicing events and promoted resistance to osimertinib or RMC-6236. Knockout cells showed enhanced survival during long-term drug exposure, with little effect in short-term assays, suggesting a drug-tolerant state. These findings indicate RNA splicing regulation enhances tolerance to RAS/MAPK inhibitors. RNA binding protein expression and splicing signatures may be therapeutic response biomarkers.
O2-04: Background: Since January 2014, we have conducted multi-omics analyses of cancer patients undergoing surgery at a single institution, enrolling and analyzing > 10,000 cases. In this cohort, we observed three cases of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) and performed multi-omics analysis using whole-genome sequencing (WGS), RNA sequencing, gene expression profiling (GEP), in situ spatial analysis, and immunohistochemistry. Methods and Materials: All experimental protocols were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shizuoka Cancer Center (Authorization Number: 25-33). WGS and RNA sequencing were performed using the NovaSeq 6000 System, and GEP was conducted using a microarray platform. Xenium was used for spatial transcriptomic analysis. Immunohistochemical staining was performed by a pathologist. Results: All three patients were clinically diagnosed with MEN1 before genomic analysis. Pathogenic germline MEN1 mutations were identified using WGS, and loss of heterozygosity was confirmed in the tumors of the patients. Immunohistochemical staining for menin further supports the pathogenic significance of these alterations. In the most recently registered case, spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed differential MEN1 expression between tumor and normal tissues, which was not detected by conventional GEP. The tumor microenvironment is currently under investigation. Discussion: Further analyses and additional cases are needed; however, these findings may provide novel insights into the molecular pathogenesis of MEN1-associated neuroendocrine tumors.
O2-05: To improve diagnostic efficacy and therapeutic strategy in breast cancer, we selected URST4 (Up regulated in solid tumor 4) and investigated its biological role and potential as a candidate diagnostic and therapeutic target. Real-time qPCR, western blotting, and immunocytochemistry revealed that URST4 was overexpressed in breast cancer cell lines and clinical breast cancer tissues compared with normal breast epithelial cells and normal breast tissues. Immunohistochemistry using tissue microarrays revealed that URST4 was expressed in 72.3% (188 out of 260) of breast cancer tissues but was barely detectable in normal breast tissues. Higher expression of URST4 was significantly correlated with a poor prognosis in patients with breast cancer (P = 0.0105). Knock-down of URST4 expression using siRNAs significantly inhibited breast cancer cell growth through G2/M cell cycle arrest, mitotic program disruption as well as senescence formation, and also suppressed invasive ability of breast cancer cells. In contrast, overexpression of URST4 by plasmid transfection increased growth and invasion of cells. These findings suggest URST4 could be a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for breast cancer.
O2-06: The implementation of routine next-generation sequencing (NGS) in clinical genetics has led to a high prevalence (∼40%) of variants of uncertain significance (VUS). We evaluated a Fujitsu-developed deep learning model (FDLM) for reanalysis of germline VUS in genes related to DNA repair. These have been linked to hereditary cancer syndromes (HCS) such as Lynch Syndrome and Hereditary Breast- Ovarian Cancer. The model, trained on ClinVar (2023), was applied to historical HCS cases (2017–2025) from Complexo Hospitalario Universitario de Ourense (Spain) carrying germline VUS, totalling 61 variants. Updated expert re-classification per ClinGen-ACMG/AMP specifications (03/2026) identified 35 VUS, 25 benign/likely benign (B/LB), and 1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP). Among 25 expert B/LB variants, for 23 (92%) variants FDLM showed concordant predictions; 1 (4%) was reclassified P/LP and 1 (4%) inconclusive. The single expert-classified P/LP variant was concordantly identified by FDLM. Out of the 35 expert VUS, FDLM reclassified 14 (40%) as P/LP, 18 (51.4%) as B/LB, and 3 (8.6%) as inconclusive. Ongoing work integrates tumour mutational signature analysis to evaluate whether tumours carrying reclassified germline variants exhibit the expected genomic profiles, thereby validating FDLM classification. Concordance between FDLM predictions and tumour mutational patterns may provide orthogonal biological evidence supporting variant pathogenicity and algorithm predictive capability.
O3-01: Background: Reports of status epilepticus associated with fever (SEF) and acute encephalopathy (AE) are frequent in East Asia, particularly in Japan. Although a genetic predisposition has been suggested, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Methods: We analyzed mainly pediatric patients with SEF/AE referred for genetic testing at Kobe University from 61 collaborating institutions across Japan. Genetic analyses included either a targeted encephalopathy 331-gene panel or whole-exome sequencing (WES). Results: A total of 118 patients were enrolled, including 38 with SEF and 80 with AE. WES was performed in 75 cases. According to ACMG guidelines, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in 18 patients, including 10 with SEF and 8 with AE; variants in SCN1A accounted for approximately half of these cases. Notably, in patients without identified pathogenic variants, rare variants were observed in genes previously implicated in epilepsy, mitochondrial disorders, or related conditions. Additionally, some de novo variants of uncertain significance were identified in immune-related genes. These variants are relatively more frequent in Japanese, suggesting a potential contribution to the higher incidence of SEF/AE in this region. Conclusion: This is the first large-scale comprehensive study investigating monogenic disease-associated variants in SEF/AE. The overall diagnostic yield among the analyzed cases was about 20%. A substantial number of candidate variants were identified, highlighting the need for further functional studies to clarify their pathogenic roles.
O3-02: Background and Objectives: GNAS-Gsα mediates signal transduction of multiple G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). We investigated functional and structural properties of four germline GNAS-Gsα variants associated with ligand-independent gain-of-function (GOF) phenotypes, including nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (NSIAD), osteolytic bone lesions (OPLBD), and peripheral precocious puberty (PPP). Identified Variants and Clinical Features: (1) p.T55A on paternal allele identified in NSIAD and OPLBD and that on parent-of-unknown allele found in NSIAD, OPLBD, and borderline PPP; (2) p.I56F on maternal allele found in NSIAD, OPLBD, and borderline PPP; (3) p.N167K on maternal allele found in NSIAD; and (4) p.L198F on paternal and maternal-alleles identified in NSIAD and OPLBD. The three variants other than p.T55A were also associated with borderline pseudohypoparathyroidism when present on the maternal allele. Functional and Structural Analyses: Luciferase assays revealed ligand-independent GOF or its tendency for AVPR2 and PTH1R signaling, together with ligand-dependent loss-of-function (LOF) for PTH1R signaling. Structural analyses showed that the four variants destabilized both inactive and active conformations. Discussion: The results indicate that the four variants have constitutive GOF effects on specific GPCR pathways while preserving tissue-specific imprinting. GPCR selectivity may depend on interactions between GPCRs and the Gsα α5-helix, and ligand-dependent LOF may be masked by constitutive signaling.
O3-03: Background: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by genetic defects affecting bile secretion and transport. PFIC type 7 is caused by mutations inUSP53 and is known to be associated with cholestasis and occasionally hearing loss. Case: A 7-month-old girl presented with generalized purpura and was found to have vitamin K deficiency-associated coagulopathy and cholestatic liver dysfunction. She received treatment with fat-soluble vitamins and hepatoprotective drugs, and her symptoms improved. A targeted PFIC gene analysis was negative. During outpatient follow-up, hepatobiliary enzymes normalized. At 1 year and 5 months of age, intact-PTH levels increased, and vitamin D administration was started. However, hypocalcemia and rickets progressively worsened despite dose escalation. No pathogenetic variants were identified in VDR or CYP27B1 by further examination at 2years of age. However, comprehensive genetic analysis through IRUD identified a homozygous mutation in USP53, leading to a diagnosis of PFIC type 7. By 4 years of age, liver function including bile acid levels normalized and rickets findings gradually improved. No hearing impairment has been identified to date. Conclusion: The clinical symptoms of PFIC are diverse. Symptoms can be intermittent and can change over time. Currently available targeted PFIC gene analysis does not cover all types of PFIC. This case highlights the clinical importance of comprehensive genomic analysis in patients with unexplained cholestasis and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
O3-04: Background ROHHAD syndrome is a rare pediatric disorder characterized by rapid-onset obesity, hypothalamic dysfunction, and autonomic dysregulation The association with neural crest tumors and the recent identification of ZSCAN1 autoantibodies suggest a possible tumor-associated autoimmune mechanism; however, the genomic background of associated tumors remains poorly understood. Objective To explore somatic genomic alterations in a neural crest tumor associated with ROHHAD syndrome using paired tumor-germline whole-genome sequencing. Methods Paired WGS was performed using tumor tissue and peripheral blood DNA obtained from a patient with ROHHAD syndrome and neural crest tumor. Somatic alterations including copy number abnormalities and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) were evaluated. Results Multiple chromosomal regions demonstrating LOH were identified in tumor tissue compared with germline DNA. Several affected regions included loci potentially relevant to tumor biology, genomic imprinting, and immune regulation. No clearly pathogenic germline coding variants explaining the phenotype were identified. These findings suggest possible tumor-associated genomic instability in ROHHAD syndrome. Additional epigenomic and transcriptomic analyses are currently ongoing to further investigate the biological significance of these alterations. Conclusion Comprehensive paired tumor-germline WGS identified multiple somatic LOH regions in a ROHHAD-associated neural crest tumor, suggesting possible genomic and epigenomic mechanisms underlying disease pathophysiology.
O3-05: Background: In recent years, molecular genetic analysis for pediatric severe obesity has rapidly advanced in Western countries, but Japanese data remain limited. Methods: We analyzed 35 patients with pediatric severe obesity [BMI at least 120% of the 95th percentile, obesity index at least 50% for ages 6-17 years, or at least 30% for children under 6 years]. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) panel analysis for obesity-related genes and copy number variation (CNV) analysis using MLPA were performed. Results: One patient carried a previously reported pathogenic heterozygous MC4R variant, c.164G-to-A (p.G55D). In addition, microdeletions were identified in 3 patients (proximal 16p11.2 deletion, 15q13.2 deletion), and a 15q13.2 microduplication was detected in 1 patient. Overall, genetic abnormalities were identified in 5 patients (14.3%). Deletions involving 16p11.2 and 15q13 are CNVs that have attracted international attention in recent years because of their association with neurodevelopmental and obesity-related phenotypes, and our findings suggest that these CNVs may also contribute to Japanese pediatric obesity. Conclusion: Pediatric severe obesity has a highly heterogeneous genetic background involving both monogenic abnormalities and CNVs. Comprehensive genetic evaluation including CNV analysis in addition to NGS may help clarify disease mechanism and support future precision medicine approaches.
O3-06: Distal Deletion 14q Syndrome is a rare chromosomal disorder characterized by developmental delay, growth restriction, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Most cases are diagnosed after developmental delay becomes apparent, and neonatal diagnosis remains uncommon because early phenotypic findings are often subtle. We report a male infant born at 37+6 weeks of gestation with fetal growth restriction, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, mild dysmorphic features, and cardiopulmonary instability requiring NICU admission. Echocardiography demonstrated mild pulmonary artery branch narrowing and distal aortic arch tapering without significant hemodynamic obstruction. Bilateral hearing loss was confirmed by auditory brainstem response testing. These subtle multisystem neonatal findings raised suspicion of an underlying genetic condition, and research-based trio exome sequencing was performed and suggested a terminal deletion of chromosome 14q. Chromosomal microarray subsequently confirmed a 6.5Mb deletion at 14q32.2-q32.33 (GRCh37: Chr14:100,801,148-107,287,505). The deletion was absent in both parents, consistent with a de novo event. Early genetic diagnosis provided important information regarding prognosis and recurrence risk, enabling timely genetic counseling and multidisciplinary planning, including growth and neurodevelopmental follow-up, audiological intervention, and cardiovascular assessment.
O4-01: Introduction We report a case in which a fetus was diagnosed with Meckel Gruber syndrome (MKS) on consecutive pregnancies. Following exome sequencing,preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT M) was performed,resulting in a non affected fetus pregnancy. Case Report At 12 weeks of gestation, a mass was noted in the head of fetus. The patient was referred to Hospital A for prenatal diagnosis (PD). The karyotype was normal. An encephalocele and renal enlargement were detected by ultrasonography leading to a diagnosis of MKS. Following genetic counseling, the patient opted for termination of pregnancy. Subsequently, a pregnancy was achieved and head mass was detected at 11 weeks of gestation. The patient decided to terminate the pregnancy. We explained that on the results of genetic testing (GT) of the miscarried fetus, PD or PGT M might be possible. Initially, GT was not requested. However, since a subsequent pregnancy was also diagnosed with MKS, the patient requested GT. Exome sequencing was performed, and heterozygous variants in TMEM231 gene exon 1 and 3 were detected in both the affected specimen and parental blood. PGT M were performed after approval by the Japan Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology. A pregnancy was established following the second transfer of a non-affected embryo. The patient is currently 25 weeks pregnant, and the pregnancy is progressing with no apparent fetal morphological abnormalities. Discussion The results of GT allowed us to support the clients decision to proceed with another pregnancy through PGT M.
O4-02: Background: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a hereditary renal disorder associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and renal deterioration. Although ADPKD carries a 50% transmission risk to offspring, reports on preconception support are limited. Objective: To investigate pregnancy-related risk perception and preconception care practices among women with ADPKD. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed pregnancies complicated by ADPKD and pregnancies in women with a family history of ADPKD managed at our institution between 2016 and 2026. Renal deterioration, awareness of genetic inheritance, and implementation of genetic counseling and preconception care were evaluated. Results: Nine pregnancies complicated by ADPKD and two pregnancies with a family history of ADPKD were included. Most women recognized ADPKD as hereditary; however, some had limited understanding of the genetic nature of the disease, pregnancy-related renal deterioration, and perinatal risks. No patients had received preconception care. In two women with a family history of ADPKD, concerns regarding transmission to offspring emerged after pregnancy, leading to nephrology referral. Among nine ADPKD pregnancies, three developed hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and two showed renal deterioration after pregnancy. Discussion: Women with ADPKD may have insufficient understanding of pregnancy-related risks and long-term renal prognosis despite recognizing the disease as hereditary. These findings highlight the importance of preconception care and genetic counseling before pregnancy.
O4-03: When embryos classified as euploid with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) are transferred, many people assume that fetal chromosomal abnormalities are unlikely, although a residual risk remains. We encountered three pregnancies in which chromosomal abnormalities not predicted by PGT-A were identified after conception. In the first case, detailed fetal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities; however, SNP microarray analysis of amniotic cells revealed a pathogenic 1.4 Mb duplication in the 17q12 region, below the resolution detectable by PGT-A. In the second case, an XX embryo was selected at a non-authorized facility. During pregnancy, male external genitalia were observed, and NIPT ordered from a non-accredited clinic showed a positive result for XXY, suggesting mosaic XXY constitution. In the third case, amniocentesis revealed 20% mosaic trisomy 12. Retrospective review of the original PGT-A data demonstrated evidence of trisomy 12 below the reporting threshold for mosaicism, resulting in classification as euploid. Although PGT-A is highly accurate, it cannot detect small chromosomal deletions or duplications, as well as uniparental disomy. Furthermore, in embryos with chromosomal mosaicism, the chromosomal status of biopsied cells for PGT-A may not correspond to that of the fetus. At our clinic, SNP microarray analysis with amniocentesis is offered as an option after transfer of a euploid embryo, although uptake is approximately one-third. For patients, appropriate and balanced information provision regarding the limitations of PGT- A is important.
O4-04: [Objective] Increased fetal nuchal translucency (NT) in early pregnancy is associated with chromosomal and cardiac abnormalities, serving as a key prenatal marker. This study aimed to investigate the outcomes of cases with increased NT and negative non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) or normal amniocentesis karyotypes to improve future clinical management. [Methods] This retrospective study included cases with increased NT (defined as NT >= 3.5 mm) identified at our hospital or affiliated clinics between November 2016 and December 2025, with negative NIPT or normal karyotype. [Results] Out of 67 cases meeting the criteria, structural anomalies were detected in 25 (37.3%). Out of these, 10 cases presented with isolated congenital heart defects, and another 10 cases presented with multiple structural anomalies including heart defects. Other identified structural abnormalities included diaphragmatic hernia (n=1), left radial defect/aplasia (n=1), biliary atresia (n=1), a complex case presenting with thoracic hypoplasia, horseshoe kidney, bilateral lower leg shortening, and right fibular absence (n=1), and sacrococcygeal teratoma (n=1). [Conclusions] Even in cases with negative NIPT or a normal karyotype, structural anomalies occurred in approximately one-third of cases with NT >= 3.5 mm, with cardiac defects representing 80% of these anomalies. Detailed mid-trimester ultrasound evaluation targeting a wide range of anomalies is essential, and appropriate counseling should be provided to patients regarding these risks.
O4-05: Objective: To identify a predictive marker for the outcome of labor induction in late-term pregnancy. Methods: Maternal plasma miRNAs within the chromosome 19 miRNA cluster (miR-515-3p, miR-517a, miR-517c, miR-518b) and chromosome 14 miRNA cluster (miR-323-3p) were evaluated as candidate markers. Plasma samples at 30 and 36 weeks of gestation were collected from women who subsequently delivered at term following spontaneous labor (n = 21) and those who underwent labor induction in late-term pregnancy (n = 20). Maternal plasma cell-free microRNA levels were quantified using RT-qPCR. The late-term pregnancy group were further classified into successful (n = 13) and failed (n = 5) groups of labor induction. Results: Plasma cell-free miR-517a and cell-free miR-518b levels at 36 weeks of gestation were significantly higher in the failed labor induction group than in the successful labor induction group (miR-517a: median, 368.6 [9.9-1223.0] vs 30.0 [2.7-441.0], P = 0.030; miR-518b, 37.9 [5.5-58.2] vs 5.6 [1.5-20.3], P = 0.014). A receiver operating characteristic analysis comparing term delivery and successful labor induction (n = 34) with failed labor induction (n = 5) showed that plasma cell-free miR-518b levels at 36 weeks of gestation discriminated induction failure (area under the curve: 0.871, 95% confidence interval: 0.70-1.00). The optimal cutoff value was 23.3, with a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 94%. Conclusion: Maternal plasma miR-518b at 36 weeks were associated with failed labor induction and showed a better discriminatory performance than the Bishop score.
O4-06: A woman with clinically diagnosed hypochondroplasia based on characteristic radiographic findings and marked short stature (120 cm) experienced three consecutive pregnancies between 2019 and 2025. Genetic testing in the mother revealed no identifiable pathogenic variant. During the first pregnancy, threatened preterm labor developed at 24 weeks of gestation, and emergency cesarean delivery was required at 32 weeks and 1 day because of uncontrollable uterine contractions. The first daughter subsequently showed clinical findings consistent with hypochondroplasia. During the second pregnancy, elective cesarean delivery was performed at 33 weeks and 0 days considering the previous obstetric course. The second daughter also exhibited clinical features compatible with hypochondroplasia. During the third pregnancy, recurrent preterm labor developed and emergency cesarean delivery was required at 32 weeks and 5 days. In contrast, the male infant showed normal growth and development without evidence of skeletal dysplasia during follow-up. Thus, among three offspring, two inherited the maternal phenotype while one was unaffected. This family demonstrated segregation consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance and highlights the importance of prenatal surveillance, delivery planning, and genetic counseling for women with skeletal dysplasia.
O5-01: Background: The Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization (ToMMo) has pioneered the return of genomic results (ROGR) to BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant (PV) carriers in the general population, and their subsequent medical care is essential for evaluating the significance of ROGR. Objective: To assess healthcare utilization after ROGR and identify related challenges. Methods: This retrospective study analyzed participants in the ROGR study within the ToMMo cohort. Individuals who received BRCA1/2 PV results between Dec 2020 and Oct 2025 and visited Tohoku University Hospital (TUH) at least once were included. Results: Of 113 individuals (23 men and 90 women), 89 (17 men and 72 women) visited TUH. Prior cancers included breast (n=19), ovarian (n=3), prostate (n=1), and pancreatic (n=1). Four had undergone risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM) before ROGR; after ROGR, one developed breast cancer and two underwent RRM. Eight underwent bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy before ROGR for risk reduction or gynecologic disease, while 14 underwent risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO) after ROGR; one had ovarian cancer. Among women, continued surveillance at TUH or other institutions was observed in 52/68 in breast surgery and 55/71 in gynecology, indicating discontinuation in approximately 20%. Conclusion: The ROGR study showed relatively high follow-up adherence. Seamless collaboration between research institutions and hospitals may facilitate access to care for BRCA1/2 PV carriers, while long-term cancer prevention requires prevention strategies that are feasible and sustainable for each individual.
O5-02: Background: MRI is recommended for surveillance of BRCA-positive breast cancer, whereas mammography (MG) and ultrasound (US) are considered less accurate. We evaluated the sensitivity of each modality and related factors in BRCA-positive cases treated at our institution and explored a feasible surveillance strategy. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 36 women (47 breasts) with BRCA-positive breast cancer. Clinical and pathological data and imaging findings (MG, US, MRI) were reviewed. Sensitivity was defined as category >3, and category sensitivity as >4. Results: ER positivity was 53.8%, median tumor size was 19 mm, lymph node metastasis was present in 29.8%, and 48.9% were stage >2. Lesions were mainly located in the central to posterior regions (56.7%). Sensitivity (category sensitivity) was 76.1% (50%) for MG, 89.4% (76.6%) for US, and 95.5% (93.2%) for MRI. MG showed low sensitivity regardless of tumor size, especially in dense breasts and posterior lesions. US frequently missed tumors <10 mm and centrally or deeply located tumors, and calcifications. Combined MG and US achieved 100% sensitivity, indicating complementary value, although category sensitivity remained around 70% for tumors <20 mm. Adding MG and US to MRI provided minimal improvement. Conclusion: BRCA-positive breast cancers are often located posteriorly, requiring careful assessment of dense breast tissue on MG and US. A practical surveillance strategy may include annual MRI, with combined MG and US at 6 months, comparison with prior images, and additional MRI when new findings are detected.
O5-03: Background: Cancer whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is being implemented in Japan under the national Whole Genome Analysis Project, but real-world data on interpretation and disclosure of germline secondary findings (SFs) remain limited. Methods: Tumor-normal WGS from 198 patients with intractable or rare cancers (May- Oct 2025) was processed with DeepVariant and ANNOVAR, filtered by ToMMo allele frequency <1%. A multidisciplinary panel reviewed SFs against ACMG SF v3.2 and the Kosugi list, cross-checked with a commercial pipeline, and reassessed via ClinVar, IGV, and phenotype review. Results: Disclosed hereditary cancer variants included BRCA1/2, RAD51D, BARD1, ATM, SDHA, and SDHB. Other ACMG SF disclosures included PKP2 frameshifts in two asymptomatic ARVC cases, a PAX6 splice variant with congruent ocular phenotype, a FLNC splice variant in cardiomyopathy reviewed with cardiology, and a COL3A1 nonsense in a patient with intraoperative bleeding. Non-disclosed variants included TTN truncations in cardiac-only isoforms, EPCAM nonsense outside Lynch regions, and low-penetrance FLG/KCNQ4. A recurrent TSC2 splice variant was deemed false-positive by IGV. Commercial cross-checking identified five P/LP-annotated variants not flagged by the in-house annotation due to ClinVar-version lag. Conclusion: A systematic expert-panel workflow integrating curated gene lists, manual inspection, and multi-pipeline cross-validation enabled meaningful SF disclosure while avoiding false positives. Database maintenance and specialist consultation for incompletely penetrant genes are essential.
O5-04: Background: Tumor-normal paired (T-N) comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) directly assesses germline pathogenic variants (GPVs), whereas tumor-only (T-only) CGP requires confirmatory testing when presumed germline pathogenic variants (PGPVs) are detected. GenMineTOP, a DNA/RNA-based T-N CGP, became available at our institution in April 2024. Whether increased use of T- N CGP is associated with higher GPV detection in clinical practice remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed consecutive tissue-based CGP reimbursed under Japan's national health insurance system from our prospective clinical database. We evaluated the proportion of T-only and T-N CGP, GPVs confirmed by germline testing after T-only CGP, and GPVs identified by T-N CGP in Period 1 (June 2019-March 2024) and in Period 2 (April 2024-March 2026). Overall GPV detection rates were compared using Fisher's exact test. Results: Among 1,133 tissue-based CGP, T-N CGP accounted for 49/705 (7.0%) and 258/428 (60.3%) in Periods 1 and 2, respectively. In Period 1, PGPVs were detected in 46/656 T-only CGP (7.0%), and GPVs were confirmed in 11 cases (1.7%). One GPV was identified among 49 T-N CGP (2.0%). In Period 2, PGPVs were detected in 27/170 T-only CGP (15.9%), and GPVs were confirmed in four cases (2.4%). Fifteen GPVs were identified among 258 T-N CGP (5.8%). Overall GPV detection was 12/705 (1.7%) in Period 1 and 19/428 (4.4%) in Period 2 (p=0.0081). Conclusions: Increased use of T-N CGP was associated with higher overall GPV detection and may provide more opportunities to detect germline findings in clinical practice.
O5-05: Background: BRACAnalysis is used to diagnose HBOC and guide genetic counseling and risk-reducing care. We evaluated which insurance-coverage criteria best detect BRCA pathogenic variants. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 811 breast cancer patients who underwent BRACAnalysis under Japanese insurance coverage between July 2022 and November 2025, excluding tests performed for PARP inhibitor eligibility. Criteria assessed were age 45 years or younger, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) at age 60 years or younger, multiple primary breast cancers, family history, ovarian/ fallopian tube/peritoneal cancer, male breast cancer, and known familial BRCA variants. Sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), and Youden index were calculated. Results: BRCA pathogenic variants were detected in 57 patients (7.0%). Family history showed the highest sensitivity (71%). TNBC at age 60 years or younger showed the highest PPV (20%) and Youden index (0.19). Age 45 years or younger and multiple primary breast cancers showed intermediate performance (PPV 8% and 10%; Youden index 0.12 and 0.13, respectively). Ovarian/fallopian tube/peritoneal cancer and male breast cancer had high PPVs (29% and 25%, respectively), although few patients met these criteria. Conclusions: Family history showed the highest sensitivity, whereas TNBC at age 60 years or younger showed the highest PPV and Youden index. Criterion utility should be assessed using both diagnostic performance and the number of eligible patients.
O5-06: Approximately 15% of pediatric patients with cancer are genetically predisposed to cancer. However, clinical management and surveillance strategies are still based on limited evidence. To provide real-world data to guide clinical management and future directions, we conducted a retrospective review of cases seen in our Cancer Genetics Program from 2001 to 2024. Over 2,000 children were referred, of whom 620 patients had a genetically confirmed diagnosis of cancer predisposition (67 different diagnoses). The most common indications for germline testing were a personal history of cancer (42%), cascade testing (40%), and non-tumor manifestations associated with known cancer predisposition syndromes (12%). In 6% of cases, diagnoses were made through genetic testing performed for non-cancer indications. Across major cancer predisposition syndromes, surveillance facilitated early tumor detection. In Li-Fraumeni syndrome, the most common diagnosis in this cohort, no patients died of 10 surveillance-detected tumors, while 3 deaths occurred among 8 symptomatically diagnosed tumors during the surveillance interval, suggesting the need for more sensitive methods. Surveillance-detected tumors were associated with less intensive therapy compared to symptomatically detected tumors, highlighting an important impact on morbidity in this young population. Additionally, analysis of our long-term follow-up data led to modifications of surveillance protocols. These findings highlight the significant impact of a cancer genetics program on improving clinical management of at-risk patients.
O6-01: Introduction: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a developmental disorder primarily caused by mutations in NIPBL. Despite advancements in sequencing technology, a significant proportion of clinically diagnosed CdLS cases remain genetically undiagnosed after standard whole-exome sequencing (WES), likely due to variants in non-coding regions. We aimed to identify the underlying genetic cause in a patient presenting with classic CdLS features who remained undiagnosed after standard WES analysis. Methods and Results: To reveal unexpected pathogenic variants in our WES-negative patient with typical CdLS, we performed long-read whole-genome sequencing (LRS) using Oxford Nanopore Technologies. Manual inspection of the genomic data revealed a ~2.9 kb insertion within a deep intronic region of NIPBL (intron 44). The insertion was characterized as a de novo SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) type D element. This deep intronic variant was not detectable by standard WES due to its location and the nature of the repetitive sequence. Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that de novo SVA type D insertions in deep intronic regions of NIPBL can cause CdLS. Notably, this represents one of the very few reported instances of a Mendelian disorder caused by an active SVA_D retrotransposition. This study not only highlights the clinical utility of LRS in resolving WES-negative rare genetic disorders, but also provides crucial evidence that evolutionarily older SVA_D elements retain pathogenic mobilization capacity in the human genome.
O6-02: Background: Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) features PTH resistance due to reduced Gs α expression. Maternal GNAS pathogenic variants cause PHP1A, while methylation defects in GNAS differentially methylated regions (DMRs) lead to PHP1B. Although STX16 enhances NESP transcription, and NESP55 transcription is required to establish maternal imprints for AS2-DMR and A/B-DMR, the regulatory mechanisms of methylation imprint for GNAS-DMR remain unclear. Methods and Results: Using targeted long-read sequencing (T-LRS), we evaluated allele-specific methylation and structural variants in six patients. Patient 1 (PHP1A), with a deletion from 3' A/B-DMR to GNAS exon 1, showed normal methylation in the intact A/B-DMR, narrowing its critical maternal imprinted region. Among five PHP1B patients, Patient 2 with an STX16 deletion exhibited AS2-DMR hypomethylation, helping define precise AS2- DMR boundaries. Patient 3, carrying a maternal duplication that increased the STX16 - AS2-DMR distance, also showed AS2-DMR hypomethylation, proving that increased distance from STX16 drives hypomethylation. Patient 4, with a maternal retrotransposon insertion, exhibited marked A/B-DMR hypomethylation alongside mild AS1- and XL-DMR hypomethylation on the maternal allele, which was undetected by conventional methods. Patients 5 and 6, presenting with atypical GNAS-DMR methylation patterns, had mosaic abnormalities across all DMRs, indicating early embryonic epigenetic errors. Conclusion: T-LRS is a powerful tool for clarifying the complex genomic and epigenetic regulation underlying GNAS-DMR methylation.
O6-03: Introduction Spastic paraplegia type 62 (SPG62; MIM:615681) is a complex form of hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic deleterious variants in the ERLIN1 gene. We report a case of SPG62 resulting from complete paternal uniparental isodisomy (UPiD) of chromosome 10 with a novel variant in the ERLIN1 gene. Case Report The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation, weighing 3,412 g, by spontaneous vaginal delivery without neonatal asphyxia. At 4 years and 5 months of age, the patient developed toe-walking and was referred to our hospital for further evaluation. At the initial examination, restricted ankle dorsiflexion was observed. The patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes were hyperactive, the Babinski sign was positive, and spasticity was evident. Routine blood tests and brain and spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no abnormalities. Given the suspicion of a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder, whole-exome sequencing was performed as part of Rare and Undiagnosed Diseases (IRUD). Genetic analysis identified a homozygous deletion encompassing exon 4 of the ERLIN1 gene, derived from complete paternal uniparental isodisomy. This deletion was determined to be the pathogenic variant responsible for SPG62. Discussion Although etiology due to uniparental isodisomy - as seen in this case -is extremely rare, parental segregation analysis remains essential during genetic counseling for homozygous variants involving an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
O6-04: Background: CHARGE syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder mainly caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in CHD7 and shows variable phenotypes. We report a neonate in whom a synonymous CHD7 variant was considered causative through aberrant splicing. Case: A male infant had an atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) at 34 weeks of gestation and was delivered vaginally at 41+0 weeks, weighing 3242 g. Apgar scores were 4 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes, and he required intubation after birth. He had a coloboma, right facial nerve palsy, micrognathia, retrognathia, cleft right earlobe, and mild scrotal anomaly. Cardiac findings included unbalanced AVSD, right atrioventricular valve atresia, moderate left atrioventricular valve regurgitation, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. These findings led to a clinical diagnosis of CHARGE syndrome. His parents and sister had no anomalies or developmental delay. Genetic testing identifiedCHD7 NM_017780.4:c.5841A>G p.(Glu1947=), absent in both parents. SpliceAI predicted donor gain. RT-PCR using leukocyte RNA detected an abnormal band only in the proband. Sequencing showed an aberrant transcript with a 53-bp deletion, predicted to cause a frameshift. Discussion: The phenotype was compatible with a CHD7-related disorder. Although synonymous variants do not alter the encoded amino acid, they may be pathogenic when they cause aberrant splicing and loss of function. Conclusion: Synonymous CHD7 variants should not be dismissed solely because no amino acid substitution is predicted. Prediction tools, parental testing, and RNA analysis are important.
O6-05: Kabuki syndrome is a relatively common congenital anomaly syndrome characterized by distinctive facial features, neurodevelopmental disorders, short stature, and other clinical manifestations. Pathogenic variants in KMT2D (formerly MLL2) are recognized as the major cause of this condition. The KMT2D protein functions as a histone methyltransferase that catalyzes the methylation of lysine 4 on the tail of histone H3 (H3K4), thereby promoting gene expression through alterations in chromatin structure. In recent years, several disorders caused by pathogenic variants in other enzymes that similarly catalyze H3K4 methylation have been identified. We encountered and genetically diagnosed patients with Kleefstra syndrome 2, caused by variants in KMT2C, and ODLURO syndrome, caused by variants in KMT2E. In addition, we evaluated a patient with Kleefstra syndrome 1, which results from pathogenic variants in EHMT1, a gene encoding an enzyme that catalyzes methylation of another lysine residue on the histone H3 tail, H3K9. We discuss the shared neurodevelopmental phenotypes observed among these patients, as well as the characteristic facial features associated with each disorder. Furthermore, the diagnostic pathways that ultimately led to the identification of these conditions were particularly informative, and we present these clinical courses as part of our analysis.
O6-06: Joubert syndrome (JS) is a genetically heterogeneous ciliopathy characterized by hypotonia, developmental delay, abnormal ocular movements, and the molar tooth sign (MTS). Recently, heterozygous truncating variants in SUFU have been recognized as a cause of a mild neurodevelopmental phenotype within the JS spectrum with reduced penetrance. Our patient was a 3-year-old boy referred because of delayed motor and language development. He was born at 38 weeks of gestation after an uneventful pregnancy and delivery. He achieved independent walking at 23 months and had no meaningful words at 3 years of age. Neurological examination revealed congenital ocular motor apraxia, hypotonia, and macrocephaly without characteristic dysmorphic features. Brain MRI demonstrated an incomplete MTS. No retinal, renal, or hepatic involvement was identified. Comprehensive genetic testing revealed a heterozygous frameshift variant in SUFU (p.Gln217Profs*21). Unlike most forms of JS, which are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner,previously reported SUFU-related disorders have shown autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance. Consistent with these reports, our patient carried a heterozygous SUFU variant inherited from an unaffected parent. He showed no neonatal respiratory abnormality or multiorgan involvement. As previously reported, our case suggests that SUFU haploinsufficiency represents a relatively mild neurological subtype within the JS spectrum. Accurate phenotypic understanding is essential for genetic counseling and developmental support.
O7-01: Background: BRCA1/2 gene alterations are identified in approximately 10% of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). We analyzed the results of BRACAnalysis testing and the clinical outcomes of olaparib (Ola) treatment at our institution. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients with mCRPC who underwent BRACAnalysis testing at our institution between April 2021 and December 2025, including those subsequently treated with olaparib. The prevalence of BRCA1/2 alterations detected by BRACAnalysis, additional alterations identified by comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP), and the efficacy of olaparib treatment were evaluated. Results: A total of 92 patients were included, with a median age of 74 years. Metastatic sites included lymph node metastases in 79.3%, bone metastases in 82.6%, lung metastases in 5.4%, and liver metastases in 5.4% patients. BRACAnalysis identified BRCA1/2 alterations in 7 patients (7.6%), including BRCA2 alterations in 6 patients and a BRCA1 alteration in 1 patient. Among the 85 patients who were negative by BRACAnalysis, FoundationOne CDx (F1CDx) testing subsequently detected BRCA2 alterations in 2 additional patients, resulting in an overall BRCA1/2 positivity rate of 9.8% (9/92). Olaparib was administered to 8 of the 9 patients with BRCA1/2 alterations, and the median progression-free survival was 12 months (range, 0.5-50 months). Conclusions: Our retrospective analysis demonstrated that the prevalence of BRCA1/2 alterations in patients with mCRPC at our institution was generally consistent with previous reports.
O7-02: Objective: To clarify the molecular and clinical characteristics of anterior-segment dysgenesis (ASD)/aniridia and microphthalmia/ anophthalmia caused by monogenic variants. Methods: A total of 111 patients and their family members were recruited through a multicenter collaborative study in Japan. Next-generation sequencing using custom-designed panels for 11 genes associated with ASD/aniridia and 12 genes associated with microphthalmia/anophthalmia. We analyzed the clinical information of patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. Results: We achieved genetic diagnosis rates of 50.0% for ASD/aniridia and 37.5% for microphthalmia/anophthalmia. De novo variants in the PAX6, PITX2, or GJA8 genes, and parentally derived variants in the FOXC1 and CYP1B1 genes were the major causes of ASD/aniridia. Microphthalmia/anophthalmia-associated variants in the ABCB6, BMP4, and OTX2 genes were predominantly inherited from parents with no or different ocular phenotypes. We observed phenotypic diversity and variable ocular and systemic complications in variant-positive patients. Conclusions: Our targeted panel approach effectively clarified the mutation spectrum and phenotypic characteristics of ASD/aniridia and microphthalmia/ anophthalmia due to monogenic variants. Our genetic study confirmed that various phenotypes classified as ASD, such as Peters anomaly and Axenfeld anomaly, constitute a group of disorders on the same spectrum, may overlap with aniridia, and exhibit genetic heterogeneity.
O7-03: Case 1: A 38-y.o. male had atopic dermatitis (AD) since childhood. He had esophageal stenosis, scoliosis, recurrent pneumonitis and asthma followed by esophageal cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Serum IgE 12304 U/mL, TARC 1925 pg/mL, peripheral eosinophils 2500/μL. Genetic test identified a novel heterozygous ERBIN variant (NM_018695.4: c.3781C>T, p.Arg1261Trp). Case 2: A 44 y.o. male had AD since childhood, with cystic lung disease, recurrent pneumonia, multiple skin abscesses, and delayed exfoliation of primary teeth. Cervical lymph node biopsy demonstrated fungal infectious granulomas. Serum IgE 55,435 U/mL, TARC 1545 pg/mL, eosinophils 300/μL. A previously reported heterozygous STAT3 variant (NM_139276.3: c.1414A>G, p.Asn472Asp) was identified. Case 3: A 19 y.o. extremely obese male developed AD in childhood, with recurrent otitis media, paronychia, cutaneous candidiasis, and sinusitis. He exhibited a broad nasal base and prominent forehead. Serum IgE 4670 U/mL, TARC 789 pg/mL, eosinophils 900/μL. A novel heterozygous ZNF341 variant (NM_001282933.2: c.2165G>A, p.Arg722His) was identified. Case 4: 44-y.o. male had AD since childhood. He repeated subcutaneous abscess on his buttocks, otitis media and multiple fungal granulomas in his scrotum. He had diffuse large B cell lymphoma at the age of 35. Serum IgE 38319 U/mL, TARC 997 pg/mL, Eosinophils 868 μ/mL. Splice site variant in STAT3 gene; NM_139276.3: c.1139+2dup (T/TA) was identified. Conclusion: Detailed history taking is a key to identify hyper IgE syndrome overlooked until adulthood.
O7-04: Alport syndrome (AS) is characterized by locus heterogeneity(i.e. COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5) and significant variable expressivity . A 36-year-old man with childhood-onset hematuria progressed to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and developed hearing loss in his 30s. Multiple maternal relatives had microscopic hematuria and his deceased father had ESKD. Whole exome sequencing identified two rare COL4A4 variants: c.2165-5A<G, predicted by SpliceAI to cause aberrant splicing and frameshift, and c.1323_1340del, an in-frame deletion previously reported in autosomal dominant AS. Because parental samples were unavailable, long-read sequencing (LRS) was performed and demonstrated the two variants were in trans. The compound heterozygous state likely produced an allelic dose effect, resulting in severe disease with early-onset ESKD and extrarenal manifestations, whereas heterozygous family members showed only mild renal findings. These findings suggest that COL4A4-related disease severity may be better understood as a phenotypic spectrum influenced by allelic dose effects rather than a simple autosomal dominant/recessive classification. In genetic counseling, precise long-read phasing was particularly important in the context of potential living donor kidney transplantation. Some reports support kidney donation from relatives carrying a single COL4A4 variant, even with hematuria, whereas others warn of increased risk of kidney failure. Thus, LRS-based phase determination is clinically valuable for accurate genetic counseling and medical management, even without parental samples.
O7-05: Background: The retina reflects central nervous system pathology. However, shared polygenic networks among retinal morphology, brain structures, and tau/APOE-related neurodegeneration remain unmapped in East Asians. Purpose: This study elucidated genetic overlaps to establish ethnicity-specific imaging-genetics foundations. Methods: In the Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization (ToMMo) cohort, we conducted GWAS for retinal metrics from Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images (N=40,714) and integrated results with Brain-MRI GWAS (N=12,218). LDSC, Bayesian colocalization, and Mendelian Randomization identified genetic correlations and causal variants. An age-related polygenic risk score (PRS) was tested against Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) subscales. A linear mixed-effects model evaluated longitudinal Delta Retinal Neural Fiber Layer/Ganglion Cell Layer Slope, adjusting for glaucoma/myopia variants. This study followed relevant ethical guidelines, with informed consent obtained from all participants. Results: GWAS identified significant loci for retinal traits and brain volumes, peaking at the right parahippocampal area. We pinpointed causal colocalizing loci shared between eye and brain. Joint PRS showed these risks significantly drive MMSE "Orientation to Time" subscores. Adjusting for glaucoma PRS unmasked novel tau-pathway pleiotropic loci governing structural atrophy speed. Conclusion: This triangulation uncovers the shared retina-brain genetic architecture, establishing an ethnicity-specific foundation for precision screening of preclinical neurodegeneration.
O7-06: Background: Inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs) are a major cause of blindness. In Japan, voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna R) and its companion diagnostic, the PrismGuide TM IRD Panel System, were approved in 2023 for RPE65-retinopathy. We evaluated outcomes of expert panel review following insurance-covered genetic testing. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 275 cases discussed at the Ophthalmic Genetics Expert Panel between December 2023 and May 2026. Eligibility for insurance-covered testing required suspected autosomal recessive disease, childhood-onset severe night blindness with visual impairment, and markedly reduced full-field electroretinogram responses. Variant interpretation followed ACMG specifications adapted by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society. Results: Seventeen of 275 cases (6.2%) underwent insurance-covered genetic testing. Median age was 29 years (range 2 to 53). Six patients (35.3%) were eligible for Luxturna, four (23.5%) had RPE65-retinopathy without treatment eligibility, five (29.4%) received alternative genetic diagnoses, and two (11.8%) had other outcomes. Conclusions: Expert panel review identified Luxturna candidates in over one-third of tested patients. Despite potential referral bias, the high frequency of RPE65-retinopathy suggests that current eligibility criteria effectively enrich for affected patients, supporting the clinical utility of genetic testing and expert panel review.
O8-01: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor neuron degeneration. Age at onset (AAO) influences disease progression and survival; however, whether genetic determinants of AAO are shared across populations and analytical frameworks remains unclear. We performed a genome-wide association study of AAO using data from 9,252 European ancestry ALS patients from dbGaP (phs000101). We used REGENIE for linear regression model and gwasurvivr with a Cox proportional hazards model to evaluate associations between SNPs and AAO. The Cox model identified no genome-wide significant loci, whereas linear regression identified a novel significant locus, with SNP X as the lead variant (p = 2.05 × 10-8, β = -1.443). These findings suggest that linear regression and survival models may detect different genetic effects on disease onset. SNP X was observed only in European ancestry populations and is in strong linkage disequilibrium with SNP Y, previously associated with eosinophil-related traits, suggesting possible involvement of immune-related pathways in ALS onset timing. In contrast, the ADAM29-GPM6A locus previously reported in Japanese ALS patients (Nakamura et al. Commun Biol 8:1720 2025) was not replicated in European ancestry patients. These findings suggest ancestry-related differences in AAO-associated loci and model-dependent association patterns, providing new insights into ALS heterogeneity.
O8-02: [Background] Sequencing analysis provides detailed information at the nucleotide level. However, detecting complex structural abnormalities is often challenging. In contrast, genome mapping analysis (GMA) enables visualization of structural variants. We report on complex chromosomal structural abnormalities that were identified and solved by combining these two methods. [Patients and Methods] We performed short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) analysis in a family with suspected axonal neuropathy, including hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy (HNA) and other related conditions. No pathogenic variants had been identified in previous genetic testing. Since srWGS analysis suggested an abnormality spanning 17q25.1 to q25.3 in affected individuals, we performed GMA and HiFi long-read sequencing analysis (HiFi sequencing) using high molecular weight DNA extracted from blood to further elucidate the details. [Results] GMA yielded a contig of over 1 Mb spanning 17q25.1 to q25.3. Within this region, we identified an inverted duplication exceeding 500 kb, including the SEPTIN9 gene, and a duplicated insertion exceeding 151 kb. Detailed analysis of this region using HiFi sequencing revealed additional insertions of multiple small DNA fragments (less than 50 bp). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of such a complex structural abnormality in the SEPTIN9 region in patients with HNA. [Conclusion] Combining GMA with Hi-Fi sequencing is highly effective in identifying and elucidating complex chromosomal structural variants.
O8-03: A 50-year-old woman presented with hypotonia from 3 months of age. At 7 months, she developed decreased activity, recurrent vomiting, and impaired consciousness, and was hospitalized with suspected acute encephalopathy. Head control was achieved at 12 months. At 3 years, she developed acute cerebellar ataxia following a febrile illness. A metabolic disorder was suspected, and vitamin B1 administration partially improved her symptoms. Epileptic seizures occurred between 3 and 9 years of age, and antiseizure medication was continued until age 13. At 13 years, reduction of vitamin supplementation resulted in generalized weakness and bulbar symptoms, which improved after intravenous vitamin B1 administration. A vitamin B1-responsive disorder was suspected, and supplementation was continued thereafter. Her condition remained stable. At age 47, she was referred for follow-up. Neurological examination revealed gaze-evoked nystagmus, dysarthria, limb and truncal ataxia, spasticity, rigidity, hyperreflexia, and bilateral positive Babinski and Chaddock signs. She required assistance for walking. Brain MRI demonstrated encephalomalacia in the bilateral caudate heads and cerebellar vermian atrophy. Whole-genome sequencing identified pathogenic variants consistent with TPK1 deficiency. TPK1 encodes thiamine pyrophosphokinase, which converts vitamin B1 into thiamine pyrophosphate. Early vitamin B1 supplementation is crucial in this disorder. In this case, empirical vitamin B1 supplementation before genetic diagnosis was considered effective in preventing further neurological deterioration.
O8-04: Background: Gelsolin amyloidosis is an autosomal dominant hereditary amyloidosis caused by deposition of mutant gelsolin fragments as amyloid in multiple organs. We report a case of gelsolin amyloidosis presenting with aortic regurgitation (AR). Case Presentation: A 72-year-old woman presented with ptosis and drooping of the mouth corners beginning in her 40s and had undergone three previous surgeries for ptosis. Several family members, including her mother, second son, one sibling, maternal grandmother, and maternal cousin, had similar symptoms, all developing ptosis in their 40s. Neurological examination revealed muscle weakness and atrophy involving the facial, tounge, and cervical muscles. No sensory disturbance was observed. Laboratory tests showed elevated BNP levels of 836 pg/mL and renal dysfunction with a serum creatinine level of 1.72 mg/dL and. Echocardiography demonstrated moderate-to-severe AR. No definitive findings suggestive of cardiac amyloid deposition were identified. Results: Whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous pathogenic variant in the GSN gene, c.487G>A (p.Asp163Asn), which has been previously reported. Discussion: Clinically significant cardiomyopathy in gelsolin amyloidosis is considered rare; however, several small case series have reported cardiac involvement and conduction abnormalities. Only one case with AR was found to the best of our knowledge. Conclusion: We experienced a case of gelsolin amyloidosis presenting with AR. This case highlights the importance of cardiac screening in patients with this disease.
O8-05: Proximal 18q deletion syndrome is a rare contiguous gene deletion disorder primarily associated with neurodevelopmental abnormalities. Although tremor and other movement disorders have occasionally been described, involvement of the dopaminergic system has not been clearly demonstrated. We report a 53-year-old woman with intellectual disability since childhood who developed adult-onset tremor. Neurological examination revealed postural and intention tremor involving the neck and both upper limbs, accompanied by orofacial dyskinesia. Brain MRI showed mild atrophy of the dorsal pons and midbrain. Dopamine transporter scintigraphy demonstrated reduced bilateral striatal uptake, suggesting nigrostriatal dysfunction. Cardiac MIBG scintigraphy was normal, and the overall findings were not suggestive of an underlying α-synucleinopathy. Targeted next-generation sequencing did not detect pathogenic variants associated with hereditary parkinsonism. Chromosomal microarray analysis identified a 5.5-Mb interstitial deletion at 18q12.1-q12.3. The deleted region encompasses multiple genes involved in neuronal development and synaptic regulation, including CELF4, ZNF24, MAPRE2, and ELP2. Haploinsufficiency of these genes may contribute not only to neurodevelopmental abnormalities but also to vulnerability of the dopaminergic system. This case provides evidence that proximal 18q deletion can be associated with dopaminergic dysfunction and adult-onset movement disorder, expanding the phenotypic spectrum of this condition.
O8-06: LAMB1 encodes laminin subunit β1, a basement membrane protein critical in neurodevelopment. Biallelic LAMB1 variants, especially loss-of-function alleles, are classically associated with severe pediatric-onset neurodevelopmental disorders, including cobblestone lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, and cortical malformations. More recently, heterozygous end-truncating variants, predicted to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, have been linked to a distinct adult-onset disorder characterized by neurological symptoms and diffuse white matter lesions on brain MRI. Because heterozygous end-truncating LAMB1 variants have been reported in only a few cases, the associated clinical and radiological spectrum remains unclear. Here, we report affected individuals from two unrelated families carrying novel heterozygous end-truncating variants in LAMB1 (NM_002291.3:c.5263_5269del and c.5224+5G>C), identified by whole exome or genome sequencing. The first variant was identified in six affected relatives and segregated with neurological symptoms and diffuse white matter lesions, already evident at 6 years of age in the youngest individual. The second variant occurred de novo in a 5-year-old girl with multiple brain malformations including cobblestone lissencephaly, resembling the phenotype of biallelic LAMB1 variants. These findings expand the clinical spectrum associated with heterozygous end-truncating LAMB1 variants, suggesting that their clinical phenotypes range from childhood-onset white matter disease and severe neurodevelopmental abnormalities to adult-onset leukoencephalopathy.
O9-01: Introduction: Recent genomic sequencing enables early diagnosis of pediatric genetic diseases, and gives a chance of considering palliative care (PC). This report indicated our experiences of integration of PC into the management of pediatric genetic diseases. Methods: Data drive from our hospital between 2018 and 2025. Patients with pediatric genetic diseases who received PC by PC health professionals were included. Results: Of the 69 patients who received PC, 34 (49%) were pediatric genetic diseases including 4 patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, 4 patients with Mitochondrial disease, 3 patients with Down syndrome and 2 patients with Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy. In addition, there were 21 cases of other rare genetic diseases, such as Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease. The total number of advance care planning (ACP) sessions was 114. ACP was conducted repeatedly depending on the trajectory of patients, ranging from 1 to 11 sessions per patient (median, 2). The initial ACP age ranged from 4 to 35 years (median age 14 years). Two patients died at 12 years of age (Down syndrome) and at 15 years of age (SENEBAC syndrome), respectively. Bereavement care was conducted to both families. Conclusions: Integration of PC into genomics is important. However, a policy gap related to integrating PC into genomics exists. Genetic health professionals need the knowledge about PC and collaborate with PC health professionals, providing more appropriate management of pediatric genetic diseases.
O9-02: <Background> Management of congenital heart disease in infants with trisomy 18 remains controversial. Our center increasingly considered cardiac surgery beginning around 2020. We evaluated the association between this change and clinical outcomes. <Methods> This retrospective cohort study compared cardiac intervention rates and survival in infants with trisomy 18 born at our center between Era 1 (2015-2019) and Era 2 (2020-2024) using Fisher's exact test and Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank test, respectively. Cardiac interventions included catheter-based and surgical procedures. <Results> A total of 31 infants were identified, including 17 in Era 1 and 14 in Era 2. Five infants whose families did not choose intensive care were excluded (4 in Era 1 and 1 in Era 2), leaving 26 infants for analysis. Baseline characteristics were similar between eras. Cardiac intervention was more frequently performed in Era 2 than Era 1, although the difference was not significant (46.2% vs 7.7%, p = 0.07). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly longer survival in Era 2 (p < 0.05). Infants who underwent cardiac intervention showed significantly longer survival than non-surgical patients (p < 0.05). <Conclusions> Cardiac intervention gradually increased following changes in institutional practice and was associated with improved survival. Although limited by small sample size, selection bias, and temporal improvements in neonatal care, these findings suggest a potential role for cardiac intervention in selected infants with trisomy 18.
O9-03: Background; Rett syndrome-like neurodevelopmental disorders (RTT-like NDDs) form a phenotypic cluster defined by combinations of stereotypic movements, autistic traits, developmental delay, sleep disturbance, autonomic dysfunction, feeding difficulties, and epilepsy. This cluster is clinically recognizable but independent of classic Rett criteria and genetically heterogeneous. Without a guiding framework, prediction and treatment remain uncertain, and families manage care without clear direction. This study aimed to describe real-world diagnostic trajectories of RTT-like cases. Methods; We retrospectively reviewed eight patients seen between 2021 and 2026 with RTT-like features who received molecular diagnoses through insurance-based testing, IRUD, national research programs, or self-funded external analyses. Results; Only one patient underwent MECP2 testing at a referring institution; Rett syndrome was excluded at our center, and the final diagnosis was Lessel-Kreienkamp syndrome. Six patients were diagnosed through varied routes, with genetic causes spanning RNA-related, chromatin, metabolic, chromosomal, imprinting, and synaptic disorders, showing mechanisms beyond MECP2. Conclusions; RTT-like NDDs constitute a coherent clinical cluster, yet diagnostic routes and management remain inconsistent, increasing uncertainty for clinicians and families. Flexible genetic evaluation using broad panels or comprehensive genomic testing, together with a structured care framework tailored to this cluster, is needed.
O9-04: Introduction: PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PTEN variants. It is characterized by hamartomas and an increased risk of malignancy, requiring surveillance. Although PHTS is often diagnosed in adulthood, it may also present in childhood with macrocephaly and intellectual disability (ID). We analyzed five children with PHTS. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients with pathogenic PTEN variants identified between August 2020 and March 2026. Genetic testing was performed using next-generation sequencing and Sanger sequencing. This study was approved by the ethics committees of Kobe University and Hyogo Prefectural Kobe Children Hospital. Results: There were two males and three females. Age at diagnosis ranged from 1 to 5 years. Macrocephaly ranged from +2.5 to +4.9 SD, whereas tall stature was absent. Developmental quotient ranged from 41 to 82 (mean 64.8). Brain MRI showed T2 hyperintensities in the peritrigonal white matter in three patients. One patient had gastrointestinal hamartomas with hypoalbuminemia and punctate palmoplantar keratosis. Missense variants were identified in two patients, nonsense variants in two, and one patient harbored both missense and splice-site variants. Discussion: In children with macrocephaly and ID, Sotos syndrome is often suspected; however, PHTS should also be considered. PHTS carries a tumor risk from childhood and requires follow-up; therefore, genetic testing should be actively considered when this disease is suspected based on clinical findings.
O9-05: Multiple genetic factors can contribute to acute recurrent pancreatitis (ARP) in children. We report a 3-year-old girl with ARP requiring four hospitalizations, who carried a SPINK1 variant and compound heterozygous UBR1 variants. Targeted next-generation sequencing identified a heterozygous SPINK1 splice-site variant (c.194+2T>C), predicted to cause loss of function of pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor. This variant was also present in her unaffected father, suggesting that SPINK1 alone was insufficient to explain the phenotype. Whole-exome sequencing identified two rare UBR1 missense variants, c.2924T>C (p.Ile975Thr) and c.4856A>T (p.Asp1619Val) in trans. Both variants were predicted to be deleterious by multiple in silico tools. p.Ile975Thr is located in the WHD domain and p.Asp1619Val in the CHD domain; structural analysis suggested possible effects on interactions or folding. No variants were found in other major pancreatitis-associated genes. UBR1 encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause Johanson- Blizzard syndrome, although milder impairment may produce variable phenotypes. The patient had no syndromic features except pancreatic involvement. Given that Ubr1-knockout mice show exocrine pancreatic dysfunction and susceptibility to injury, partial UBR1 dysfunction may have contributed to her pancreatitis susceptibility. Although the risk of compound heterozygous UBR1 variants or coexistence with SPINK1 variants remains unclear, UBR1 may be involved in a subset of idiopathic pancreatitis, including pediatric cases.
O9-06: Background: Congenital malformations (CM) and genetic pathology significantly drive neonatal morbidity and mortality. We evaluated clinical and genetic features in neonates to optimise diagnostic algorithms. Materials and Methods: A retrospective analysis of 167 neonates was conducted, assessing prenatal screening, ultrasound, clinical phenotypes, cytogenetic, and molecular genetic findings. Results: Dysmorphism/stigmata of dysembryogenesis were identified in 52 infants (31.1%), multiple CM in 18 (10.8%), and confirmed chromosomal anomalies in 14 (8.4%; 10 Down syndrome, 1 Turner, 1 Triple X, 1 Edwards, 1 microdeletion/microduplication). Cardiovascular CMs were most frequent (30.5%), followed by genitourinary (16.2%), gastrointestinal (13.2%), and pulmonary (9.6%) defects. Monogenic diagnoses included Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (n=2). A comparative analysis revealed that all 14 verified chromosomal cases occurred in 2025 (n=121), whereas zero were registered among live births in 2026 (n=46). This shift reflects enhanced prenatal screening, ultrasound quality, and NIPT coverage, enabling timely antenatal detection. Concurrently, non-chromosomal CM referrals increased in 2026. Conclusion: The high prevalence of dysmorphism (31.1%) contrasted with low chromosomal resolution (8.4%) highlights the limitations of standard karyotyping. Effective prenatal screening successfully reduced postnatal chromosomal births in 2026. Transitioning to chromosomal microarray analysis and next-generation sequencing as a standard is essential to improve diagnostic yield and genetic counselling.
O10-01: Objectives: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix- Saguenay (ARSACS) is a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder caused by SACS gene. The aim of this study was to elucidate the clinical and genetic characteristics of 22 Japanese patients in our cohort. Methods: We examined the clinical presentation and MRI findings. We performed Sanger sequencing of the SACS gene after obtaining consent for genetic testing. Results: A total of 24 variants in the SACS gene were identified in 22 Japanese patients from 16 families. Most of these variants were located in different regions of the gene, and the majority were nonsense or insertion/deletion variants; only 5 were missense variants. The mean age at onset was 6.95 years. Clinical symptoms included cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy in nearly all cases; however, 8 cases lacked hyperreflexia, 6 cases lacked lower limb spasticity, and 4 cases lacked pathological reflexes. No retinal hypermyelination was observed in 10 patients, and 9 patients had intellectual impairment. In almost all cases where MRI findings could be confirmed, atrophy of the superior vermis and cervical spinal cord, as well as T2 low signal intensity in the pons, were observed. However, T2 high signal intensity around the thalamus and thinning of the corpus callosum were observed in only about two-thirds of cases. Conclusion: In our cohort which genetic analysis was performed and variants in the SACS gene were identified, the clinical manifestations, MRI findings and the genetic variant locations were highly diverse.
O10-02: Background: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is caused by abnormal CTG repeat expansion in the 3' untranslated region of the DMPK gene. Somatic instability has been associated with disease progression, whereas repeat interruptions are known to be linked to delayed onset and milder symptoms. Objective: To characterize somatic instability and repeat interruptions in Japanese patients with DM1 using multiple methods. Methods: Lymphocyte DNA was analyzed. Repeat interruptions were screened by triplet repeat-primed PCR (TP-PCR), followed by Sanger sequencing and long-read sequencing (LRS) using PureTargetTM Repeat Expansion Panel (Pacific Biosciences).
