Somatic instability was evaluated by small-pool PCR (SP-PCR) and LRS. Results: Genomic DNA was obtained from 116 Japanese patients with DM1. TP-PCR followed by Sanger sequencing identified CCG interruptions in six samples from four families. Sanger sequencing and LRS demonstrated variation in the number and position among clones and reads. Interruption sites were relatively conserved within families. SP-PCR and LRS showed similar modal repeat lengths and distribution ranges in most samples, although discrepancies were observed in congenital cases. Expansion bias was more pronounced in samples with modal repeat lengths <600, whereas it tended to plateau in those with repeat lengths >600. Conclusion: LRS showed results largely consistent with SP-PCR and TP-PCR while enabling detailed analysis of somatic instability and repeat interruptions, supporting its utility in DM1 genetic research.
O10-03: [Objective] Recent advancements in disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) have optimized hereditary ATTRv amyloidosis management. Although predictive genetic testing identifies at-risk individuals, standardized clinical protocols for pre-emptive monitoring remain poorly established. This study systematically compared international consensus guidelines regarding clinical surveillance for asymptomatic ATTRv carriers. [Methods] International consensus frameworks and guidelines published since 2013 regarding asymptomatic ATTRv carrier management were evaluated. [Results] Frameworks universally converge on four core principles: (1) comprehensive baseline evaluation upon variant identification; (2) individualized surveillance tailored to mutation type and family history; (3) continuous subclinical assessments; and (4) mandatory care coordination through multidisciplinary teams with genetic counseling. Conversely, significant discrepancies remain regarding tissue biopsy recommendations and non-invasive modalities like bone scintigraphy. [Conclusion] While ATTRv amyloidosis is a paradigm model for pre-emptive medicine, harmonizing diagnostic discrepancies remains essential to maximize therapeutic efficacy. To facilitate sustainable surveillance, establishing minimally invasive monitoring methodologies, such as longitudinal serum biomarker assays, remains critical
O10-04: Background: Adult-onset non-5q spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is genetically heterogeneous, and many cases remain molecularly undiagnosed. We tested whether LRP12 CGG repeat expansions are enriched in patients with clinically diagnosed adult-onset non-5q SMA. Methods: Eight consecutive Japanese families with clinically diagnosed adult-onset non-5q SMA meeting prespecified criteria were analyzed after excluding SMN1-related SMA, SBMA, and pathogenic variants in known SMA-, ALS-, and neuropathy-associated genes. LRP12 expansions were defined by a sawtooth repeat-primed PCR pattern and sized by Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing. Expansion frequencies were compared with 1,000 controls using two-sided Fisher's exact test. Results: LRP12 CGG repeat expansions were found in 6/8 probands (75.0%; 5/5 familial, 1/3 sporadic). Seven affected individuals carried heterozygous expansions of 58-92 repeat units, shorter than typical LRP12-OPDM expansions. They showed adult-onset, slowly progressive, proximal-predominant pure lower motor neuron weakness, preserved bulbar and sensory function, and no upper motor neuron signs throughout follow-up. The expansion frequency was markedly higher than in controls (2/1,000; P=5.4 x 10-13), whereas expansions were rare in an ALS series (2/496, 0.40%). Conclusions: LRP12 CGG repeat expansions may represent an underrecognized genetic cause of unresolved adult-onset lower motor neuron syndromes with SMA-like features and broaden the clinical spectrum of LRP12-related disease. LRP12 repeat-expansion testing should be considered in such patients.
O10-05: Digenic TBP/STUB1 spinocerebellar ataxia (SCATBP/STUB1) is a recently proposed disorder characterized by the coexistence of an intermediate TBP repeat expansion and a STUB1 variant. However, its pathology remains poorly understood. We report a 44-year-old woman with progressive myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia, and cognitive impairment. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed cerebellar atrophy with hyperintense dentate nuclei (Crab sign). Muscle biopsy revealed ragged-red fibers with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency and scattered succinate dehydrogenase-positive fibers, consistent with mitochondrial myopathy. Despite these findings, no pathogenic variants were detected in mitochondrial DNA or in nuclear genes associated with mitochondrial disease. Whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variant in STUB1 [NM_005861.4: c.146A>G p.(Tyr49Cys)], while ONT target long-read sequencing confirmed an intermediate TBP repeat expansion (36/42 repeats), establishing the diagnosis of SCATBP/STUB1. This is the first description of skeletal muscle pathology in SCATBP/STUB1, which expands the pathological spectrum of this recently recognized digenic disorder and suggests that mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to its pathogenesis. The findings also suggest that intermediate TBP expansions may modify the clinical impact of STUB1 variants and contribute to disease expression. The SCATBP/STUB1 should be considered in patients with suspected mitochondrial disease, particularly those with MERRF-like features and negative mitochondrial genetic testing.
O10-06: Background: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants have been reported in hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), but their role in HSP cohorts remains unclear. Methods: Using MitoHPC, we called mtDNA variants from exome data of 646 patients with HSP collected through the Japan Spastic Paraplegia Research Consortium (JASPAC). Variants with allele fraction >0.1 were annotated using ClinVar, APOGEE2, population databases, and literature. Candidates were prioritized by rarity, disease reports and predicted impact. Results: In MT-ATP6, five rare missense variants with APOGEE2 probability >0.1 were found, including the homoplasmic m.9176T>C, p.(Leu217Pro), reported in maternally inherited spastic paraplegia, and four additional variants classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Among these four VUS, one was found in a family that did not show maternal inheritance, and another in a patient with a likely pathogenic variant in a nuclear gene. Heteroplasmic MT-ATP6 m.9205_9206del, p.(Ter227MetextTer?), a likely pathogenic variant reported in neonatal-onset mitochondrial disease, was also identified, although its relevance to HSP remains unclear. In MT-TV, homoplasmic m.1661A>G, previously reported in spastic paraplegia, was found in three unrelated patients. Pathogenic mtDNA variants related to hearing loss and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy were also found. Conclusions: This exome-based mtDNA screening identified candidate mtDNA variants in patients with HSP. Further family studies and functional validation are needed to clarify their clinical significance.
O11-01: Background: Transcriptome analysis can improve the diagnostic yield for neurodevelopmental disorders. However, identifying pathogenic non-coding variants remains challenging when exome sequencing detects only a single heterozygous pathogenic variant in a recessive disease. Case Report: We applied RNA-seq using urine-derived cells (UDCs) to a family with two affected brothers with muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy and dilated cardiomyopathy. Exome sequencing identified a maternally inherited heterozygous B3GALNT2 splice-site variant (NM_152490.5:c.261-2A>G) but no second pathogenic allele. UDCs RNA-seq with OUTRIDER detected markedly decreased expression of B3GALNT2 in the proband and a milder decrease in the father, suggesting a paternally inherited non-coding variant. Genome sequencing revealed a 357-bp heterozygous deletion encompassing the B3GALNT2 promoter and transcription start site, which segregated with the phenotype. RNA-seq supported aberrant splicing from the splice-site allele and reduction of transcripts from the deletion allele. Conclusion: These findings provide proof of concept that UDCs RNA-seq-guided outlier-expression analysis can identify non-coding second hits and support genetic diagnosis. They also suggest that cardiac surveillance may be warranted in B3GALNT2-related disorder as affected individuals age.
O11-02: Cancers of unknown primary (CUP) and diagnostically challenging cases remain a major obstacle in precision oncology. Genome- Derived-Diagnosis Ensemble (GDD-ENS) is a deep learning model trained on MSK-IMPACT genomic profiles to predict cancer type. We examined whether GDD-ENS can be implemented in a Japanese comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) setting to support diagnostic reinterpretation and cancer type inference. We analyzed 2,133 non- CUP cases from 13 institutions. While GDD-ENS showed high discrimination (macro-averaged AUC 0.87 in tissue CGP), concordance with pathological diagnosis was modest. UMAP-based dimensionality reduction of predictive scores revealed clusters enriched for specific cancer types with varying heterogeneity. Focusing on discordant cases between genomic prediction and pathological diagnosis, we identified 160 candidates for diagnostic reconsideration using cluster- and neighborhood-based criteria. Among these, 126 showed higher genomic similarity to alternative cancer types than to their original diagnoses. Expert review confirmed clinically meaningful discordance in selected cases, particularly metastatic lesions and ambiguous samples. We further applied this framework to 68 CUP cases. Neighborhood-based inference enabled cancer type estimation in a subset with low entropy in neighboring cancer composition. These results demonstrate that GDD-ENS-derived genomic clustering identifies diagnostically ambiguous cases and supports cancer type inference in CUP, complementing pathology by incorporating genomic similarity into clinical decisions.
O11-03: Genome sequencing in patients with suspected genetic disorders increasingly identifies variants of uncertain significance (VUS), including putative splicing variants. Although prediction tools support initial prioritization, direct clinical or functional evidence for the query variant is often unavailable. Evidence from analogous variants affecting the same gene, region/domain, and molecular consequence can provide contextual support, but systematic collection and integration of such evidence remain labor-intensive. We developed CLAVI, an LLM agent-based framework for hypothesis generation on the functional impact and disease relevance of VUS. CLAVI searches literature and variant resources to identify high-grade similar variant evidence, defined as evidence from analogous variants supported by functional studies and/or patient reports. It summarizes the findings in the context of gene and domain information, and interprets the potential functional impact of the query VUS. Benchmarking across repeated runs showed that CLAVI achieved reliable recall and precision despite run-to-run fluctuation inherent to LLM agents, while generating interpretable evidence summaries. We are also applying CLAVI to approximately 1,000 putative splicing VUS extracted from SRA-derived genomic data. CLAVI prioritizes VUS lacking direct variant-specific evidence by leveraging analogous variant evidence, without assigning ACMG/AMP classifications. This approach may help efficiently identify candidate variants for expert review or functional validation in genetic disorders.
O11-04: Diagnosis of rare diseases remains a major clinical challenge because of the limited number of reported cases. Existing systems, such as PubCaseFinder and GestaltMatcher, are useful as diagnostic aids; however, they are limited by the types of data they can accept and are often biased toward a narrow range of diseases. In recent years, generative AI such as ChatGPT has attracted attention for clinical use, but simple prompt-based use alone lacks sufficient medical accuracy and carries the risk of hallucinations. To address these limitations, we developed ZebraSeek, a diagnostic support tool that integrates information from generative AI, existing diagnostic support programs, medical databases, and search engines. ZebraSeek uses generative AI as its core and applies a custom workflow to sequentially process and integrate information from multiple sources. This enables the system not only to present accurate diagnostic candidates but also to provide detailed textual explanations for why each disease is suggested. We evaluated the system using data derived from actual case reports. While the diagnostic accuracy of conventional methods and standalone generative AI with simple prompting was approximately 30-50%, ZebraSeek achieved an accuracy of over 60%. By efficiently organizing and integrating previously scattered medical information, ZebraSeek may reduce the physical and psychological burden on clinicians and help address the long-standing challenge of the diagnostic odyssey in rare disease care.
O11-05: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a common type of dementia, and its prevalence is increasing worldwide including in Japan. Early intervention is essential for delaying disease progression, highlighting the urgent need for novel biomarkers for early diagnosis. In this study, we aimed to identify blood-based biomarkers through gene- and transcript-level expression patterns associated with AD using long-read RNA sequencing. Long-read RNA sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies was performed using blood samples from 116 AD patients (mean age=75.2±4.5) and 72 cognitively normal individuals (mean age=72.0±4.8) aged >64 years, obtained from the National Center for Geriatrics and Gerontology Biobank. Differential expression analyses were conducted at both the gene (DEG) and transcript (DET) levels. DEG analysis identified 525 significantly differentially expressed genes (FDR < 0.05, FC > 1.2) and four enriched KEGG pathways. DET analysis, excluding genes identified in the DEG analysis, identified 449 significantly altered transcripts and two enriched KEGG pathways. Notably, the Neutrophil extracellular trap formation pathway was detected in both DEG and DET analyses. Among the genes in this pathway, six neutrophil-enriched gene exhibited significant alterations at the transcript level, without corresponding gene-level changes. These findings demonstrate that transcript-level analysis can detect expression changes that are undetectable by conventional gene-level approaches. Such transcript-specific alterations may contribute to the development of early diagnostic biomarkers.
O11-06: Long-read sequencing (LRS) is a powerful tool for detecting structural variants (SVs), which are major causes of genetic diseases. However, the application of trio-based analysis to LRS data remains challenging due to the complexity of merging and comparing SVs across individuals. Here, we established a workflow to prioritize pathogenic SVs using trio-based LRS whole-genome sequencing. The workflow integrates high-accuracy basecalling, trio-based phasing, and multiple SV callers (CuteSV and Sniffles2). We employed the PanPop Realign and Thin (PART) process to merge SVs and utilized the JSV1 Japanese population-specific SV frequency dataset to filter common variants. We evaluated this workflow using 12 family trios from the Initiatives for Rare and Undiagnosed Diseases (IRUD) project. The workflow successfully prioritized candidate SVs by narrowing down tens of thousands of loci to less than approximately 20 with X-linked homozygous and de novo models for manual inspection. Notably, we identified a pathogenic AluY element insertion in the GPC3 gene in a patient with Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome. This variant had been missed by previous short-read whole-exome sequencing but was clearly prioritized by our LRS workflow. Our workflow effectively prioritizes pathogenic SVs from LRS data, demonstrating the clinical utility of LRS for diagnosing rare diseases involving complex SVs without prior knowledge of candidate genes or loci.
O12-01: Background: Marfan-related disorders are one of the congenital diseases which is known to elevate the risk of aortic dissection during the perinatal period. This study aimed to investigate the incidence of aortic dissection during the perinatal period in women with Marfan-related disorders by using a nationwide administrative claims database. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data extracted from the Japanese Diagnosis Procedure Combination database. Women diagnosed with Marfan-related disorders who delivered between 2010 and 2023 were included in the study. Results: We identified a total of 226 deliveries by 175 women with Marfan-related disorders. Cesarean section accounted for 69.0% of deliveries. Among all deliveries, 15.0% of patients received beta-blockers from admission until postpartum day 2. The prevalence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy was high among patients who experienced aortic dissection. During pregnancy, 1.8% of cases (4/226) experienced aortic dissection and required aortic surgery. In the postpartum period, 2.7% of cases (6/226) experienced aortic dissection during postpartum hospitalization. Within 1 year after delivery, 2.7% of cases (6/226) were re-hospitalized for aortic dissection. Conclusions: Women with Marfan-related disorders were at a high risk of aortic dissection even in the postpartum period. The prevalence of cesarean delivery was higher than that in the overall population in Japan. Beta-blockers may be underused to prevent aortic dissection in women with Marfan-related disorders.
O12-02: Genome-wide non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) can detect chromosomal abnormalities beyond common trisomies, including rare autosomal trisomies (RATs) and sex chromosome aneuploidies (SCAs). However, the clinical significance of these findings remains unclear because they are not routinely disclosed in Japan. We retrospectively evaluated the association between RATs/SCAs and perinatal outcomes in 30,373 pregnancies with known delivery outcomes among 46,082 women who underwent NIPT between 2015 and 2021. RATs and SCAs were identified through cfDNA-based NIPT data reanalysis, and cases were classified into RAT, SCA, and normal groups. Maternal characteristics and perinatal outcomes, including miscarriage or stillbirth, fetal growth restriction, and fetal abnormalities, were compared among groups. RATs were detected in 187 cases (0.62%) and SCAs in 117 (0.39%). Compared with the normal group, both RAT and SCA groups showed significantly higher rates of miscarriage or stillbirth (RAT: 3.7% vs 0.7%; SCA: 7.7% vs 0.7%) and fetal abnormalities (RAT: 13.9% vs 4.7%; SCA: 7.8% vs 4.7%) (all P values were less than 0.001). Overall adverse outcomes occurred in 13.9% of RAT cases and 18.8% of SCA cases, exceeding those in the normal group, although more than 80% of pregnancies showed favorable outcomes. Because NIPT reflects placental cfDNA, these findings may support careful prenatal and perinatal assessment in selected cases and may provide clinically relevant information for perinatal risk assessment in current Japanese practice.
O12-03: Background: Turner syndrome (TS) features haploinsufficiency of SHOX (short stature) and ovarian-function genes (BMP15, DIAPH2), causing premature ovarian insufficiency. Mosaic TS may confer better live-birth rates via oocyte donation than non-mosaic 45,X. A 2024 meta-analysis reported HDP in 8-14% of TS pregnancies, though karyotype-specific risk differences remain unclear. Pregnancy eligibility depends on aortic pathology severity. Methods: Four TS patients (five pregnancies, six deliveries) achieving live births via oocyte donation at St. Mother Hospital were reviewed. Karyotypes were confirmed by G-band analysis. All underwent frozen-thawed blastocyst transfer with hormone replacement. Informed consent was obtained. Results: Karyotypes: 45,X (case 1), mos 45,X/46,X,i(X) (q10)/47,X,i(X)(q10)x2 (case 2), mos 46,X,del(X)(p11.4)/ 46,X,idic(X)(p11.4) (case 3), mos 46,X,i(X)(q10)/45,X (case 4). Pregnancy was achieved within 1-2 transfers. Case 1 (45,X) developed HDP at 16 weeks, progressing to superimposed preeclampsia at 35 weeks; emergency cesarean at 37 weeks (2,030 g, Apgar 7/9). Mosaic cases were uncomplicated. Case 3 delivered vaginally twice at 40 weeks (148 cm). No neonatal anomalies were detected. Conclusions: When cardiovascular evaluation is reassuring, oocyte donation enables live birth even in TS with aortic-risk gene haploinsufficiency (e.g., TIMP1). Early diagnosis and timely Kaufmann therapy are critical for uterine development and favorable perinatal outcomes.
O12-04: Case: A 43-year-old woman, gravida 3, visited our clinic at 37 for primary infertility. After unsuccessful intrauterine insemination, she began IVF at age 38. She underwent nine oocyte retrievals and seven embryo transfers, with two miscarriages. In January 2025, ICSI and transfer of two frozen embryos resulted in a singleton pregnancy. Because of advanced maternal age and recurrent miscarriage, transabdominal chorionic villus sampling was performed under local anesthesia at 12 weeks 0 days. Results: NGS detected a 21q22.3 deletion. SNP microarray confirmed 21q22.3(45,044,960-46,673,449)x1. The same deletion was found in the mother. According to ACMG/ ClinGen criteria, it was classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) and clinically interpreted as a normal variant. The 1.6-Mb deleted region contained four genes/regions related to haploinsufficiency and phenotypic abnormalities: DIP2A, LSS, 21q22.3 population region, and FTCD. None had a haploinsufficiency score of 3, indicating pathogenicity by deletion alone. DIP2A showed little evidence for haploinsufficiency, and the other three were judged normal variants. FTCD haploinsufficiency does not cause disease, but if the remaining allele carries a pathogenic variant, glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency (OMIM 229100) may rarely occur. Conclusion: Although prenatal diagnosis for advanced maternal age usually relies on chromosomal testing, NGS detected a deletion that conventional analysis could miss. Detailed evaluation enabled accurate clinical interpretation and assessment of possible future genetic risks.
O12-05: Introduction The significance of mildly increased nuchal translucency (NT) below 3.5 mm remains controversial in prenatal genetic counseling. We report a prenatal case initially presenting with mildly increased NT, followed by cystic hygroma and diagnosis of 5p abnormality. Case Presentation A 27-year-old nulliparous woman underwent first-trimester combined screening at 12 weeks. Crown-rump length was 65.6 mm and NT measured 2.8 mm, above the 95th percentile. Nasal bone was present. Tricuspid regurgitation, abnormal ductus venosus flow, and structural abnormalities were not observed. The estimated risk for trisomy 21 was 1/676, higher than the background risk; however, no additional genetic testing was requested after counseling. Ultrasonography at 16 weeks revealed septated cystic hygroma. No hydrops or structural abnormalities were observed. Amniocentesis was performed. G-banding and FISH demonstrated 46,XX,add(5)(p15.1). Chromosomal microarray was not requested. The abnormality was considered to involve chromosome 5p deletion with duplication of unknown origin. After information sharing, the couple opted for pregnancy termination. Because the couple hoped for future pregnancy, parental karyotyping was subsequently performed and showed normal results, suggesting a likely de novo abnormality. Discussion This case suggests that chromosomal abnormalities beyond common trisomies may occur even in fetuses with mildly increased NT. Individualized genetic counseling, information on additional testing, and follow-up ultrasound evaluation should therefore be considered in such cases.
O12-06: Noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is a screening test for fetal chromosomal trisomies using cell-free DNA in maternal plasma. Because NIPT uses next-generation sequencing, it can also provide maternal genetic information. Although most copy number variations (CNVs) are benign, some have been associated with pathological phenotypes, and population-specific CNV profiles have attracted increasing attention. However, most large-scale CNV studies have been conducted in Western populations, and data from Japanese cohorts remain scarce. In this study, we conducted the first multicenter, large-scale cohort analysis of maternal CNVs detected by NIPT in Japanese women. A total of 46,082 participants were analyzed to establish a reliable detection threshold and to evaluate the clinical significance of maternal CNVs. Detected CNVs were validated using array CGH, and ROC curve analysis identified 0.8 Mb as the minimum threshold achieving 100% specificity. Using this criterion, maternal CNVs were identified in 2,907 cases (6.3%), most frequently as an 8p23.2 duplication. Comparison with public genomic databases, including ToMMo and gnomAD, showed that all CNVs detected in this study had been previously reported, with particularly high concordance with ToMMo. Several rare CNVs were also identified. These findings indicate that NIPT can reliably detect maternal CNVs of 0.8 Mb or larger. The presence of these CNVs in ongoing pregnancies also suggests that they are unlikely to exert a major adverse effect on fertility or very early pregnancy loss.
O13-01: Background: Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) for hematologic malignancies can identify potential germline pathogenic variants (PGPVs) as secondary findings. However, interpretation is often complicated by tumor-derived variants, clonal hematopoiesis, and mosaicism. At our institution, CGP is performed with the Division of Clinical Genetics, and certified genetic counselors provide GC. Real-world data on PGPV interpretation and management remain limited. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 23 patients who underwent CGP between June 2025 and April 2026. Patients with PGPVs were evaluated for GC, confirmatory testing, and subsequent management. Results: PGPVs were identified in 4 of 23 patients (17%), involving CHEK2, DDX41, CDKN2A, and BRCA1. All four received GC. Confirmatory testing was performed in three cases: CHEK2 and DDX41 were confirmed as germline variants, whereas CDKN2A remained indeterminate due to suspected mosaicism. Testing was not performed in the BRCA1 case because of patient preference. No relatives underwent cascade testing. Management varied according to confirmatory test results, variant interpretation, and patient preferences. Conclusions: In this single-institution analysis, PGPVs were detected in 17% of patients undergoing CGP for hematologic malignancies. Variant interpretation was occasionally complicated by suspected mosaicism, and cascade testing was not implemented despite a structured GC program. Further studies are needed to establish clearer criteria for confirmatory testing and to identify factors influencing cascade testing.
O13-02: Background: Paired tumor-normal CGP testing with GenMineTOP enables direct identification of germline pathogenic variants (GPVs). We characterized GPVs across solid tumors, focusing on non- BRCA1/2 GPVs and challenges in low variant allele frequency (VAF) findings. Methods: We analyzed 8,109 solid tumor patients in C-CAT who underwent GenMineTOP testing (August 2023 to March 2026). Pathogenic/likely pathogenic GPVs were summarized by cancer type/ gene. HBOC-related cancers were breast, ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancers. Results: GPVs were detected in 410/8,109 patients (5.1%; 424 variants). Frequent genes were BRCA2 (n=83), BRCA1 (n=53), TP53 (n=46), ATM (n=31), NF1 (n=30), RAD51D (n=29), and PALB2 (n=22). Non-BRCA1/2 GPVs comprised 67.9% of all GPVs (288/424) and 33.6% of GPVs detected in HBOC-related cancers (38/113). The proportion of BRCA1/2 among GPVs in HBOC-related cancers differed significantly: 78.9% (breast), 66.7% (ovarian), 100% (prostate), 51.4% (pancreatic) (Fisher's exact test, p=0.0199). In pancreatic cancer, PALB2 (n=6), TP53 (n=4), and ATM (n=3) were prominent. TP53 was the most common GPV in brain tumors (14/61) and soft tissue sarcomas (13/59). Across all cancers, low-VAF findings were observed in TP53 (n=9), NF1 (n=2), and CHEK2 (n=1), with VAF 0.169-0.299. Conclusions: Among GPVs detected by GenMineTOP, 67.9% were non-BRCA1/2, supporting clinical systems for managing GPVs beyond BRCA1/2. BRCA1/2 proportions varied significantly across HBOC-related cancers. Low-VAF findings require careful interpretation for mosaicism or clonal hematopoietic changes
O13-03: Background: Genomic profiling for hematologic malignancies can identify variants suspicious for germline predisposition in addition to clinically relevant somatic alterations. These findings may affect family counseling, confirmatory testing, and related donor selection for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. However, the clinical workflow linking Expert Panel (EP) review to clinical genetics assessment and genetic counselling remains poorly characterized. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients discussed at the institutional hematologic malignancy EP after HemeSightR testing at Kyushu University Hospital and affiliated centers between June 2025 and March 2026. Patients requiring clinical genetics collaboration because of suspected germline findings were identified. Results: Among 121 patients, median age was 61 years (range, 9-85), and 61% were male. Nine patients (7.4%) required clinical genetics involvement for disclosure and post-test management. Suspected genes included TP53 (n=3), BRCA1/2 (n=3), DDX41 (n=2), and ATM (n=1). Relevant family history was identified in six patients. Two patients required additional multidisciplinary discussion regarding suitability of related hematopoietic stem cell donors. Conclusions: EP review served as an important pathway linking patients with suspected germline findings to clinical genetics care. Integration of clinical genetics into hematologic malignancy genomic practice may improve management of suspected germline findings, particularly in transplantation settings where donor selection can be affected.
O13-04: Background: Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) has been reimbursed in Japan since 2019, but its clinical use is limited by interpretive complexity and the burden on expert panels (EPs). Scalable decision-support systems are required. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed CGP data from Kyoto University Hospital between 2019 and 2022 (FoundationOne CDx and OncoGuide TMNCC OncoPanel). Our originally-developed structured EP rules were integrated into the Chrovis platform (Xcoo, Inc., Tokyo), which automatically matched alterations to therapeutic recommendations using curated databases and YAML (a human-readable format)-based rules. EP interpretations served as the reference, and concordance was assessed by two specialists, with discrepancies resolved using validated evidence. Actionable variants were defined as Evidence Levels A to D under JSMO/JSCO/JCA criteria. Results: Of 356 patients, 305 were eligible after excluding trial referrals and VUS. Concordance was achieved in 271 cases (88.9%), including 67 with actionable findings (82 genes), of which 33 (10.8%; 38 genes) were Evidence Level A; 204 had no actionable annotations. Overall, 237/305 (77.7%) were amenable to streamlined EP review. Discordances occurred in 34 cases (11.1%): 26 (8.5%) from pending EP rule updates, and 8 (2.6%) were attributable to annotation-related inconsistencies. Conclusion: Auto-annotation using YAML-based rules showed high concordance with EP interpretations, indicating that it can streamline CGP interpretation for individual physicians and supporting its feasibility as a decision-support tool.
O13-05: Background: Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) is increasingly important in prostate cancer, particularly for identifying BRCA1/2 mutations to guide PARP inhibitor therapy. However, CGP test failure due to poor DNA quality of FFPE specimens remains a critical issue. This study aimed to characterize DNA quality impairment in prostate cancer across multiple CGP platforms. Methods: Cases submitted to NCC Oncopanel (NCC) or GenMineTOP (TOP) between August 2023 and April 2025 were analyzed. Failure rates were assessed by DNA quantity and delta-delta Cq-based DNA quality metrics. Results: A total of 2,716 NCC and 4,700 TOP cases were included. DNA quantity-related failure rates in prostate cancer were low (NCC: 2.0%; TOP: 3.5%). In contrast, delta-delta Cq-based failure rates were markedly elevated and the highest among all cancer types on both platforms (NCC: 15.3%; TOP: 17.2%). Conclusions: CGP failure in prostate cancer is predominantly driven by DNA degradation rather than insufficient tumor quantity, consistent across both platforms. This likely reflects tissue-intrinsic characteristics of prostate cancer. Optimizing pre-analytical procedures and considering liquid biopsy are essential strategies. Further analysis incorporating FoundationOne CDx data will be reported in future work.
O13-06: Background: Low-variant allele fraction (VAF) clinically significant variants in blood-based hereditary cancer testing may suggest constitutional mosaicism, but may reflectclonal hematopoiesis, blood-restricted events, tumor contamination, or artifacts. Accurate classification is key for surveillance, counseling, and testing of relatives. Methods: We reviewed a case series of patients with suspected hereditary cancermosaicism involving TP53, CHEK2, NF1, and ATM. Variant allele fraction, age,phenotype, treatment exposure, hematologic findings, clonal hematopoiesis relevance,and available tissue results were assessed. Results: Constitutional mosaicism was supported by non-hematopoietic tissue positivityand gene-consistent phenotypes. TP53 mosaicism was favored in young patients withLi-Fraumeni syndrome-spectrum tumors and non-blood positivity. One CHEK2 caseshowed low-level detection in multiple non-blood tissues, consistent with constitutionalmosaicism and possible blood-clone expansion. In contrast, blood-only variants in olderor treated patients, especially with cytopenia or no confirmatory tissue results, favoredclonal hematopoiesis/blood-restricted events. Conclusions: Low-VAF blood variants require interpretation beyond allele fraction. Integrating tissue distribution, phenotype, treatment exposure, hematologic findings,and clonal hematopoiesis relevance, together with multi-tissue validation, helpsdistinguish constitutional mosaicism from acquired blood-restricted events and guideshereditary cancer management.
O14-01: Recent proteomic studies have focused on gout flares or symptomatic hyperuricemia, with limited investigation of circulating proteomic profiles in relation to serum urate (SU) level as a continuous trait. This study examined associations between SU level and serum proteomic profiles. We enrolled 176 Japanese individuals aged >=50 years from participants of the Kita-Nagoya Genomic Epidemiology (KING) Study and measured serum protein using Olink Explore 3072. Associations were analyzed using linear regression adjusted for age, sex, renal function and insulin resistance, with a false discovery rate of 5%. Tissue-specific and gene set enrichment analyses were performed. Among 2886 proteins, 63 were significantly associated with SU; uromodulin (UMOD) showed the strongest association (padj=2.21×10-5). These proteins were enriched in the liver, kidney and duodenum. We further examined the dysfunctional ABCG2 single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) p.Q141K. In minor allele carriers (n=91), 11 SU-associated proteins were identified, whereas none were detected in wild-type homozygotes (n=85). Gene set enrichment analysis indicated xenobiotic metabolism in wild-types and additional inflammation- and disease-related pathways in carriers. We confirmed UMOD SNP rs77924615 showed a strong association with serum UMOD levels (p<5×10-8), but no significant association with SU level was observed. This study identifies a proteomic signature of SU level and suggests that SU-associated proteomic profiles differ by ABCG2 genotypes, highlighting genetic contributions to SU-related pathophysiology.
O14-02: Despite the large-scale genomic cohort studies that identified many novel genetic variants associated with the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), the direct biological relevance of these variants remains unresolved. We have explored LOAD-risk genetic factors in Japanese patients and identified a rare functional SHARPIN variant, rs572750141 (p.Gly186Arg), that is associated with LOAD. Recent large-scale Caucasian GWAS meta-analyses have identified additional common SHARPIN variants associated with LOAD, suggesting SHARPIN's significant role in LOAD pathogenesis. To elucidate the role of SHARPIN variants in disease pathogenesis, we performed functional analyses using knock-in cells and mice generated through genome editing using CRISPR/Cas9. We performed the knock-in of the targeted SNV into cultured cells and obtained SHARPIN G186R homozygous cells by single-cell cloning. Using these knock-in cell lines, we found a suppressed NF-κB pathway and increased amyloid-β secretion into the culture medium. Then, we introduced the Sharpin G183R, which is equivalent to the human SHARPIN G186R, into mice and conducted behavioral analyses that revealed increased persistent behavior and anxiety toward stimuli. Furthermore, we prepared primary microglia from the knock-in mice and performed RNA-Seq analysis. We are now conducting comprehensive analyses of gene expression, pathways, and networks. The differential expression analysis has identified genes with altered expression in knock-in microglia. Further investigation may elucidate the mechanism underlying the onset of LOAD.
O14-03: Narcolepsy type 2 (NT2) is a sleep disorder characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness without cataplexy, a symptom of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1). Almost all NT1 patients carry HLA-DQB1*06:02. Although the positivity of DQB1*06:02 is higher in NT2 (30-50%) than in the general population, it remains considerably lower than in NT1. Previous studies suggest that NT2 comprises heterogeneous subgroups based on DQB1*06:02 status. However, whether NT2 shares a polygenic background with NT1, independent of HLA status, remains unclear. We performed polygenic risk score analyses (PRS) using data from a genome-wide association study of NT1 (5,339 cases and 20,518 controls). Target datasets included 275 NT2 patients, 228 idiopathic hypersomnia (IH) patients, and 1,509 controls. SNPs within the HLA region were excluded to evaluate non-HLA polygenic effects. NT1-derived PRS showed a significant association with NT2 (P = 2.0×10-11). This association remained significant in both DQB1*06:02-positive (P = 2.5×10-7) and -negative NT2 (P = 7.5×10-7) subgroups, indicating that NT2 shares a polygenic background with NT1 independent of HLA status. In contrast, only modest associations were observed between NT1-derived PRS and IH (P = 6.9×10-3). The number of sleep onset REM periods (SOREMPs) in IH patients was associated with higher NT1-derived PRS (P = 3.7×10-4). These findings support genetic continuity between NT1 and NT2 beyond the well-established HLA effect and suggest that non- HLA polygenic factors contribute to susceptibility to NT2, including in DQB1*06:02-negative individuals.
O14-04: We previously reported that the HBV basal core promoter mutations A1762T/G1764A markedly increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in patients homozygous for HLA-DPB1*05:01 (OR=8.8), whereas HBV mutation alone has been associated with a lower risk (OR=4.1). These findings highlight the importance of monitoring HBV mutation emergence. We aimed to estimate HBV mutation rates using longitudinal serum samples and survival analysis. Serum samples were collected from chronic HBV patients in Japan. HBV mutation status was determined by sequencing serial serum samples. Assuming irreversible mutations and an exponential distribution of waiting time to mutation, mutation rates were estimated using maximum likelihood methods with censored observations. As of January 2025, 881 cases had been collected, and 406 had undergone mutation analysis. HBV mutations were detected in 140 cases, while 73 remained wild type throughout follow-up. Preliminary analysis of 17 patients with wild-type HBV at baseline estimated the mutation rate of A1762T/G1764A to be 8.2×10^-4 per week (approximately 4.2% per year). The exponential model was consistent with Kaplan-Meier estimates, and simulations suggested that >100 cases would provide stable estimates. No reversion from mutant to wild type or emergence of new mutations during nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy was observed. These findings demonstrate that survival analysis of longitudinal serum samples enables estimation of HBV mutation rates and may contribute to prediction of HBV-related hepatocarcinogenesis.
O14-05: Hereditary α-tryptasemia is an autosomal dominant trait defined by an increase in the copy number of the TPSAB1 gene coding for α or β tryptase. Several studies have demonstrated that an increase in the copy number of α tryptase-coding sequences within the TPSAB1 gene significantly elevates basal serum tryptase levels and raises the prevalence of severe anaphylaxis. Despite these findings in white populations, the relationship between TPSAB1 region CNVs and the anaphylaxis and food allergies in other racial groups, including Asians, remains under-investigated. In this study, we analyzed the TPSAB1 locus in Japanese pediatric samples and examined its association with food allergy and anaphylaxis. The considerable sequence homology between TPSAB1 and TPSB2, which exceeds 97%, makes it difficult to use conventional single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array-based genotyping techniques. Thus, we used a stepwise genotyping strategy combining long-range PCR, deletion-specific PCR, direct sequencing, quantitative PCR, and droplet digital PCR in a subset of samples to characterize structural variation within the region. The results showed that in Japanese population, increased α-tryptase allele count was rare, whereas the TPSAB1 deletion allele was frequently observed. Furthermore, α-tryptase, β-tryptase, and deletion allele distributions were not associated with food allergy or anaphylaxis. Our findings highlight the importance of population-specific assessment of structurally complex immune-related loci.
O14-06: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory disease of the central nervous system characterized by demyelination disseminated in space and time. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in European populations have identified over 200 MS susceptibility loci, but no GWAS has been conducted in East Asian populations. Moreover, recent advancements in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics technologies hold considerable promise for interpreting GWAS findings in MS, which is characterized by spatial heterogeneity, but have not been fully leveraged for this purpose. Here, we performed the first Japanese MS GWAS using 688 cases and 205,199 controls and identified an East Asian-specific risk variant in 11q24. Furthermore, through cross-population GWAS meta-analyses using a total of 29,374 cases and 1,843,563 controls from four ancestral populations, we identified 22 novel loci. To detect cell types associated with MS susceptibility, we integrated our MS GWAS and sc/snRNA-seq datasets. In PBMC scRNA-seq data, MS genetic risk was enriched in CD4+ T cells. In snRNA-seq data from MS subcortical lesions, T cells, myeloid cells, endothelial cells, and B cells showed significant enrichment. Furthermore, we integrated our MS GWAS with spatial transcriptomics of MS subcortical lesions. MS genetic risk was enriched in the "vascular infiltrating" and "lesion rim" regions, specifically in active lesions. Our study underscores the value of investigating spatio-cellular features of disease genetics across diverse populations and omics modalities.
O15-01: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA) is an adult-onset, X-linked neuromuscular disorder caused by CAG repeat expansion in the androgen receptor (AR). While S-nitrosylation (SNO), a redox-dependent post-translational modification of cysteine thiols, is implicated in aging, cancer, and neurodegeneration, its role in SBMA remains unknown. Here, we identify SNO as a key regulator of AR function by modulating liquid liquid phase separation (LLPS). We focused on Cys406 in the activation function-1, a low-complexity intrinsically disordered region critical for LLPS, and generated a cysteine-to-serine substitution (C406S) in both wild-type AR and polyglutamine-expanded AR (polyQ-AR), abolishing SNO at this site. Confocal imaging revealed that C406S markedly enlarged nuclear AR condensates. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching demonstrated reduced molecular dynamics in C406S mutants, indicating a shift toward more static condensates, with greater effects in polyQ-AR. Functionally, C406S impaired androgen-dependent transcriptional activity, resulting in decreased expression of the AR target genes TMPRSS2 and ERG and reduced MED1 recruitment to AR condensates. Our findings demonstrate that SNO at Cys406 regulates the material properties of AR condensates and transcriptional output, revealing a redox-dependent mechanism linking LLPS dysregulation to SBMA pathogenesis, and suggest that nitrosative stress may contribute to the transcriptional dysfunction observed in this disease.
O15-02: [Introduction] Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by autonomic failure, cerebellar ataxia, and parkinsonism. Although several MSA-associated genetic factors have been reported, the molecular pathogenesis of MSA remains incompletely understood. [Methods] Whole-genome sequencing was performed for a patient with familial MSA. The AGG repeat expansion in BIN1 was screened for 224 patients with clinically diagnosed MSA, 67 patients with pathologically confirmed MSA, and control groups including 574 blood samples and 65 brain samples from neurologically healthy individuals. [Results] Long-read sequencing identified an AGG repeat expansion in the first intron of BIN1 in the proband. Patients with MSA carried a higher frequency of repeat expansions exceeding 80 repeats in the pathological MSA group compared to the brain control group (frequency: 13.4% vs. 0%; odds ratio: infinity; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.1 to infinity; P = 0.003) and in the clinical multiple system atrophy group compared to the blood control group (frequency: 4.5% vs 2.4%; odds ratio: 1.87; 95% CI, 0.8 to 4.5; P = 0.16). Neuropathological analysis revealed BIN1-positive glial cytoplasmic inclusions more frequently in the brains of patients with repeat expansions. In immunoblot analysis, insoluble BIN1 was increased in the brains of multiple system atrophy, irrespective of repeat status. [Discussions] Our findings indicate that the AGG repeat expansion in BIN1 and BIN1 protein aggregation play an important role in the pathogenesis of multiple system atrophy.
O15-03: Amyloid-β protein (Aβ), the primary component of neuritic plaques in late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), is considered a key molecular trigger underlying its pathogenesis and progression. However, the Aβ accumulation rate varies substantially among individuals with LOAD, suggesting that individual genetic background may contribute to this variability. In this study, we aimed to identify genetic variants associated with the Aβ accumulation rate using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data. A total of 139 cognitively normal individuals aged ≥60 (mean age 73.6±5.8 years, 52 females, mean follow-up year 3.1±2.8 years, baseline Centiloid value 15.3±23.1) were included. The Aβ accumulation rate was defined as the annual change in Centiloid values derived from longitudinal Aβ-PET scans. WGS analysis identified common variants and rare variants. Genome-wide association studies for common variants were performed using the Aβ accumulation rate as the dependent variable. Three genome-wide significant and eleven suggestive association signals were identified and further evaluated in an independent validation cohort of 20 participants. As a result, two variants, rs200006811 near AGAP6 and rs142619754 near HAO1, reached genome-wide significance. For rare variants, gene-based association analyses identified eight candidate genes comprising 17 rare variants. Among these, rs61754856 on ADAMTSL3 reached genome-wide significance in replication analysis. These findings may contribute to the development of early-stage prediction models for LOAD and support personalized prevention strategies.
O15-04: Purpose: GABAA receptor (GABR) mutations are known to cause a variety of epilepsy syndromes. GABR consists of five subunits (SUs) α, β, and γ, that assemble to form a central anion channel. Each SU is a four-transmembrane protein with a common structure in which the second transmembrane domain (M2) faces the center. We will examine the relationship between molecular information on GABR subunit gene mutations in epilepsy cases and epilepsy diagnosis. Methods: We selected 12 cases diagnosed with SU gene mutations in GABR from patients treated at our center and estimated the functional impact (LOF, GOF) using databases such as Clin Var. Results: The 12 cases consisted of 2 cases with GABRA1 mutations, 1 case with a GABRB2 mutation, 4 cases from 3 families with GABRB3 mutations, and 5 cases from 3 families with GABRG2 mutations. Five of the eight amino acid substitution mutations were located in the M2 region. The three extracellular domain mutations were presumed to be LOF. Three of the five M2 mutations were presumed to be LOF, one was a mixed LOF+GOF type, and one was presumed to be GOF. Two of the three LOF extracellular domain mutations followed a course of generalized epilepsy. Three of the five M2 mutations were LOF and followed a mild course with GEFS+. The one case presumed to be a GOF mutation in the M2 region followed the course of the most severe type of EIMFS. Discussion: It is possible that only mutations in the M2 region are GOF, and these may contribute to the onset of EIMFS, a severe form of early-infancy epilepsy, related with increased GABR excitability.
O15-05: Non-coding CGG repeat expansions in NOTCH2NLC cause neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease and have also been associated with a broad spectrum of neurological phenotypes including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. NOTCH2NLC-associated disorders show a distinct East Asian predominance, yet previous studies have not identified a single shared founder haplotype among expanded alleles. We sought to clarify the population-genetic background underlying this regional enrichment. To resolve haplotypes flanking the repeat locus, we analyzed long-read whole-genome sequencing data from eight NOTCH2NLC repeat expansion carriers. In parallel, publicly available whole-genome sequence data of 1,011 individuals from diverse populations were analyzed to examine the distribution of repeat-size classes and linked variants among populations. We found no evidence of a single extended founder haplotype flanking expanded NOTCH2NLC alleles, consistent with previous studies. Instead, large-normal alleles, defined as 35-43 repeat units, were observed exclusively in East Asian individuals. We further identified five single-nucleotide variants on chromosome 1 (149365556G>A, 149383714C>T, 149414210C>T, 149426030G>C, and 149428432A>G) linked to the expanded alleles in affected individuals and to large-normal alleles in the East Asian population. The frequency of these variants increased with repeat size in East Asians, but not in Europeans. Our findings suggest that susceptibility to NOTCH2NLC CGG repeat expansion arises from a population-specific genetic background rather than from a single founder allele.
O15-06: Parkinson disease (PD) is a complex genetic disorder with multiple variants, yet conventional genome-wide approaches can explain its heritability insufficiently. In neurodegenerative diseases, the importance of tandem repeat expansions and structural variants has been demonstrated in several disorders, exemplified by the GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9orf72 in ALS. In PD, tandem repeat expansions such as the ATXN2 CAG repeat and structural variants in SNCA have been recognized; however, the contribution of tandem repeat expansions and structural variants to PD pathogenesis has not been systematically investigated. Recent advances in long-read sequencing have expanded the spectrum of analyzable genetic variation, including tandem repeat expansions and structural variants. Noncoding CGG repeat expansions in oculopharyngodistal myopathy (OPDM)-related genes LRP12, GIPC1, and NOTCH2NLC have been implicated in some disorders, but the role of these expansions in PD has been poorly explored. In this study, we screened 1,011 Japanese patients with PD using repeat-primed PCR and GC-rich PCR targeting these three genes and identified 23 individuals suspected of harboring intermediate or larger repeat expansions. Long-read sequencing provided a powerful approach for resolving the detailed structures of these repeat expansions and evaluating their pathogenic relevance to PD. These findings highlight the contribution of LRP12 and NOTCH2NLC repeat expansions to the genetic architecture of PD and suggest the utility of long-read sequencing for molecular stratification and precision medicine.
O16-01: Background: Universal tumor testing for mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency is recommended for Lynch syndrome (LS) detection. However, prospective data in young Asian patients remain limited, and the implications of specific MMR loss patterns are not fully defined. Methods: This prospective observational study included patients aged under 50 years with endometrial cancer (EC) at a single Japanese institution (2021-2024). Immunohistochemistry for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 was performed. Clinicopathologic features, MMR loss patterns, and germline testing results were analyzed. Results: Among 111 patients, 26 (23.4%) exhibited dMMR. Loss patterns included MLH1/PMS2 (n=12), MSH2/MSH6 (n=8), and isolated MSH6 loss (n=6). Germline testing was performed in 12 patients, identifying LS in 9 (75%). Detection rates appeared to vary across patterns: MSH2/MSH6 loss (4/4), isolated MSH6 loss (2/3), and MLH1/PMS2 loss (3/5). dMMR tumors were more likely to present with advanced stage and higher-grade histology. MLH1/PMS2 loss accounted for nearly half of dMMR cases. Conclusions: In young Japanese patients with EC, dMMR frequency was comparable to that in unselected populations. Germline testing yield appeared to differ across MMR loss patterns, with high detection rates in MSH2/MSH6 loss and non-negligible rates in MLH1/PMS2 loss. LS was identified across patterns, including MLH1/PMS2 loss. In young patients, such cases should not be assumed to represent sporadic methylation, supporting the importance of MMR IHC-guided genetic evaluation.
O16-02: Purpose: Sustainable surveillance for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC) remains an important issue in genetic medicine. This study aimed to clarify challenges in HBOC surveillance in Japan. Methods: 1) A web-based questionnaire survey was conducted among participants of a public seminar held at Keio University Hospital in 2024, including HBOC carriers, healthcare professionals, and the general public. The survey assessed surveillance practices, financial burden, and barriers to sustainable surveillance. 2) Based on the survey findings, our institution introduced a surveillance program for unaffected HBOC carriers. Results: 1) Responses were obtained from 121 of 274 participants. Among 66 HBOC carriers, 57 were affected. Surveillance uptake among affected carriers was 89.5%, although nearly half attended multiple institutions. Across respondent groups, annual out-of-pocket costs below 50,000 yen were considered acceptable. Healthcare professionals identified interfacility collaboration and shortages of genetic medicine specialists as major barriers. 2) Twenty-five unaffected HBOC carriers participated in the surveillance program, accounting for 48 visits. All participants continued surveillance, and two subsequently underwent risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy. Conclusion: Sustainable HBOC surveillance in Japan may require improved care coordination, reduced financial burden, and expansion of the genetic medicine workforce. Structured surveillance programs may support long-term adherence and may also become important in the management of secondary findings.
O16-03: Background: With the increasing use of multigene panel testing (MGPT) and comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP), multi-locus inherited neoplasia allele syndrome (MINAS), characterized by germline pathogenic variants (GPVs) in multiple cancer predisposition genes, is increasingly identified. However, its clinical characteristics remain incompletely characterized. We report nine individuals with MINAS identified at our institution. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of nine individuals with MINAS identified through germline genetic testing at our institution. Results: The identified gene combinations included ATM/SDHA, BRCA1/ATR, BRCA1/BRCA2, BRCA1/BRIP1, BRCA2/ATM, BRCA2/BARD1, BRCA2/BRIP1, MSH2/BRIP1 and MSH6/RAD51D. Among the nine individuals, seven had breast cancer (unilateral, n=4; synchronous bilateral, n=2; metachronous bilateral, n=1), one had endometrial cancer, and one had multiple cutaneous cancers. The median age at initial cancer diagnosis was 49 (range, 28-68). Six were identified by MGPT, two by CGP, and one by BRACAnalysis. Discussion: Eight of the nine individuals may not have been identified as MINAS without MGPT or CGP, highlighting the risk of missing a second GPV through through syndrome-specific genetic testing. Most combinations involved high- and moderate-risk genes, consistent with previous reports. Clinical management of MINAS requires individualized risk assessment based on the penetrance and cancer risks of each involved gene. Although limited by a small sample size, further accumulation of clinical data is warranted.
O16-04: Background/Objective: Endometrial cancer (EC) occurs in 21-57% of women with Lynch syndrome (LS), with less than 1% reportedly developing EC before age 40. However, in Japan, LS cases of EC onset before age 40 have been occasionally observed. This study aimed to clarify the clinical characteristics of LS-related EC and provide foundational data on EC development in Japanese patients with LS. Methods: Among patients diagnosed with LS by genetic testing (GT) at our institution between January 2000 and May 2026, we analyzed EC frequency, age at onset, multiple primary cancers, and gene-specific characteristics. Results: Of 220 patients suspected of LS following EC diagnosis who underwent GT, 138 (62.7%) were confirmed as LS. Among the 237 women with LS, EC frequency by gene was as follows: MLH1: 41/73 (56.2%), MSH2: 80/120 (66.7%), MSH6: 20/35 (57.1%), and PMS2: 1/9 (11.1%) (MSH2 vs. PMS2: p=0.0016). Median age at EC onset was MLH1: 47.0, MSH2: 45.0, and MSH6: 48.5 years (p=0.0313). Among patients with LS who developed cancer, the 1st primary cancer type was EC in MLH1: 43.8%, MSH2: 54.2%, MSH6: 63.0%, and PMS2: 16.6% (p=0.1063). EC onset before age 40 occurred in MLH1: 8.2%, MSH2: 20.0%, MSH6: 8.6%, and PMS2: 11.1% of LS women (p=0.0986). Discussion: In our cohort, especially MSH6 carriers developed EC before age 40, exceeding previously reported rates. Limitations include its single-center design and potential selection bias, as early onset prompted GT. Nonetheless, this finding may serve as informative foundational data for optimizing surveillance timing in Japanese female LS.
O16-05: Background: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS), caused by germline TP53 alterations, often remains undiagnosed due to the lack of public insurance coverage for dedicated genetic testing in Japan. We investigated LFS prevalence using comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP). Methods and Results: Among 912 patients who underwent CGP at our hospital, three were diagnosed with LFS. Case 1: A teenage female with recurrent glioblastoma. CGP identified a germline TP53 pathogenic variant with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of 29%. Despite a low VAF suggesting mosaicism, multi-site testing confirmed a non-mosaic constitutional variant, likely skewed by sequencing artifacts of CGP. Case 2: A female in her 60s with unresectable pancreatic cancer and a history of triple primary malignancies including early-onset sarcoma. A TP53 loss-of-function variant with a VAF of 49% was omitted from the standard CGP report but confirmed via subsequent germline testing. Case 3: A teenage female presented with glioblastoma. Both her mother and a sibling had been diagnosed with LFS at another hospital. CGP was utilized for both therapeutic target screening and definitive genetic confirmation. Conclusion: The LFS prevalence in our cohort was 0.3%. It is markedly higher than the historical estimate of 0.005-0.02%. When interpreting CGP results, clinicians must remain vigilant for low VAFs or variants excluded from standard reporting criteria to avoid overlooking LFS.
O16-06: Background: Standard germline BRCA testing occasionally yields inconclusive results, preventing diagnosis of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC). Cryptic germline alterations such as structural variants, mosaic events, and intronic retrotransposon insertions may escape detection by conventional assays. We evaluated the diagnostic utility of integrated genomic analyses in patients with inconclusive BRCA test results. Methods: Three patients with HBOC-associated malignancies and inconclusive germline BRCA1/2 test results underwent whole-genome sequencing (WGS), Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing, direct RNA sequencing, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Results: Case 1 was a patient with prostate cancer diagnosed at age 67. WGS identified a germline mosaic translocation involving chromosomes 13 and 3, accompanied by a deletion encompassing BRCA2. FISH confirmed mosaic BRCA2 deletion in peripheral blood. Cases 2 and 3 were patients with breast cancer diagnosed at ages 31 and 26 years, respectively. Long-read sequencing identified a 2.7-kb SVA_E retrotransposon insertion within intronic regions of BRCA1 and BRCA2. Direct RNA sequencing demonstrated loss of BRCA1/BRCA2 function at the transcript level. All three patients were ultimately diagnosed with HBOC. Conclusions: Clinically significant pathogenic variants may underlie inconclusive BRCA test results. Integrated genomic approaches combining WGS, long-read sequencing, and RNA sequencing can improve the diagnostic yield of hereditary cancer testing and support appropriate clinical management.
O17-01: Hereditary transthyretion amyloidosis (ATTRv) is characterized by various symptoms including cardiomyopathy, polyneuropathy and other organs disorders. We experienced a case of ATTRv with transthyretin genotype of c.238A>G (p.Thr80Ala). A 65-year-old man was referred to our hospital because of edema of lower extremities and dyspnea on exertion. His mother died of congestive heart failure due to ATTRv with same genotype at the age of 72. His older sister has been followed as cardiomyopathy for 20 years and genetic test lately revealed ATTRv with p.Thr80Ala. Echocardiography showed ejection fraction of 19%. He was diagnosed as severe congestive heart failure of at least NYHA III and admitted. Endomyocardial biopsy using Congo red staining showed the deposition of amyloid fibrils. 99mTc-pyrophosphate scintigraphy showed uptake in heart. He also has noticed hand and foot paresthesia. He was found to be a carrier of the p.Thr80Ala pathological variant. He was diagnosed with ATTRv. He has underwent the treatment of Vutrisiran, an RNA interference therapeutic that reduces TTR production. When six months elapsed after Vutrisiran administration start, echocardiography showed ejection fraction of 38%. In the Irish population, ATTRv with p.Thr80Ala has been recognized as the most common. Meanwhile, in the Japanese population, there is only one case report, that was his mother's report, as far as we investigated. The genotype manifests both cardiac and neurological phenotypes.
O17-02: Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) testing is increasingly essential for cancer care, making the appropriate evaluation of germline variants as secondary findings ever more important. We previously reported "Varporter," a CGP support software (https:// web.sapmed.ac.jp/canmol/varporter.html) that consolidates multi-panel results into Excel, extracts germline variant candidates (PGPVs and GPVs) based on the Secondary Findings disclosure list, and incorporates ACMG classifications from GeneBe, ClinVar pathogenicity, gnomAD/ToMMo allele frequencies, and functional prediction scores via auto-generated database links. Building on this, we developed an AI chatbot integrated with Varporter for assessing germline pathogenicity. Static information is retrieved from a pre-built RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) model. In contrast, frequently updated resources, including ClinVar, gnomAD, guidelines, therapeutic evidence, and clinical trial information, are queried via web search APIs, limiting the AI's role to information synthesis and suppressing hallucinations. This enables AI-assisted ACMG classification referencing gene-specific ClinGen guidelines, with dedicated support for TP53 (ClinGen TP53 guidelines v2.1) and BRCA1/BRCA2 (ClinGen ENIGMA criteria). The chatbot also performs automatic liftover between GRCh37 and GRCh38 and HGVS normalization from free-text input, addressing key technical challenges in multi-panel CGP. This system is expected to improve the quality and efficiency of germline variant assessment in CGP.
O17-03: Kabuki syndrome (KS) is characterized by multiple congenital anomalies and distinctive dysmorphic features caused by loss-of-function variants in KMT2D or KDM6A. We identified a novel de novo RBBP5 variant in a patient with KS-like phenotypes and mild intellectual disability by trio exome sequencing. No pathogenic variants were identified in KMT2D or KDM6A by whole-gene sequencing. Genome-wide DNA methylation analysis of peripheral blood demonstrated an episignature highly similar to that of KS. RBBP5 is a component of the MLL/COMPASS histone methyltransferase complex together with KMT2D and ASH2L, and it directly binds to the SET domain of KMT2D. To evaluate the functional impact of the identified variant on MLL/COMPASS complex formation, co-immunoprecipitation assays were performed using the KMT2D SET domain and ASH2L. The assays demonstrated that the variant selectively impaired binding to the KMT2D SET domain, whereas interaction with ASH2L was preserved. These findings indicate that the novel RBBP5 variant disrupts SET domain binding within the KMT2D/ASH2L/RBBP5 complex. Previously reported RBBP5 variants, including p.T232I and p.E296D, are thought to impair nucleosome binding while preserving the complex's intrinsic catalytic activity. In contrast, the novel RBBP5 variant affects a residue critical for interaction with the KMT2D SET domain. This defect is expected to impair KMT2D-dependent histone methyltransferase function, providing a possible mechanistic explanation for the KS-like phenotype observed in this case.
O17-04: Recently, spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) and lysosomal storage disease were added to newborn screening test (NBS). Until Jan. 31, 2026, totally 33,870 newborn babies were tested in Miyazaki Prefecture. Among them, 10 cases (7 male and 3 female) were positive in screening and verified with genetic testing. Incidence of the Fabry disease was higher than expected (One to 3081case). And, interestingly, 7 cases had same variant (GLA M296I) suggesting founder effect. This variant classified as late onset type, in other words, clinical symptom suspects to appear 20 to 30 years later. Therefore, not only strict follow up of newborn but also investigation of the family member is very important. In this situation, we started clinical trial. In this trial not only pediatricians but cardiologists, nephrologists, neurologists, obstetrician, doctor of emergency center, geneticist and genetic counselor joined the meeting. We shared information of each family in periodical meeting. We found 2cases of grandfather have a renal and heart failure with unknown etiology. Genetic testing verified M296I variant, then, started enzyme replacement therapy. In conclusion, newborn screening test of Fabry disease is effective for identification and treatment of the family member. However, strict follow up of the identified baby and translation from pediatrician to cardiologist, nephrologist and neurologist seems to be essential procedure. In addition, genetic counseling to the mother also important to understanding importance of follow up.
O17-05: Background Chromosomal microdeletions involving Xp11.3 are associated heterogeneous clinical phenotypes depending on the genes included. Haploinsufficiency of KDM6A causes Kabuki syndrome type 2 (KS2), whereas contiguous gene deletions may result in more complex phenotypes. We report a man whose genetic etiology was redefined through re-evaluation of genomic copy number variations (CNVs). Case Presentation The patient was a 22-year-old man with severe intellectual disability, intractable epilepsy, and retinitis pigmentosa. Although an Xp11.3 deletion had been identified by a BAC-based microarray analysis during childhood, detailed molecular characterizations were unavailable. A CGH+SNP-based microarray analysis revealed a 2.4 Mb hemizygous deletion encompassing KDM6A, RP2, and SLC9A7. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with KS2. The retinal phenotype was consistent with RP2-associated retinal degeneration. Previous studies have suggested that male patients with pathogenic KDM6A variants exhibit more severe manifestations than females. Although SLC9A7 has been implicated in X-linked neurodevelopmental disorders, the contribution of SLC9A7 haploinsufficiency remains uncertain. Conclusion This case expands the clinical spectrum of Xp11.3 contiguous gene deletion involving KDM6A and RP2. Genomic re-evaluation established a molecular diagnosis and improved access to medical support programs. These findings highlight the importance of genomic re-evaluation and careful interpretation of contiguous gene effects in chromosomal microdeletion syndromes.
O17-06: Background Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by CTG repeat expansion in the DMPKgene and characterized by anticipation. DM1 may first be suspected during pregnancy based on abnormal blood test findings or fetal ultrasound findings, although pregnant women may have no subjective symptoms or apparent family history. Cases We experienced three cases in which DM1 was first suspected during pregnancy. Common features were pregnancy through in vitro fertilization, elevated maternal serum creatine kinase levels leading to suspicion of DM1, and polyhydramnios. In contrast, reactions to the suspected diagnosis varied among the cases, including difficulty accepting the diagnosis by both partners, limited understanding by the patient and difficulty accepting the diagnosis by the husband, and good acceptance by both partners. Accordingly, the timing and target of genetic testing also varied, including postnatal testing of both mother and neonate, postnatal maternal testing alone, and maternal testing during pregnancy. Discussion Advances in reproductive medicine would increase pregnancies among previously undiagnosed patients with hereditary disorders, and such cases would increase in the future. Although perinatal care requires maternal treatment, fetal evaluation, and management decisions under time constraints, responses to diagnosis acceptance and decision-making differed among the cases.
O18-01: Mucolipidosis (ML) is an ultra-rare lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in GNPTAB or GNPTG, encoding subunits of GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase. There is no established treatment response monitoring biomarker in ML, and we present heparan sulfate (HS) as a candidate biomarker based on a case with ML III α/β, whose clinical condition stabilized and urinary HS levels markedly decreased following unrelated cord blood transplantation (UCBT). The patient presented at age 3 with mitral regurgitation, growth delay, and dysostosis multiplex. Compound heterozygous GNPTAB variants were identified, and she was diagnosed with ML. She underwent UCBT at age 5. Neutrophil engraftment occurred on day 16, with stable donor chimerism (>95%). At 2 years post-UCBT, cardiac and respiratory function remained stable, and joint range of motion improved slightly. Cognitive development was maintained (WISC-V FSIQ: 101; pre-transplant KSPD DQ: 90). Urinary HS as a proportion of total glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) decreased from 46% to 13%, paralleling clinical improvement. Ammer et al. suggested that therapy for ML, through mechanisms such as cross-correction, decreases urinary GAGs. Blood, urine, and CSF HS are established biomarkers in mucopolysaccharidosis. Although several studies have reported elevated blood and urinary HS levels in ML, a reduction in urinary HS following therapies such as UCBT has not been previously described. Our findings suggest that HS may represent a candidate biomarker in ML.
O18-02: Background: Mitochondrial diseases are characterized by impaired energy production and often remain genetically unresolved despite advances in next-generation sequencing. Focusing on non-coding regions, we identified two patients with the same de novo RNU4-2 variant, implicating spliceosome dysfunction in mitochondrial disease. Aim: To investigate the relationship between spliceosomal dysfunction and mitochondrial disease, focusing on the impact of RNU4ATAC variants on mitochondrial-related splicing abnormalities and mitochondrial function. Method: Patient-derived fibroblasts harboring the RNU4-2 variant were analyzed by RNA sequencing to detect aberrant splicing events. Whole genome sequencing re-analysis also identified a patient with compound heterozygous pathogenic/ likely pathogenic variants in RNU4ATAC. Results: RNA sequencing revealed clear aberrant splicing of NDUFV1, a nuclear-encoded component of mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I, in RNU4-2 variant fibroblasts, despite no pathogenic variants in NDUFV1 itself. In addition, we identified a patient with compound heterozygous pathogenic RNU4ATAC variants previously reported in ClinVar. The patient presented with short stature, diabetes mellitus, and intellectual disability. Conclusion: Abnormalities involving RNU4-2 and RNU4ATAC may represent an underrecognized mechanism, which is likely aberrant splicing, contributing to mitochondrial disease. Our findings highlight the importance of reanalyzing non-coding spliceosomal genes in genetically unresolved mitochondrial disease cases.
O18-03: Background: DGUOK-related mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome (MTDPS) is a rare, fatal disorder causing early-onset liver disease. Although an international cohort of 202 patients clarified its natural history, Japanese data remain limited. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed genetically confirmed DGUOK-related cases in the Japanese mitochondrial disease database. Clinical features, hepatic and extrahepatic involvement, liver transplantation, and prognosis were compared with the international cohort. Results: Thirteen Japanese patients were identified. Most presented in the neonatal or infantile period, and 8 of 13 developed severe liver disease, including acute liver failure. This spectrum was consistent with the international cohort, in which neonatal and infantile onset accounted for 55.7% and 32.3% of cases, and hepatocerebral disease was the most common phenotype. Liver disease was the main determinant of morbidity and mortality in both cohorts. Two Japanese patients with neurological manifestations underwent liver transplantation, but both had unfavorable outcomes, suggesting that neurological involvement may worsen post-transplant prognosis. Conclusions: Japanese patients with DGUOK-related disease show a clinical spectrum similar to that reported internationally, dominated by early-onset liver disease. DGUOK deficiency should be considered in neonates and infants with cholestasis, progressive liver dysfunction, or acute liver failure. Early molecular diagnosis and assessment of extrahepatic involvement are essential for prognosis and transplant decisions.
O18-04: Background: Mitochondrial diseases are clinically and genetically heterogeneous. Genetic counseling regarding recurrence risk and reproductive options including prenatal diagnosis (PND) and preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M) requires substantial expertise. We evaluated the clinical and genetic background, and counseling outcomes of families seeking reproductive medicine. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 24 families with mitochondrial disease who underwent PND or PGT-M at our hospital. Results: Among 18 families with nuclear DNA defects, which were generally severe and inherited in an autosomal recessive or X-linked manner, PND (n=14) and PGT-M (n=6) were feasible options depending on clinical severity and familial preference. For 6 families with mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) defects, PND (n=4) was viable when maternal blood and urine were negative for the variant, suggesting a de novo mutation; no variant was identified in fetuses tested by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. In contrast, when mothers carried the same mtDNA variant (n=2), PND was difficult to interpret due to obligatory transmission and limited phenotype predictability, whereas PGT-M remained a potential option for selected variants. Conclusions: Reproductive options for mitochondrial disease differ according to whether the causative defect is located in nuclear DNA or mtDNA and, in mtDNA disease, whether the variant is de novo or maternally inherited. Precise molecular diagnosis and individualized genetic counseling are essential for informed reproductive decision-making.
O18-05: Background: Propionic acidemia (PA) is a severe inherited metabolic disorder caused by pathogenic variants in PCCA or PCCB, resulting in propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC) deficiency. Current treatment is mainly supportive, and novel treatment strategies are needed. In an individual with neonatal-onset PA, we identified a homozygous deep-intronic variant of PCCA causing inclusion of an 84-bp pseudoexon. We evaluated antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated skipping of the 84-bp pseudoexon as a potential treatment strategy for PA. Methods: ASOs targeting the 84-bp pseudoexon were transfected into fibroblasts from the affected individual. We evaluated splicing, transcripts, PCCA protein, and PCC activity. Fibroblasts harboring other mutations were also analyzed. Results: In fibroblasts from the individual, the 84-bp pseudoexon was included in the majority of PCCA transcripts. PCCA protein was undetectable, and PCC activity was markedly reduced to 0.5% of wild-type (WT).
