ASO treatment restored normal splicing to 98.9% of transcripts (p<0.001), increased PCCA protein expression, and improved PCC activity to approximately 300% of WT (p<0.001). In fibroblasts carrying other mutations retaining >1% of WT PCC activity, ASO treatment also increased PCC enzyme activity. Conclusion: ASO-mediated correction of the 84-bp pseudoexon represents a viable molecular therapeutic approach for PA caused by the deep-intronic PCCA variant and may have broader applicability. Further in vivo studies are required to validate the efficacy and generalizability of ASO-mediated pseudoexon skipping.
O18-06: Introduction: Apolipoprotein C-II (apoC-II) is a cofactor of lipoprotein lipase, and apoC-II deficiency, mostly caused by APOC2 coding-region mutations, leads to severe hypertriglyceridemia (HTG). In several atypical cases, mutations in the promoter region or a splice site of APOC2 cause markedly reduced but detectable plasma apoC-II with massive HTG (hereafter referred to as hypoapoC-II). We previously reported a case of hypoapoC-II with severe HTG (Case 1) in which no rare APOC2 coding variant was identified; however, the clinical entity remains controversial as evidence of causality is weak. Methods: Case 1 and an additional case (Case 2) of hypoapoC-II were analyzed by whole genome/exome sequencing, Southern blot hybridization (APOC2 or APOC4 cDNA probes), breakpoint analysis (PCR, subcloning, and direct sequencing), custom-made array CGH around the APOE/APOC4/APOC2 gene cluster, and microarray-based haplotype analysis. Results: Whole genome sequencing of Case 1 revealed a two-fold increase in coverage spanning APOC4 and the noncoding exon of APOC2. Array CGH, Southern blot, and breakpoint analyses confirmed a homozygous tandem duplication. Case 2 harbored the same tandem duplication as Case 1. Although apparently unrelated, Cases 1 and 2 shared a founder haplotype. Conclusions: We found two independent cases of hypoapoC-II harboring the same founder tandem duplication containing APOC4 and a noncoding exon of APOC2, representing a distinct clinical subtype of hyperchylomicronemia with markedly reduced apoC-II.
O19-01: In CGP, EGFR variants in lung cancer are usually interpreted as therapeutic biomarkers, but some may indicate germline pathogenic variants (GPV). We report a 50-year-old man with disseminated lung adenocarcinoma. His father and sister had lung cancer at 65 and 54 years, respectively. Initial OncomineDx testing detected the activating EGFR driver p.G719S, and afatinib provided disease control for 3 years. At progression, repeat OncomineDx testing did not detect resistance-associated EGFR p.T790M. After another 3 years of chemotherapy, liver metastasis developed; FoundationOne CDx on this biopsy newly revealed EGFR c.2327G>A (p.R776H; VAF 0.488), outside OncomineDx coverage, together with p.G719S. Based on VAF and family history, p.R776H was suspected to be germline and confirmed by germline testing. In our 247-case institutional lung cancer series, 60 EGFR variants were detected in 42 cases. Among reported EGFR GPV, p.V843I and p.P848L were not detected, and p.T790M was detected in 7 cases but was not considered suggestive of germline origin based on VAF, co-occurring EGFR variants, and clinical context. EGFR p.R776H was first observed in this case and co-occurred with p.G719S. This case highlights the need to distinguish potential EGFR GPV from co-occurring therapeutic drivers and to link selected patients to germline testing and counseling.
O19-02: Lung cancer is an immunogenic cancer for which immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) work. However, current biomarkers cannot perfectly predict ICI response. Analysis of the tumor microenvironment (TME) is important to predict and improve the outcome. We performed bioinformatic analysis of TCGA data to identify key molecules distinguishing hot from cold TMEs. Chemokines and their receptors whose mRNA levels were strongly associated with CD8A were identified in lung adenocarcinoma (Ad). In particular, CXCL9/10/11 and their receptor CXCR3, which are essential for ICI response, as well as XCL1/2, which recruit cDC1, were highly correlated with CD8A in Ad. EGFR-mutated (EGFRmt) Ad represents a cold TME characterized by exclusion of CD8+ T cells. We demonstrated that CXCL9/10/11 are epigenetically suppressed through induction of HDACs under oncogenic EGFR signaling. We also focused on tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm) that are specialized T cells adapted for long-term residence within tissues. A high frequency of Trm cells, which are considered terminally differentiated precursor exhausted T cells (Tpex), a presumed target of anti-PD-1 Ab, correlates with favorable prognosis in lung cancer. TCGA data revealed that ITGAE (CD103), a marker of Trm cells, and Trm-associated effector molecules including GZMH, GZMA, and GZMB were significantly decreased in EGFRmt Ad. We confirmed a significant reduction of CD103+ cells in EGFRmt Ad tissues. These findings suggest that analysis of public databases can provide important insights into mechanisms underlying impaired antitumor immunity.
O19-03: Multiple primary lung adenocarcinomas are often associated with somatic driver alterations in such as EGFR, HER2 or MET. However, the contribution of germline variants to lung cancer susceptibility remains poorly understood. Here, we report monozygotic twin sisters harboring multiple lung adenocarcinomas in a family with an apparent aggregation of lung cancer. In the proband, three tumors harbored independent EGFR L858R mutations, whereas her co-twin developed distinct tumors carrying MET exon 14 skipping or no detectable driver mutation. Whole-exome sequencing identified a shared heterozygous germline variant in PCLO encoding the presynaptic cytomatrix protein Piccolo. PCLO mutations near the variant detected in this pedigree have been reported in EGFR- or KRAS-mutant lung cancer cell lines PC-9, HCC2279 and DFCI024, suggesting its role in oncogenesis. Our findings indicate that a germline PCLO variant may predispose to multiple lung adenocarcinomas by enhancing susceptibility especially to EGFR/MET-driven tumorigenesis in genetically identical individuals.
O19-04: The risk variability of hereditary cancer remains poorly characterized, limiting personalized clinical management. Given the importance of verifying the impact of epidemiologic factors in carriers of hereditary cancer genes, we assessed their effects on cancer risk and age at diagnosis. We used our previously reported data on 8 hereditary cancer genes (BRCA1, BRCA2, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PTEN, and TP53) across 12 significantly associated cancer types from BioBank Japan. Epidemiologic factors included smoking, alcohol consumption, family history, age at menarche/menopause, and cancer-specific polygenic risk scores. Parallel analyses in noncarriers were conducted as references. Statistical significance was set at q<0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. In 59,503 cases and 38,212 controls, we found that family history of gastric cancer was significantly associated with the same cancer risk in BRCA2 carriers (OR 4.9, q=2.9x10-3), with a descriptively higher OR than in non-carriers (OR 2.2, q=2.9x10-206). Notably, for breast (BRCA1, BRCA2) and ovarian cancer (BRCA2), age at menarche =<12 years was significantly associated with a younger mean age at diagnosis, with differences ranging from 8.1 to 12.5 years, despite having no significant impact on these cancer risks. In summary, our findings suggested that some epidemiologic factors impact disease risk with a different magnitude in carriers compared to non-carriers. Furthermore, they implied the importance of independently evaluating cancer risk and onset age, supporting surveillance and risk-reduction strategies.
O19-05: Biliary tract cancer (BTC) is a highly lethal malignancy with poor prognosis due to challenges in early detection. Both environmental and genetic factors are considered to contribute to its development. To identify genetic variants associated with BTC and its anatomical subsites, we conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) and gene-based analysis in a Japanese population. The GWAS included 529 BTC cases and 4,454 apparently healthy controls. Cases were further classified into four subsites: gallbladder cancer, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and ampullary cancer. GWAS were performed for overall BTC as well as for each subsite separately. Subsequently, gene-based analyses were conducted using MAGMA based on the GWAS summary statistics. Although no single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) reached genome-wide significance, subsite-specific analyses identified X, Y, and Z as statistically significant genes in gallbladder cancer. These genes were located in close proximity to one another. Previous studies in European populations have reported associations between these genes and gallstone disease, a known risk factor for gallbladder cancer. Our findings suggest that this genomic region may contribute to susceptibility to both gallstone disease and gallbladder cancer in the Japanese population. Further validation studies in independent cohorts are warranted.
O19-06: Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes cervical cancers. HPV is epidemiologically classified, but unclassified-risk HPVs exist. This study comprehensively elucidates HPV infection status in cervical cancer using next-generation sequencer analysis. With the approval of the ethics committee and the patient consent, DNA was extracted from cervical cytology specimens from 48 patients with cervical cancer. Following target capture of HPV genomic DNA, next-generation sequencing was performed. Multiple HPVs were detected in all samples and all samples had at least one high-risk HPV. Notably, the infection rate of HPV16 was higher than in previous reports. Hybridization capture detected HPV16 genomic DNA in all samples, while E7-specific PCR detected HPV16 in only 35 of 48 samples(73%). It is possible that conventional HPV testing may have underestimated the HPV16 infection rate. Assuming HPV16 infection is a prerequisite for carcinogenesis, persistent multiple infections with at least one high-risk HPV may play a significant role in cancer progression.
O20-01: Background: Molecular QTL enable functional interpretation of GWAS risk loci for immune-mediated diseases (IMDs). Chromatin accessibility QTL (caQTL) complements expression QTL (eQTL) by providing additional regulatory insights. Methods: Peripheral blood immune cells from 72 healthy individuals were FACS-sorted into 29 cell types. Bulk RNA-seq and ATAC-seq were performed to map eQTL and caQTL. Additionally, 5' scRNA-seq was conducted on >350,000 cells across all cell types from five donors. Results: We identified 7,250 eQTL and 11,243 caQTL in 29 immune cell types, including substantial signals in rare populations such as pDC (1,907 eQTL and 3,317 caQTL). caQTL were more enriched in enhancer regions than eQTL, indicating regulatory mechanisms beyond gene expression. Colocalization with GWAS of 12 IMD traits in East Asian populations identified loci colocalizing with eQTL and caQTL (e.g., the SHOC2 locus in pDC for SLE), highlighting cell-type-specific regulatory effects. GWAS risk projection onto scRNA-seq data revealed trait-relevant cellular enrichment (e.g., SLE in pDC). Using 5' scRNA-seq, we identified 2,896-13,022 bidirectionally transcribed candidate enhancers (btcEnhs) per cell type, enriched for both eQTL and caQTL within related lineages. Stratified LDSC analysis using ATAC peaks and btcEnhs further revealed cell-type-specific heritability enrichment (e.g., Th17/Tfh in RA and B cells/pDC in SLE). Conclusion: Integrative analysis of eQTL and caQTL across FACS-sorted immune cell types reveals cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms underlying IMD pathogenesis.
O20-02: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia (SZ) are clinically distinct, but genomic studies show partially shared liability. We asked which WGS-detectable risk layers are shared or disorder-preferential. We analyzed PCR-free short-read WGS from 11,335 Japanese participants (ASD/SZ cases, controls and relatives), using harmonized variant calling, ancestry QC and pedigree-aware designs. We evaluated rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs), exonic and recurrent genomic-disorder CNVs, PRS (PRS-CSx), rare genic-proximal TRE outliers detected by ExpansionHunter Denovo/STRling with 5-fold cross-fitting, and rare deletions/duplications overlapping developmental topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries. TAD boundaries are genomic borders organizing local regulatory contacts, including enhancer-gene contacts; here we focused on boundaries differing across developing brain cell types. Rare coding and CNV analyses recovered known risk layers. Rare TRE outlier carriage was increased in both ASD and SZ (OR=1.37-1.61 across callers), with no clear ASD- SZ heterogeneity. In contrast, rare deletions overlapping developmental cell-type-differential TAD boundaries were enriched in ASD (OR=1.43, P=2.9e-5), but not in SZ or duplications. This ASD deletion signal was supported by independent ASD cohorts (IVW OR=1.25, P=2.2e-3) and retained in joint-layer models. These findings support a layered WGS architecture: ASD and SZ share TRE burden, whereas rare deletions overlapping developmental 3D-genome regulatory borders show an ASD-preferential pattern.
O20-03: Large-scale genome studies have advanced rapidly with high-throughput sequencing. While single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) have been extensively characterized across diverse populations, multiple-nucleotide variants (MNVs), defined as clusters of adjacent nucleotide substitutions occurring simultaneously, remain comparatively underexplored, especially in Japanese populations. In this study, we analyzed MNVs using the 60KJPN whole-genome sequencing dataset from the Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization. By comparing MNV allele frequencies with gnomAD, we identified many MNVs observed only in the Japanese dataset (969,700 MNVs; 85.5% of jMorp MNVs). Annotation analysis showed that more than 80% of Japanese MNVs were located in non-coding regions, mainly intergenic and intronic regions, suggesting that their effects may not be captured by coding-focused interpretation. To investigate the potential functional impact of these non-coding MNVs, we applied AlphaGenome, a genome language model, to predict changes in gene expression and epigenomic features. We also compared the predicted effects of MNVs with those of the corresponding SNVs, enabling evaluation of effects that may emerge only when adjacent substitutions are considered jointly. A subset of Japanese-specific MNVs showed predicted regulatory effects that were not fully captured by analysis of the corresponding SNVs alone. These findings highlight the importance of MNV-aware analyses for characterizing population-specific genomic variation and improving the interpretation of disease risk in Japanese populations.
O20-04: Background: Mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtCN) reflects mitochondrial content and cellular bioenergetic capacity and is influenced by nuclear genetic variation and systemic physiology. However, most genetic determinants of mtCN have been identified in populations of European ancestry, and their transferability to non- European populations remains incompletely understood. Methods: We quantified blood mtCN by quantitative PCR in 857 participants from the Shika population-based cohort in Japan. We applied effect-size equivalence testing to evaluate the transferability of 66 previously reported mtCN-associated variants. We also performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) to identify novel loci and a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) to characterize phenotypic correlates of mtCN. Results: Sixty-two of 66 previously reported mtCN-associated variants showed statistically equivalent effects in our cohort, supporting cross-ancestry transferability of mtCN-associated genetic effects. GWAS identified three loci exceeding the suggestive significance threshold, although none reached genome-wide significance. PheWAS revealed a significant positive association between mtCN and serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels after false discovery rate correction (q = 0.02). Conclusion: These findings support the transferability of previously reported mtCN-associated variants to a Japanese population and suggest that the genetic architecture of mtCN is largely conserved across ancestries. The association between blood mtCN and AST warrants further investigation.
O20-05: [Introduction] We demonstrated a strong association between HLA- B*15:11 and carbamazepine (CBZ)-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) in the Japanese population. In contrast, HLA-A*31:01 is an established risk allele for CBZ-induced drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome/drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DIHS/DRESS), but its contribution to SJS/TEN susceptibility remained unclear. We investigated whether the association between HLA-A*31:01 and SJS/TEN could be replicated by a trans-ethnic meta-analysis of Japanese and Korean cohorts and evaluated the predictive performance of combined HLA biomarkers. [Methods] Meta-analyses were conducted using Japanese and Korean cohorts with CBZ-induced SJS/TEN and DIHS/DRESS. ROC analyses were performed. [Results] The association between HLA-B*15:11 and SJS/TEN was replicated in Japanese and Korean populations. HLA-A*31:01 showed a strong association with DIHS/DRESS and a moderate but statistically significant association with SJS/TEN in the meta-analysis (OR = 3.18, p = 1.1 × 10 -4 ). In the Japanese SJS/TEN cohort, the area under the ROC curve (AUC) increased from 0.698 to 0.749 after adding HLA- A*31:01 to HLA-B*15:11 alone. Similarly, in the Korean SJS/TEN cohort, the AUC improved from 0.681 to 0.793 after adding HLA- A*31:01. [Discussion] These findings suggest that HLA-A*31:01 contributes not only to DIHS/DRESS but also to SJS/TEN susceptibility. Combining HLA-A*31:01 with HLA-B*15:11 substantially improves the prediction of CBZ-induced SJS/TEN in East Asian populations.
O20-06: Complex structural variations (cxSVs) are often overlooked in genome analyses due to detection challenges. We developed ARC-SV, a probabilistic and machine learning-based method that enables accurate detection and reconstruction of cxSVs from standard datasets. Applying across 4,262 genomes representing all continental populations, we identified cxSVs as a significant source of natural human genetic variation. Rare cxSVs have a propensity to occur in neural genes and loci that underwent rapid human-specific evolution, including those regulating corticogenesis. By performing single-nuclei multiomics in postmortem brains, we discovered cxSVs associated with differential gene expression and chromatin accessibility across various brain regions and cell types. Additionally, cxSVs detected in brains of psychiatric cases are enriched for linkage with psychiatric GWAS risk alleles detected in the same brains. Furthermore, our analysis revealed significantly decreased brain region- and cell type-specific expression of cxSV-genes specifically for psychiatric cases, implicating cxSVs in the molecular etiology of major neuropsychiatric disorders.
O21-01: Conventional cytogenetic analyses may not fully resolve complex chromosomal rearrangements (CCRs). We applied optical genome mapping (OGM) to three patients with developmental delay and suspected CCRs. Case 1 was a 4-year-old boy with macrocephaly, developmental delay, and autistic features. G-banding, FISH, and chromosomal microarray (CMA) identified five structural variants (SVs) involving chromosomes 2, 8, and 14 and a 4.2-Mb deletion at 2q13-q14.1, whereas OGM detected at least 12 SVs, including a breakpoint disrupting CHD8 at 14q11.2. Case 2 was a 6-year-old boy with seizures, developmental delay, and cleft lip and palate. CMA and spectral karyotyping suggested a CCR involving chromosomes 2, 10, 12, and 14, and OGM identified at least 11 translocation breakpoints, clarifying the rearrangement architecture. Case 3 was a 6-year-old boy with developmental delay and infantile epileptic spasms syndrome. G-banding showed 46,XY,t(2;11)(p21;p15.1),t(8;21)(p11.2;q11.2), but OGM identified chromosome 3, rather than chromosome 11, as a rearranged chromosome, revealing a CCR involving chromosomes 2, 3, 8, and 21, four translocation breakpoints, and a 1.13-Mb deletion at 21q21.1. Across all three cases, OGM revealed substantially greater structural complexity than conventional methods. OGM corrected a chromosome misidentification in Case 3 and identified gene-level disruption of CHD8 in Case 1, providing a plausible molecular basis for the phenotype. These findings support OGM for comprehensive characterization of CCRs in patients with developmental delay.
O21-02: Introduction) Healthcare transition (HCT) from pediatric to adult care is critical for patients with congenital genetic disorders requiring lifelong multidisciplinary management. To develop an HCT system tailored to patient needs, we surveyed families of patients with Mowat- Wilson syndrome (MWS). Methods) In collaboration with the MWS Family Association, we conducted a web-based questionnaire survey on transition support and adult medical care between December 2025 and January 2026 (ethics approval R7-03). Results) Fifty families responded (response rate 68.3%); 54% had patients under 15 years and 46% were aged 15 or older. All recognized the need for adult medical care, and 86% had a primary physician (pediatrics 50%, neurology 25%, genetics 10%, pediatric surgery 10%, home-visit care 5%). The most desired specialty for future care was general internal medicine (61.1%), followed by neurology and genetics (16.7% each). Among the 10 families under pediatric care, only one wished to continue with a pediatrician; others preferred adult specialists. Only 26.1% had received transition support, and just one-third of those felt it was adequate. Only 15% reported being informed about adult-onset complications or future medical needs. Conclusion) This survey reveals a substantial gap between patient needs and the reality of HCT support for rare genetic disorders. There is an urgent need to organize disease-specific medical data and establish effective systems for transition support and information provision.
O21-03: Post-zygotic correction of chromosomal monosomy, monosomy rescue, can result in whole-chromosome uniparental isodisomy. Recently, post-zygotic correction of partial chromosomal deletion, deletion rescue, has been proposed as a mechanism underlying segmental uniparental isodisomy. Here, we report a girl with mosaic partial monosomy of chromosome 9p arising from deletion rescue. The proband was a 10-year-old girl. She was born to non-consanguineous parents at 40 weeks of gestation. Developmental milestones were delayed: head control achieved at 3 months, sitting at 7 months, creeping at 2 years, and pulling herself up at 7 years of age. At 10 years of age, she was able to speak only a few words. She developed epilepsy at 10 years of age with generalized spike-and-wave discharges observed on electroencephalography during sleep. She showed linear pigmentation along the lines of Blaschko, suggesting a mosaic disorder. G-banding confirmed mosaic partial monosomy 9p (mos 46,XX,del(9) (p22)[7]/46,XX[23]). Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) of peripheral blood identified a region of homozygosity on 9p24.3-p22.3 without detectable copy number loss. In contrast, CMA of buccal mucosa revealed a deletion on 9p24.3-p22.3 with a normalized log2 ratio of -0.8: mosaic ratio of the deletion was estimated 86%. These results indicated that the 9p24.3-p22.3 deletion was orthotopically corrected during post-zygotic cell division. In conclusion, the coexistence of partial monosomy mosaicism and a region of homozygosity in the corresponding region is a clue of deletion rescue.
O21-04: Background: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), caused by pathogenic NF1 variants, is characterized by cafe-au-lait macules (CALMs) and neurofibromas. However, diagnosis is challenging when CALMs are the sole feature, particularly in differentiating NF1 from Legius syndrome (LS). We evaluated the clinical utility of genetic testing (GT) for suspected NF1. Methods: We reviewed patients with suspected NF1 who underwent GT (targeted sequencing and chromosomal microarray) at Tottori University Hospital between January 2017 and January 2026. Results: Of the 23 patients included, the median age at the initial visit was 5 years (0-67). Manifestations included multiple CALMs in 22 (95.7%), freckling in 7 (30.4%), and neurofibromas in 4 (17.4%). Definitive diagnosis was established in 12 patients (52.2%), comprising 10 with NF1 (43.5%) and 2 with LS (8.7%). Among 9 patients meeting NF1 clinical criteria, 6 were genetically diagnosed (66.7%, 5 NF1, 1 LS). Notably, among 15 patients with CALMs alone, 8 achieved definitive diagnosis (53.3%, 7 NF1, 1 LS). Identified NF1 variants included 4 nonsynonymous, 3 frameshift, 1 splice-site, and 2 NF1 whole-gene deletions. Conclusion: GT confirmed diagnoses in 53.3% of patients presenting solely with CALMs, supporting its utility when clinical signs are insufficient. Furthermore, pathogenic variants such as frameshifts and NF1 whole-gene deletions were identified in NF1, allowing for accurate assessment of complication risks based on genotype-phenotype correlations. GT is valuable for early diagnosis and tailored follow-up.
O21-05: [Introduction] Skeletal dysplasias are a heterogeneous group of rare genetic disorders affecting ~ 1 in 5,000 individuals, encompassing 771 conditions caused by pathogenic variants in 552 genes. Next-generation sequencing has accelerated detection of causative variants. [Aim] To evaluate the diagnostic utility of whole-exome sequencing (WES) in patients with skeletal dysplasia at a single center. [Method] Between December 2016 and November 2025, WES was performed in 192 patients referred nationwide to the University of Osaka. Our pipeline integrated SNV/CNV detection, annotation, and disease-specific gene filtering. [Result] The overall diagnostic yield was 58.9% (113/192), ranging from 52% (26/50; Osteogenesis imperfecta) to 90% (9/10; Type II collagenopathy). Heterozygous variants predominated (n=94), including missense (n=41), frameshift (n=20), nonsense (n=14), splice-site (n=12), CNVs (n=4), in-frame (n=2), and delins (n=1). In 22 patients, diagnoses were revised after genetic analysis; for instance, a case initially diagnosed with brachydactyly was reclassified as aggrecanopathy due to an ACAN variant. [Discussion] WES showed high diagnostic yield with expert clinical evaluation. Limitations included reduced sensitivity for deep intronic variants and imprecise CNV breakpoint resolution, requiring whole-genome sequencing (WGS). [Conclusion] WES is an effective first-tier tool for skeletal dysplasia diagnosis. However, complementary approaches, including WGS, transcriptome/methylome analyses, and collaboration, are needed to improve yield.
O21-06: Noonan syndrome and related disorders (RASopathies) are known to be the most common conditions associated with cases where fetal nuchal translucency (NT) thickening was observed in early pregnancy but chromosomal testing yielded normal results. We provide information on these conditions during genetic counseling and offer Noonan/RASopathies panel testing to those who request it. We investigated the ultrasound findings and the diagnostic process for cases of RASopathies diagnosed at our hospital. Among the 9 cases in which prenatal RASopathies panel testing was performed due to nuchal translucency (NT) thickening between January 2022 and January 2026, variants were identified in 4 cases. The breakdown was as follows: 2 cases with pathogenic BRAF variants, 1 case with a pathogenic SOS1 variant, and 1 case with a variant of unknown significance (VUS) in LZTR1. In addition, there was one case in which multiple anomalies were detected by ultrasound, and a pathogenic variant in SOS1 was identified through chorionic exome sequencing following termination of pregnancy. There was also one case in which the pregnant woman herself exhibited suspicious physical characteristics; testing revealed a pathogenic variant in her RIT1, and it was considered likely that this variant had been transmitted to the fetus. If nuchal translucency thickening is observed during the first trimester, the possibility of RASopathies must always be kept in mind when planning genetic counseling and testing.
O22-01: Backgrounds: SCN5A encodes a cardiac sodium channel, and its loss-of-function (LOF) variants cause various cardiac phenotypes, such as Brugada syndrome (BrS), sick sinus syndrome (SSS) and so on. The penetrance of these phenotypes is variable depending on age and sex, however, the detailed phenotypes in families with the same SCN5A variant have not been well elucidated yet. Purpose: We aimed to clarify age and sex-dependent differences in phenotypes caused by the same SCN5A variants in families. Methods and Results: The study cohort consisted of 41 probands (male n=24) with LOF SCN5A variants and their parents with the same variants as the probands. The median age for genetic testing of probands is 15 (7-24) years old. The phenotypes of probands were classified into BrS (n=24, male n=18), SSS (n=21, male n=9) and others (n=1). Five probands showed overlapping phenotypes of BrS and SSS. In 24 BrS probands, SCN5A variants were inherited from 11 fathers and 13 mothers. Ten (90%) fathers and 4 (31%) mothers showed BrS phenotype, and 1 mother without BrS phenotype was SSS. Among 11 male probands who inherited SCN5A variants from their mothers, only 3 (27%) mothers showed BrS phenotype. In 21 SSS probands, SCN5A variants were inherited from 9 fathers, none of whom had SSS, but 2 of whom showed BrS phenotype. In contrast, 5 (42%) out of 12 mothers suffered SSS, and 4 of them were implanted with pacemakers. Conclusions: Phenotypes of LOF SCN5A variants are variable even within a family. We must be careful when providing genetic counseling to patients with LOF SCN5A variants.
O22-02: The clinical importance of genetic medicine in the cardiovascular field has increased in recent years; however, the real-world characteristics of genetic counseling in this field remain insufficiently understood. We retrospectively reviewed 122 cases related to cardiovascular and connective tissue disorders among 2,018 genetic counseling cases performed at our institution between April 2016 and March 2025. The 122 cases included Fabry Disease in 44 (36%), connective tissue disorders in 33 (27%), inherited arrhythmia disorders in 27 (22%), mitochondrial diseases in 10 (8%), cardiomyopathies in 6 (5%), and other disorders in 2 (2%). Suspected and disease-related cases were also included in each category. Only 38 cases (31%) were referred from the cardiology department, whereas 40 (33%) were referred from other departments and 43 (36%) were self-referred at-risk individuals without formal physician referral. Family-based cascade screening was observed particularly in patients with Fabry Disease, connective tissue disorders, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy-related conditions. Genetic medicine in the cardiovascular field encompasses multisystem disorders, including metabolic diseases, connective tissue disorders, highlighting the need for multidisciplinary collaboration across departments. In addition, many at-risk individuals do not initially present to a specialized department. Establishing a clinical framework in which cardiology departments actively accept and evaluate at-risk individuals may therefore be desirable in future clinical practice.
O22-03: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder characterized by ventricular dilatation and impaired systolic function, leading to heart failure and sudden cardiac death. Despite advances in genomic technologies, the genetic causes of DCM remain unidentified in more than half of patients. Here, we performed an integrative analysis of genomic and transcriptomic data from patient-derived cardiac tissue to identify causative variants in genetically undiagnosed DCM. This approach enabled us to identify a homozygous splice-site variant, c.243+6T to A, in the sarcoglycan gene SGCB, which results in exon 2 skipping. This variant was significantly enriched in patients with DCM compared with the general population, with consistent genotype-phenotype correlations observed across multiple families. Protein-level analysis of cardiac tissue from homozygous individuals revealed loss of beta-sarcoglycan, the protein product of SGCB, and destabilization of the sarcoglycan complex. Although SGCB has been previously associated with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, these homozygous individuals showed no biochemical or clinical signs of skeletal muscle involvement, indicating an absence of myopathy. Compared with patients with DCM without this variant, homozygous individuals also had a higher risk of early-onset adverse cardiac events. Together, these findings identify c.243+6T to A in SGCB as a cause of isolated DCM associated with unfavorable clinical outcomes.
O22-04: Background: Pediatric idiopathic and heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension (IPAH/HPAH) is increasingly recognized as biologically distinct from adult-onset disease. Although the RNF213 p.R4810K founder variant has been implicated in East Asian vasculopathy, the broader spectrum and clinical significance of non-p.R4810K RNF213 variants in pediatric PAH remain unclear. Methods: We retrospectively investigated 203 Japanese and Chinese patients diagnosed with IPAH/ HPAH before 20 years of age. The result of genetic testing, clinical characteristics and outcomes were evaluated according to RNF213 variant status, including comparisons between p.R4810K and non-p.R4810K carriers. Results: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants of disease-causing genes were identified in 79 patients (38.9%). In addition, isolated RNF213 rare variants in 34 patients (16.7%). Non-p.R4810K carriers demonstrated higher pulmonary arterial pressure than did p.R4810K carriers. Survival differences between RNF213 subgroups were not statistically significant. Several non-p.R4810K variants demonstrated high predicted deleteriousness, supporting their potential clinical relevance. Conclusions: East Asian pediatric IPAH/ HPAH demonstrates an expanded RNF213 variant spectrum extending beyond the canonical p.R4810K founder variant. The identification of clinically significant non-p.R4810K variants broadens the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of RNF213-associated pulmonary vasculopathy and suggests genetic heterogeneity in pediatric PAH susceptibility across East Asian populations.
O22-05: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) are both primary cardiac muscle diseases but with morphologically and functionally contrasting phenotypes. The genetic architectures distinguishing between them remain unresolved. We conducted the largest-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in non-European populations to date, analyzing 2,385 DCM and 2,089 HCM Japanese individuals in parallel (N = 150K). We identified three novel risk loci (CACNA1D, SORCS1, GAREM1) in Japanese HCM GWAS. Cross-population GWAS meta-analyses with 23,000 DCM and 11,113 HCM cases (N = 1,900K) identified 64 and 56 significant loci each, including 12 novel loci, and demonstrated shared and distinct risk variants across populations. Two cardiomyopathies showed genome-wide opposing architectures by comparing polygenic risk scores (PRS). Comprehensive cross-trait association analyses of DCM/ HCM-PRS in BioBank Japan and UK Biobank revealed that both PRSs predicted other cardiovascular and metabolic phenotypes in the same positive direction, while echocardiographic and cardiac MRI parameters showed consistently inverse associations between DCM- PRS and HCM-PRS. When integrating GWAS with human heart single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, both cardiomyopathies are spatiotemporally associated with stressed cardiomyocytes, but with gene expression profiles in opposite directions. This study highlights the polygenetic, cellular, and spatial contrasts between DCM and HCM and provides further insights into their unresolved pathogenesis.
O22-06: Background: Rapid implementation of cardiovascular genomic medicine has highlighted critical ethical, legal, and social issues (ELSI). While monogenic disorders provide clear actionability, polygenic risk scores involve probabilistic risks, complicating results return. Objective: To characterize ELSI and practical challenges in establishing frameworks for returning genomic results in cardiovascular diseases. Methods: From January to March 2026, we conducted multi-stakeholder deliberations within our AMED project. Concurrently, we investigated domestic return practices at Shizuoka Cancer Center. In March 2026, we performed international inquiries with key stakeholders implementing national genomics in the UK (NHS, Genomics England, Our Future Health) and Singapore (PRECISE) to analyze global infrastructure and engagement strategies. Results: Three core ELSI themes emerged: (1) Divergent protocols for monogenic vs. polygenic risks; explaining shifting risk models requires robust literacy support. (2) Longitudinal accountability; managing the reinterpretation of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) and post-mortem disclosure requires pre-obtained consent. (3) Workforce gaps; lack of pathways for non-specialists handling secondary findings hinders heart-team and genetic-professional synergy. Conclusion: Cardiovascular genomic delivery requires a life-course knowledge loop rather than one-time disclosure. Developing cross-disciplinary guidance and pilot infrastructure to evaluate behavioral outcomes is urgent.
O23-01: Variants in the MSL2 gene were newly established as a disease entity in 2024 and registered in OMIM as Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (KBHS). KBHS is a rare disorder characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, epilepsy, and ophthalmologic abnormalities caused by loss-of-function MSL2 variants. An 8-year-old boy, born at 38 weeks of gestation, presented with developmental delay, refractory epilepsy consistent with Lennox-Gastaut spectrum, and ophthalmologic abnormalities including hyperopia and astigmatism. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous nonsense variant in MSL2 (NM_018133(MSL2): c.1429C>T, p.Arg477Ter). This variant is located in the terminal exon and is predicted to escape nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), resulting in a truncated protein. The variant has not been registered in ClinVar or population genome databases, including ExAC and the 1000 Genomes Project. According to ACMG guidelines, the variant was classified as pathogenic (Class Ia) based on PVS1 and PS2 evidence, together with previously reported iPSC-based functional analyses of MSL2 and localization within a DNA-binding domain. Among 25 previously reported cases, variants predicted to undergo NMD were predominantly associated with severe phenotypes and early-onset epilepsy. Although the present variant is predicted to escape NMD, the patient exhibited refractory epilepsy, suggesting this case may provide important insights into the disease mechanism of KBHS.
O23-02: Background: Mobile element insertions (MEIs), including LINE-1 (L1) and Alu insertions, are established causes of human genetic disease but are often overlooked in routine genome analysis. We investigated the clinical utility of dedicated MEI detection in unresolved rare disease cases. Methods: We analyzed 4,570 Illumina short-read whole-genome sequencing datasets from patients and relatives using MEGAnE. Coding-disrupting MEIs were evaluated according to phenotype and inheritance pattern. Results: We identified four patients in whom MEIs represented the disease-causing mechanism. Patient 1, with Angelman syndrome, harbored a de novo L1 insertion in exon 5 of UBE3A on the maternally derived allele. Patients 2 and 3, both with retinitis pigmentosa, carried the same heterozygous AluY insertion in exon 4 of RP1 together with different frameshift variants. Patient 4, with Joubert syndrome, carried an L1 insertion in exon 7 of CC2D2A together with a splice-site variant in exon 29. The recurrent RP1 and CC2D2A MEIs were identified in 14 and 10 individuals, respectively, among 4,570 analyzed subjects, suggesting ancestry-enriched pathogenic alleles. Discussion: Dedicated MEI analysis identified pathogenic variants missed by standard SNV/indel-focused pipelines and provided diagnoses for previously unresolved cases. Recurrent coding-disrupting MEIs in RP1 and CC2D2A may represent founder alleles in the Japanese population. These findings support incorporating MEI detection into routine genome analysis to improve rare disease diagnosis.
O23-03: Background: Fabry disease is a systemic hereditary disorder that frequently leads to complications such as renal failure, cardiomyopathy, and stroke. Urinary mulberry cells and bodies, which appear in the early stages of Fabry disease, serve as highly sensitive and specific non-invasive diagnostic markers, with near 100% sensitivity and specificity. At our institution, we collaborate with multiple departments to conduct high-risk screening, termed "Mulberry Screening", using urinary sediment analysis. Methods: This was a single-center, retrospective observational study conducted between May 2024 and April 2025. Patients were eligible for screening if they presented with any of the following conditions: unexplained renal dysfunction, proteinuria, cerebrovascular disease (age < 60 years), left ventricular hypertrophy (13 > mm), or cardiac dysfunction. Urinary sediment was examined for the presence of mulberry cells or bodies. Results and Discussion: Mulberry screening was performed in 76 patients: 28 from the Department of Cardiology, 28 from Nephrology, 13 from Neurosurgery, and 7 from Cardiovascular Surgery. One true-positive case was identified, and treatment was initiated. Two false-positive cases were also noted. In these false-positive cases, phospholipid accumulation in glomerular epithelial cells, potentially due to medications such as amiodarone, was considered a contributing factor. Given that patients with left ventricular hypertrophy may be on anti-arrhythmic agents such as amiodarone, careful interpretation of mulberry screening results is warranted.
O23-04: Background The detection and interpretation of structural variants (SVs), including copy number variants (CNVs), is the key function of modern cytogenetic laboratories and are important for diagnosis, clinical management, and genetic counseling. Current cytogenetic laboratory methods such as chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and chromosome banding chromosome analysis (CBA) can each provide structural genomic information, but each technique has specific limitations in their ability to resolve certain types or sizes of SVs. Electronic genome mapping (EGM) enables genome-wide analysis of SVs using long DNA molecules in a single workflow. We present a proof of concept for the use of EGM for the detection of SVs in a cohort of constitutional and prenatal samples with findings previously characterized by conventional cytogenetic testing. Methodology EGM, a solid-state nanochannel-based platform, is a high-resolution technology capable of detecting a broad range of structural genomic variations. To evaluate the utility of EGM for cytogenetic testing of constitutional disorders, peripheral blood specimens referred for follow up of known chromosomal abnormality were analyzed in this study. DNA was extracted using NEB Monarch® HMW DNA Extraction Kit and processed using a dual-enzyme workflow and the OhmX™ Platform. SVs were identified using Human Chromosome Explorer® (HCE) de novo assembly, while copy number alterations was assessed using a CNV analysis pipeline. The study cohort included samples with genomic findings previously characterized using orthogonal methods such as CMA, qPCR and CBA. Results EGM enabled assessment of structural and copy number alterations across the analyzed cohort, with findings concordant with previously characterized genomic abnormalities. HCE de novo assembly enabled the detection of SVs less than one megabase, while the CNV analysis pipeline was configured to detect larger copy number alterations (>1 Mb), with both approaches demonstrating findings consistent with prior orthogonal characterization. EGM was able to detect abnormalities as small as ~80kb and up to whole chromosome aneuploidies in our cohort. Conclusions EGM represents a promising, emerging technology for integrated genome-wide assessment of SVs in constitutional and prenatal samples. The combination of de novo assembly and CNV analysis enables identification of genomic abnormalities across multiple size ranges, highlighting the potential utility of EGM as a tool to simplify and improve the clarification of SVs in standard cytogenetic workflows.
O23-05: Many genetic disorders are caused by simple sequence repeat expansions, including Fragile X syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. Accurate sizing of these expansions is critical for determining pathogenicity. Conventional PCR and sequencing methods are unreliable for long repeat regions. Electronic genome mapping (EGM) uses solid-state nanodetectors to survey long DNA molecules and detect structural variants, including those caused by repeat expansions. We assessed EGM’s ability to detect FMR1, FXN, DMPK, and c9orf72 repeat expansions. Single injections and replicates were analyzed for concordance with published repeat lengths using the custom RepX™ Repeat Expansion Analysis pipeline. Results were concordant with expectations across all FMR1 cell lines, but some FXN cell lines did not match published findings. Because FXN has been shown to be an unstable repeat within the same cell line, we analyzed the FXN cell lines by PCR and EGM. Some cell lines were found to have multiple repeat alleles via PCR, and these patterns were mirrored by the single-molecule EGM results. This confirms the accuracy and robustness of EGM for detecting and sizing repeat expansions that are challenging to analyze by standard techniques. In addition, we have customized the FMR1 and FXN assays by including specific nicks and blocks to optimize the interval size for calling premutation alleles. The impact of CRISPR customization will be shown for these repeat expansion assays. EGM offers integrated workflows for high-resolution analysis of repeat regions in either whole-genome or gene-specific mode.
O23-06: Cas9’s ability to bind both targeted and non-targeted sites, and its functional interactions with other proteins and domains, have been studied using many technologies. We show how electronic genome mapping (EGM), which can detect DNA nicks in single molecules covering the whole genome, can be used to determine how gRNA mismatches affect target versus off-target binding and how Cas9 interacts with other proteins when bound to DNA. Cas9 binding to perfectly matched gRNA sites was examined and compared with binding to sites with mismatches at each position in the gRNA. The PAM site and nearby bases in the seed region were found to be critical for binding activity, while single mismatches in positions toward the 5’ end of the recognition region allowed significant off-target binding. The impact of mismatches varied by gRNA. In addition, we used EGM to determine, at base-pair resolution, how physically close the bound CRISPR/dCas9 complex can be relative to nearby nickase recognition sites and still allow activity. Using gRNAs that each bind many different sites in the human genome, we determined the minimum distance between the bound CRISPR/dCas9 complex and nearby nickase recognition sites required for nickase activity. Nickase recognition sites 4-7 bp from the gRNA showed reduced activity, while those 8 bp or more from the gRNA were minimally impacted. Coupled with EGM’s ability to simultaneously evaluate hundreds of singly and doubly mismatched off-target sites, these findings provide insight into Cas9 activity that may be extended to other CRISPR systems.
O24-01: Background: Stigma-free, standardized terminology in genetics has been increasingly encouraged. The ACMG/AMP sequence variant interpretation guideline recommended replacing terms such as "mutation" and "polymorphism" with "variant." However, regional uptake of these recommendations remains unclear. We examined long-term trends in genetics-related terminology in PubMed abstracts. Methods: PubMed baseline and update XML files were parsed to extract bibliographic and affiliation data. English-language records published from 1996 to 2025 containing "gene" in the title or abstract were defined as the gene corpus. Countries were grouped into Asia, Europe, and North America, with separate G7 analyses. Twenty-nine genetics-related terms were assessed across six 5-year periods by Poisson regression with token count as an offset. Results: The gene corpus included 7,592,401 abstracts and 1.62 billion tokens. Over time, "mutation" decreased (IRR per 5 years 0.87, 95% CI 0.85-0.88), whereas "variant" increased (1.08, 1.07-1.10) and "pathogenic variant" markedly increased (3.10, 2.25-4.27). In 2021-2025, among the 3 regions, "mutation" and "polymorphism" were most frequent in Asia, "variant" in Europe, and "pathogenic variant" in Europe. Among G7 countries, "mutation" and "polymorphism" were most frequent in Japan, "variant" in Italy, and "pathogenic variant" in France. Conclusion: Genetics terminology shifted from mutation-centered wording toward variant- and pathogenicity-oriented language, but the pace of change differed across regions and countries.
O24-02: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable neurodevelopmental disorder. To gain insights into its complex genetic architecture, family-based genomic analyses can provide insights into shared and inherited variants associated with ASD. In this study, we performed whole-genome sequencing (WGS) using saliva samples from a mother and her two daughters, all of whom were clinically diagnosed with ASD. Their clinical features were assessed in detail by the ADOS-2, K-ABCII, SRS-2, and AQ. Genomic DNA was extracted from saliva samples and subjected to WGS. The data obtained were processed using standard pipelines, including alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome and variant calling with the GATK. Variants were annotated using snpEff and filtered by SnpSift based on their population frequencies and predicted functional impacts. ASD-associated candidates were further searched for in the following order: (1) variants shared among the three individuals or transmitted from the mother to both daughters; (2) rare variants; (3) loss-of-function and predicted damaging missense variants; and (4) annotations based on ASD-associated genes from the SFARI Gene database. Shared copy number variants (CNVs) were identified using Control-FREEC. In this presentation, we will report ASD-associated genetic variants shared by all three family members and those specific to the siblings, and explore associations between genetic variants and phenotypic profiles.
O24-03: <Background> Nephrotic syndrome (NS) is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by proteinuria due to glomerular filtration barrier dysfunction. Podocyte injury is central to its pathogenesis, with genetic and immune-mediated mechanisms implicated. While monogenic causes and genome-wide association studies have identified susceptibility loci, many cases remain unexplained. The contribution of rare variants is not well defined. <Methods> Whole genome sequencing data from 10,659 Japanese individuals (1,290 cases and 9,369 controls) were analyzed. Rare variants were restricted to predicted loss-of-function variants and aggregated at the gene level. The dataset was randomly divided into a training set (70%) and a test set (30%). In the training set, gene enrichment was assessed using Fishers exact test followed by Bayesian gene-based analysis. Genes with high posterior probability and multiple variants were selected. In the test set, burden analysis was performed. <Results> A total of 150 genes were identified in the discovery phase, from which a subset was prioritized. In the test set, rare variant carriers were more frequent in cases than controls (17.0% vs 15.6%, odds ratio 1.11, p=0.26), although not statistically significant. At the gene level, several candidates showed relatively large effect sizes, including PARP2 and ERO1B. Expression data indicated that these genes are expressed in podocytes and immune-related cell types. <Conclusion> This study identifies biologically plausible candidate genes for NS and suggests that rare variants may contribute in a polygenic manner.
O24-04: Gout develops after prolonged hyperuricemia with elevated serum uric acid (SUA) levels. Sex, overweight/obesity, heavy drinking, aging and menopause (if female) are its risks, in addition to two common dysfunctional SNPs in ABCG2/BCRP. Here we evaluate the individual and population genetic effects in 9,244 Japanese to implement genome-personalized nurse-led hyperuricemia/gout care. First, ABCG2 SNPs had a higher population-attributable fraction (PAF; approximately 30%) for hyperuricemia than those for other typical environmental risk factors except for menopause. In premenopausal individuals, the PAF for ABCG2 SNPs was 45.8%, much higher than that after menopause (29.6%). Second, all these factors also showed significant individual risk of increased SUA level, and ABCG2 SNPs had sufficient effect size to allow them to be converted into other environmental factors. For example, a 25% ABCG2 dysfunction was equivalent to the effects of a 1.67 kg/m2 increase in BMI in females from the viewpoint of SUA increase. Third, to implement genome-personalized nursing with these results above, we mapped onto the process a theoretical framework that is based on a psychological model from behavioral change theory. Because the present results for convertibility will improve the predictability of genetic effects, cognitive interventions could encourage behavioral change through efficacy expectations (self-efficacy) and outcome expectations. We conclude that this framework would function effectively and has potential as a basis for implementing genome-personalized nurse-led care.
O24-05: Case matchmaking supports diagnosis of ultra-rare genetic diseases and rare disease research by identifying related cases across institutions. However, sharing clinical and genomic data raises privacy and practical concerns. We developed a matchmaking function in CaseSharing, a web-based platform within PubCaseFinder, to discover related cases while keeping sensitive information under user control. CaseSharing stores case records locally in the browser and represents clinical information as standardized data. The function searches cases using diagnosis names, candidate genes, and phenotypic profiles. Inheritance and zygosity are contextual information to prioritize matches, while avoiding disclosure of variant-level or identifying information. Users can register, manage, and search cases through one interface. Once a query is submitted, matchmaking is performed immediately against registered cases. When a match is identified, contact information is shared with both parties, enabling collaboration or joint research. The system supports domestic discovery and future interoperability with Matchmaker Exchange. Combining standardized data and controlled exposure, CaseSharing links local management with collaborative diagnosis and research. To our knowledge, CaseSharing is the first platform to integrate local rare disease case management with privacy-conscious case matchmaking. It may accelerate diagnosis, promote discovery of novel disease entities, and provide a foundation for future interoperability with Matchmaker Exchange.
O24-06: Objective: To investigate the prevalence of germline pathogenic variants (GPVs) in cervical cancer and their possible contribution to carcinogenesis. Methods: Using the C-CAT (Center for Cancer Genomics and Advanced Therapeutics) database, we collected variant data from cervical cancer patients. Variant annotations and pathogenicity classifications were re-evaluated according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines. GPVs were extracted from tumor-normal paired analyses. For tumor-only testing, presumed GPVs (PGPVs) of 26 genes with high germline conversion rates were extracted according to the "Guideline for handling GPV/PGPV in comprehensive genomic profiling (2025)"; for liquid biopsy testing, PGPVs of 73 genes were identified using our original germline/somatic sorting algorithm. GPV/ PGPV frequencies were calculated and compared with other cohorts. Results: A total of 2,585 cervical cancer cases were analyzed. Median age was 51 years (range: 15-90). Pathological diagnoses included 1,259 squamous cell carcinomas, 808 adenocarcinomas, 164 neuroendocrine carcinomas, and 354 others/unclassified. Among 299 tumor-normal paired cases, eight GPVs (2.7%) were identified. From 2,076 tumor-only and 210 liquid biopsy panels, 158 (7.6%) and seven PGPVs (3.3%) were detected, respectively. For BRCA1/2, five GPVs (1.7%) and 62 PGPVs (2.7%) were found, slightly exceeding the C- CAT off-tumor cohort prevalence (1.2%). Conclusions: A relatively high GPV/PGPV prevalence in cervical cancer was observed in C- CAT, suggesting a possible association between germline alterations and carcinogenesis.
O25-01: Argyrophilic grain (AG) is an age-associated neurodegenerative accumulation of 4-repeat (R) tau in dendritic spines. Dementia with grain (DG) is defined as AGs with a sole pathological basis for cognitive decline. As with other multifactorial diseases, DG could result from interactions of environmental and genetic factors. Other neurogenerative disorders characterized by abnormal aggregates of 4R tau, corticobasal degeneration (CBD) and progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), have the major genetic risk factor, the H1 haplotype of MAPT locus. However, the genetic basis of DG is largely unknown. To clarify the genetic architecture of DG pathogenesis, we conducted a genome-wide association studies (GWAS) with 214 DG cases versus 12,405 controls (DG-GWAS) and 214 DG cases versus 4,015 Alzheimer's disease (AD)(DG-AD GWAS). We have identified three candidate loci associated with the risk of DG, the SVIL locus on chr10, the NBAS locus on chr2, and the PLPPR1 locus on chr9 at both GWAS. Transcriptome-wide association analysis using summary statistics for DG-GWAS identified DAPK2 as a novel candidate causal gene for DG pathogenesis in the brain frontal cortex. The genetic association analysis for the APOE locus revealed that the APOE allele did not affect DG pathogenesis. We also identified new variants in MAPT encoding tau protein that could potentially affect DG pathology. This is the first report on the genetic basis for DG. Our findings provide biological and clinical insights into the pathogenesis of DG.
O25-02: Background and Aims: Up to half of patients switch or discontinue antihypertensive drugs within the first year, but underlying mechanisms remain elusive. We identified genetic predictors of antihypertensive drug use trajectories in the first year. Methods: Using longitudinal drug data from >400,000 genotyped antihypertensive drug users in FinnGen, the UK Biobank, and the Estonian Biobank, we classified short-term antihypertensive drug use trajectories as Continue, Switch, or Discontinue. We then performed genome-wide association studies and downstream analyses across five drug classes. Results: We identified 14 genome-wide significant loci for switching from angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI) and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (dCCB) to other antihypertensive drugs. For ACEI switching, evidence converged on the neurotensin-NTSR1 pathway, including a 320-fold Finnish-enriched protective missense variant in the neurotensin receptor gene NTSR1 (rs148569146 [G301R], odds ratio [OR] 0.49, P=3.3×10-43) and a variant near RASSF9 (rs181941187, OR=0.74, P=1.2×10-49) tagging the neurotensin gene NTS. In drug-gene interaction analyses, NTSR1 G301R conferred reduced ACEI-induced cough risk (OR=0.39, P=8.1×10-4). The dCCB switching locus at CYP3A43 was in near-complete linkage (r2=0.99) with the functional CYP3A4*22 allele (rs35599367, OR=1.23, P=6.1×10-10). Conclusions: We extend the bradykinin hypothesis of ACEI-induced cough by implicating neurotensin-NTSR1 signaling and pinpointing CYP3A4*22 as a novel functional predictor of dCCB switching.
O25-03: Vascular dementia (VaD) is the second most common subtype of dementia and a complex neurocognitive disorder influenced by both environmental exposures and genetic susceptibility. Although previous studies have linked genetic predisposition to individual vascular risk factors with VaD, an integrated polygenic architecture underlying VaD was unexplored. We therefore investigated the associations of a cardiometabolic multi-trait polygenic risk score (mPRS) with VaD. This study targeted 9,503 Japanese adults (Mean age: 73 years old, Women: 57.5%) who participated in the Japan Prospective Studies Collaboration for Aging and Dementia (JPSC-AD) Study. We applied the PRS-CS method to calculate 12 single-trait PRSs using summary statistics from genome-wide association studies in the Biobank Japan Project. We integrated these PRSs to construct mPRS, with trait-specific weights from leave-one-site-out ridge regression. After the 5-year follow-up period, 985 participants developed all-cause dementia, including 146 VaD cases. Single-trait PRS analyses showed that PRSs for systolic blood pressure and chronic heart failure were positively associated with VaD (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05). Cardiometabolic mPRS showed an independent association with VaD (odds ratio per SD: 1.46, p=1.47×10-5), while it showed modest discriminatory capacity for VaD with an area under the curve of 0.569. These findings highlight that cardiometabolic polygenic burden contributes to VaD, suggesting potential utility for early risk stratification and primary prevention.
O25-05: Metabolome-genome-wide association studies (MGWAS) have improved our understanding of the genetic factors of metabolites, providing valuable insights into how lifestyle influences disease development. We performed an MGWAS of 48 plasma metabolites measured using NMR in 31,232 Japanese participants from the Tohoku Medical Megabank Community-Based Cohort Study. We identified 317 independent variant-metabolite associations, including 161 new associations. These results build on previous MGWAS by expanding both ancestry and metabolite coverage. As the East Asian-enriched variant rs671 showed the broadest pleiotropic associations, we examined rs671 in detail, including models of rs671, daily alcohol consumption, and their interactions. Rs671 showed significant direct associations with only four metabolites, suggesting that most rs671-metabolite links depend on alcohol consumption. In contrast, daily alcohol consumption was associated with a wide range of metabolites and biochemical traits that are often modified by the rs671 SNP. These findings imply that rs671 influences metabolism not only through differences in drinking behavior but also by changing how alcohol affects metabolism. The association patterns were well-matched to the glutathione-related metabolic responses, leading us to propose a mechanism involving disruption of glutathione balance in rs671_A carriers. Our study underscores the East Asian-specific genetic architecture of metabolites and highlights rs671 as a key regulator of alcohol-related metabolic variations.
O25-06: Background: In radiation-affected regions, assessing whether ambient dose, exposure age, and BRCA1/2 spectra increase the posterior probability of a radiation-origin hypothesis is clinically and scientifically important. Methods: We analyzed 177 breast cancer patients who underwent BRCA1/2 testing after counseling from July 2020 to December 2025. BRCA positivity was limited to pathogenic variants. HER2 2+/FISH-negative tumors were HER2-negative, PgR negativity was 0%, and two or more primary breast cancers included bilateral, ipsilateral multiple, or metachronous cancers. We used Bayes' formula, P(R|D)=P(D|R)P(R)/[P(D|R)P(R)+P(D|non-R)P(non-R)], with robust Poisson regression. Results: Pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants were found in 34 patients (19.2%): BRCA1 in 15 and BRCA2 in 19. PgR negativity and TNBC at 60 years or younger were associated with BRCA positivity in univariable analyses. In multivariable analysis, two or more primary breast cancers remained independently associated with BRCA positivity (IRR 2.30, 95% CI 1.23-4.29; p=0.009), whereas PgR negativity was attenuated and young-onset TNBC retained an association. These features showed no association with dose, distance, or exposure age. Variants were mainly loss-of-function, without structural enrichment, domain clustering, abnormal hotspot, or C-to- T/G-to-A pattern. Conclusion: Bayesian interpretation suggests that the data support general germline BRCA1/2 clinical-genetic features more than low-dose radiation-specific effects, providing a Fukushima baseline for counseling and precision medicine.
O26-01: Purpose: Eyes shut homolog (EYS) is the most common genetic cause of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa (RP) in Japan. This study aimed to investigate the ethnic distribution of EYS pathogenic variants detected in Japanese patients by calculating their cumulative allele frequencies (CAF) across multiple ethnic groups in an international genomic database. Methods: We evaluated EYS pathogenic variants detected in 1,204 previously reported Japanese patients with RP (Koyanagi Y et al., J Med Genet. 2019). CAF was calculated for seven ethnic groups in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD): East Asian (EAS), South Asian (SAS), Admixed American (AMR), Non- Finnish European (NFE), African/African American (AFR), Finnish (FIN), Ashkenazi Jewish (ASJ). Results: EAS showed the highest CAF at 1.318%, markedly exceeding the total population CAF of 0.129%. All other ethnic groups showed substantially lower frequencies: SAS (0.080%), AMR (0.053%), NFE (0.044%), AFR (0.025%), FIN (0.016%) and ASJ (0.000%). Conclusions: EYS pathogenic variants detected in Japanese patients show marked East-Asian specificity, with substantially lower frequencies in South Asian and American populations, and exceedingly low rates in other global groups. These findings provide a foundation for population-tailored medicine and genetic counseling for RP.
O26-02: Background: Interpretation of genetic variants associated with pediatric inherited arrhythmia syndromes may change over time as genetic knowledge evolves. However, variant reclassification in pediatric arrhythmia cohorts remains insufficiently characterized. Methods: Pediatric patients with inherited arrhythmia syndromes followed at Aichi Childrens Health and Medical Center between 2005 and 2025 were retrospectively included. Genetic variants identified through clinical genetic testing in 77 pediatric probands and their family members (200 genetic tests) were systematically re-evaluated at the variant level using updated American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics criteria. Re-evaluation incorporated population databases, ClinVar, published literature, in silico prediction tools, and functional evidence. Results: A total of 62 variants across 10 arrhythmia-related genes were re-evaluated. The most frequently affected genes were KCNQ1 (n=19), KCNH2 (n=13), and RYR2 (n=10). Following re-evaluation, 49 variants (80%) remained classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, whereas 12 variants (20%) were reclassified as variants of uncertain significance or likely benign. No benign or likely benign variants were upgraded to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. Conclusions: Systematic re-evaluation of genetic variants in pediatric inherited arrhythmia syndromes corrected potential overclassification while preserving the stability of benign variants. Periodic reinterpretation may improve long-term genetic diagnosis and clinical management in pediatric patients.
O26-03: Mitochondrial diseases are clinically and genetically heterogeneous disorders that often present with multisystem involvement, including growth failure, neurological symptoms, liver dysfunction, and impaired mitochondrial function. We have performed genetic investigations in patients suspected of having mitochondrial disease using whole-exome sequencing (WES), whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). Through this comprehensive diagnostic approach, we unexpectedly identified pathogenic variants in SBDS, the causative gene of Shwachman- Diamond syndrome, in six patients initially suspected for mitochondrial disease. All six patients carried combinations of a known stop-gain variant and splice variant in SBDS that were identified by WES or WGS. In selected cases, RNA-seq confirmed aberrant splicing, providing functional evidence for pathogenicity. Clinically, many patients showed features overlapping with mitochondrial disease, including liver involvement and reduced oxygen consumption in patient-derived fibroblasts. These findings suggest that Shwachman- Diamond syndrome can mimic mitochondrial disease and may be associated with secondary mitochondrial dysfunction. Integrated genomic and transcriptomic analyses are valuable for identifying noncanonical mitochondrial disease mimics and improving diagnostic accuracy.
O26-04: Background: Thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (TAAD) exhibits genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, and data on Asian patients are limited. We aimed to clarify the genetic landscape and clinical features of TAAD in a large Japanese cohort. Methods: We performed whole-exome sequencing in 282 Japanese patients with TAAD. Variants in 40 established TAAD-associated genes were classified according to ACMG guidelines as pathogenic (P), likely pathogenic (LP), or variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Clinical data, including age at onset, family history, and syndromic features, were collected and compared between variant-positive and variant-negative patients. Results: P/LP variants were identified in 2-3% of patients, mainly in FBN1 and rarely in other TAAD genes. Several variants recurred in unrelated families, suggesting possible founder mutations. Many unreported variants were observed across multiple genes, most classified as VUS and broadly distributed without a single dominant gene. The median age at onset in the overall cohort was 59 years, whereas patients with P/LP variants presented at a median age of 36 years, indicating earlier onset in monogenic cases. Conclusions: This study provides a population-specific overview of the genetic landscape of TAAD in Japanese patients. It highlights founder-like recurrent variants, many unreported changes, and earlier onset in P/LP carriers, and may inform future functional studies, longitudinal phenotyping, and consideration of updates to diagnostic criteria and testing strategies.
O26-05: Background: Diagnostic criteria and intervention thresholds for heritable thoracic aortic disease (HTAD) have been established primarily based on Western cohorts, and their applicability to Japanese patients remains unclear. We evaluated the utility of genetic analysis for risk stratification and clinical outcome assessment in Japanese HTAD. Methods: A total of forty-one unrelated probands and five relatives, classified as syndromic (n=14), non-syndromic (n=17), or systemic-only phenotype (n=10), were analyzed by HTAD panel sequencing. Results: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants were identified in 27% of probands (11/41). FBN1 was the predominant disease gene (10/11 P/LP cases) and accounted for 50% of the syndromic subgroup (7/14). Compared with Western patients, Japanese FBN1 carriers exhibited milder systemic manifestations, including lower Ghent scores and fewer skeletal and ocular features, despite a comparable risk of aortic events. Three novel variants were identified, and four variants were reclassified from VUS to P/LP, improving genetic counseling and family screening. Notably, 55% of patients with P/LP variants experienced aortic dissection at near-normal aortic diameters. Conclusion: Japanese HTAD patients exhibit milder systemic phenotypes while remaining susceptible to aortic dissection at diameters below conventional surgical thresholds. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating genetic information into risk assessment and the need for population-specific diagnostic and management strategies to advance precision medicine in HTAD
O26-06: Background : The patient was a boy born at 37 weeks by uneventful normal spontaneous delivery with unremarkable antenatal progress. He was admitted at day 23 for prolonged neonatal jaundice and irritability. The head circumference, weight, and length were below the third percentiles. Biochemical, hematological, and sepsis workups were unremarkable. However, the patient exhibited persistently elevated plasma lactate (3.4–9.4 mmol/L) and a high cerebrospinal fluid lactate of 3.5 mmol/L. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) demonstrated prominent lactate peaks within the bilateral basal ganglia and the frontal and parieto-occipital white matter, highly suggestive of an underlying mitochondrial disease. Methods : In our previous investigations into undiagnosed rare diseases, whole-exome sequencing (WES) was used to identify novel disease genes in patients with diagnostic odysseys. The novel gene in the present case was identified through trio-based WES and bulk RNA sequencing of peripheral blood. Results : WES identified hemizygous EOLA1: c.368_369del p.(Val123Aspfs*13) in the patient inherited from the asymptomatic mother. RNA sequencing showed mRNA with the frameshift variant, suggesting that the mRNA transcript with the frameshift variant escapes nonsense-mediated decay. EOLA1 was previously shown to localize within the mitochondria and EOLA1-knockout cells exhibit reduced mRNA and protein levels of mitochondrially translated subunits within the electron transport chain. Conclusions : In summary, we have identified EOLA1 as a novel cause of X-linked mitochondrial translation defects in an infant presenting with developmental delay and persistent lactic acidosis. The EOLA1 gene should be incorporated into targeted gene panels for the evaluation of undiagnosed inherited metabolic and neurodevelopmental diseases.
O27-01: Background: Retinoblastoma (RB) is a rare pediatric tumor occurring in one in 15,000 individuals, with 40-50% of cases caused by pathogenic germline RB1 variants. Preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M) for RB was approved in Japan for the first time in 2023. This study explored perceptions of family planning among patients with RB and their families in the current medical and social context. Methods: We reviewed patients with RB who visited our genetic counseling clinic between January 2022 and April 2026. Medical records were examined to identify reasons for consultation, and patient and family member statements were extracted and qualitatively analyzed. Results: Seventy-five individuals visited during the study period: 40 pediatric probands with their parents, 31 adult probands, and 4 other cases. Some adult probands (67.7%) attended the consultation accompanied by family members or partners. Eight thematic categories emerged, including: desire to understand genetic testing for future children, desire to obtain information necessary for decision-making, feelings of difficulty in undergoing PGT-M. Conclusion: This study identified adult RB survivors who sought information about their hereditary conditions and reproductive options in relation to life events, as well as parents of patients with RB. Given that some patients experience anxiety about the inheritance of RB and wish to take proactive steps, providing tailored medical options may support their family planning and decision-making.
O27-02: Background: Intrafamilial communication of genetic risk is important for relatives' health management, yet remains insufficient. Psychological processes underlying family communication and subsequent interactions remain unclear. Objective: This study aimed to clarify genetic risk perceptions, family communication processes, and post-communication interactions from the perspectives of clients and relatives. Methods: Questionnaire surveys were conducted with 62 clients and 52 relatives who received genetic counseling at the University of Tsukuba Hospital. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 33 participants. Data were analyzed using Steps for Coding and Theorization with reference to the Health Belief Model. Results: Genetic risk perceptions were reconstructed through lived experiences and risk communication, shaping readiness for family communication. Post-communication interactions included emotional sharing, relationship adjustment, relational distance, and differences in perceptions. Anxiety, relief, acceptance, and regret coexisted depending on context. Through these interactions, perceptions of genetic risk were integrated into the lifeworld through reinterpretation of values, emotional stabilization, and reorganization of daily life. Conclusions: Family communication of genetic risk was a dynamic process involving reconstruction of genetic risk perceptions, readiness formation, family interactions, and lifeworld integration. The findings suggest the importance of support that considers post-communication interactions and changes in meaning-making.
O27-03: Background; The APOE gene is included in a multigenic panel test targeting familial hypercholesterolemia(FH). Genome-wide association studies have linked APOE to various phenotypes, including Alzheimer Disease(AD), hyperlipidemia, myocardial infarction, aortic aneurysm and coronary artery disease. Apolipoprotein ε4 variant(rs429358) is a common DNA variant substituting arginine for cysteine at codon 112. Based on the allele frequency in Japanese, about 15% of Japanese people have at least one ε4 allele. Detection of common ε4 variant suggests a possible modifier of the hyperlipemia such as familial combined hyperlipidemia, while ε4 variant is one of the established risk factors for the onset of Alzheimer disease (AD) and appropriate disclosure of the APOE-related secondary findings in genetic counseling is ethically important issue. Case Report; In FH genetic testing, the ε4 variant is detected in over 40% of cases, underscoring the need for pre and post-test counseling on future AD risk. We conducted a qualitative analysis of result disclosure, patient preferences, psychological responses, and challenges in risk acceptance. Results and Discussion; In most ε4 heterozygotes, AD shows incomplete penetrance with onset in the late 70s, while dyslipidemia precedes by decades. As APOE4 indicates future dementia risk, disclosure preferences varied. For APOE4 carriers, preventive information reduced psychological burden and supported acceptance.
