Because her cousin's results could not be confirmed, MGPT was performed. No pathogenic variants were detected. Family history Paternal cousin: 65y. Small bowel cancer in her 40s, renal cancer at 50y, and colorectal cancer at 62y; diagnosed with Lynch syndrome by genetic testing. Father: d.68y. Rectal cancer at 30y; gastric cancer at 56y. Brother: d.55y. Colorectal cancer at 45y; gastric cancer at 55y. Paternal uncle: d.29y. Colorectal cancer. Discussion When a pathogenic variant is identified in a proband, single-site analysis is often used for familial testing. However, even when no variant is detected, other hereditary cancer syndromes cannot be excluded. In this case, comprehensive evaluation using MGPT contributed to the patient's health management and reduced anxiety. Conclusion While MGPT may therefore be beneficial for individuals seeking information for health management, many problems still present, such as the fact that it is not covered by insurance.
P1-04-17: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is expected to show higher accuracy than target-capture sequencing to detect structural variants (SVs) by identifying breakpoints (BPs) in non-coding regions. However, short-read WGS (SR-WGS) pipelines often suffer from insufficient accuracy and discrepancies between analytical tools, posing challenges for clinical interpretation. We evaluated 7 germline SVs previously detected by SR-WGS using target adaptive sampling long-read sequencing (TAS-LRS). The target region spanned 13 Mb (approximately 0.4% of the genome), covering 147 hereditary tumor-related genes and 20 kb flanking each SV. Alignment was performed using minimap2, followed by SV analysis with nanomonsv. TAS-LRS achieved an average on-target coverage of 28.5x and a 7.0-fold enrichment. Consistent BPs were confirmed for 6 out of 7 variants. The single discrepant case involved a suspected PMS2 translocation in SR- WGS, which TAS-LRS identified as a false positive due to a 174-bp insertion of a PMS2-homologous sequence insertion in a distinct region on chromosome 4. Furthermore, TAS-LRS enabled nucleotide-level evaluation of all BPs and clarified complex rearrangements, such as SVA retrotransposon insertions in BRCA2, which were previously misclassified or unclear in SR-WGS. While SR-WGS is effective for detecting various SVs, it remains prone to false positives and misinterpretations of complex genomic structures. Integrating TAS- LRS into the diagnostic workflow significantly enhances the accuracy of germline SV detection, providing a robust framework for precise genomic medicine.
P1-04-18: Background: Although comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) is widely used in lung cancer (LC), germline pathogenic variants (GPVs) identified through CGP are rarely reported. We report a young-onset non-small cell LC (NSCLC) patient in whom CGP led to the diagnosis of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC) and familial surveillance. Case Presentation: A 32-year-old never-smoking man was diagnosed with stage IV NSCLC harboring an EGFR exon 20 insertion and PD-L1 expression. He received multiple lines of therapy, including carboplatin (CBDCA) + pemetrexed (PEM), docetaxel + ramucirumab, and amivantamab + CBDCA + PEM. CGP using tumor tissue identified EGFR V774_C775insHV (variant allele frequency [VAF] 66%), BRCA2 D427fs*3 (VAF 63%), and CDKN2A/CDKN2B/ MTAP losses, without a detectable BRCA2 second-hit event. Germline testing confirmed the BRCA2 variant as a GPV. Genetic testing of three relatives identified the same variant in his mother. Discussion: Although CGP is primarily used for treatment selection, it identified a BRCA2 GPV. While the causal relationship between BRCA2 GPV and LC remains unclear, PARP inhibitors may be an option. Risk-reducing surgery may also be considered for his mother. A Japanese paired tumor-normal sequencing study reported GPVs in only 2.2% of LC patients, whereas BRCA2 variants showed a 67% conversion rate. Conclusion: Although LC is generally considered to have a limited association with heredity, BRCA2 variants detected in LC may show a high germline conversion rate. The present case is consistent with these findings.
P1-05-01: Biallelic repeat expansions in intron 2 of RFC1 are a major cause of cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS). Pathogenic alleles harbor repeat motifs such as (AAGGG) or (ACAGG) instead of the reference (AAAAG) motif. Accurate detection of CANVAS-associated pathogenic repeat expansions by short-read sequencing remains challenging because of the large repeat size, GC-rich composition, and high sequence similarity among repeat motifs. Recent advances in long-read sequencing technologies, including Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT), enabled full-length characterization of these repeat expansions. However, precise discrimination among pathogenic motifs remains technically challenging because of platform-specific systematic errors and basecalling characteristics. Here, we compared the accuracy of pathogenic RFC1 repeat motif analysis between the two platforms using the latest sequencing chemistries and basecalling algorithms in more than 10 recently sequenced CANVAS cases. ONT more frequently mis-genotyped the (ACAGG) motif, whereas PacBio more frequently mis-genotyped the (AAGGG) motif. We also observed repeat-size misestimation associated with mis-genotyping of specific repeat motifs, as well as allele dropout resulting in failure to detect the second allele. Based on these findings, we characterized platform-specific error profiles and discuss optimal genotyping strategies for RFC1 repeat expansion analysis.
P1-05-02: Introduction: Risdiplam (RIS), an SMN2 splicing modifier, is effective in improving condition in patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). We examined urinary occult blood (OB) findings in SMA patients treated with RIS. Subjects: Eighteen SMA patients (type 2/3: 9/9, SMN2 gene copies 3/4: 15/3, M/F: 11/7, age 25.2 to 69.8 years (mean 44.2)). Method: We investigated the frequency of positive OB in urine tests before and after RIS start. Results: The data collection period before RIS start ranged from 1 to 5649 days (mean 3167), and the observation period after start ranged from 239 to 1450 days (1132). The number of urine tests before start ranged from 1 to 35 times (16.3), and from 4 to 24 times (11). after start. The positive rate of urinary OB test before start ranged from 0 to 25% (3.6) and from 0 to 100% (34.8) after start. Five cases showed negative urinary OB both before and after start. Six negative urinary OB cases before start became positive after start. In 6 cases with positive both before and after start, the percentage of positive rate increased after start. One case with positive before start turned negative after start. In one patient, urinary OB became negative after discontinuation of RIS. In another case, edema appeared during RIS administration, and the edema and the degree of OB reduced after dose reduction. Conclusion: In many cases, positive findings for urinary OB increase after RIS start. There are only a few reports of positive urine OB in post marketing surveillance. Large-scale investigation and elucidation of the causal mechanism are required.
P1-05-03: Background: Heterozygous loss of function variants in CTNNB1 cause neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity and visual defects (NEDSDV; OMIM 615075). We report a patient with a novel CTNNB1 variant presenting with neurodevelopmental disorder and lower limb dystonia. Case: The patient is an 11 years and 2 months old girl. Prenatal findings included fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios. At 10 months, she was evaluated for motor delay, but brain MRI and blood tests were unremarkable. At 1 year 9 months, she presented with short stature, microcephaly, distinctive facial features, hypotonia, and lower limb dystonia. From age 6, her dystonia worsened, accompanied by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and tantrums. At 7 years and 5 months, levodopa was initiated for dystonia and emotional dysregulation, leading to symptom stabilization. At 11 years 2 months, IRUD analysis identified a novel heterozygous CTNNB1 variant, c.1469_1470dup (p.Leu491Aspfs*17), classified as pathogenic based on her clinical features. Discussion:β - catenin encoded by CTNNB1 regulates dopaminergic neuron development. Dystonia in CTNNB1 related disorders likely reflects dysfunction in this pathway. Prior reports suggest levodopa may improve both motor symptoms and behavioral problems. Our findings indicate that early levodopa may benefit not only dystonia but also broader neurodevelopmental outcomes in CTNNB1-related disorders.
P1-05-04: The patient is a 19-year-old male. He had repeatedly exhibited altered consciousness during fevers since early childhood. Brain MRI revealed extensive lesions in the entire corpus callosum and bilateral white matter in the centrum semiovale, characterized by high signal intensity on DWI and FLAIR images, and low signal intensity on ADC maps. The symptoms and imaging findings resolved spontaneously, and the patient was diagnosed with mild encephalitis/encephalopathy with a reversible splenial lesion (MERS) Type II. His 10-year-old sister also had a history of recurrent altered consciousness during fevers since early childhood, and brain MRI revealed findings consistent with MERS Type II. No similar symptoms were observed in his parents or 16-year-old brother. Direct sequencing of the MYRF gene revealed a heterozygous missense variant c.1208A>G (p.Q403R) in the proband, his father and younger sister. The same variant was not found in his mother or younger brother. MYRF is a transcription factor essential for oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelin maintenance. This variant is located in a highly conserved DNA-binding domain of the MYRF gene, and previous functional analyses have shown that it reduces N-terminal transcriptional activity and may lead to reversible myelin vacuolization. Based on these findings, we diagnosed a pedigree of MERS with the MYRF gene mutation. Although MERS caused by a MYRF gene mutation was first reported in Japan in 2018, subsequent reports have been limited; we report this pedigree in conjunction with the review of literature.
P1-05-05: Background: Variants in the superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) gene are associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a progressive motor neuron disease leading to fatal respiratory failure. Gene-specific therapies have increased the clinical importance of determining the pathogenicity of individual SOD1 variants. We report a novel SOD1 p.Gly42Cys variant in a Japanese ALS family. Methods: Clinical, genetic, biochemical, and neuropathological analyses were performed in two affected family members. Results: The proband developed left-sided limb weakness at age 73 and died of respiratory failure 11 months after onset. Neuropathology showed anterior horn degeneration with SOD1-positive inclusions. His mother developed right leg weakness at age 68, required mechanical ventilation at age 71, and died at age 88. Neuropathology revealed degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons and multiple brain regions. Both cases harbored a heterozygous SOD1 c.124G>T (p.Gly42Cys) variant absent from HGMD and ClinVar. In silico analyses predicted pathogenicity. Biochemical studies showed preserved enzymatic activity and circular dichroism spectra, but reduced thermal stability. SDS-PAGE showed SOD1 oligomer formation, which was also detected in autopsied tissues. According to ACMG criteria, the variant was classified as pathogenic. Conclusions: We identified a novel pathogenic SOD1 p.Gly42Cys variant associated with late-onset, rapidly progressive familial ALS. Functional and neuropathological analyses supported its pathogenicity and the rationale for gene-specific therapies.
P1-06-01: [Background] Desmoplakin (DSP) cardiomyopathy is an arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy characterized by left ventricular fibrosis, late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), ventricular arrhythmias (VA), and myocarditis-like episodes. However, its clinical phenotype and outcomes have not been systematically quantified because existing studies are small and heterogeneous. [Methods] We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. PubMed and Embase were searched from inception to May 2026 for studies reporting clinical phenotypes and outcomes in carriers of pathogenic or likely pathogenic DSP variants. Primary outcomes were pooled prevalence of LGE on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and VA. Secondary outcomes included reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), myocarditis-like episodes, and heart failure hospitalization. [Results] A total of 122 studies including DSP variant carriers were analyzed. The pooled prevalence of LGE was 71% (95% CI, 63-79%), and the pooled prevalence of VA was 43% (95% CI, 37-49%). Myocarditis-like episodes occurred in 13% of patients, and reduced LVEF was observed in 24%. DSP cardiomyopathy commonly showed a left-dominant phenotype with extensive subepicardial fibrosis, despite moderate interstudy heterogeneity. [Conclusions] DSP cardiomyopathy is characterized by a high prevalence of myocardial fibrosis and ventricular arrhythmias, often disproportionate to the degree of systolic dysfunction. LGE may represent an early imaging marker preceding overt ventricular dysfunction.
P1-06-02: Early-stage diagnosis of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (PAF) is challenging owing to its asymptomatic nature. However, the genetic factors underlying PAF and predictive utility of polygenic risk scores (PRSs) remain elusive. We aimed to explore the PAF-associated genetic variants in a Japanese cohort and evaluate the predictive performance of PAF-specific PRSs. This study included 2,604 participants. Following exclusion, quality control, and genotype imputation, a genome-wide association study (GWAS) was conducted. The predictive performance of 30 sets of PRS models constructed across various thresholds was evaluated using three machine learning methods. Model performance was assessed using area under the curve (AUC) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). The GWAS using 1,038 PAF cases and 744 controls identified 82 genome-wide significant variants (P < 5 × 10-8), all on chromosome 4q25. Of these, 80 variants clustered upstream of PITX2. Fine mapping identified two independent intergenic signals, with rs2200732 as the lead single-nucleotide polymorphism. The best PRS-only model achieved an AUC of >0.70, which was improved up to 0.737 in additive models incorporating PRS and clinical variables. SHAP analysis consistently ranked PRS as the most influential predictor among the clinical variables included in this study. These results suggest that genetic risk, particularly at the established 4q25/PITX2 locus, contributes substantially to PAF susceptibility in this Japanese cohort and that PRS may improve early risk stratification when integrated with clinical risk factors.
P1-06-03: [Introduction] SCN5A-related disorders exhibit diverse electrophysiological phenotypes. Loss-of-function cause Brugada syndrome (BS) and sick sinus syndrome (SSS), whereas gain-of-function lead to long QT syndrome (LQTS). Variants associated with overlap syndromes have also been reported. We report a family with a pathogenic SCN5A variant identified in a child with LQTS-like electrocardiographic findings and a family history of BS and SSS. [Case] The proband was a previously healthy 10-year-old girl referred for QT prolongation detected during school-based cardiac screening. Holter electrocardiography demonstrated marked nocturnal QT prolongation, with a maximum corrected QT interval of 550 ms. Her father had been diagnosed with BS after syncope at 33 years of age and underwent cardioverter-defibrillator implantation with cilostazol therapy. The paternal grandfather developed SSS in his 50s and underwent pacemaker implantation. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic SCN5A (NM_000335.5) variant, c.5347G>A (p.Glu1783Lys). [Discussion] The SCN5A p.Glu1783Lys variant is associated with overlap syndrome phenotypes exhibiting both gain-of-function and loss-of-function properties. In this family, carriers of the same variant showed diverse arrhythmic phenotypes, including LQTS, BS, and SSS, supporting the concept that SCN5A-related disorders represent a continuous phenotypic spectrum rather than a single disease entity. Because phenotypes may differ even within the same family, comprehensive arrhythmia evaluation and proactive genetic testing are important.
P1-06-04: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is an inherited cardiomyopathy mainly caused by pathogenic variants in desmosomal genes including PKP2. Several studies have reported copy number variations (CNVs) in desmosomal genes associated with ARVC, most of which have been identified in PKP2. In this study, we aimed to detect CNVs in PKP2 in Japanese ARVC patients. The study cohort consisted of 65 probands diagnosed with definite, borderline, or possible ARVC based on the 2010 Task Force Criteria excluding Category IV (Family history), in whom no pathogenic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) or small insertions/deletions(indels) had been detected in ARVC-associated genes. Distinct CNVs in PKP2 were identified in five probands (7.7%) using multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification analysis. One proband had a whole-gene deletion, two had duplications (exon 8 and exon 8-10), and the remaining two had deletions (exon 8-10 and exon 8-14). All five probands were male and were diagnosed as "definite" ARVC. The mean age at diagnosis was 42 ± 25 years. During follow-up, all five probands developed sustained ventricular tachycardia and right ventricular dysfunction, with no evidence of left ventricular involvement. In conclusion, we identified PKP2 CNVs in approximately 8% of ARVC probands who had been negative for pathogenic SNVs and small indels. Screening for CNVs in PKP2 is indispensable for elucidating the genetic background of ARVC.
P1-06-05: Abstract Background: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) associated with sarcomeric gene variants exhibits diverse clinical phenotypes. While right ventricular (RV) involvement is recognized in HCM, marked hypertrophy isolated to the RV septum and apex remains a relatively rare manifestation. Case Presentation: A 54-year-old man with a maternal history of HCM underwent genetic screening following the birth of his child to assess hereditary risk. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated asymmetric septal hypertrophy (ASH), along with thickened RV septal and apical walls. Subsequent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed diffuse left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), sparing the posterior wall, in addition to significant ASH. Notably, MRI further confirmed extensive hypertrophy involving the RV septum and RV apex. Genetic testing identified a pathogenic in-frame deletion variant in TNNI3 (NM-000363.5:c.547_549del, p.K183del). Discussion: TNNI3-related HCM is characterized by phenotypic variability, often presenting with severe hypertrophy and apical involvement. However, concomitant RV septal and apical hypertrophy is uncommon and may represent a distinctive biventricular remodeling pattern associated with this specific sarcomeric variant. Conclusion: This case emphasizes the necessity of comprehensive phenotypic characterization, including RV morphology, in sarcomeric HCM. It also underscores the diagnostic utility of cardiac MRI in precisely evaluating complex biventricular involvement that may be initially detected by conventional imaging.
P1-07-01: Joubert syndrome is a congenital ciliopathy characterized by the molar tooth sign on brain MRI and may involve severe renal and respiratory manifestations. Biallelic TMEM67 variants cause overlapping phenotypes, including Joubert syndrome and Meckel-Gruber syndrome; however, rare missense and atypical splice-region variants are often classified as variants of uncertain significance. We report two Japanese siblings with a perinatal lethal Joubert syndrome phenotype who were born to healthy, non-consanguineous parents and re-evaluate shared TMEM67 variants. Both siblings showed oligohydramnios, bilateral cystic kidneys, cerebellar malformations suggestive of the molar tooth sign, and pulmonary hypoplasia. The first child was delivered at 35 weeks and 1 day and died 11 hours after birth due to severe respiratory failure. The second child was delivered at 30 weeks and 6 days and died approximately 2 hours after birth. Whole-exome sequencing of the first child identified compound heterozygous TMEM67 variants, c.1243G>A (p.Val415Met) and c.2100+3A>G. Sanger sequencing showed maternal inheritance of c.1243G>A and paternal inheritance of c.2100+3A>G, confirming a trans configuration. The same variants were identified in the second sibling. Both variants were extremely rare in population databases, and c.2100+3A>G is located at the +3 donor splice-region position. Rarity, trans configuration, co-segregation, and phenotype specificity support reclassification of both variants as likely pathogenic.
P1-07-02: In patients with congenital disorders, dual pathogenic variants are rare. However, comprehensive genomic analysis is gradually identifying cases involving multiple genetic mutations. We report a Japanese patient with double de novo pathogenic variants. He was a 19-month-old boy and had cafe-au-lait spots, macrocephaly, pectus carinatum, and developmental delay. Trio whole-exome sequencing analysis identified double de novo pathogenic variants. One was a recurrent missense variant in NF1 , and the other was a novel frameshift variant in H1-4 . NF1 is the causative gene for Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) (OMIM: 162200). NF1 is characterized by multiple cafe-au-lait spots, fibromatous skin tumors, and learning or behavioral difficulties. H1-4 is the causative gene for Rahman syndrome (OMIM: 617537). Rahman syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by mild to severe intellectual disability, overgrowth including increased head circumference, hypotonia, bone abnormalities, and dysmorphic facial features. H1-4 is a single-exon gene encoding histone H1.4. The variant identified in this study was a C-terminal frameshift variant, consistent with previously reported pathogenic variants in H1-4 . Such protein-truncating variants have been suggested to escape nonsense-mediated decay (NMD). In this patient, NF1 was suspected based on cafe-au-lait spots. However, macrocephaly and developmental delay were also observed, which could not be fully explained by NF1 alone. Careful interpretation of the clinical and genetic findings is necessary in such cases.
P1-07-03: CRYGC has been recognized as the gene responsible for congenital cataract. Recently, we identified a novel CRYGC frameshift variant in a 28-year-ol female patient with congenital cataract. The patient had a family history of cataract. Her father and paternal grand-mother also had cataract. Due to the congenital cataract, she had surgery to insert lenses at 18 years old. At that time, microphthalmia was suggested. Before having pregnancy, she intended to know whether her congenital cataract can be inherited. After genetic counseling and obtaining written informed consent, exome sequencing was performed and the CRYGC variant was disclosed. There are several types of crystallin proteins, including alpha, beta, and gamma. These types are related to the autosomal dominant trait. Although the information cannot be used for PGT-M, this likely helped her prepare mentally for pregnancy.
P1-08-01: Cleidocranial dysplasia (CCD) is characterized by delayed cranial suture closure, hypoplastic clavicles, and dental anomalies. Although most cases are caused by RUNX2 variants, rare CCD-like phenotypes have been linked to alterations involving MSX2. We report two unrelated patients with persistent anterior fontanelles carrying microduplications upstream of MSX2. Microarray analysis identified smaller duplicated regions than previously reported, refining the critical regulatory interval. To investigate the mechanism, we performed in silico analyses using public datasets. Epigenetic analysis of the minimal overlapping region (chr5:173848716_173888281) identified two transcriptionally active subregions with high chromatin accessibility in osteoblasts, suggesting regulatory activity during osteogenic differentiation. ATAC-seq analysis also showed preferential accessibility in osteoblasts over chondrocytes in human and mouse datasets, supporting a role in cranial bone development. The duplicated interval was entirely located within a single topologically associating domain (TAD), suggesting that intra-TAD duplications may alter MSX2 regulation and contribute to the CCD-like phenotype. Phenotypic differences, including synpolydactyly, may reflect involvement of regulatory elements outside the minimal overlapping region. These findings support a causal association between upstream MSX2 duplications and CCD-like phenotypes and highlight the importance of epigenetic regulation and chromatin architecture in skeletal development.
P1-08-02: Background: ANKRD17-related disorder is mainly recognized as a neurodevelopmental disorder. ANKRD17 encodes an ankyrin repeat-containing protein involved in cell-cycle progression. Whether ANKRD17-related disorder can resemble Noonan syndrome (NS) with short stature, characteristic facial features, congenital heart disease (CHD), and developmental delay (DD) remains unclear. We report a girl with ANKRD17-related disorder who was initially suspected to have NS. Case: A 6-year-old girl had atrial septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus at birth, auricular anomalies, characteristic facial features, epilepsy from 5 months, DD, and growth deceleration from around 1 year. Height at 4 years was 91.4 cm (-3.0 SD). An arginine stimulation test did not support growth hormone deficiency, and brain MRI showed no pituitary abnormality. NS was suspected. However, pulmonary valve stenosis (PS) was absent, and an NS gene panel was negative. Exome analysis identified a de novo heterozygous in-frame indel in the ankyrin repeat domain of ANKRD17. Discussion: Literature review identified one reported patient with ANKRD17-related disorder and an NS-like phenotype. Shared features included short stature, CHD, suggestive facial features, DD, absence of PS, and an in-frame indel in the ankyrin repeat domain. Domain-specific in-frame variants may affect ANKRD17 interactions. ANKRD17-related disorder could partly overlap with NS in phenotype and gene regulation. Conclusion: ANKRD17-related disorder should be considered in patients with short stature, CHD, characteristic facial features, and DD.
P1-08-03: More than 300 genes have been identified as causative genes for inherited retinal dystrophy (IRD), among which retinitis pigmentosa is the most common phenotype. The inheritance patterns of retinitis pigmentosa are genetically heterogeneous. We report a family with retinitis pigmentosa involving three affected siblings, two sisters and one brother. All patients became aware of night blindness during their late teens and were diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa in their twenties. Ophthalmological examination revealed bilateral retinal degeneration with characteristic pigmentary changes. Electroretinography showed non-recordable responses, and visual field testing demonstrated concentric constriction in all patients. The affected siblings exhibited remarkably similar ocular findings without systemic manifestations. Their parents were non-consanguineous, and no other family members had a history of retinal disease. Genetic analysis were performed and identified two variants in the EYS gene, c.4957_4958insA (p.Ser1653LysfsTer2) and c.2528G>A (p.Gly843Glu) in a compound heterozygous state common in all three cases. According to the ACMG/AMP guidelines for variant interpretation, both variants were assessed as pathogenic. The same pathogenic variants were shared among affected siblings. The EYS gene is a well-established cause of autosomal recessive IRD. This family is considered to represent autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa associated with compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in EYS, showing consistent phenotypes among affected siblings.
P1-08-04: Background: Germline BRCA (gBRCA) mutations and homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) may influence hematologic toxicity during platinum-taxane chemotherapy in ovarian cancer. This study evaluated the association between these molecular features and hematologic adverse events. Methods: Patients with stage III-IV ovarian cancer treated with platinum-taxane chemotherapy between 2022 and 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Hematologic adverse events were compared according to gBRCA and HRD status. A meta-analysis of published studies was also performed. Results: Eight gBRCA mutation carriers and 33 non-carriers were analyzed. Although gBRCA mutation carriers tended to show lower neutrophil counts, no significant differences in hematologic toxicities were observed during treatment. In the pooled meta-analysis, gBRCA mutation carriers showed increased risks of neutropenia (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.16-2.44) and G-CSF use (OR 3.09, 95% CI 1.19-8.03). No significant associations were observed for anemia, thrombocytopenia, dose delay, or dose reduction. Additionally, 23 HRD-positive and 15 HRD-negative patients were evaluated, and HRD positivity was not associated with increased hematologic toxicity. Baseline hemoglobin levels tended to be lower in HRD-positive patients; however, these differences were observed before chemotherapy initiation. Conclusion: gBRCA mutation carriers may have a modestly increased risk of neutropenia during platinum-taxane chemotherapy; however, treatment delivery was not compromised. HRD positivity itself was not associated with hematologic toxicity.
P1-08-05: <Introduction> Duplications of the Xq28 region are the most frequent chromosomal aberrations observed in patients with intellectual disability (ID), especially in males. Among them, the incidence of duplication including MECP2 is relatively high, and the ID is severe. The small duplication distal to MECP2 also cause ID. Here we report a case of ID having about 250 kb copy gain. This region contains GDI1 which is responsible for non-specific ID. <Patient> A 5-year-old male was born at 40 weeks gestation without no remarkable prenatal history. His birth weight and length were 3,184 g and 52 cm, respectively, and Occipitofrontal Circumference (OFC) was 33 cm. He was referred to our hospital due to delay of language development. An ophthalmologic evaluation revealed strabismus. He has no epilepsy so far. No family history about ID was recorded. He has moderate ID, currently, achieves some two-word sentences. <Genetic test results> Array CGH analysis showed copy gain at Xq28 with the size of 255 kb and log2 ratio of 1.189. The region does not contain MECP2, but FLNA and GDI1 located to distal. Digital PCR confirmed that the Xq28 duplication also exists on his mother without clinical findings. <Conclusion> This case having 255 kb duplication region at Xq28 including GDI1 shows moderate ID and no seizures. This implies that the phenotype of this small duplication distinguishes from that of duplications including MECP2. From the point of view of genetic counseling, genetic tests for the mother having the possibility of the same copy variant should be considered.
P1-08-06: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RTS) is a malformation syndrome caused by heterozygous variants in the CREBBP or EP300 genes, characterized by developmental delay, characteristic face, and broad thumbs and halluces. Although over 90% of individuals with RTS reportedly survive into adulthood, studies on its natural history are extremely limited. Our patient was clinically diagnosed with RTS during infancy. At his initial visit to our hospital at age 24, he showed multiple pilomatricomas on both thigh and left buttock and mild kyphosis but was able to extend his spine as instructed. From age 38, he developed low back pain and gait disturbance and was diagnosed with spinal canal stenosis, scoliosis, and kyphosis centered at T12/L1. At age 40, his femoral bone mineral density (BMD) was 0.544 g/cm2 (61.47% of the reference), and he was diagnosed with osteoporosis. Blood tests showed a slightly elevated 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D3 level, but serum calcium, phosphate, ALP, and intact PTH were within normal ranges. Genetic analysis identified a frameshift variant in CREBBP (NM_004380.3: c.4037del, p.Leu1346CysfsTer30). To our knowledge, there has been only one reported pediatric case of abnormal bone density in RTS. RTS is known to be associated with pilomatricomas, and studies using model mice have suggested possible abnormalities in calcium metabolism or calcification. These findings imply a potential link between RTS and bone metabolism. Further case accumulation and analysis are required to elucidate the prevalence and mechanisms of bone metabolic abnormalities in adult RTS patients.
P1-08-07: Background: Multigene panel testing (MGPT) enables comprehensive analysis of hereditary cancer-related genes and may identify pathogenic variants (PVs) in unexpected genes. We report a case in which an LZTR1 PV was identified by MGPT. Case: A woman in her 40s had a family history notable only for colorectal cancer in her mother. In her 30s, she developed right breast ductal carcinoma in situ and underwent total mastectomy. BRCA1/2 testing at that time was negative. Five years later, she developed contralateral invasive lobular carcinoma and underwent total mastectomy. Because of metachronous bilateral breast cancer, she was referred for further genetic evaluation. MGPT targeting 70 cancer-related genes identified a heterozygous LZTR1 variant NM_006767.3:c.1786-1G>A, registered in ClinVar as likely pathogenic (single submitter). Discussion: LZTR1 is mainly associated with schwannomatosis and Noonan syndrome. The patient had no personal or family history suggestive of either disorder. Noonan syndrome associated with LZTR1 PVs can follow either dominant or recessive inheritance; this variant is considered consistent with recessive inheritance. Considering clinical reports and family data on LZTR1 PVs, the risk as a hereditary cancer predisposition is considered limited, and no specific surveillance was recommended. However, family testing was offered because future evidence may clarify associations with malignancy. The patient understood the explanation well and showed no significant psychological distress. Follow-up will continue as new evidence emerges.
P1-08-08: Purpose: With advances in molecular genetics and the growing importance of clinical genetics, there is an increasing need to convey information to patients accurately and in an easily understandable manner. Our hospital established a Genetic Counseling Office in April 2025, where board-certified clinical geneticists and certified genetic counselors provide care. We will review the current status of our services and the challenges we face, and report on our future prospects. Subjects and Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of cases in which genetic counseling was provided at our hospital between April 2025 and January 2026. Results: We conducted genetic counseling for 66 cases. The most common topic of consultation was perinatal issues, including prenatal testing, accounting for 60 cases (90.9%); this was followed by familial tumors (4 cases, 6.1%) and mitochondrial diseases (2 cases, 3.0%). Regarding referral sources, 62 cases (93.9%) were referred internally; of these, 60 were referred from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology and 2 from the Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism. Conclusion: Our immediate challenge is to raise awareness of the Genetic Counseling Office among other departments within the hospital and at other institutions, encouraging them to utilize our services. We also consider it important to organize joint conferences and study sessions with nearby medical institutions and other departments to foster engagement in the field of clinical genetics.
P1-08-09: Introduction: Down syndrome regression disorder(DSRD) is characterized by the acute or subacute onset of cognitive decline, insomnia, mutism, catatonia, and psychotic symptoms in adolescents or young adults with down syndrome. Although the etiology of DSRD remains unclear, recent studies have suggested that immune dysregulation may contribute to its pathogenesis and the effectiveness of immunological therapies. We report two cases with Down syndrome and DSRD who were treated with oral corticosteroids. Case : Both patients were women with Down syndrome in their 20s who were living independently with minimal support. One patient developed a sudden decrease in speech output, decline in activities of daily living (ADL), psychiatric symptoms, catatonia, and insomnia without an identifiable trigger. The other patient developed cognitive decline, decline in ADL, psychomotor slowing, and obsessive behaviors following an environmental change. Both were diagnosed with DSRD. Oral steroid therapy was initiated, after which improvement in clinical symptoms was observed. Discussion: Reliable diagnostic biomarkers and standardized treatment strategies for DSRD have not been established. Although several reports have described the therapeutic efficacy of intravenous immunoglobulin(IVIg), there are few reports regarding treatment with oral corticosteroids. Further accumulation of cases is needed to clarify the role of immune dysregulation in DSRD and to evaluate the efficacy and indications of steroid therapy.
P1-08-10: Cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS) is an autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia caused by biallelic repeat expansions in intron 2 of RFC1. AAGGG and ACAGG repeat expansions are considered pathogenic, whereas AAAGG repeat expansions are thought to be pathogenic when the repeat size exceeds 500 units. Several other repeat motifs have been observed at this locus, making it highly complex. We screened 192 families with genetically undiagnosed spinocerebellar degeneration (SCD) and 56 families with hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) collected from 2000 to 2023. PCR using flanking primers was followed by repeat-primed PCR in patients without normal-length bands. Long-read sequencing was performed in three families (families 1-3) in whom no normal-length band was detected by flanking PCR, but pathogenic repeat expansions could not be identified by repeat-primed PCR. In family 2, an AAAGG repeat expansion of fewer than 500 repeats was detected. In family 1, an allele with complex repeat configuration containing AAAGG repeats together with interspersed AAAGGG and AAAAGG repeats was identified, whereas in family 3, an allele with AAAGG and AAAGGG repeats was suggested. Both configurations were considered unlikely to be pathogenic. In total, pathogenic RFC1 expansions were found in six families with homozygous (AAGGG)exp and two with compound heterozygous (AAGGG)exp/(ACAGG)exp. These results indicate that long-read sequencing can help determine the clinical significance of AAAGG expansions by confirming repeat number and motif structure.
P1-08-11: Background: Intellectual disability (ID) is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). In April 2014, the "ID clinic" was established at the Center for Medical Genetics, Shinshu University Hospital. We provide clinical diagnosis, systematic genetic evaluation, and genetic counseling to individuals with ID and families. We previously reported interim findings at the 69th annual meeting and now present the overall progress from 2014. Methods: Genetic testing has been basically carried out in the following order unless a specific genetic disorder was clinically suspected: (1) G-banded chromosome analyses and chromosomal microarray analyses (CMA); (2) Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) using custom gene panels for NDDs; (3) Some individuals underwent trio-based whole-exome sequencing (WES) through the Initiative on Rare and Undiagnosed Diseases. Results: Up to March 2026, we had recruited 335 individuals (187 males, 148 females) with ID/DD (developmental delay). Seizures and autistic behavior were observed in 155 and 128 individuals, respectively. The total diagnostic yield was 47% (159/335). CMA and trio-based WES identified pathogenic variants in 28 of 211 (13%) and 31 of 70 (46%), respectively. Targeted NGS using various custom gene panels led to diagnoses in 76 individuals. Inherited pathogenic variants included 14 autosomal dominant, 8 autosomal recessive, 5 X-linked, and 1 imprinting disorder. Conclusion: The current genetic evaluation framework at the "ID clinic" appears effective for establishing diagnosis and providing genetic counseling.
P1-08-12: Background: Tumor-only comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) can identify presumed germline pathogenic variants (PGPVs) in hereditary cancer genes. Single-site germline testing is often selected to confirm CGP-reported PGPVs for economic reasons. We report a breast cancer case in which testing for a CGP-reported PALB2 pathogenic variant failed to detect the target but identified another nearby variant. Case: A 47-year-old woman was diagnosed with bilateral breast cancer in year 20XX. She developed recurrence in year 20XX+3 and received systemic therapy. In year 20XX+6, when standard options were nearly exhausted, tumor-only CGP reported PALB2 c.3202-1G>A as pathogenic. After genetic counseling, single-site testing for this variant was performed. The target was not detected; instead, PALB2 c.3350+5G>A was identified. The CGP laboratory later revealed that c.3350+5G>A had also been detected by CGP but was filtered out because it was classified as benign under the then-current laboratory pipeline. After a ClinVar-based pipeline update, the variant was called pathogenic. Her younger sister carries the same variant and will undergo high-risk surveillance. Conclusion: PGPVs detected by tumor-only CGP suggest possible germline origin, but discordance with germline testing may reflect reporting filters and later variant reclassification rather than absence from CGP data. This case highlights the need to review unreported CGP-detected variants and current classifications when single-site testing confirms secondary findings, as discrepancies can affect familial risk assessment.
P1-08-13: Introduction: Haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is a rare monogenic autoinflammatory disorder caused by heterozygous TNFAIP3 variants. It is characterized by dysregulated NF-κB signaling and frequently presents with Behcet-like manifestations, including recurrent oral and genital ulcers, fever, and systemic inflammation. However, pediatric-onset HA20 may present with organ-limited manifestations, complicating early diagnosis. Case Presentation: We report a Japanese girl with recurrent genital ulcers accompanied by only one febrile episode without other systemic manifestations. Given the non-herpetic nature of the lesions and a strong family history of immune dysregulation, genetic evaluation was pursued. Targeted sequencing identified a novel heterozygous nonsense variant in TNFAIP3 (c.491G>A, p.Trp164Ter), which was absent from public variant databases. Functional analysis demonstrated that the mutant protein failed to suppress TNF-induced NF-κB activation, confirming its pathogenic loss-of-function effect. The patient was diagnosed with HA20 and clinical improvement was observed following treatment with prednisolone and colchicine. Conclusion: This case highlights the diagnostic importance of genetic and functional analyses in pediatric patients presenting with unexplained recurrent genital ulcers. Identification of a novel pathogenic TNFAIP3 variant further expands the clinical and molecular spectrum of HA20 and underscores the need to consider monogenic autoinflammatory diseases in atypical, organ-limited presentations.
P1-09-01: ATP6V0A1 encodes the a1-subunit of the V0 domain of vacuolar H+- ATPase (V-ATPase), which plays an essential role in lysosomal acidification and intracellular proton transport. ATP6V0A1 variants are associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, with phenotypic severity varying depending on the variant. Particularly, the R804H variant is reported in severe phenotypes including stillbirth, although its molecular pathogenesis is not yet fully understood. We report a stillborn fetus at 28 weeks of gestation in which a de novo ATP6V0A1 p.R804H variant was identified by trio-based whole-exome sequencing. To investigate the molecular pathogenesis of this variant, we performed in silico structural analyses using AlphaFold3, mCSM-membrane, and the AlphaFold Server. Structural analysis demonstrated that the R804H variant caused only mild destabilization of the ATP6V0A1 monomer (δδG = -0.159 kcal/mol), while suggesting weakened interactions between the V0A1 and V0C subunits, potentially impairing V-ATPase complex stability and proton transport function. The R804H variant may impair V-ATPase function by disrupting inter-subunit interactions at the c-ring interface, potentially contributing to the severe fetal phenotype. Functional validation studies are ongoing.
P1-09-02: Background: RAPADILINO syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in RECQL4. This syndrome is characterized by skeletal abnormalities, short stature, gastrointestinal manifestations, and cancer predisposition, while cognitive function is typically preserved. Adult cases are rarely reported. Case: A 43-year-old woman presented for genetic evaluation of an undiagnosed disorder. She had severe short stature, patellar hypoplasia, radioulnar synostosis, chronic diarrhea, and early-onset malignancy. Despite repeated evaluations since childhood, no diagnosis had been established. RAPADILINO syndrome was suspected based on her symptoms. Genetic testing identified a homozygous pathogenic variant in RECQL4, confirming the diagnosis. In adulthood, she developed Hashimoto disease, osteoporosis, iron deficiency anemia, chronic inflammatory manifestations, and spastic paralysis, requiring multidisciplinary care. Genetic diagnosis enabled integrated understanding of her symptoms, cancer surveillance, and genetic counseling. However, psychosocial and healthcare-related challenges emerged due to the rarity and complexity of the disorder. Discussion: This case demonstrates that RAPADILINO syndrome may remain undiagnosed until adulthood and that multisystem manifestations can progress over time. Although genetic diagnosis improved disease understanding, it also revealed psychosocial and healthcare-related challenges. Conclusion: Comprehensive post-diagnostic management and support are essential for adults diagnosed with rare hereditary disorders.
P1-09-03: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type (AMDM) is a congenital bone dysplasia caused by bialleic mutation in the natriuretic peptide receptor 2 (NPR2) gene. A Japanese man was born to consanguineous parents of normal stature. He learned to walk by the age of two. After injuring his back on the horizontal bar at around 11 years of age, he became difficult to stand and walk and eventually became wheelchair-bound. He developed quadriplegia and restrictive ventilatory impairment with recurrent pneumonia after the age of 52 due to cervical compressive myeloradiculoneuropathy. Although foramen magnum decompression surgery and a C1 laminectomy were performed at the age of 54, no improvement was observed. He eventually became bedridden, underwent tracheostomy, required mechanical ventilation, and underwent gastrostomy. His height was 93 cm. he had acromesomelic limb shortening with brachydactyly. Skeletal radiological findings revealed disproportionately shortening of forearm bones, short and wide metacarpals and phalanges, and flattened vertebral bodies. Based on these findings, he was clinically diagnosed with AMDM. Whole exome sequencing using genomic DNA identified a homozygous missense variant in the NPR2 gene (NM_003995): c.653G>C (p.Arg218Pro), This variant is not listed in ClinVar, has not been reported in population databases of healthy individuals, and was not detected in 49 in-house control samples. p.Arg218Pro was predicted to be deleterious by MutationTaster and possibly damaging by PolyPhen-2, suggesting an association with AMDM.
P1-09-04: CLDN19 variants cause familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis type 2 (FHHNC2), with renal and ocular features; sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is not part of the established spectrum. Burgos Martin et al. (Nefrologia 2024) reported a Spanish patient with the same homozygous variant and SNHL but did not systematically exclude alternative deafness genes. We evaluated an Ecuadorian family whose 26-year-old male proband presented with congenital nephrocalcinosis (stage 5 CKD on hemodialysis), bilateral SNHL diagnosed in 2011, refractory anemia, secondary hypertension, femorotibial deformity, and unilateral visual loss. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) of the proband, mother, and sister was performed, and all hearing loss genes curated by the ClinGen Hearing Loss Gene Curation Expert Panel (DiStefano et al., 2019) were screened. WES identified a homozygous CLDN19 c.59G>A, p.(Gly20Asp) (ClinVar Pathogenic; gnomAD AF 2.25×10-5), a recurrent allele in Spanish/ Hispanic populations (Martin-Nunez et al., 2014); his mother and sister are unaffected heterozygous carriers, supporting autosomal recessive inheritance. ClinGen-curated hearing loss gene screening detected no additional pathogenic variants, excluding alternative monogenic causes. This represents the second independent occurrence of CLDN19 p.(Gly20Asp) homozygosity with SNHL. Whether SNHL belongs to the CLDN19-related spectrum remains an open question; further studies in larger FHHNC2 cohorts are needed to clarify this and to disentangle direct from hypomagnesemia-mediated effects.
P1-09-05: [Objective] Short-read next-generation sequencing (NGS) is widely utilized for genetic testing of monogenic and hereditary disorders. However, variant detection remains challenging in complex regions containing highly homologous sequences or tandem repeats. Recently, long-read NGS approaches have been applied to overcome these limitations. Therefore, we have evaluated a long-amplicon sequencing strategy combining long-range PCR and Nanopore sequencing. Here, we report findings on the ABCC6 gene as a model case harboring a highly homologous pseudogene across exons 1-9. [Methods] Long-range PCR for amplification of the target region exceeding 23 kb was performed using a commercial reference genomic DNA. The purified amplicon was processed using the Native Barcoding Kit24 V14 and sequenced on the MinION Mk1C platform. Sequencing data were analyzed through a bioinformatic workflow, including quality control, read mapping, and haplotype-resolved consensus sequence generation. [Results and Discussion] A sufficient amount of target amplicon for library preparation was obtained by long-range PCR. The optimized bioinformatic processes reduced Nanopore sequencing error and enabled accurate variant calling. The specific short-read variant call errors were identified by comparison of the obtained Nanopore sequencing data with publicly available short-read NGS reference datasets. In conclusion, the long-amplicon sequencing strategy is a powerful approach for resolving difficult genomic regions that cannot be accurately determined by conventional short-read NGS platforms alone.
P1-09-06: Background: Vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy is characterized by seizure cessation or improvement following vitamin B6 administration. The causative genes of ALDH7A1 and PNPO are well-established entities, and more recently PLPBP has been reported. Case Report: The patient was the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous Japanese parents. His first seizure occurred at 9 months of age during a febrile illness. Thereafter, he developed both febrile and afebrile seizures and was diagnosed with epilepsy. At 3 years of age, he developed convulsive status epilepticus triggered by fever. He showed generalized hyperkinetic seizures accompanied by vocalization and agitation. Based on the clinical presentation, febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome (FIRES) was suspected, and barbiturate coma therapy was initiated. Attempts to wean him from coma therapy were unsuccessful except for intrathecal dexamethasone therapy. However, seizure relapses continued to occur every 1-2 months. His general condition progressively deteriorated, and he died of intracranial hemorrhage at 5 years of age. Genetic Analysis: Targeted epilepsy gene panel testing performed shortly before death identified a homozygous PLPBP variant, NM_007198.4:c.122G>A:p. (Arg41Gln), leading to the diagnosis of vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy caused by PLPBP deficiency. Conclusion: This case expands the phenotypic spectrum of PLPBP-related vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy. The disorder should be considered in the differential diagnosis of late-onset, fever-triggered refractory epilepsy.
P1-09-07: Background: CYP21A2, responsible for 21-hydroxylase deficiency (21OHD), and TNXB, responsible for classical-like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (clEDS), are located adjacently within the RCCX module containing highly homologous pseudogenes. Non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) can generate a 30 kb deletion from CYP21A2 to TNXB (CAH-X allele); and biallelic CAH-X alleles cause clEDS. CAH-X alleles are classified into CH1, CH2, and CH3 from the chimeric junctions; detailed molecular mechanisms of which remain unclear. This study aimed to clarify the mechanisms of CAH-X allele formation. Methods: We recruited 144 cases with clinically diagnosed 21OHD, confirmed genetically by long-read sequencing. Cases carrying the CAH-X alleles were analyzed through our custom TNXB analysis. Results: CAH-X alleles were identified in 33 alleles (11.5%) from 31 cases. Two homozygous cases also had clEDS. 16 cases (18 alleles) had CH1, 9 had CH2, and 6 had CH3. Two cases had an atypical allele with the characteristic 120 bp deletion of CH1 but without a missense variant in exon 40. From mRNA analysis, the 120 bp deletion was suggested to cause aberrant splicing leading to a frameshift. Discussion: The frequency of CAH-X alleles was comparable to previous reports in Asian cohorts. The atypical alleles could not be explained by a simple NAHR event, suggesting complex rearrangements with gene conversion. Phenotypic variability in CAH- X might be related not only to TNXB protein deficiency by splicing abnormality but also to impaired trimer formation of remaining protein by the missense variant.
P1-09-08: Introduction: KDM6B-related neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) was initially described in 2019 as NDD with coarse facies and mild distal skeletal abnormalities (NEDCFSA). However, a 2023 cohort study revealed that these features are infrequent, while the disorder involves multisystem manifestations. Despite this prognosis, the number of reported cases remain limited, and Japanese cases are poorly characterized. Case: A 6-year-old boy presented with macrocephaly, overgrowth, severe global developmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder. At 5 years and 11 months, he had no meaningful words, and his developmental index was 28. Electroencephalography and brain MRI were normal. Prominent forehead, macrocephaly, low-set ears, a pointed chin, and a long face prompted chromosomal microarray analysis, which revealed no causative findings. Whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous frameshift variant (NM_001080424.2:c.43delG, p.(Glu15Lysfs*8)) in KDM6B, leading to a diagnosis of KDM6B-related NDD. Parental testing suggested a de novo variant absent from gnomAD and databases, indicating a novel pathogenic variant. Discussion: In this case, macrocephaly, overgrowth, and core manifestations of NDD were observed, whereas coarse facies and skeletal abnormalities were absent. This phenotype was more consistent with the clinical spectrum redefined in the 2023 analysis than with the 2019 definition. Therefore, genetic evaluation should be considered for suspected KDM6B-related NDD based on neurodevelopmental manifestations, regardless of facial or skeletal abnormalities.
P1-09-09: Introduction: Biallelic variants in FARSA reduce cytosolic phenylalanyl tRNA synthetase (FARS1) activity, leading to a multisystem disorder including congenital alveolar proteinosis (PAP). Here, we report the genetic diagnosis of an infant with FARSA-related disease and our assessment of preimplantation genetic testing for a subsequent pregnancy in this family. Case: The patient was a boy born at 36 weeks' gestation with fetal growth restriction. He subsequently developed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and interstitial lung disease consistent with PAP. His phenotype included cholestatic liver disease, cystic periventricular leukomalacia with global developmental delay, hypothyroidism, and pituitary posterior lobe atrophy. He died at 11 months of age from multiorgan failure with gastrointestinal bleeding associated with DIC. Targeted sequencing for PAP identified two heterozygous missense variants in FARSA. In our multidisciplinary genetics conference, one variant, corresponding to a previously reported amino acid substitution, was classified as likely pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines, whereas the other was a novel variant interpreted as VUS. Therefore, preimplantation genetic testing was not considered applicable at that time. Discussion: In disorders where residual enzymatic activity shapes the phenotype, variant interpretation must go beyond in silico prediction to include functional assays. Responsibly incorporating research based genomic findings on ultra rare diseases into clinical and reproductive decision making remains a major challenge.
P1-09-10: Background Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) are occasionally encountered among patients with undiagnosed diseases. CDG IIc is characterised by severe psychomotor developmental delay, mild morphological abnormalities and impaired neutrophil motility, and is known to be an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the GDP-fucose transporter (SCL35C1). There have been no reports of this disease in Japan. Case A 2 year and 4 month old girl. The child was born at 32 weeks and 3 days gestation. She was followed up for SGA and short stature. Her short stature became pronounced, with height at -5SD to -6SD and weight at -3SD to -4SD. She presented with developmental delay, characteristic facial features, hearing loss, elevated serum ALP levels, and abnormalities on bone X-ray. Genetic testing for FGF3 revealed no pathogenic variants, and the patient was enrolled in the IRUD. Methods: After written informed consent from the parents, trio whole-exome sequencing, comprehensive glycan analysis of plasma, and glycan analysis using established B-cell lines (fuc-loaded) were performed. Results Genomic analysis revealed a homozygous SCL35C1 nonsense variant in the patient. Glycan analysis in plasma and blood cells confirmed that fucose residues were almost entirely absent from all glycans. Recovery of fucose residues was observed following fucose loading of cultured B cells. Conclusion We report the first case of CDG IIc in Japan. We have demonstrated the potential for correction of glycan abnormalities through the administration of large doses of fucose.
P1-10-01: Chromosomal copy number variations (CNVs) and aneuploidies are major causes of fetal structural anomalies. Current standard methods, including G-banded karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis, require 7-21 days, limiting timely decision-making. We evaluated low-pass nanopore sequencing as a rapid, portable alternative for prenatal CNV detection. Genomic DNA was extracted from six validation cases: male and female controls, trisomy 13, a 6.3- Mb deletion at chr11, a 1.4-Mb deletion at 16p13.11, and a mosaic isochromosome 18p (15% mosaicism). Libraries were prepared using Rapid Sequencing Kit V14 and sequenced on MinION, terminated at 1-4 Gb of sequencing data. Reads were aligned to GRCh38 using minimap2 and CNVs called using QDNAseq with 1-Mb bins. Trisomy 13 was detected at 1 Gb (0.31x coverage; log2 ratio +0.58, matching theoretical value). A 6.3-Mb deletion on chromosome 11 was identified at 1 Gb, establishing 5-Mb or larger CNVs as reliably detectable at this threshold. The 15% mosaic isochromosome 18p produced detectable signal at chromosome 18p across all quantities tested (1, 2, and 4 Gb), exceeding theoretical predictions. The 1.4-Mb deletion at 16p13.11 was not detected at 2 Gb. The workflow from DNA extraction to result was completed within 5-6 hours at 1 Gb. These findings support a two-tier strategy: MinION at 1 Gb for same-day screening of aneuploidies and CNVs of 5 Mb or larger, and PromethION at higher coverage for smaller CNVs and mosaic variants, offering advantages in turnaround time, portability, and accessibility for regional medical settings.
P1-10-02: Background: Pallister Killian syndrome (PKS) is a rare chromosomal disorder characterized by mosaic tetrasomy 12p caused by an isochromosome of chromosome 12p [i(12p)]. Because PKS exhibits tissue-limited mosaicism, cytogenetic testing may yield false-negative results. We report a case in which WES-derived CNV analysis using umbilical cord tissue after termination revealed a 12p copy gain suggestive of PKS. Case Presentation: A 27-year-old primigravida was referred at 15 weeks of gestation. Fetal ultrasound demonstrated long bone shortening, atrioventricular septal defect, and generalized edema. Chorionic villus sampling revealed a normal female karyotype on SNP array. Pregnancy was terminated at 20 weeks. Babygram suggested skeletal dysplasia but was inconclusive. WES using DNA extracted from uncultured umbilical cord tissue identified no pathogenic variants. However, CNV analysis derived from WES data detected a copy gain involving chromosome 12p, raising suspicion of PKS. Discussion & Conclusion: Prenatal diagnosis of PKS remains challenging, and many cases are diagnosed incidentally during evaluation of increased nuchal translucency. Mosaic fractions may decrease during cell culture. In this case, WES-derived CNV analysis using uncultured umbilical cord identified a 12p copy gain that had not been detected by SNP array using chorionic villus samples. Although the phenotype strongly suggested PKS, partial trisomy 12p could not be excluded because chromosomal structure was not directly evaluated. This approach may aid detection of copy number abnormalities in mosaic cases.
P1-10-03: Introduction: Karyotyping is mainly used for detecting chromosomal aneuploidies and structural aberrations in patients with congenital anomalies and developmental delay. However, certain genomic imbalances remain undetectable by conventional G-banding. Recent advances in molecular cytogenetic analysis, particularly chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), have clarified the presence of submicroscopic or cryptic chromosomal imbalances that may escape detection by karyotyping. We report three cases of cryptic unbalanced translocations which were clarified by CMA. Case: The three patients, all of whom had normal karyotypes, included a 1-year-old boy with multiple congenital anomalies (Case 1), a 5-year-old girl with developmental delay (Case 2), and an 11-month-old girl with holoprosencephaly (Case 3). CMA identified a 27-Mb duplication at Xp22.33p21.3 and a 38-Mb deletion at Yq11.222q12 in Case 1; a 4.6- Mb deletion at 6q27 and a 5.1-Mb duplication at 10p15.3p15.1 in Case 2; and a 3.8-Mb deletion at 18p11.32p11.31 with a concomitant 1.4- Mb duplication at 21q22.3 in Case 3. Discussion: CMA is widely used for detecting submicroscopic copy number variants (CNVs) that are difficult to identify by karyotyping. Moreover, the presence of concomitant terminal deletions and duplications strongly suggests underlying unbalanced translocations, even in cryptic rearrangements. Conclusion: Combined genomic approaches using karyotyping and CMA improve the diagnostic yield in patients suspected of harboring structural chromosomal aberrations, particularly cryptic translocations.
P1-10-04: Structural abnormalities of the sex chromosomes involve unique mechanisms such as X-chromosome inactivation and X-Y pairing. Therefore, careful consideration is warranted regarding both phenotypic expression and genetic counseling implications. The patient was a 3-year-old boy with speech delay and congenital left clubfoot. Cytogenetic analysis using G-banding and chromosomal microarray analysis, performed to investigate the underlying cause, revealed a karyotype of 47,XY,dic(X;X)(qter->p11.22::p22.2->qter). While the presence of multiple regions with excess X chromosomal material is expected to result in clinical features resembling Klinefelter syndrome, the SHOX gene located in the PAR1 region was present in only a single copy, suggesting that tall stature is unlikely to occur. Dicentric chromosomes are known to arise as recombinant chromosomes derived from parental inversions. In this case, involvement of the X chromosome suggested a maternal origin. The karyotype was considered to result from recombination associated with a paracentric inversion and nondisjunction. The patient has a male sibling. If he also carries the pericentric inversion of the X chromosome, chromosomal imbalance is unlikely in the next generation due to X-Y pairing but may appear in subsequent generations. Only a limited number of cases of male patients with dicentric chromosomes derived from paracentric inversion of the X chromosome have been reported. This case illustrates the underlying genetic mechanism and underscores the importance of long-term risk assessment in genetic counseling.
P1-10-05: Background: Chromosomal heteromorphisms, among which inv(9) is the most well-known, are common constitutional chromosomal variants that generally carry no clinical relevance. The prevalence of inv(9)(p12q13) has been reported to vary among ethnic groups and institutions, while data from Japanese laboratories remain limited. To date, no large cohort studies have investigated the prevalence of chromosomal heteromorphisms other than inv(9)(p12q13). Here, we retrospectively investigated the frequencies of chromosomal heteromorphisms in Japanese pediatric patients. Methods: We reviewed the results of karyotyping obtained between April 2016 and March 2026. Subsequently, the frequencies of chromosomal heteromorphisms were calculated. Results: Among 2,674 cases, inv(9) (p12q13) was identified in 35 (1.31%), representing the most frequent variant. Other variants, including inv(1)(p11q12), inv(1)(p13q21), inv(1)(p13q12) and inv(2)(p11.2q13), were observed in 5 (0.19%), 2 (0.07%), 1 (0.04%) and 1 (0.04%) cases, respectively. Conclusions: The prevalence of inv(9)(p12q13) was consistent with previously reported data (1-3%). Our study may contribute to a better understanding of the prevalence of chromosomal heteromorphisms beyond inv(9).
P1-11-01: Background: Radiotherapy response in cervical cancer varies among patients. We developed an ensemble machine learning approach to identify radiosensitivity associated missense variants in DNA damage response genes. Methods: Somatic missense variants from 307 TCGA- CESC patients were analyzed. Variants were annotated using ANNOVAR and dbNSFP with pathogenicity and conservation metrics. Random Forest and XGBoost models were integrated by ensemble prediction. Biological relevance and clinical significance were evaluated using pathway and survival analyses. Results: Seventy missense variants were analyzed, and ensemble learning identified 22 high confidence radiosensitivity associated variants, including BRCA2, CHEK2, TP53, ATM, POLE, XRCC2, and PRKDC alterations. Key predictive features included CADD, REVEL, and conservation metrics. Enriched pathways involved homologous recombination and DNA double-strand break repair. Carriers of high-confidence variants showed significantly improved overall survival compared with noncarriers (log-rank P=0.029). Noncarriers also showed worse survival in multivariable Cox analysis (HR 3.06, 95% CI 1.10-8.48). Conclusions: Ensemble machine learning identified clinically relevant radiosensitivity associated variants in cervical cancer, supporting AI-assisted radiogenomic approaches for precision radiotherapy.
P1-11-02: RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) is a powerful technique for the quantification of transcripts and the analysis of alternative splicing. Previously, our laboratory developed the targeted RNA long-amplicon sequencing (rLAS) method, which has the advantage of allowing deep analysis of targeted specific transcripts. The computational tools for analyzing RNA-Seq data have boosted alternative splicing research by detecting and quantifying splicing events. However, the performance of these splicing tools has not yet been investigated for rLAS. Here, we evaluated the performance of four splicing tools (MAJIQ, rMATS, MISO, and SplAdder) using samples with different types of known splicing events (exon-skipping, multiple-exon-skipping, alternative 5 splicing, and alternative 3 splicing). MAJIQ was able to detect all of the types of events, but it was unable to detect one of the exon-skipping events. On the other hand, rMATS was able to detect all of the exon-skipping events. However, rMATS failed to detect other types of events besides exon-skipping events. Both MISO and SplAdder were unable to detect any of the events. These results indicate that MAJIQ presents better performance for the different types of splicing events in rLAS and that rMATS shows better performance for exon-skipping splicing events.
P1-11-03: For a better understanding of the molecular pathogenesis caused by genomic variants in non-coding regions, many of which appear to be associated with characteristic phenotypes of recessive metabolic disorders, we applied deep learning-based models to evaluate RNA structures and RNA processing in silico. Clinical investigations and genome-wide association studies have identified numerous potentially pathogenic variants in non-coding regions. However, the pathogenic mechanisms of these variants remain largely unclear, partly because experimental analyses of transcripts, non-coding RNAs, and intronic regions are technically challenging in vivo, and also because these regions are less well characterized than protein-coding genes. Recent advances in deep learning technologies, including SpliceAI, have substantially improved transcriptome analysis, enabling more accurate prediction of splice pattern alterations caused by cryptic splice variants and facilitating estimation of the pathogenic effects of mutations. Using these approaches, we investigated variants located in regions adjacent to genes responsible for urea cycle disorders. We further examined the relationships between the energy imbalances observed as phenotypic traits in heterozygous carriers of the variants we previously reported and the splice pattern alterations predicted in silico.
P1-11-04: Background While conventional eQTL studies have provided significant findings, most of them did not analyze isoform level expression. Recently, we and other groups analyzed association between genetic variations and isoform expression level and identified isoform eQTLs (ieQTLs). However, these studies have not analyzed structural variations (SVs). Methods We integrated SV obtained from the 1000 Genomes Project with full-length isoform expression profiles derived from long-read sequencing of 67 human B-cell lines. We performed a eQTL analysis followed by identifying causative SVs associated with isoform expression levels (SV-ieQTLs). We also examined association of SVs with expression level of gene (SV gene eQTLs). Results Among 9556 SVs, 56 were identified as causative SVs, of which 41.1% (23 SVs) were classified as ieQTL-specific, modulating expression level of specific isoforms without significant effect in total gene expression level. Functional enrichment analysis shows different feature between gene-level eQTL and isoform specific eQTL. A comparison with genome-wide association studies (GWAS) data revealed 6 SV-ieQTLs linked GWAS hit of immune-related, hematological traits, suggesting that analysis of SV-ieQTL can uncover previously hidden causative variants. Conclusions To our knowledge, this is the first study to characterize SVs associated with isoform-specific expression at a genome-wide scale. Our study suggests that SVs can affect the expression level of isoform, and analysis of SV-ieQTL reveals regulatory mechanism of isoforms and novel causative genes of GWAS.
P1-11-05: We investigated structural biases in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), particularly the tendency for minor alleles to be preferentially detected as risk alleles. Using p-value simulations and analyses of publicly available GWAS catalogs, we evaluated whether the imbalance between minor and major risk alleles could be explained solely by statistical detection power. We confirmed that this tendency was especially prominent among variants with low minor allele frequency (MAF), particularly below 0.1. Although the overall magnitude of the imbalance was modest in many traits, several diseases showed a substantial excess of reported risk alleles corresponding to minor alleles. In particular, traits with relatively low average risk allele frequency, such as myopia and sudden cardiac arrest, demonstrated patterns that exceeded expectations based on statistical power differences alone. These observations suggest that structural and evolutionary factors, including negative selection, may contribute to systematic biases in GWAS risk allele detection. Such biases may also influence downstream analyses, including polygenic risk prediction and cross-population transferability. To address these issues, we are currently exploring statistical correction approaches based on causal inference frameworks. Our long-term goal is to improve the robustness and interpretability of GWAS findings and to contribute to more reliable and equitable genetic risk prediction across populations. In this presentation, we report recent findings and ongoing developments related to these bias-aware approaches.
P1-11-06: While over half a million distinct LINE-1-related loci comprise ~17% of the human genome, a limited number of these loci remain active, i.e. capable of mobilizing. Molecules generated by active LINE-1 are proposed to trigger inflammation. However, which LINE-1 loci are mobile, and the extent of inter-individual presence/absence polymorphism of these active LINE-1, is incompletely resolved. Analysis of long-read sequencing data from 1,019 individuals recently enumerated 208 transpositionally-active LINE-1 "source" regions, based on evidence that these LINE-1 have mobilized adjacent unique sequences during their transposition in human germlines; all but 17 of these "source" LINE-1 are polymorphic in the population studied. To understand how these recently-active LINE-1 varied in other populations, we used MEGAnE, which genotypes LINE-1 polymorphisms using short-read sequencing data, to analyze 2,503 genomes from 1000 Genomes Project participants and 4,653 genomes in a US-based cohort (PEGS). Of the 837 LINE-1 variants detected in both cohorts, 61 were among the recently-active LINE-1 defined above. These findings provide a foundation for investigating active LINE-1 element polymorphisms, genome-wide dosage of active LINE-1, and potential associations of these genotypes with human phenotypes.
P1-12-01: The indications for BRCA1/2 genetic testing(GT) covered by insurance in breast cancer(BC) patients are: 1) aged 45 or younger; 2) triple-negative BC aged 60 or younger; 3) two or more primary BC; 4) a family history of breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer within third-degree relatives; 5) male BC; and 6) with a history of ovarian, fallopian tube, or peritoneal cancer. Detailed assessment of family cancer history is important, but it is difficult to obtain comprehensive information. In our hospital, Certified Genetic Counselors (CGC) interview family cancer history prior to the physician examination. We evaluate the effectiveness of collaboration with CGC. A total of 366 patients underwent BRCA GT between 2019 and 2025. The indication for GT was CDx for Olaparib in 81 cases and HBOC diagnosis in 283 cases. 2 were out-of-pocket. 16 were found to carry a pathogenic variant(PV) in BRCA1 , 24 in BRCA2 , and 12 had a VUS. Regarding the criteria for insurance coverage, 99 cases(35%) met the criteria solely on family history 4). Among the 400 BC patients who underwent surgery between 2022 and 2025, 218 (55%) met the criteria for insurance-covered genetic testing. Among 218 cases, only 16(7%) were not performed due to a lack of consent . Through collaboration with CGC, the identification of patient groups eligible for insurance-covered BRCA GT has been appropriately facilitated. This has also enabled smooth counseling for individuals with PV and their relatives, representing a significant achievement in the establishment of a genetic counseling system.
P1-12-02: In 46,XY disorders of sex development (DSD) with a female phenotype, androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is often suspected. However, discordant endocrine findings may cause diagnostic uncertainty, complicating genetic counseling (GC). We report three cases. Case 1(15-year-old) presented with primary amenorrhea, absent uterus, and inguinal gonads. Although AIS was suspected, endocrine findings suggested adrenal steroidogenic defects. After inconclusive evaluation, CYP17A1 variants confirmed 17α-hydroxylase deficiency. GC was challenging due to diagnostic revisions and conflicts regarding gonadectomy and disclosure. Case 2(16-year-old) showed amenorrhea, and inguinal gonads. Low testosterone with elevated gonadotropins suggested gonadal dysfunction, inconsistent with AIS; diagnosis remains inconclusive. GC was complicated by parental reluctance toward disclosure. Case 3(17-year-old) presented with amenorrhea and mild clitoromegaly. Testosterone increased after hCG stimulation but did not fit a single diagnosis. GC was limited by family involvement and incomplete evaluation due to relocation. Diagnostic uncertainty necessitates revising assumptions, decision-making under limited information, and careful disclosure, while limiting discussion of prognosis, fertility, and malignancy risk. Unlike AIS, where a confirmed diagnosis guides counseling, these cases lacked a clear basis for explanation and decision-making. In conclusion, diagnostic uncertainty complicates GC in 46,XY DSD by obscuring the basis for explanation and decision-making. Ongoing, adaptive counseling is essential.
P1-12-03: Introduction Oncofertility care requires management of treatment-related fertility impairment and counseling based on genetic background in patients with hereditary cancer syndromes. Because fertility preservation is often performed before cancer treatment, clinical information may be incomplete at referral. We report a case highlighting the importance of confirming hereditary cancer-related information during oncofertility counseling.
