Case A 35-year-old unmarried man was referred for sperm cryopreservation before adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery for appendiceal cancer (cT3N2M0). Review of referral documents revealed microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), prompting further inquiry. The referring institution had suspected Lynch syndrome and performed additional immunohistochemical evaluation. Discussion Further confirmation revealed that the patient had been diagnosed with Lynch syndrome, although this had not been shared at referral. In addition to standard oncofertility counseling, we explained the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, 50% transmission risk, and future reproductive options including preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M), followed by sperm cryopreservation. This case demonstrated that hereditary cancer-related information may not be fully communicated in time-sensitive oncofertility practice. Conclusion Hereditary cancer syndromes should be considered in young cancer patients undergoing oncofertility counseling. Proactive confirmation of pathology and genetic background is essential.
P1-12-04: Introduction: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) is characterized by generalized joint hypermobility and multisystem symptoms and has recently been associated with mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS). We report a family with hEDS in whom genetic counseling contributed to symptom improvement. Case: The patients were three siblings (two females aged 18 and 16 years and a 9-year-old male) with generalized joint hypermobility and chronic pain since childhood. The eldest sister required an electric wheelchair, and the second sister had recurrent anaphylaxis and syncope. Although no causative variant was identified, all siblings were clinically diagnosed with hEDS. Their mother had sought detailed information and comprehensive care at multiple institutions but had not received sufficient support. After referral to our hospital in 2025, genetic counseling facilitated information sharing regarding MCAS and multidisciplinary collaboration, resulting in a marked reduction in anaphylactic episodes. Discussion: Because hEDS presents with heterogeneous symptoms and lacks established molecular markers, affected families often experience difficulty obtaining appropriate support. In this case, genetic counseling promoted information sharing and multidisciplinary collaboration regarding MCAS, leading to symptom improvement. This case highlights the potential role of genetic counseling in connecting families with appropriate medical care and support.
P1-12-05: Objective: To evaluate the disclosure and genetic counseling (GC) process for patients with suspected or confirmed hereditary tumor syndromes identified through comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP). Patients and Methods: Electronic medical records were retrospectively reviewed for 314 CGP tests submitted between December 1, 2019, and March 25, 2026. Results: Testing included 251 tumor-only patients (FoundationOne, n=200; FoundationOneLiquid, n=51) and 63 tumor-normal paired patients (Oncoguide, n=33; GenMineTOP, n=30). Disclosure for suspected hereditary tumor syndromes was recommended in 26 patients: 24 (9.6%) from tumor-only testing and 2 (3.1%) from paired testing, representing 30 variants total. Variants included BRCA2 (n=6), ATM (n=5), MSH6 (n=3), CDH1/MEN1/TP53 (n=2 each), and BRCA1/BRIP1/MSH2/ RAD51C/RAD51D/SDHB/SMAD4/STK11/TSC2/VHL (n=1 each). Following disclosure, 7 patients and 2 family members (whose affected relatives declined GC) received counseling with a certified genetic counselor. Only 2 of 26 patients (7.7%) completed confirmatory germline testing; one was diagnosed with Lynch syndrome. Separately, one pancreatic cancer patient underwent germline BRCA1/2 testing as part of routine clinical care and was diagnosed with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. Conclusion: Fewer than 10% of patients with suspected hereditary tumors identified through CGP at our institution proceeded to confirmatory germline testing. The institutional process from CGP submission through result disclosure and genetic counseling is under review to improve uptake.
P1-12-06: In 2026, Japanese National Health Insurance coverage of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC) cascade testing was expanded to first-degree relatives. However, HBOC cascade testing has conventionally relied on single-site testing for the germline pathogenic variant (GPV) identified in the proband. This expansion raises a counseling issue how to explain the implications of limiting testing to the known familial GPV versus pursuing broader analysis when the client's diagnosis or the opposite parental lineage suggests additional hereditary risk. We report a woman in her 40s whose mother had undergone BRACAnalysis four years earlier and was found to carry a BRCA2 GPV. Cascade testing was offered at that time but deferred. Her paternal family history was notable for ovarian cancer in her grandmother and aunt. After being diagnosed with breast cancer, she underwent genetic evaluation for HBOC. Insurance-covered BRACAnalysis identified the known maternal BRCA2 GPV and an additional BRCA1 GPV suspected to be of paternal origin. If cascade testing had been limited to single-site testing, the BRCA1 GPV might have remained undetected. This case illustrates a practical dilemma in HBOC cascade testing whether to restrict testing to the known familial GPV or to consider broader analysis based on the client's diagnosis and opposite parental lineage. In this report, we discuss how genetic counselors can support informed decision-making regarding test selection while balancing clinical utility, health-economic considerations, and unexpected findings.
P1-12-07: Background: HHT is characterized by arteriovenous malformations affecting organs and can lead to serious complications even in pediatric patients (pts). We therefore proactively offer consultation regarding genetic testing (GT) not only to probands but also to their relatives, irrespective of age. Method: Pts who were clinically suspected of having HHT and were seen for genetic counseling (GC) between January 2021 and January 2026 were identified from the medical records. Results: In this period, 78 pts with HHT were managed at our institution. GC was attended by 24 pts (30.8%). Following GC, 21 pts (87.5%) proceeded with GT. Fifteen pts (71.4%) were genetically confirmed to have HHT. Among those with ENG variants, multi-exon deletions were detected, and some pts underwent MLPA analysis. Although ten pts (41.7%) were genetically diagnosed as probands, all had at-risk relatives, 60% expressed interest in GT for their family members. Eleven relatives subsequently presented for GC. The ages of the relatives ranged from 0 to 73 years. In relation to the probands, 8 were children. GT was performed in 10 relatives (90.9%), of whom 5 (50.0%) were confirmed to have HHT. Discussion: Most pts who underwent GC proceeded to GT, and the diagnostic yield was comparable to, or slightly lower than previous reports. The potential addition of MLPA analysis remains an issue for further consideration. Approximately 40% of at-risk relatives did not attend GC, which may be attributable to factors such as residence outside the prefecture or prior clinical diagnosis.
P1-12-08: Background: VHL syndrome is a hereditary tumor syndrome that often cause multiple tumors during childhood and requires long-term disease management, making psychosocial support essential. This study focused on how patients and families live with VHL. Methods: Participants were recruited from Kyoto University Hospital and a patient advocacy group. Sixty-minute semi-structured interviews were conducted and analyzed using thematic analysis. Result: A total of 28 VHL syndrome-related individuals participated, including 16 affected relatives, 8 unaffected relatives, 3 spouses, and one parent of a sporadic case. Participants diagnosed during childhood or not fully aware of their condition tended to be optimistic, whereas those with severe symptoms or intensive treatment were often preoccupied with treatment and unable to focus on their heredity and future. Over time, participants came to accept VHL syndrome as part of themselves, found meaning in living with VHL syndrome, and hoped to inspire their children by showing that they were living fulfilling and enjoyable lives. Children wanted honest disclosure of the hereditary nature without parental guilt, as they felt grateful for their birth and wished to be respected as autonomous individuals. Discussion: Diagnosis experiences shape initial perceptions of VHL syndrome, which may change over time as individuals integrate the disease into their lives. Genetic professionals are expected to support reflection on these experiences and facilitate parent-child communication when emotional expression is hindered.
P1-12-09: Background: Lynch syndrome(LS) is caused by germline variants in mismatch repair (MMR) genes. In colorectal cancer, mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry(MMR IHC) and microsatellite instability(MSI) testing are used as screening tools for LS in Japan. We report a case of somatic BRAF V600E-mutated colorectal cancer with a pathogenic variant in MLH1. Case: The client(CL) was a 70-year-old man. He had a history of rectal cancer at 45 years of age and gastric cancer at 59 years of age. At 70 years of age, he developed ascending colon cancer and MSI-high status was detected in the surgical specimen, was referred for suspected LS. Pre-assessment of the family history revealed no relatives with a history of cancer, and the referral letter did not include information regarding somatic BRAF mutation analysis. However, documents brought by the CL on the day of consultation included a positive result for the somatic BRAF V600E mutation. After explanation of the standard diagnostic workflow, the CL and his wife requested germline genetic testing, which identified a pathogenic variant in MLH1. Discussion: BRAF V600E mutation generally suggests sporadic colorectal cancer and argues against LS; however, exceptions have been reported. The CL may represent such an exception, or the current colorectal cancer may have been sporadic while some previous tumors were associated with LS. These findings suggest the importance of comprehensive clinical assessment and involvement of genetic department even in patients with BRAF V600E-mutated colorectal cancer.
P1-12-10: Background: Selective termination of pregnancy (TOP) for fetal structural anomalies causes profound parental grief. In multiple anomalies, genomic autopsy is crucial to establish a definitive diagnosis. Unconfirmed etiologies often cause self-blame and anxiety regarding future pregnancies. Genomic autopsy is vital in perinatal grief care to alleviate guilt and enable genetic counseling with precise recurrence risks. Case: A woman in her 30s presented with multiple fetal anomalies at 13 weeks, including increased nuchal translucency, cystic hygroma, congenital heart disease, radial hypoplasia, and a single umbilical artery. Transport challenges precluded the scheduled amniocentesis. Under diagnostic uncertainty, maternal depression worsened, leading to termination at 19 weeks. Post-mortem G-band karyotyping did not yield results because of insufficient metaphase cells. Subsequently, cell culture-independent droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) successfully identified Trisomy 18. This definitive diagnosis provided profound relief, resolving guilt and restoring hope for future pregnancies. Discussion and Conclusion: This case highlights ddPCR as a rapid genomic autopsy modality when conventional cytogenetics is inconclusive. Establishing sporadic Trisomy 18 through post-mortem genomic autopsy served as a vital psychological turning point, resolving self-blame with evidence-based reassurance of low recurrence risk. Genomic autopsy for fetuses with structural anomalies is a critical intervention supporting parental mental health and safeguarding reproductive self-determination.
P1-13-01: Background: Japan's 2022 NIPT certification framework requires decision-making support for pregnant women and their partners. We quantified (1) perceived vs. actual concordance on primary NIPT purpose, (2) gender asymmetry in information gathering, and (3) gender differences in post-negative guilt. Methods: Women with negative NIPT results (n=98) and partners (n=79) completed questionnaires independently on disclosure day (June 2025-April 2026). 64 couples (65% pairing rate) were analyzed with Cohen's kappa, Fisher's exact test, and Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: Although 84.8% of couples reported aligned views, concordance on primary NIPT purpose was 58.9% among concordant couples. Women more often identified as the primary information seeker (75.5% vs. 50.6%; intra-couple concordance 31.3%); more women read clinic information thoroughly (75.5% vs. 36.7%; p<0.001). Guilt was reported by 40.8% of women and 21.5% of men (Fisher p=0.009; Wilcoxon p=0.028). Women citing "options including pregnancy termination" showed higher prevalence of guilt (48.2%); no difference in men (p=0.972). Counseling satisfaction, information volume, and perceived agreement were unrelated to guilt. Conclusions: Perceived joint decision-making may mask clinically relevant discordance, even after genetic counseling. Information-gathering burden fell disproportionately on women, and post-negative guilt was more prevalent among women and associated with testing purpose among women only. Assessing each partner's purpose may reveal unmet needs; gender-sensitive post-test care may be warranted.
P1-13-02: [Background] As genomic medicine advances, understanding public perceptions of genetic information-related health conditions is important. Genetic discrimination and disability stigma have been studied in East Asia, but acceptance in personal relationships has not yet been compared among Japan, Korea, and Taiwan. [Methods] Web survey, October 2025; adults aged 20~69 in metropolitan areas (N=1,200; 400/country). Acceptance of persons with four health conditions as a dating partner, spouse, colleague, or friend, perceived discrimination, and views on prevention measures were compared. [Results] Acceptance declined with relationship intimacy across all conditions and countries. Mental disability had the lowest acceptance as a friend: Japan 30.3%, Korea 29.5%, and Taiwan 54.8%. The highest acceptance was for family history of cancer in Japan and Korea (50.5%, 63.5%) and physical disability in Taiwan (81%). For physical disability, rare disease, and family history of cancer, acceptance was highest in Taiwan and lowest in Japan. "No discrimination exists" was highest in Japan (51.8%; Korea 26%, Taiwan 27%); so was "no measures needed" (38.3%; Korea 11%, Taiwan 4.5%). [Discussion/ Conclusion] Social acceptance varied by health condition across all countries. In Japan, lower acceptance and recognition of discrimination suggest that discrimination may be latent. The findings provide data for discussing public perception and legal measures against genetic discrimination. The interpretation of responses selecting "none of the listed relationships" requires further analysis.
P1-13-03: Background Interest in Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) in genomic medicine and research has grown substantially. However, competencies required for researchers to implement PPI have not been well defined. This study explored competencies required for PPI practice through discussions with experts and patient/public contributors. Methods A draft competency framework was developed based on literature, guidelines, and practical PPI models. An opinion exchange workshop was conducted with 18 researchers in genomics and PPI and six patient/ public members in five groups. Participants wrote comments on sticky notes for each item, followed by group discussion. Comments were analyzed qualitatively. Results The draft framework consisted of 28 items across three domains: knowledge, skills, and attitudes. A total of 33, 50, and 30 comments were collected for the knowledge, skills, and attitudes domains, respectively. For knowledge, participants suggested tiered competencies according to experience level. For skills, comments highlighted the importance of clearly explaining technical terms and research concepts and coordinating communication between researchers and contributors. For attitudes, participants emphasized respect for contributors as equal partners, psychological safety, and understanding the core philosophy of PPI. Discussion These findings suggest that, in addition to knowledge and skills, attitudes emphasizing collaboration with patient/public contributors and understanding PPI principles are important. Further evaluation of this framework is needed.
P1-13-04: Polygenic scores (PSs) are increasingly expected to be used in clinical and preventive healthcare settings for predicting risks of common diseases. While discussions on the ethical, legal, and social implications (ELSI) of PSs have mainly focused on theoretical concerns, less attention has been paid to the practical challenges faced by institutions attempting to return PS results to patients or service users. We conducted exploratory interviews with stakeholders involved in pilot attempts to return PS information in Japan, including researchers, healthcare professionals. The aim was to identify practical concerns arising during implementation and to examine how stakeholders understand and manage the uncertainties associated with PSs. Interviewees commonly recognized the probabilistic nature of PSs as a major communication challenge. Difficulties were reported in explaining limited predictive power, population differences, and appropriate responses following disclosure. Concerns were also raised regarding user misunderstanding and the lack of established social norms surrounding PS use. At the same time, several institutions emphasized the importance of gradual implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and communication strategies adapted to non-specialist users. These findings suggest that PS implementation raises broader questions regarding social understanding and governance under conditions of scientific uncertainty. This poster discusses emerging themes from the interviews and their implications for future ELSI frameworks for PS implementation in Japan.
P1-13-05: Since fetal surgery for myelomeningocele (MMC) was introduced in Japan in 2020, options after prenatal diagnosis have expanded. However, eligibility is limited by gestational age, requiring rapid decision-making. Although criteria are defined, how families decide in Japan remains unclear. This study clarifies the decision-making process after prenatal MMC diagnosis in this emerging context. We conducted semi-structured interviews with five women whose fetuses had MMC and were considered for fetal surgery at The University of Osaka Hospital between April and August 2025. Interviews covered diagnosis to decision-making. Data were analyzed using thematic narrative analysis focusing on emotion, cognition, decision-making over time. The process was categorized into three phases: pre-diagnostic, diagnosis, decision-making. All five participants were multiparous, with four undergoing fetal surgery and one choosing termination of pregnancy. Pre-diagnostic phase involved anxiety due to uncertainty. At diagnosis, participants experienced distress and time pressure due to gestational limits and surgery eligibility. In decision-making, factors included prognosis, attachment, disability views, family impact, support, information consistency. These findings suggest that prenatal decision-making for MMC after the introduction of fetal surgery in Japan is time-sensitive and complex. Support should start at the suspicion stage and provide balanced prognostic information under uncertainty. Continuous, nondirective, and value-sensitive care is essential for decision-making.
P1-13-06: Polygenic scores (PGS) may support risk stratification and personalized prevention for common diseases and health-related traits. However, returning PGS results to non-specialists requires careful communication, because PGS are probabilistic, population-based, and do not determine disease onset or individual outcomes. In this study, we describe the implementation of PGS-based results in a Japanese direct-to-consumer genetic testing service and examine communication issues for general users. In our implementation, to improve comprehensibility for general users, genetic risk is classified into five risk groups. We present odds ratios relative to the average group and using our own data, provide information on disease prevalence by sex, age, and genetic risk group. We also show standardized scores so that users can understand their relative position in the distribution. To date, we have not received notable feedback indicating that these explanations or displays are difficult to understand, suggesting that the current presentation is generally accepted by users. We will further evaluate whether PGS-based results are accurately understood without major misconceptions and whether they promote behavioral change by conducting a user survey. By combining a real-world service implementation case with user survey data, this study aims to identify communication challenges in the social implementation of PGS in consumer genomics services and to provide insights for developing best practices.
P1-13-07: <Background> Research involving sex and gender may raise ethical issues, including bias in study design and stigmatization resulting from the presentation of findings. Addressing these concerns requires not only ethics review but also appropriate publisher policies. This study examined ethical considerations required at the publication stage for sex and gender related research in human genetics. <Methods> We identified the top 30 journals in the "GENETICS & HEREDITY" category of the 2024 Clarivate Journal Citation Reports. Between January and March 2026, we collected the latest versions of each journal Guide to Authors, Editorial Policies, and related documents available through primary links. Two researchers independently analyzed the content. <Results> Considerations regarding sex or gender in study design were described in 19 journals (63.3%), whereas considerations regarding the potential impact of findings on groups appeared in only six journals (20.0%). Design related considerations included reporting sex or gender disaggregated data and clarifying definitions and assessment methods. Considerations related to group impact included careful use of terminology and avoidance of potential harms to particular groups. <Conclusion> Ethical considerations related to sex and gender are not comprehensively addressed in the publisher policies of human genetics journals. Further efforts by researchers and publishers are needed to mitigate potential harms and ensure socially responsible communication of research findings.
P2-01-01: Objective: We report on three cases of azoospermia in couples in which rare X-chromosome-related chromosomal abnormalities were identified. Case 1: The G-banding analysis of a 30-year-old man revealed a karyotype of 46,XX, so we performed FISH and detected a single SRY signal on one of the X chromosomes. We concluded that he was an XX male and explained that the likelihood of recovering sperm from the testis was not possible. Case 2: A 30-year-old man underwent TESE. Two fertilized embryos were obtained via ICSI treatment, and transferred. However, pregnancy did not occur. G-banding examination revealed a balanced reciprocal translocation of 46,XY,t(X;7)(p22.3;p15). We proposed genetic counseling regarding PGT-SR treatment. However, they declined. Case 3: The G-banding analysis of a 28-year-old man revealed a karyotype of 46,X,i(Y) (q11.2)?[27]/45.X,[3], and AZF gene testing identified a deletion encompassing the AZFb+c regions (Y chromosome long arm partial deletion type III). Although we explained that there was virtually no chance of obtaining sperm even if TESE were performed, the patient requested TESE treatment because the condition was not Y chromosome long arm partial deletion type II (Y del-q2). No sperm was recovered and so the patient did not request FISH testing to confirm the Y chromosome breakpoint. Conclusion: In cases of male infertility presenting with azoospermia, conducting genetic counseling and testing at an appropriate time is important as above.
P2-01-02: Introduction: Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Structural Rearrangement (PGT-SR) is indicated for couples with chromosomal structural abnormalities. Chromosomal structural abnormalities are associated with a high risk of miscarriage and are often diagnosed through chromosomal testing during investigations for recurrent pregnancy loss. We report a case of a couple with no history of pregnancy or miscarriage, in whom a balanced reciprocal translocation was identified following an evaluation for severe oligozoospermia, and who subsequently underwent PGT-SR. Patients: A 36-year-old woman, G0P0, and her 37-year-old husband consulted a local clinic after two years of infertility, and they were referred to our hospital due to severe oligozoospermia. G-banding analysis revealed a balanced reciprocal translocation. As the couple requested PGT-SR, they underwent oocyte retrieval and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) following genetic counseling. PGT-SR was performed on nine blastocysts, resulting in one transfer-grade embryo. A frozen-thawed embryo transfer was performed in a natural ovulatory cycle, resulting in pregnancy that ended in early miscarriage. The couple underwent a second ICSI cycle, and PGT-SR was performed on two blastocysts. One showed mosaic monosomy 5 and the other exhibited multiple aneuploidies. We are planning the third ICSI cycle. Conclusion: Even in a couple with no history of pregnancy or miscarriage, chromosomal structural abnormalities may be identified as a result of male infertility. PGT-SR could serve as useful tool for infertility treatment.
P2-01-03: Background: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is a hereditary tumor syndrome caused by germline pathogenic variants in STK11. Surveillance for gastrointestinal polyps and malignancies is important in PJS, and women may develop ovarian tumors, including sex cord tumor with annular tubules (SCTAT) and mucinous tumors. Because ovarian tumor surgery may affect future fertility, reproductive perspectives should be considered alongside tumor management. Case: A 40-year-old nulligravid woman with PJS had undergone multiple gastrointestinal polypectomies since childhood. At 21 years, she underwent bilateral ovarian cystectomy for SCTAT. At 31 years, she underwent unilateral ovarian cystectomy for a 24-cm mucinous ovarian tumor. At 35 years, she developed torsion of a 17-cm mucinous ovarian tumor, requiring unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. At 40 years, she visited reproductive medicine because of a desire for pregnancy and primary infertility. Her anti-Mullerian hormone level was 1.13 ng/mL. Two stimulation cycles yielded two good-quality embryos in total. Pregnancy was not achieved after frozen embryo transfer. Conclusion: This patient required multiple ovarian surgeries for bilateral SCTAT and recurrent large mucinous ovarian tumors reported in PJS, and fertility-related issues became apparent during infertility treatment. In women with PJS, the potential impact of ovarian surgery on future fertility should be assessed early, together with genetic counseling, tumor surveillance, and reproductive counseling according to life stage and reproductive intentions.
P2-01-04: Chromosomal abnormalities involving the X chromosome contribute to female infertility, but their phenotypic impact is variable. Case 1 was a 30-year-old woman with primary infertility who underwent repeated ART. Despite 38 oocyte retrieval cycles, most oocytes showed cytoplasmic degeneration and only a few reached maturity, and two embryo transfers were unsuccessful. Case 2 was a woman with 46,X,del(X)(q23q25). Although blastocyst formation was observed, pregnancy was not initially achieved; however, she subsequently conceived a twin pregnancy following ART. Whole-exome sequencing and copy number analysis were performed in both cases, with X-chromosome inactivation analysis as appropriate. No pathogenic variants in known infertility genes were identified. In Case 1, a deletion at Xq27.3-q28 and a duplication at 18p11.23 suggested an unbalanced translocation, der(X)t(18;X)(p11.23;q27.3), with markedly skewed X-chromosome inactivation. In Case 2, a deletion at Xq23-q25 with presumed selective inactivation was observed, without structural rearrangement. Both cases shared partial monosomy of the X chromosome and may involve ovarian dysfunction similar to Turner syndrome. However, Case 1 showed severe oocyte maturation defects associated with an unbalanced translocation, whereas Case 2 retained reproductive potential and achieved pregnancy. These findings suggest that infertility associated with X chromosome deletions is not determined solely by gene dosage, but is also influenced by structural abnormalities and differences in the deleted regions.
P2-01-05: In recent years, our genetic counseling practice has increasingly encountered individuals considering oocyte donation or those who conceived through oocyte donation abroad. This presentation summarizes issues related to oocyte donation as observed through our clinical practice. Oocyte donation may be considered when women cannot produce oocytes, when repeated attempts with their own oocytes fail to result in a successful pregnancy, or when they wish to avoid transmitting a hereditary condition to their offspring. Oocyte donation is most commonly conducted using unrelated donors. Disclosure to donor-conceived children is recommended, yet there is no consensus regarding how much information about the donor should be available, including identity, appearance, education, occupation, or personal characteristics. Legal approaches to a child's right to know donor information differ among countries. Challenges include protecting donor privacy and establishing long-term systems for preserving donor information. Additional issues include donor recruitment and evaluation, oocyte cryopreservation, recipient assessment, donor-recipient matching, donor compensation, treatment costs, reproductive tourism, eligibility of unmarried or LGBTQ individuals, and the prevention of commercialization. Although broad discussion is important, the development of an appropriate regulatory framework is urgently needed. Furthermore, improving healthcare professionals' understanding of the diverse psychosocial backgrounds and motivations of both donors and recipients is critical.
P2-01-06: [Case] A couple in their late twenties conceived their first child naturally. At 29 weeks of gestation, fetal ventriculomegaly, polyhydramnios, and fetal growth restriction were detected. Prenatal ultrasonography revealed holoprosencephaly. The infant was delivered by elective cesarean section at 36 weeks and died on day 3 of life due to total anomalous pulmonary venous return. Chromosomal analysis and chromosomal microarray analysis identified an unbalanced translocation: 46,XX,der(18)t(18;20)(p11.2;q13.3). The couple attended genetic counseling to assess recurrence risk. [Clinical Course and Results] Parental chromosome testing and preimplantation genetic testing for structural rearrangements (PGT-SR) were discussed. Chromosome analysis revealed that the father carried a balanced reciprocal translocation, 46,XY,t(18;20)(p11.2;q13.3). The couple elected to undergo PGT-SR. No category A embryos were obtained during the first two cycles, and genetic counseling was provided regarding the interpretation and residual risks of category B embryos. A category A embryo was obtained in the third cycle, and embryo transfer resulted in an ongoing pregnancy. [Discussion] Identification of the genetic etiology shortly after birth enabled recurrence risk assessment and reproductive decision-making. Continuous genetic counseling, including grief support following the loss of the first child and discussion of the interpretation and residual risks of category B embryos, facilitated informed decision-making, reduced anxiety regarding recurrence, and contributed to a successful pregnancy.
P2-02-01: Background: Stickler syndrome is a hereditary disorder characterised by the Pierre Robin sequence, severe myopia, hearing loss, and joint abnormalities. Prenatal diagnosis is particularly challenging in cases involving an isolated cleft palate, but no cleft lip. Case report: A 31-week pregnant woman was referred to our hospital due to fetal limb shortening. The fetus's father had visual impairment, hearing loss, and characteristic facial features, and the paternal grandfather had similar findings, suggesting familial Stickler syndrome. Fetal ultrasound revealed mild limb shortening without any obvious skeletal abnormalities. As both FGR and limb shortening were present, chromosomal abnormalities and other syndromic disorders could not be excluded. No obvious micrognathia or cleft palate was detected prenatally. As the prenatal diagnosis remained inconclusive and specialised neonatal care might be required, delivery was planned at our institution. Following birth, the neonate was diagnosed with Pierre Robin sequence due to micrognathia and a cleft palate. Stickler syndrome was strongly suspected based on postnatal findings and family history. Discussion: Although familial Stickler syndrome was suspected prenatally, foetal findings were limited to non-specific features such as fetal growth restriction (FGR) and mild limb shortening. The absence of typical prenatal findings, together with the difficulty in detecting an isolated cleft palate, may have contributed to the diagnostic challenge.
P2-02-02: Background: Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) is increasingly used in prenatal genetic testing in Japan. However, genetic counseling is challenging when variants of uncertain significance (VUS), including copy number variants (CNVs), are detected. We report a case of a VUS microdeletion identified after abnormal first-trimester ultrasound findings. Case: A 36-year-old, gravida 4, para 1, woman was referred at 13 weeks of gestation. First-trimester ultrasound revealed increased nuchal translucency (3.5mm) and tricuspid regurgitation, with estimated risks of T21 >1:4, T18 1:31, and T13 1:64. At 16 weeks of gestation, amniocentesis with FISH and SNP- CMA was performed. Trisomies 21, 18, and 13 were excluded, but a 1.75-Mb microdeletion was identified on chromosome 10q. Deletions involving this region have been associated with developmental delay and intellectual disability, although unaffected carrier parents have also been reported. The exact extent of the deletion could not be confirmed. Second-trimester ultrasound revealed no apparent structural abnormalities, and parental testing results were unavailable by 22 weeks. The couple remained anxious and elected termination of pregnancy. The deletion was later shown to be inherited from the healthy father, but its clinical significance remained unclear. Discussion: CNVs detected by prenatal CMA may have uncertain boundaries and unclear clinical significance. Their interpretation is particularly difficult in prenatal care, where counseling and decision-making must occur within a limited timeframe.
P2-02-03: Background: In Japan, non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) has been provided under a government-involved certification system. Maternal age affects the prior risk of fetal aneuploidy, and ultrasound findings may suggest conditions beyond NIPT. Therefore, NIPT results should be interpreted with maternal age and fetal ultrasound findings. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 141 patients who underwent NIPT. Maternal age, indications, ultrasound findings, NIPT results, pregnancy outcomes, and postnatal findings were reviewed. Results: Among 141 cases, 136 were negative and 5 were positive: four for trisomy 21 and one for trisomy 18. All positive cases had abnormal fetal ultrasound findings, including increased NT, absent nasal bone, reversed ductus venosus flow, abnormal four-chamber view, and suspected cardiac anomalies. Of 14 cases with ultrasound findings, 5 were NIPT-positive, while none of the 127 cases without such findings were positive. Pregnant women of positive cases were aged 25-39 years, and none were aged 40 years or older. Among 9 NIPT-negative cases with ultrasound findings, no chromosomal abnormality was found after birth, although cardiac anomalies, cleft palate, micrognathia, low birth weight, and hydronephrosis were noted. Conclusion: All NIPT-positive cases had fetal ultrasound findings, which may be associated with positive NIPT results more than advanced maternal age. NIPT is useful for trisomy 13, 18, and 21, but should be interpreted with fetal ultrasound findings. Continued fetal and postnatal follow-up is important when ultrasound findings are present.
P2-02-04: Introduction: As a certified facility, our hospital has been offering NIPT for three types of trisomy. However, we occasionally encounter cases where family history suggests a higher risk of other conditions. This report presents three cases of patients who requested NIPT and underwent genetic counseling. Case 1: The first child has 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Chromosomal testing has not been performed on the parents. If they were concerned about a recurrence, they would have needed to undergo a FISH test, but they didn't. A healthy child was born. Case 2: The 31year old woman's older brother died in 1987 at 16 days of age due to OTC deficiency. The woman's mother is a carrier of OTC deficiency, but the woman and her older sister were diagnosed in childhood as non-carriers. It is unclear whether they underwent genetic testing. Therefore, if she is pregnant with a boy, we should be aware of the risk of OTC deficiency. A healthy baby girl was born. Case 3: The younger brother of a woman was diagnosed with Brugada syndrome at age 30. Brugada syndrome is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is possible to be a carrier even without symptoms. The outcome is unknown after GA20weeks. Conclusion: All three cases underwent NIPT, and the results were negative. Couples tend to focus on fetal abnormalities. However, assessing the couple's own risk, promoting an understanding of congenital anomalies, and monitoring the pregnancy are crucial for the health management of both mother and child.
P2-02-05: Background We report on a case in which NIPT was performed for a monochorionic triamniotic (MT) pregnancy. Case The client was a 21-year-old woman. She was diagnosed with an MT pregnancy following a spontaneous conception. An ultrasound examination at 11 weeks and 6 days of gestation revealed NT(nuchal translucency) measurement of 5 mm in one fetus. The client expressed anxiety about chromosomal abnormalities associated with increased NT and requested genetic counseling. During genetic counseling, she was informed that an increased NT may be associated with chromosomal abnormalities or congenital heart disease. To alleviate her anxiety, options for prenatal genetic testing were presented. Concerned about the risk of miscarriage associated with amniocentesis, the client underwent NIPT at 14 weeks. Results The NIPT result was negative. We explained that the likelihood of the three trisomies was considered quite low; that the increased NT was thought to be due to an imbalance in blood flow; and that even when twins share the same chromosomes, one may still have a heart condition, so continued ultrasound follow-up would be necessary. Subsequently, the client was admitted for management of MT pregnancy and threatened preterm labor starting at 17 weeks of gestation, and a scheduled cesarean section was performed at 34 weeks and 4 days. Due to prematurity, the infant was admitted to the NICU. Discussion It was suggested that NIPT was a useful option for multiple pregnancies in which abnormalities were identified during an ultrasound examination.
P2-02-06: Preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M) in muscular dystrophy raises complex issues regarding disease severity, predictability, and ethical considerations. In this study, we comparatively examined Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy (FCMD), and myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), focusing on disease characteristics, genetic uncertainties, and the current regulatory framework in Japan. A multidisciplinary approach involving clinical geneticists, genetic counselors, neurologists, pediatric neurologists, reproductive specialists, and obstetricians was employed to analyze the decision-making process. PGT-M should be considered one of several reproductive options, rather than being uniformly recommended or discouraged. Given the inherent uncertainties in genotype - phenotype correlations and disease progression, supporting informed and autonomous decision - making is essential. This study integrates clinical, genetic, ethical, and social perspectives to clarify current challenges and future directions for PGT-M in muscular dystrophy.
P2-02-07: Background: Myotonic dystrophy type1 (DM1) is caused by CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene, with anticipation and predominant maternal transmission in the congenital form(CDM1). Polyhydramnios is a known antenatal finding, yet prenatal diagnosis remainschallenging when other sonographic features are absent. Case Report: A 36-year-old primigravida (G1P0) with prior myomectomy underwent cervical cerclage at 24 weeks. Polyhydramnios was noted from 30 weeks: OGTT was negative. Fetal movement was preserved with no sonographic signs of hypotonia. At 34 weeks and 4 days, emergency cesarean was performed for threatened uterine rupture. A female infant (2007g: Apgar 5/5: pH 7.441) required immediate intubation due to hypotonia and SpO2 <60%. CDM1 was confirmed postnatally (1800 - 1900 CTG repeats). Parental testing revealed the mother carried 150 - 200 CTG repeats (allele 1: <34), with grip myotonia and cataracts onretrospective assessment, confirming previously undiagnosed DM1. The father's result wasunavailable. Conclusion: This case illustrates the diagnostic challenge of CDM1 when polyhydramnios is the sole antenatal finding. The marked CTG repeat expansion from mother to infant exemplifies anticipation in maternally transmitted DM1. The mother's diagnosis was madeonly after her child's birth, highlighting the importance of DMPK testing in unexplainedpolyhydramnios. Genetic counseling including PGT-M was provided postnatally, facilitatinginformed reproductive decision-making.
P2-02-08: Objective This study evaluated the clinical significance of combining NIPT with first-trimester screening (FTS) via detailed ultrasound. Methods This study reviewed 240 cases undergoing NIPT at our institution from November 2025 to April 2026. Clinical backgrounds were compared among three groups: 55 NIPT-only cases and 185 combined-testing cases, subdivided into NIPT-first (n=103) and FTS-first (n=82) groups. Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's, and Bonferroni tests were used for statistical analyses. Results The median maternal age was significantly higher in the NIPT-first group [35 years(range: 33-39)] than in the NIPT-only [32 (30-35)] and FTS-first [33 (31-37)] groups (p < 0.001). The median gestational age at NIPT was 11.9 weeks for the NIPT-only group, 11.0 weeks for the NIPT-first group, and 12.9 weeks for the FTS-first group; the NIPT-first group underwent testing significantly earlier, while the FTS-first group was evaluated at the latest (p<0.001). No significant difference was observed in median NT thickness between the NIPT-first (1.9 mm) and FTS-first (1.8 mm) groups. Three cases tested positive on NIPT (all NIPT-first: 1 T21, 2 T18). FTS detected NT thickening or abnormalities in the T21 case and one T18 case; the other T18 case showed normal FTS findings and was confirmed as a false-positive via amniocentesis. Discussion Older clients preferring NIPT earlier suggested heightened anxiety about the fetus. Although FTS confirmed anomalies in two NIPT-positive cases, its normal findings in the false-positive case served as a vital psychological buffer before invasive testing.
P2-02-09: Background: Fetal hydrops is a severe condition characterized by abnormal fluid accumulation in multiple fetal compartments. Its etiology is diverse, including chromosomal abnormalities, cardiovascular disorders, infections, and hematologic diseases. Despite advances in prenatal diagnosis, prognosis remains poor. Objective: To retrospectively evaluate clinical characteristics, etiology, prenatal diagnostic testing, and outcomes of fetal hydrops cases at our institution. Methods: We reviewed 35 cases diagnosed between 2016 and 2025. Data included maternal age, gestational age at diagnosis, genetic testing, non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), and outcomes. Etiologies were classified based on diagnostic findings. Results: The mean maternal age was 36.3 years. Outcomes were poor: 13 cases resulted in intrauterine fetal death (IUFD) before 22 weeks, 11 in termination, and 4 in IUFD after 22 weeks. Only 7 cases resulted in live birth, of which 5 neonates died early. Five cases had normal karyotypes, while 13 had no confirmed chromosomal abnormalities. Two cases were due to blood group incompatibility. Conclusion: Fetal hydrops remains associated with poor outcomes, with chromosomal abnormalities as the leading cause. Early genetic evaluation and standardized prenatal counseling are essential to support clinical decision-making.
P2-02-10: Objective: To evaluate initial fetal findings and timing of prenatal diagnosis in fetuses with trisomy 18 (T18). Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 34 fetuses diagnosed with T18 between 2015 and 2025. Initial fetal findings, gestational age at first abnormal finding, referral, and definitive diagnosis were analyzed. Results: The most common referral indication was fetal growth restriction (FGR)/ small-for-date (SFD) in 17 cases (50.0%), followed by congenital heart disease (CHD) in 15 (44.1%), limb abnormalities in 9 (26.5%), amniotic fluid abnormalities in 7 (20.6%), and central nervous system abnormalities in 6 (17.6%). Median gestational age at first abnormal finding was 27 weeks in the FGR/SFD group and 22 weeks in the CHD group. Median gestational age at definitive diagnosis was 30 weeks in the FGR/SFD group, 24 weeks in the CHD group, and 15 weeks in the high-risk noninvasive prenatal testing group. Conclusion: FGR/SFD and CHD were the major initial fetal findings in T18. Cases presenting with FGR/SFD tended to be diagnosed later in gestation, whereas cases with CHD or high-risk prenatal screening results were diagnosed earlier.
P2-03-01: Background: Kearns Sayre syndrome (KSS) classically presents with progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction defects. Primary adrenal insufficiency is rare, especially in early childhood. Case: A boy developed progressive hyperpigmentation from age 2 and was diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency at age 4 . He subsequently showedgrowth failure, pancreatic atrophy, hearing loss, and Fanconi syndrome. At8 years 10 months, muscle weakness and tremor emerged. Brain MRI revealed new symmetric high intensity lesions in subcortical white matter, globus pallidus, and midbrain. Genetic testing for adrenal insufficiency related genes and whole exome sequencing were unremarkable. Mitochondrial genome analysis identified a large deletion, m.8636_16073del, confirmed by droplet digital PCR, with markedly elevated heteroplasmy in urinary sediment cells (90.4%). Discussion: This case considered to belong to the PS/KSS spectrum, beginning with adrenal insufficiency and progressing to multisystem dysfunction. Despite theextensive deletion, typical ocular and cardiac findings were absent, suggesting that clinical expression may depend more on tissue heteroplasmy and metabolic demand than deletion size. mtDNA deletion syndromes dominated by adrenal insufficiency are extremely uncommon, and this case illustrates the sequence and variability of organ involvement. Conclusion: In children with primary adrenal insufficiency accompanied by multisystem abnormalities, mitochondrial disease should be considered even when classic KSS features are lacking.
P2-03-02: In 2013, ASXL3 was first identified as the gene responsible for neurodevelopmental disorder and recognized as a transcriptional regulator. There is no specific tissue in which ASXL3 is highly expressed. Recently, we encountered a 3-year-old female patient with developmental delay with only few words. She often repeats what others say. Thus, communications with others are challenging for her and she was diagnosed as having autism spectrum disorder. Distinctive features including hypertelorism, epicanthus, and high-arched palate were noted. Neurological examination revealed truncal hypotonia. Because there was no specific finding, comprehensive genomic analysis was performed. As a result, de novo nonsense variant was identified in ASXL3. Most of the previously reported ASXL3 variants were nonsense or frameshift. Therefore, loss-of-function was considered as the mechanism for this condition.
P2-03-03: Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome (BRPS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmental delay, moderate-to-severe intellectual disability, and hypotonia. BRPS is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in ASXL3 on chromosome 18q12.1. We experienced a 5-year-old girl diagnosed with BRPS following the identification of a novel frameshift variant in ASXL3 through a diagnostic workup for developmental delay. Her prenatal, perinatal, and family history were unremarkable. At a 10-month health checkup, she presented with developmental delay and was referred to the pediatric department of a regional hospital. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed no remarkable findings. Developmental testing at 3 years of age revealed a total developmental quotient (DQ) of 47, indicating moderate intellectual disability. She was subsequently referred to our institution for further diagnostic evaluation. A NGS-based target genetic analysis using a custom panel for neurodevelopmental disorders identified a novel heterozygous frameshift variant in ASXL3, leading to the diagnosis of BRPS.ASXL3 belongs to the ASXL gene family, which regulates chromatin remodeling and is highly expressed in the fetal cerebral cortex and other tissues. The clinical features of BRPS overlap with those of Bohring-Opitz syndrome, caused by ASXL1 pathogenic variants, and Shashi-Pena syndrome, caused by ASXL2 pathogenic variants. Considering this phenotypic overlap between ASXL-related disorders, accurate genetic diagnosis is essential for appropriate surveillance and genetic counseling.
P2-03-04: Background Earlier diagnosis and growth hormone (GH) therapy have improved physical outcomes in Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS), but behavioral changes across birth cohorts remain unclear. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 128 individuals with PWS treated at our institution between 1971 and 2024. Ages at diagnosis, GH initiation, body mass index (BMI), and behavioral manifestations were analyzed by birth cohort. Time-to-event analyses were performed for first occurrence of food stealing, shoplifting/theft, aggressive or destructive tantrums, wandering/absconding, and school refusal. Chart descriptions were categorized into emotional dysregulation, food-related symptoms, rigidity, aggressive/destructive behavior, body-related behaviors, and psychiatric/anxiety-related symptoms. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee (R6-14). Results Younger birth cohorts showed earlier diagnosis and GH initiation, with improved BMI trends. However, burdensome behaviors remained prevalent. Food-related behaviors increased with age, whereas aggressive/destructive tantrums emerged earlier in childhood. School refusal and wandering/absconding appeared later. Qualitative analyses suggested that body-related concerns became less prominent, whereas emotional dysregulation, rigidity, food-related symptoms, and psychiatric/anxiety-related problems persisted. Conclusion Despite improved physical outcomes, behavioral and psychosocial burdens persist in PWS. Family concerns may be changing qualitatively across birth cohorts. Lifelong psychosocial support remains essential in PWS care.
P2-03-05: Since 1989, our center has provided a group clinic (DK Clinic) for babies with Down syndrome and their families. The aims of this clinic are to provide accurate medical information and to facilitate relationships among families. The clinic is managed by a multidisciplinary team over six months with monthly sessions. Since October 2023, it has been conducted in a hybrid format with both in-person and online options. We have held an annual meeting with members of the Family Associations in Saitama Prefecture to promote collaboration. Since 2024, as a new form of collaboration, members of Family Associations have introduced their organizations and activities to participants during DK clinic sessions. Furthermore, we introduced two new initiatives in 2025. During the day-long clinic sessions, the "Saitama house Cafe", supported by Ronald McDonald House Saitama, has provided a comfortable space for participants to interact and spend time together. Additionally, we have created opportunities for staff from employment support facilities to share information about the daily lives of adults with Down syndrome. These collaborations are helpful in promoting a better understanding of Down syndrome and supporting families. The DK Clinic provides not only medical information but supports the development of relationships between families and community partners. We aim to further support children with Down syndrome and their families through continuous collaboration with Family Associations and local facilities.
P2-03-06: Background: TFE3 (Xp11.23) encodes a MiT/TFE transcription factor. Pathogenic variants cause X-linked TFE3-related neurodevelopmental disorder (MIM#301066), with distinctive facial dysmorphism, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder. Fewer than 20 patients, including few males, have been reported. Patient: A 32-month-old boy was referred at 1 year with hepatosplenomegaly, distinctive facial features, umbilical hernia, hypothyroidism, and motor delay. Speech delay, seizures, and obesity became evident. No mosaicism was observed. Methods/Results: G-banding and chromosomal microarray were unremarkable. Trio exome sequencing through IRUD identified a de novo hemizygous missense TFE3 variant, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing: NM_006521.6:c.339G<T, p.(Arg113Ser). It was absent from gnomAD and jMorp, predicted deleterious in silico (CADD:23.2,SIFT:deleterious), and classified as likely pathogenic. Discussion: Missense mutations in TFE3 may impair DNA binding and dimerization. As in this case, reported pathogenic variants cluster in the TFE3 exon 3-4 region. The highly conserved p.Arg113Ser variant in exon 3 affects the same codon as the previously reported pathogenic p.Arg113Lys. Although TFE3-related neurodevelopmental disorder tends to be more severe in males, several non-mosaic male patients have been reported, suggesting a broad phenotypic spectrum. For ultra-rare disorders, post-diagnostic genetic counseling should provide updated information, promote data sharing, and facilitate remote family support through GENIE.
P2-03-07: [Background] Newborn mass screening (NBS) is a population-based screening program for hereditary metabolic and endocrine disorders. Accurate parental recognition of NBS results is important for genetic counseling and family planning yet remains poorly characterized. [Objective] To evaluate parental awareness of NBS results and factors affecting long-term retention of NBS information. [Methods] Consecutive new patients (April 2023-March 2026) with verifiable NBS records from medical charts or maternal-child health handbooks were enrolled. At the first visit, parents completed a questionnaire regarding conventional six-disease NBS and expanded screening using tandem mass spectrometry (TMS), selecting one of four responses: normal, abnormal, unknown, or not tested. Pediatricians verified responses using maternal-child health handbooks. Awareness was defined as correct parental recognition of screening status and results. Agreement was defined as concordance between parental and verified records. [Results] A total of 452 patients (median age, 8 years; range, 0-15 years) were analyzed. Awareness rates for conventional NBS decreased with age (77.6%, 69.7%, and 67.9% in the 0-year, 1-6-year, and over 6-year groups, respectively). TMS awareness rates were low (18.4%, 34.8%, and 35.1%). Agreement rates were 73.4% for conventional NBS and 34.6% for TMS. [Conclusion] Parental awareness of NBS results decline over time, and agreement with records is insufficient, especially for TMS. Improved education and record preservation may improve long-term accessibility of NBS information.
P2-03-08: Introduction: PIK3CA-related Overgrowth Spectrum (PROS) is characterized by segmental overgrowth resulting from somatic gain-of-function variants in PIK3CA. Variant detection in blood is occasionally challenging. Therefore, analyses using multiple tissue types, including saliva, buccal mucosa, and skin fibroblasts, are often considered. We report seven cases in which disease-causing variants were identified by whole exome sequencing (WES) and deep sequencing of blood and buccal mucosa. Results: PIK3CA variants were identified in blood samples in two cases using a variant-calling pipeline with a variant allele frequency (VAF) threshold of 20%. Meanwhile, four cases required buccal mucosa for successful diagnosis. One of the four cases exhibited the left craniofacial overgrowth with the variant localized to the right buccal mucosa, demonstrating discordance between the clinical manifestations and the distribution of VAF. In the remaining case, ultra-deep sequencing with revised filtering settings was required for diagnosis. Discussion: NGS-based ultra-deep sequencing and samples from affected regions have been recommended in previous report. However, our findings suggest that molecular diagnosis in PROS may still be challenging even when using affected tissues. Conclusion: A combinational tissue-based approach is important for improving the molecular diagnosis of PROS, and clinically less affected tissues may also be informative.
P2-03-09: Background: Pediatric parathyroid carcinoma is extremely rare with only around 20 cases reported. When primary hyperparathyroidism develops in childhood, a hereditary tumor predisposition, especially a CDC73-related disorder, should be considered. Case: A 15-year-old boy was referred for gait disturbance present since age 8 years, with hip pain. Laboratory tests showed corrected calcium of 12.7 mg/dL, intact PTH of 1531 pg/mL, and ALP of 4771 U/L, leading to a diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism. Based on the suggestive imaging findings, en bloc resection was performed and the diagnosis was confirmed histopathologically. With consent from the patient and his parents, peripheral blood genetic testing using the Hereditary Hyperparathyroidism Gene Panel identified a known CDC73 variant, c.162C>G, p.Tyr54Ter. His parents declined genetic testing. At 11 months after surgery, he showed no evidence of recurrence. Discussion and Conclusion: CDC73-related hyperparathyroidism is thought to result from loss of parafibromin tumor-suppressor function, causing parathyroid tumor formation and excessive PTH secretion. In this case, symptoms appeared at age 8 years, indicating the need for surveillance from childhood. CDC73-related disorders may also involve kidney tumors, jaw tumors, and uterine tumors in females. Lifelong follow-up is warranted because recurrence may occur years after surgery. This case highlights the importance of genetic evaluation in pediatric-onset primary hyperparathyroidism, as well as long-term surveillance and genetic counseling.
P2-03-10: Background: Maternal duplication of chromosome 15q11q13 is associated with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. The 15q11q13 region contains the pigmentation-related genes OCA2, a causative gene for oculocutaneous albinism. Although hexasomy of this region is extremely rare, several cases with generalized hyperpigmentation have been reported. Case: A 21-year-old woman was born at term weighing 2626g. Marked generalized hyperpigmentation was evident immediately after birth. She showed characteristic facial features, hypotonia, and delayed head control, and developed refractory epilepsy at 8 months of age. G-banding demonstrated 47,XX,+mar idic(15)(q14), initially interpreted as 15q11q14 tetrasomy. Additional molecular analyses, including chromosomal microarray and methylation-specific MLPA for the PWS/AS region, revealed six copies and hypermethylation of 15q11.1-q13.1, leading to the diagnosis of maternal full 15q11q13 hexasomy. She currently remains bedridden with profound intellectual disability and persistent marked hyperpigmentation. Discussion: Hypopigmentation is well recognized in Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, whereas generalized hyperpigmentation has occasionally been reported in 15q11q13 hexasomy. To our knowledge, hyperpigmentation has not been reported in 15q11q13 tetrasomy, suggesting a gene dosage effect of OCA2. Furthermore, this case highlights the importance of additional molecular analyses for copy-number and parent-of-origin evaluation in patients with idic(15).
P2-03-11: Background Fabry disease (FD) is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient α-galactosidase A (GalA) activity. Expanded newborn screening (eNBS) for FD has been started in Hyogo Prefecture since 2021. We report a case diagnosed through eNBS, revealing a family with classic FD. Case A 1-month-old boy underwent evaluation because of low α-GalA activity detected by eNBS. Leukocyte α-Gal A activity was reduced (0.7 nmol/mg protein/h), and genetic testing identified a previously unreported GLA variant, c.880T>G (p.Leu294Val). Plasma Lyso-Gb3 was elevated to 37.7 ng/mL at 7 months. Family history revealed multiple maternal relatives with FD, including a great-uncle with classic FD who died of heart failure in his fifties. Based on the elevated Lyso-Gb3 level and family history, the patient was diagnosed with classic FD. Family analysis The mother and maternal aunt had childhood acroparesthesia. Both carried the same variant. The mother currently has no apparent organ involvement. The maternal grandmother was asymptomatic and declined genetic testing. Discussion/Conclusion Newborn screening for FD contributes not only to diagnosis of the proband but also to identification of affected relatives. Family-based diagnosis requires appropriate genetic counseling tailored to individual circumstances. However, the optimal timing of treatment initiation in infants with classic FD identified through NBS remains unclear. Careful monitoring of symptoms, organ involvement, and Lyso-Gb3 levels is required to determine treatment timing.
P2-03-12: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is one of relatively common spinocerebellar ataxia in Japan, but reports on the clinical features of childhood-onset cases remain limited. We retrospectively reviewed medical records of genetically confirmed childhood-onset DRPLA cases followed at our department since 1994. We examined major clinical features, disease course, and the relationship with ATN1 gene CAG repeat length. Twenty patients from 17 families were included (final follow-up age 6-49 years; 10 males and 10 females). Family history was paternal in 14 families, maternal in 1, and absent in 2. Two patients had the infantile-severe form, with 93 and 90 CAG repeats. Both showed dystonia and stagnation or regression of psychomotor development around 6 months, became bedridden by age 1, required tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation at ages 2-3, and died at ages 6 and 15. The remaining 18 patients developed symptoms after infancy, with 62-84 CAG repeats. All showed intellectual disability between ages 2-12 and developed epilepsy between ages 3-14. Thirteen became bedridden between ages 6-21, six required tracheostomy and ventilatory support between ages 7-30, and four died between ages 12-49. Age at symptom onset, initiation of medical care, and death were significantly negatively correlated with CAG repeat length. Childhood-onset DRPLA was predominantly paternally inherited, progressed rapidly with poor prognosis, and showed a strong association with CAG repeat length. Prospective natural history data in pediatric cases will be essential for future clinical trials.
P2-03-13: Background: Chromosomal microarray testing (CMA) is widely used to diagnose chromosomal microdeletion/microduplication syndromes, with a reported diagnostic yield of 15-20%. However, the relationship between genetic testing history before CMA and CMA diagnostic yield remains unclear. We evaluated the clinical implementation and diagnostic yield of CMA at our institution. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed pediatric patients who underwent CMA between April 1, 2024 and March 31, 2026. Patients were classified into two groups: Group I (G1), patients who underwent disease-specific genetic testing for suspected monogenic disorders prior to CMA; and Group II (G2), patients who underwent CMA without prior disease-specific genetic testing. Pathogenic variant detection rates were compared between the groups. Results: G1 included 9 patients and G2 included 14 patients. Pathogenic variants were identified in 1/9 patients (11.1%) in G1 and 7/14 patients (50.0%) in G2. G2 showed a higher detection rate than G1, although the difference was not statistically significant (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.153; odds ratio 8.0, 95% confidence interval 0.72-87.99). Discussion: CMA diagnostic yield may differ according to prior genetic testing. Proactive CMA implementation may improve diagnostic efficiency in patients with developmental delay and/or multiple congenital anomalies without clinical features strongly suggestive of a specific monogenic disorder. Further studies are needed to optimize genetic testing strategies in pediatric genetic practice.
P2-03-14: Background: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an inherited myocardial disorder mainly caused by sarcomere gene variants. Phenotypes may vary even within a family, and interpretation of rare variants is often challenging. We report a mother-daughter pair carrying the same MYH7 variant of uncertain significance (VUS) with distinct cardiomyopathy phenotypes. Case: The proband was a 14-year-old girl diagnosed with atrial septal defect after a heart murmur was noted at 18 months. Closure was considered before school age, but test occlusion caused marked elevation of left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and hemodynamic deterioration. Right ventricular endomyocardial biopsy showed myocyte hypertrophy, disarray, fibrosis, and endocardial fibroelastic thickening, consistent with HCM. Clinically, she has been followed as having restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM). Genetic testing identified MYH7 c.1532T>A (p.Ile511Asn), classified as a VUS. Her 55-year-old mother had cardiomegaly from 38 years and postpartum heart failure at 42 years. Imaging later showed asymmetric septal hypertrophy and late gadolinium enhancement, consistent with mild HCM. She carried the same variant. Discussion: The variant was absent from ToMMo, gnomAD, ClinVar, and HGMD, and multiple in silico tools suggested deleteriousness. However, this mother-daughter pair alone does not meet the ClinGen MYH7 VCEP threshold for PP1_supporting, and the variant remains a VUS. This case highlights the value and limitations of family analysis and the need for further case accumulation to clarify rare MYH7 VUSs.
P2-04-01: Background: Endometrial carcinoma (EC) is one of the sentinel malignancies of Lynch syndrome (LS). Although universal mismatch repair (MMR) screening for EC is internationally recommended, its implementation in Japan remains limited. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 207 patients who underwent surgery for EC between December 2023 and December 2025 at our institution. Screening was performed using a two-antibody strategy with PMS2 and MSH6 immunohistochemistry. We evaluated screening implementation, MMR-deficiency (dMMR) detection, and genetic consultation status. Results: Universal screening was explained to 175 patients (84.5%), consent was obtained from 171 (82.6%), and screening was performed in 168 (81.2%). dMMR was identified in 43 cases (25.6%); PMS2 loss in 34, MSH6 loss in 6, and combined PMS2/MSH6 loss in 3. Genetic counseling was recommended for 40 of 43 dMMR patients, of whom 29 (67.4%) completed counseling and 4 (9.3%) had scheduled appointments. Germline testing was performed in 13 patients (multigene panel in 10, MMR genes only in 3), and pathogenic germline variants were identified in 4 (30.8%). Including one case previously diagnosed at another institution, LS was diagnosed in 5 of 168 screened patients (3.0%), with pathogenic variants in MLH1 (n=3), MSH2 (n=1), and MSH6 (n=1). Of the 5 LS cases, 2 met Amsterdam II criteria. Conclusions: Universal screening using PMS2 and MSH6 immunohistochemistry effectively identified dMMR and LS in EC patients. Closer collaboration with genetic medicine specialists is needed to improve LS diagnosis.
P2-04-02: Background The relationship between genomic findings and treatment response in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) has not been fully understood. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 9 patients with RCC who underwent Comprehensive Genomic Profiling (CGP) at our institution. Results Our cohort included 8 male and 1 female patients, 7 de novo metastatic and 2 recurrent metastatic RCC, and clear cell/ chromophobe/FH-deficient subtypes in 7/1/1 cases. CGP specimens, collected after systemic therapy, were from the primary tumor/ metastatic lesions/blood in 3/3/3 cases. TMB ranged from 1 to 8.4. All tumors were microsatellite stable (MSS). Three patients have died during the observation period (median 915 days) after CGP. Pathogenic variants of VHL/PBRM1 were detected in 5 (56%)/3 (33%) cases. TP53/PTEN/MTOR pathogenic variants were identified in 3/2/1 cases, respectively. All patients received immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. Two ICI-responders had low TMB. Discussion High frequency of VHL pathogenic variants was confirmed. RCC is one of the tumor types in which ICI efficacy has been observed regardless of molecular profile. Our findings suggest that mechanisms distinct from those in other cancers may underlie ICI response in RCC. To be noted, potentially actionable pathogenic variants, including those in PTEN, were identified. These findings suggest that CGP may play an important role in the management of RCC.
P2-04-03: Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Syndrome (HBOC) is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder characterized by pathogenic variants in the tumor suppressor genes BRCA1 or BRCA2, leading to the development of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and other cancers. We report a case in which HBOC was definitively diagnosed following a cancer gene panel test for bladder cancer, and relatedness analysis was performed on two family members. The proband is an 82-year-old male who was diagnosed with bladder cancer at our hospital in 2024. Curative resection was planned after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, but was cancelled due to renal dysfunction. In 2025, he was referred to the cancer genome medicine outpatient clinic, and a bladder tumor sample was submitted for Foundation One CDx cancer genome profiling test (F1-T). The F1-T results detected a pathogenic variant in BRCA1, identified as PGPV (presumed germline pathogenic variant). The genetic testing results led to a diagnosis of germline variant, confirming the diagnosis of HBOC. Genetic counseling was also provided to the two daughters, and single-site testing for each yielded negative results. We have instructed other family members who wish to receive genetic counseling to contact the genetic counseling department. With the introduction of insurance coverage for cancer gene panel testing in 2019, opportunities to diagnose hereditary disorders from secondary findings are increasing. Building a robust genetic medicine department will become even more crucial in the future.
P2-04-04: Background: BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants (PV) confer sensitivity to platinum and PARP inhibitors (PARPi), although clinical outcomes vary among patients. Emerging evidence suggests that the functional consequences of BRCA1/2 PV may depend on their localization within domains involved in homologous recombination repair. Objective: This study aimed to clarify the significance of domain-specific BRCA1/2 PV in ovarian cancer, focusing on treatment response and outcomes. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of ovarian cancer patients harboring BRCA1/2 PV. Variants were stratified according to localization within the BRCA1 RING/BRCT domains and the BRCA2 RAD51-binding domain. Results: Among 261 patients with newly diagnosed ovarian cancer treated between 2020 and 2025, 27 had BRCA1/2 PV. Median age was 55 years. High-grade serous carcinoma was observed in 24 (89%), and 22 (81%) had stage III/IV disease. All patients received platinum-based chemotherapy, and 20 (74%) received PARPi maintenance therapy. Among PARPi-treated patients, 7 had variants localized to these domains and 13 had other variants. Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 33.2 vs 21.5 months, and median time to next treatment (TTNT) was 32.0 vs 22.6 months, respectively. In first-line maintenance cases, median PFS was 30.3 vs 28.1 months, whereas in recurrent cases, median PFS was 47.7 vs 8.4 months. Conclusion: Functional domain-based analysis of BRCA1/2 may provide prognostic and therapeutic insights beyond conventional BRCA classification in ovarian cancer.
P2-04-05: [Background] Diagnosing hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC) is crucial for early cancer detection and preventive intervention in probands and relatives. While Japan's cascade testing uptake rate is approximately 20%, the data from regional core hospitals such as our hospital remain insufficient. This study aimed to investigate the cascade testing uptake rate and evaluate clinical challenges at our hospital. [Methods] We included probands with BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants identified between April 2023 and January 2026. The primary endpoint was the cascade testing uptake rate among first-degree relatives (FDRs) by April 2026. [Results] Among 15 probands, 65 FDRs (including seven young relatives under the age of 18 years) were identified. Only five FDRs (7.7%) attended genetic counseling. Three individuals (all daughters of probands) underwent cascade testing, resulting in an overall uptake rate of 4.6%. [Conclusions] Our hospital's uptake rate (4.6%) is significantly lower than the previously reported national average of 20%. Although the presence of young relatives among FDRs may have contributed to this lower rate, the rate remains low at 5.1% even after excluding them. The low attendance rate for genetic counseling is a major contributing factor. The strengthening of genetic counseling systems and the establishing of mechanisms to support family information-sharing are urgent priorities. The proactive communication from healthcare providers and educational activities are essential to lower psychological barriers and promote regional genetic medicine.
P2-04-06: [Introduction] Lynch syndrome (LS) is an autosomal dominant hereditary disorder caused by pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, significantly increasing the risk for colorectal (CRC) and endometrial cancers (EC). We report a case of LS diagnosed via genetic testing after EC treatment in a patient with early-onset CRC, which subsequently led to detecting metachronous sigmoid colon cancer. [Case Report] A 50-year-old female with a history of rectal cancer at age 29 had undergone regular colonoscopies and multiple endoscopic resections for polyps. Her father was diagnosed with CRC at age 34 and died of gastric cancer at age 45. At age 48, she was diagnosed with EC and underwent hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and pelvic/para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Pathology showed Grade 2 endometrioid carcinoma, Stage IB (pT1bN0M0). Postoperatively, she received six cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. Given her clinical history, MMR protein immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed a loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression. Following genetic counseling, a pathogenic variant in the MLH1 gene was identified, confirming LS. Subsequent surveillance colonoscopy detected sigmoid colon cancer, which was treated with laparoscopic total colectomy. [Conclusion] In gynecology, EC and ovarian cancer are key sentinel indicators for LS diagnosis. Clinicians must prioritize not only proband treatment and surveillance but also strategies for the early detection and prevention of cancer in at-risk relatives.
P2-04-07: Background/Aim: Lynch syndrome (LS) confers a high risk of endometrial (EC) and ovarian cancers. Patient education and gynecologic surveillance with transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial cytology/biopsy are recommended. Risk-reducing hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (RRH-BSO) is offered in Western guidelines but implemented cautiously in Japan. We report three cases of endometrial atypical hyperplasia (AH) or EC diagnosed during LS surveillance. Case 1: A woman in her late 40s, an MSH2 carrier with two prior colorectal cancers, experienced anxiety with serial biopsies. An endometrial polyp with hyperplasia prompted hysterectomy and BSO. She expressed relief from surveillance. Case 2: A cancer-free woman in her 50s, an MSH2 carrier, developed abnormal bleeding in surveillance year 2. Stage IA EC was diagnosed, but positive peritoneal cytology required adjuvant chemotherapy. Case 3: A woman in her 50s, an MSH2 carrier with prior colorectal cancer, had AH confirmed on surveillance endometrial sampling and underwent hysterectomy and BSO at the precancerous stage, which she viewed favorably. Discussion/Conclusion: Surveillance enabled detection of precancerous lesions and prompt response to symptoms but did not preclude adverse features in one case. RRH-BSO may offer both oncologic and psychological benefit. Individualized, lifelong management-considering life stage, fertility, prior cancers, causative gene, and patient values-together with ongoing genetic counseling, is essential to support informed decisions.
P2-04-08: Background: Risk-reducing surgery is important for carriers of pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants, but decision-making is influenced by clinical and personal factors. We reviewed our 6-year experience to clarify implementation and factors. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 20 individuals with pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants. Primary disease, BRCA1/2 status, surgery, pathology, follow-up, and reasons for non-implementation were reviewed.
