These mappings enable linkage to international databases such as OMIM and Orphanet, allowing integrated access to disease-associated gene information. NanbyoData also provides standardized datasets, including 8,431 disease-associated genes, 1,080 glycan-related genes, 511 clinical genetic tests based on the list provided by the Japan Society of Human Genetics, 61,547 clinical phenotypes, and 32,591 rare disease-specific bioresources, along with genetic variant and literature information. In this presentation, we describe the data integration framework and key features of NanbyoData, and discuss future directions for data expansion and international collaboration.
P2-10-05: BioBank Japan (BBJ) was established in 2003 to advance personalized medicine using genetic information. Until now, BBJ collected DNA, serum, and clinical information of approximately 270,000 patients with 51 diseases (440,000 cases). Then, BBJ obtained genetic SNP data for almost all individual, increasing omics data of whole genome sequencing (WGS), metabolome and proteome analyses. These samples and data were utilized in many researchers from both academic institutions and companies, leading to a wealth of outstanding research findings. Recently, we began providing "Data Packages", which bundle clinical information, genomic information, metabolome data, and other information, to researchers. By these initiatives, the utilization of BBJ's samples and information, particularly the data, has increased significantly in recent years, contributing to the promotion of both large-scale studies and smaller-scale research. Furthermore, we have developed and partially launched a platform that enables two-way communication between research participants and BBJ. Through these new activities and the promotion of research utilization, we are contributing to drug discovery research, healthcare, and societal implementation. This report introduces the progress of these BBJ initiatives.
P2-10-06: Health-insurance coverage for orthodontic treatment in patients with congenital disorders has expanded in Japan; however, many conditions remain unrecognized. This study investigated the clinical characteristics and insurance eligibility for hereditary craniofacial anomalies in Japan. We included patients with congenital craniofacial anomalies (excluding nonsyndromic cleft lip and/or palate) who visited the Departments of Orthodontics at nine university hospitals up to December 2024. Disease names and insurance eligibility were collected using an electronic data-capture system. Among registered 1,224 patients (640 males and 584 females), 1,107 (90.4%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 88.6-92.0) were diagnosed with one of the 65 health insurance-covered disorders. The most frequent diagnoses were congenital absence of >6 teeth (343, 28.0%), followed by Down syndrome (102, 8.3%), craniofacial microsomia (67, 5.5%), craniosynostosis (53, 4.3%), and cleidocranial dysplasia (50, 4.1%). Among the 117 patients (9.6%; 95% CI, 8.0-11.4) with other disorders, 58 (4.7% of total cohort) were eligible for insurance coverage owing to symptoms overlapping those of the 65 designated disorders or diagnosis of cleft lip and/or palate or jaw deformities. The remaining 59 patients (4.8%; 95% CI, 3.7-6.2) were ineligible for coverage. Although most hereditary craniofacial anomalies are currently covered by health insurance, many rare conditions are excluded. Continued data collection and expansion of participating institutions are needed to establish a more comprehensive support system.
P2-10-07: TogoVar is a variant database that integrates allele frequencies in the Japanese population from sources such as the Japanese Genotype-phenotype Archive (JGA) and the ToMMo allele frequency panel. Because individuals with Japanese ancestry are underrepresented in international databases such as gnomAD, TogoVar is an important resource for human genetics research in Japan. In addition to Japanese allele frequencies, TogoVar includes non-Japanese allele frequencies from gnomAD, annotations by the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP), clinical significance data from ClinVar, Japanese population-derived clinical significance data from the Medical Genomics Japan Variant Database (MGeND), and literature data from LitVar and PubTator. In the latest release, TogoVar was expanded by adding structural variants, variants derived from JGA-deposited data, and splice-site creating variants. For structural variants of 51 bp or longer, TogoVar incorporated JoGo: Joint Open Genome and Omics Platform v1 (258 samples; 377,965 variants), JSV1: Japanese Structural Variation (222 samples; 72,342 variants), and gnomAD-SV v4.1 (63,046 samples; 1,931,561 variants). In addition, allele frequencies and genotype counts calculated from aggregate VCF datasets registered in JGA under JGAD000867 and JGAD000868 were added to TogoVar. These datasets were generated by variant calling of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 1,026 and 1,964 BioBank Japan individuals, respectively. Furthermore, TogoVar variants matching 48,569 variants in SSCV DB v1.1 were annotated as splice-site creating variants (SSCVs).
P2-10-08: Objective: Childhood obesity is a multifactorial disease caused by complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors and is strongly associated with obesity, hypertension, and diabetes in adulthood. Children born to mothers with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are at increased risk of obesity later in life. However, the relationship between single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and childhood obesity in children born to mothers with HDP remains unclear. This study aimed to identify obesity-associated SNPs and related biological pathways in children born to mothers with HDP. Methods: Approximately 20,000 mother-child pairs enrolled in the Tohoku Medical Megabank Project Three-Generation Cohort Study were analyzed. Children were classified into normal-weight and obese groups according to BMI percentiles at ages 3 and 5 years. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) were performed in the obese groups, and SNPs with Manhattan plot scores more than 5 were selected for Gene Ontology and pathway analyses. Results: GWAS identified 43 SNPs associated with obesity at age 3 years and 21 SNPs associated with obesity at age 5 years. Pathway analyses revealed enrichment of pathways associated with leptin signaling, glucolipid metabolism, and insulin resistance. Conclusions: Children who develop obesity at an early age may carry obesity-associated SNPs. In particular, genetic variants identified in children born to mothers with HDP may help predict future obesity risk from birth.
P2-10-09: Multigene testing for designated intractable diseases is being implemented under public health insurance in Japan. Sustainable use requires knowledge bases, as exemplified by Genomics England PanelApp, that manage disease-specific gene lists together with evidence, expert evaluations, inclusion decisions, and change history. In Japan, notification numbers, diagnostic criteria, subtypes, and external identifiers are interrelated in complex ways, requiring a framework tailored to the national system. We developed NANDO, a disease vocabulary that organizes disease names, notification numbers, and subtypes in Japan's designated intractable disease system. We also developed PanelSearch Nanbyo, a NANDO-based platform for searching, reviewing, and curating evidence-linked gene lists. It maps diseases in NANDO to external identifiers and aggregates disease-gene associations from OMIM, MedGen, Orphadata, GenCC, and literature. The platform separates public resource-derived disease-gene associations from expert reviews and curator decisions. Database and literature-derived information is not treated as a final list; evaluations and inclusion decisions by clinical geneticists, disease specialists, and curators can be recorded. Users can trace each gene's rationale, review process, inclusion process, and change history. The platform manages disease-specific gene lists as updateable knowledge resources. By accumulating reviews and expanding curation workflows, it aims to improve reproducibility in gene-list development and support the collaborative maintenance of genomic testing resources.
P2-11-01: Background: Infantile liver failure syndrome type 1 (ILFS1), caused by pathogenic LARS1 variants, is characterized by recurrent liver dysfunction triggered by inflammatory stress. We previously generated Lars1-I451F knock-in mice harboring a pathogenic variant identified in ILFS1 patients. Transcriptomic analysis of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated livers demonstrated suppression of hepatic metabolic pathways under inflammatory stress. Histological analyses also revealed aggravated hepatic steatosis and liver injury in mutant mice, but the specific metabolic alterations underlying liver injury remain unclear. Methods: Homozygous Lars1-I451F mice were challenged with LPS, and liver tissues were collected 24 hours later. Hepatic metabolomic analysis was performed to identify altered metabolic pathways. Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) activity was evaluated using NADP+/NADPH assays. Lipid peroxidation was assessed by western blotting for 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE). Results: Metabolomic analysis identified suppression of the PPP in mutant livers after LPS stimulation. NADP+/NADPH assays demonstrated reduced PPP activity in mutant mice compared with controls. Western blot analysis revealed marked accumulation of 4- HNE in mutant livers, indicating enhanced lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress. Conclusions: These findings suggest that impaired PPP activity and disrupted redox homeostasis contribute to inflammatory stress-induced liver injury in Lars1-I451F mutant mice. Accumulation of 4-HNE may represent a pathogenic mechanism and potential therapeutic target in ILFS1.
P2-11-02: Ectodysplasin A (EDA) regulates ectodermal organ development through activation of its receptor EDAR. Pathogenic EDA variants are a major cause of X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (XLHED), characterized by hypodontia, hypotrichosis, and hypohidrosis. However, the mechanisms by which missense variants impair EDA-EDAR signaling remain unclear. Here, we identified two EDA1 missense variants, p.Gln254Lys and p.Thr378Met, in individuals with XLHED. Both variants are located within the TNF homology domain responsible for EDAR binding. NF-κB luciferase reporter assays demonstrated complete loss of EDAR activation by both variants. Consistently, conditioned media containing either variant failed to bind EDAR-expressing HEK293 cells. Biochemical analysis of Fc-tagged EDA proteins showed reduced secretion of p.Gln254Lys, whereas p.Thr378Met showed secretion comparable to wild type, suggesting that impaired signaling may result from either decreased ligand availability or defective receptor interaction. AlphaFold2-based structural models demonstrated preservation of the overall TNF homology domain architecture, with only subtle local alterations near the substituted residues. The p.Gln254Lys variant may alter local interactions involved in receptor binding, whereas p.Thr378Met may affect local packing within the β-sandwich core required for receptor engagement. These findings demonstrate that subtle local structural perturbations, rather than global folding defects, can disrupt EDA-EDAR signaling and contribute to XLHED pathogenesis.
P2-11-03: Recent human genetic studies have identified pathogenic variants in angiomotin-like 1(AMOTL1) in multiple patients with orofacial clefts, suggesting that AMOTL1 may represent a novel disease-associated gene in craniofacial development. To provide functional evidence supporting the involvement of AMOTL1 in orofacial clefts, we investigated its expression during murine palatal development and examined its relationship with YAP using human embryonic palatal mesenchymal (HEPM) cells. Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated AMOTL1 expression in both epithelial and mesenchymal cells of the developing secondary palate at E13.5-E14.5 in C57BL/6 mouse embryos. In HEPM cells, AMOTL1 localized to both the cytoplasm and nucleus. Furthermore, siRNA-mediated knockdown of AMOTL1 reduced YAP1 expression. These findings suggest that AMOTL1 may contribute to palatal development through regulation of YAP signaling and provide functional support for the pathogenic relevance of AMOTL1 variants in patients with orofacial clefts.
P2-11-04: Background: Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (NBCCS) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the PTCH1 gene, characterized by bifid ribs and palmar pits, as well as a predisposition to various tumors, including basal cell carcinoma, and odontogenic keratocyst. Methods: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were obtained from patients and family members of NBCCS. Mutation analysis was performed using next-generation sequencing. NBCCS-hiPSCs were generated using a non-integrating Sendai virus vector under fully defined, serum- and feeder-free conditions. Results: A novel PTCH1 mutation, designated PTCH1_c.3298_3299insAAG, was identified. In silico analysis indicated that the detected variant was pathogenic. The established NBCCS-hiPSCs retained the mutation, could be stably maintained under defined conditions, and exhibited both pluripotency and trilineage differentiation potential. Conclusion: A novel pathogenic mutation was identified in a familial NBCCS, and disease-specific iPSCs carrying this mutation were established. These cells are expected to serve as a valuable model for elucidating the pathogenesis of NBCCS and as a resource for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for rare genetic skeletal disorders. This work has been published in Human Genome Variation 7(1):38, 2020, and In Vitro Cellular & Developmental Biology - Animal, 59(6):395-400, 2023.
P2-11-05: Background: GNAO1 is one of the genes associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Pathogenic variants in GNAO1 cause severe developmental delay, epilepsy, and involuntary movements. However, the effects of GNAO1 variants on human neurodevelopment and the underlying molecular pathways remain unclear. Objective: To generate brain organoids from patient-derived iPS cells carrying a GNAO1 variant and investigate molecular alterations associated with neurodevelopment and Rho GTPase signaling. Methods and Results: Brain organoids were generated from healthy control and GNAO1 variant iPS cells. Samples were collected at days 18, 35, and 60 for RNA extraction. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed to comprehensively evaluate transcriptomic alternations, followed by quantitative PCR validation of selected neurodevelopmental and Rho GTPase signaling-related genes. Differential gene expression was observed between control- and GNAO1-derived organoids, including genes associated with neuronal development and cytoskeletal regulation. Conclusions: These findings suggest that GNAO1 variants may alter neurodevelopmental pathways and Rho GTPase signaling during human brain development. Comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of GNAO1-derived brain organoids may provide insights into disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets for DEE.
P2-12-01: <Introduction> Marfan syndrome (MFS) is associated with serious perinatal risks. Ideally, MFS should be diagnosed before conception; however, some patients remain undiagnosed until late pregnancy. We report a case in which rapid genetic evaluation helped avoid potentially unnecessary obstetric intervention. <Case> A 36-year-old woman (G2P1) was referred to our cardiology department at 30w5d of gestation. MFS was suspected due to scoliosis and family history; however, she did not meet the Ghent diagnostic criteria, complicating perinatal management and causing anxiety. Genetic counseling was provided and genetic testing performed. Due to the advanced gestational age, we coordinated with the testing laboratory to obtain an interim report earlier than usual. No pathogenic variants were identified. Integrating the genetic and clinical findings enabled reconsideration of the planned obstetric management, including painless delivery and medication. After explanation of the results and revised management plan, the patient was reassured and later had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. <Discussion> This case highlights the role of expedited genetic evaluation when clinical findings alone are insufficient to guide obstetric management. Rapid communication among the genetic counseling team, testing laboratory, cardiology department, and obstetric team facilitated interpretation of results and refinement of management. Such coordination may be valuable in late pregnancy, when clinical decisions must be made within limited time frames and uncertainty may increase patient anxiety.
P2-12-02: Background: Recently, non-coding RNA-related disorders that are difficult to diagnose by conventional exome sequencing have been identified. This study examined family perceptions of result disclosure and genetic counseling issues in ReNU syndrome. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed counseling records of three ReNU syndrome cases, focusing on diagnosis, family reactions, and counseling needs. Results: The causative genes were RNU4-2, RNU5-2, and RNU2-5, and ages at diagnosis ranged from 6 to 14 years. During result disclosure counseling, clinicians explained that previous testing had failed because the variants were located in non-coding RNA genes and represented newly recognized disorders. Families expressed relief, expectations for future disease information, and willingness to contribute to medical knowledge despite remaining uncertainty. Discussion: Patients with ReNU syndrome often experience a prolonged diagnostic odyssey because conventional exome sequencing fails to detect non-coding RNA variants. Explanation of the relationship between non-coding RNA variants and their functional effects may help families understand why diagnosis had been difficult and facilitate acceptance of the disorder. Families also viewed the diagnosis as a hope for future medical contributions and knowledge accumulation, suggesting the importance of genetic counseling in supporting personal resilience.
P2-12-03: Since the introduction of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) to Japan in 2013, the number of institutions offering the test has continuously increased. At present, 20 certified hospitals and clinics in Saitama provide NIPT with genetic counseling required prior to testing. Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) is a molecular approach to reveal genomic alterations known to drive cancer growth, which may inform targeted therapies and clinical trial options for cancer patients. Following the implementation of CGP in 2019, increasing numbers of patients have been diagnosed with hereditary cancer syndromes. As a result, the demand and role for genetic counseling at children's hospitals has changed. We reviewed the referral reasons in 124 genetic counseling cases between 2018 and 2024. In 2018, providing information on prenatal diagnosis and recurrence risk for Down syndrome was the most frequent reason, which decreased significantly to only 3 cases in 2024. In contrast, concerns regarding the risk to family members of hereditary cancer syndromes showed a marked increase, becoming the most prevalent reason for genetic counseling in 2024. The widespread use of CGP in pediatric patients may have increased referrals for genetic counseling related to hereditary cancer syndromes. In contrast, with the increasing number of hospitals and clinics offering NIPT, the need for genetic counseling regarding prenatal diagnosis and recurrence risk for Down syndrome may have decreased. Genetic counseling in pediatric hospitals should continue to evolve to meet changing clinical needs.
P2-12-04: Introduction: Families of children with severe congenital anomalies often experience both a desire for a diagnosis and concerns about parental responsibility. We report continuous genetic counseling(GC) provided from pregnancy through diagnosis in a child with a Tubulinopathy. Case: A 34-year-old primigravida was referred for abnormal prenatal ultrasound findings. G-banding, followed by postnatal chromosomal microarray analysis, was nondiagnostic. WES identified a novel TUBB2A(NM_001069.3) variant, c.293G>A (p.Gly98Glu). The parents wished to know the cause of their child's condition but feared that one of them might carry the causative variant. The mother was particularly hesitant to pursue testing because of concerns about parental culpability. Multiple GC sessions were conducted before and after testing to discuss the purpose, benefits, limitations, and possible outcomes of genomic analysis while exploring the parents' emotions and concerns. Through ongoing GC, they reframed participation in the study as a way to help other families and agreed to proceed. At result disclosure, the parents expressed relief that a diagnosis had been established and reassurance that neither parent carried the variant, while also grieving confirmation of a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. Continued psychosocial support was provided. Conclusion: Continuous GC facilitated informed decision-making, reduced guilt and uncertainty, and supported acceptance of the diagnosis. Longitudinal counseling is essential for families undergoing genomic evaluation for severe congenital disorders.
P2-12-05: Background: Genetic information (GI) on hereditary diseases is crucial for probands and their relatives; however, attitudes toward sharing such information vary among individuals. In this study, we identified factors influencing decision making regarding sharing GI among patients with positive genetic testing (GT) results and examined associated challenges. Methods: Between 2018 and 2026, 760 individuals underwent GT at our center, of which 129 carried a pathogenic variant and were the first in their family to undergo GT. To focus on actionable conditions, 75 individuals with pathogenic variants in genes on the ACMG SF v3.3 list were included. Results: Among the 75 individuals, 69 intended to share their GI with relatives, 3 declined to do so, and the intentions of 3 individuals could not be determined. Information sharing was confirmed in 51 of 69 cases (44 had tumor-related diseases, 4 had cardiovascular diseases, and 3 had endocrine/metabolic diseases), leading to genetic testing among 23 relatives from 20 families. Analysis of the 11 individuals who postponed sharing despite expressing willingness and the 3 individuals who declined sharing identified five barriers to information sharing: patient-related, perceived characteristics of relatives, family relationships, disease-related characteristics, and healthcare/support. Discussion: Especially when at-risk relatives are minors, a long-term approach to support may be needed, considering disease acceptance, treatment status, and concerns about potential psychological burdens associated with information sharing.
P2-12-06: Approximately 90% of individuals with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) are diagnosed after developing clinical manifestations, which typically appear in adulthood. A 1-year-6-month-old girl was referred to our division to consider presymptomatic genetic testing for MEN1. Her father, paternal grandfather, and paternal aunt were all diagnosed with MEN1. The parents wished to pursue genetic testing for their child in her adulthood and obtain information regarding the indications for testing in childhood. To optimize the approach to presymptomatic diagnosis, a multidisciplinary conference was subsequently held involving endocrinologists, oncologists, geneticists, and genetic counsellors, resulting in consensus recommendations for surveillance in their respective areas of expertise. We particularly focused on the appropriate age for pediatric presymptomatic diagnosis and the disclosure of the possibility of MEN1 to the child, while respecting the child's right to know (or not to know). Based on these discussions, an institutional consensus was established and shared with the family, recommending consideration of presymptomatic genetic testing after the child reaches 10 years of age. Building consensus through multidisciplinary conferences is expected to become increasingly important in future genomic medicine practice.
P2-12-07: <Background> Recently, people can easily access disease related information on the Internet. A study conducted in the United States found that more than 80% of families used the Internet before attending a pediatric genetics clinic. <Case 1> A boy aged 10 presented with episodes of upward eye deviation beginning around 6 months of age, along with psychomotor developmental delay. Extensive evaluations at a previous hospital failed to make a diagnosis. At the initial visit, his mother mentioned that she had found a paper describing CACNA1A related disorders on the internet. As the clinical presentation were consistent with those previously reported, CACNA1A genetic testing was performed, and a previously reported pathogenic variant was identified. <Case 2> A man aged 22 with a history of growth hormone therapy for short stature during childhood, autism spectrum disorder, and mild intellectual disability visited our division. His mother had been suspected Prader Willi syndrome (PWS) as a possible diagnosis after coming across it while searching the internet. Although PWS was considered a differential diagnosis, our division recommended chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA). CMA revealed no clinically significant copy number variants. <Conclusion> In the present two cases, the parents'searches for disease names based on symptoms in children motivated them to seek medical attention. Understanding how the parents came to suspect a particular disorder may help guide the diagnostic evaluation and etiological investigation of the children.
P2-12-08: Background: A diagnosis of Marfan syndrome (MFS) in childhood contributes to early health management, but causes significant issues regarding disease disclosure to the patient and familial genetic analysis. School aged patients who have their life foundations such as school life and club activities, have to incorporate health management for MFS into their daily life with their cooperation. Objective and Methods: The purpose is to consider the role of certified genetic counselors based on mainly supporting pediatric MFS patients in understanding their diseases. Eight children were diagnosed with MFS in our hospital from April 2025 to March 2026. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of three cases of school aged patients among them. Results: Because all subjects play sports regularly, exercise restrictions were estimated to change their daily lives. In genetic counseling session, the disease information was provided to the patients as well as their parents before and after genetic testing and disclosure. Consequently, one patient could accept the diagnosis and ask a cardiologist about exercise restrictions. Another patient spoke very little about the diagnosis during genetic counseling, making it difficult to assess their understanding of MFS. From these cases, internalization of their disease and adjusting their current lifestyles turned out to be important so that the MFS patients who got a diagnosis when teenager can manage their health properly. The role of genetic counselors is to enhance patient awareness of their constitution.
P2-12-09: [Introduction] NFKB1-related immunodeficiency presents with diverse phenotypes, including antibody deficiency, recurrent infections, autoimmunity, and lymphoproliferation. This heterogeneity may obscure recognition of a shared genetic basis within a family. We report a mother and child with different phenotypes caused by the same NFKB1 variant. [Case] A 41-year-old woman developed delayed wound healing after vaginal delivery and recurrent intra-abdominal and incisional abscesses following subsequent cesarean sections. She was referred for evaluation of suspected immunodeficiency. During genetic counseling, family history revealed that her first child was receiving immunoglobulin replacement therapy for IgG2 subclass deficiency. Genetic testing identified the same heterozygous NFKB1 variant (NM_003998.4:c.157delC,p.Gln53Argfs*74) in both the mother and child. The diagnosis explained the mother's recurrent infections and the child's antibody deficiency. Because NFKB1-related immunodeficiency shows marked phenotypic variability, her other asymptomatic children were referred for immunological evaluation. [Discussion] Phenotypic diversity in NFKB1-related immunodeficiency can hinder recognition of a common genetic etiology within a family. In this case, genetic counseling and testing clarified the relationship between different clinical manifestations and enabled follow-up for at-risk relatives. Inborn errors of immunity should be considered when multiple immune-related abnormalities occur within a family, even when the phenotypes differ.
P2-12-10: PALB2 germline pathogenic variant (GPV) carriers require risk-based surveillance and shared decision-making at cancer diagnosis, yet gene-specific management protocols for PALB2 remain to be standardized in Japan. We report a case illustrating the role of sustained genetic counseling in enabling early cancer detection and informed decision-making. A woman in her 60s voluntarily sought genetic counseling based on a family history of breast/thyroid cancer in her sister and pancreatic cancer in her father. Multi-gene panel testing at the presymptomatic stage identified a PALB2 GPV. Guideline-concordant, self-funded surveillance was initiated in close collaboration with the breast surgery department. Three years later, contrast-enhanced breast MRI detected a 5-mm lesion, leading to a diagnosis of early-stage breast cancer. Following diagnosis, ongoing genetic counseling addressed surgical decision-making (including breast-conserving surgery versus mastectomy, risk of new ipsilateral primary breast cancer, contralateral risk-reducing mastectomy, and surveillance of related organs) with support tailored to the patient's values. The prior therapeutic relationship built through continuous genetic counseling from GPV identification facilitated smooth shared decision-making between the patient and the multidisciplinary team. This case suggests that presymptomatic surveillance embedded within a structured hereditary tumor screening program, combined with sustained genetic counseling, contributes to early cancer detection and supports informed treatment decisions in PALB2 GPV carriers.
P2-13-01: Background: Higher genetic literacy among the general public is expected to be achieved through an appropriate understanding of one's own family history; however, such opportunities are limited in Japan. Objective: This study aimed to improve genetic literacy through public lectures on pedigree drawing and to identify challenges for the future development of pedigree notebooks that are easy for the general public to use. Methods: Following the genetics lectures, participants practiced pedigree drawing using two mock cases. Subsequently, questionnaires were conducted to assess the participants' understanding and evaluation of the lecture. Results: Of the 13 participants, questionnaire responses were obtained from 6 participants and scanned pedigree drawings from 11 participants. Although staff support contributed to minimizing notation errors, seven of the 11 participants had difficulty aligning individual symbols within the same generation. In the questionnaire responses, a participant noted that understanding genetic information may help manage one's own health, and requested opportunities for individual consultation regarding their personal concerns. Some participants also sought consultations regarding their family history after the lectures and workshop. Conclusion: The lectures and workshop encouraged participants to view genetics as personally relevant and highlighted the need for opportunities to address genetic concerns. Providing pedigree templates with predefined generation identifiers may improve future notebook development.
P2-13-02: [Background and Objectives] In regions such as Hokkaido, where genetic healthcare resources are unevenly distributed, clinical genetics trainees may face limited access to sufficient educational opportunities and supervision. This study aimed to identify the challenges experienced by board-certified clinical geneticists (CGs) in Hokkaido during their training and the educational support they perceived as necessary. [Methods] We conducted a web-based survey regarding training experiences among 78 CGs working in Hokkaido. [Results] As of June 3, 2026, 26 CGs responded (response rate: 33%). Among them, 13 had obtained certification through the transitional system and had not undergone formal training; therefore, responses from the remaining 13 were analyzed. The key challenges included uneven distribution of case types in genetic counseling, limited opportunities for case experience and observation, and financial burdens, including travel expenses. Open-ended comments highlighted institution-dependent case disparities and a desire for systematic educational opportunities in medical genetics. Additionally, a need for online lectures and seminars was identified. [Discussion] Online platforms could address time constraints, travel expenses, and institutional case disparities by enabling trainees to experience cases from other institutions. While the genetic medicine seminar by JSHG and the GCRP by JSGC have already been fully transitioned to online formats, applying similar online approaches to case-based training may offer a potential solution to these challenges.
P2-13-03: [Background] Family trees are essential for hereditary disease risk assessment. Our hospital plans to introduce family trees in addition to traditional genograms; therefore, we assessed multidisciplinary staff awareness and educational needs. [Objective] To clarify staff awareness of family tree use, reasons for its necessity, perceived need among staff groups, and educational issues. [Methods] An anonymous web-based survey was conducted among staff who use electronic medical records. [Results] Responses were obtained from 195 staff. While 89.7% had viewed family history data in electronic medical records, only 39.0% had entered such data. On a 5-point scale of medical necessity, 53.8% rated family trees as "5" and 29.2% as "4" Reasons included understanding patients' biological relationships (69.2%) and cohabitants (67.7%), identifying carers (65.1%) and emotional support (61.0%), confirming family medical history (60.0%), and assessing hereditary disease risk (58.5%). The perceived need was highest among nurses, cancer counselors, and physicians. [Discussion] Family trees were recognized not only for assessing hereditary disease risk but also for obtaining information about family support. However, despite shared access to the data, data entry was limited compared with viewing frequency, suggesting that recording and updating may be limited to certain professions. To utilize family trees effectively in electronic medical records, profession-specific training on the purpose, clinical use, characteristics, and handling of the data is necessary.
P2-13-04: Advances in genomic medicine are transforming healthcare from a one-size-fits-all model to precision medicine. To ensure that these innovations benefit a broad and diverse population, effective communication between researchers and the public is essential. However, some populations remain insufficiently reached by existing communication strategies. To identify effective approaches for engaging these populations, we conducted a scoping review and examined existing methods for communicating genomic information. The review focused on 1) communication strategies employed and 2) target populations, with particular attention to groups that are difficult to reach. Systematic searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 965 articles published between 2005 and 2025. After the first screening based on predefined eligibility criteria, 330 studies were included. Half of them highlighted the population's literacy/ knowledge, perceptions, and feelings as a strategy to improve communication. Patients and their relatives comprised 42% of the target population. Since 2010, studies have increasingly targeted diverse groups, including the public and specific ethnic communities. From the late 2010s onward, both the range of communication strategies and the diversity of target populations increased. Among the included studies, 31 articles focusing on hard-to-reach populations were selected for full-text analysis. Our next step is to identify key characteristics of these groups for more effective and inclusive communication of genomic information.
P2-13-05: Background: To optimize information provision in genetic and genomic medicine, public awareness should first be assessed in community settings. Methods: We conducted a questionnaire survey among 2,000 randomly sampled citizens using an online survey platform. Awareness was scored as an ordinal variable (0-2). Associations between respondent characteristics, genetic counseling needs, and awareness were examined using non-parametric statistical methods. Free-text responses regarding "genetic" and "genome" were analyzed by word-frequency and co-occurrence network analyses. Results: A total of 372 citizens responded (18.6%). Awareness scores differed by education level, with higher scores in groups with higher educational attainment (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.01). Respondents with current or previous genetic counseling needs had higher awareness scores than those without such needs (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.001). Item-level analysis showed that this difference was mainly attributable to test-related items, including genetic testing and prenatal genetic testing. In qualitative analyses, frequent and connected words for "genetic" included inherited, family, good, and bad, whereas those for "genome" included gene, analysis, difficult, and afraid. Discussion: Awareness was associated with education level and genetic counseling needs. Item-level analysis showed that the difference by genetic counseling needs was mainly attributable to test-related items, suggesting that community interest may be shaped by concrete testing situations rather than abstract medical concepts.
P2-13-06: Background: With the advancement of genomic medicine, improving genomic literacy among the general public has become increasingly important. Since 2024, we have conducted annual public genomic literacy lectures in a hybrid format. Methods: The lectures covered fundamental concepts of DNA, genes, and genome; characteristics and diversity of genomic information; limitations of direct-to-consumer genetic testing; cancer genomic medicine; reproductive and perinatal medicine; genetic counseling; and perspectives from patients and their families. Results: A total of 476 individuals participated over three years, and 349 questionnaire responses (response rate: 73.3%) were analyzed. Among respondents, 54.6% were female. Participants aged 40 years or older accounted for the majority; however, junior and senior high school students participated in 2026, representing 21.9% of participants. Overall, 87.7% of respondents rated the lectures as "excellent" or "good." Although some participants found specialized topics difficult to understand, free-text responses suggested increased awareness of the relationship between genomic information, personal health, and family health. Experiences shared by patients and their families encouraged participants to view genetic information as personally relevant. Conclusions: Public genomic literacy lectures may contribute to improving public understanding of genomic medicine and genetic information. Future efforts should focus on age-appropriate educational programs and collaboration with school-based education.
P3-01-01: <case> We report a case in which Chromosome Analysis of product of conception (POC)was performed in a patient with a history of three recurrent miscarriages, identified tetraploid and a balanced translocation (BT), followed by chromosomal testing of the couple. After BT was confirmed in the wife, preimplantation genetic testing for structural rearrangements (PGT-SR) was performed, achieving a successful pregnancy. The patient was a 37-year-old woman who had spontaneous miscarriages at 5 weeks of gestation at 35 and 36 years of age; she was diagnosed with a symptomless miscarriage at 5 weeks of gestation in this instance as well. Due to this history, genetic counseling (GC) was provided for this miscarriage, and POC was performed. The results were 92,XXXX, t(3;10)(q25;q26) ×2. Based on these results, GC was conducted, and chromosomal testing was performed on the couple. The wife's karyotype was 46XX, t(3;10)(q25;q26). GC focused on recurrent miscarriage was conducted, and it was decided to perform PGT-SR to prevent recurrent miscarriage. Normal embryos or embryos with BT were obtained, and frozen-thawed embryo transfer was performed. Pregnancy was achieved.checkups. <Discussion> The determination that the wife carried the same translocation as the miscarried fetus allowed us to identify one of the causes of the miscarriage and provided information on specific steps to take in preparation for a subsequent pregnancy. Identifying a factor contributing to recurrent miscarriages is considered important for relieving anxiety regarding pregnancy.
P3-01-02: Background: In 2022, Japan revised the NIPT implementation system, allowing testing regardless of maternal age. Although prenatal genetic counseling (PGC) visits by younger women were expected to increase, the effects on test selection and results remain unclear. Objective: To examine changes in PGC clients and NIPT test takers at our hospital before and after the revision. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed first-visit PGC cases from April 1, 2021, to October 31, 2023. July 2022 was excluded as a transition month. The pre- and post-revision periods were April 1, 2021, to June 30, 2022, and August 1, 2022, to October 31, 2023; both spanned 15 months. Age, gestational age, NIPT uptake, and results were collected from medical records. Statistical analyses were performed using Python, with pp <0.05 considered significant. Results: The study included 195 cases before and 211 after revision. Mean age decreased from 36.4±3.9 to 35.5±4.7 years, and the proportion aged<35 years increased from 28.2% to 42.7%. Among NIPT test takers, mean age changed only slightly, from 37.1±3.7 to 36.7±4.1 years. Gestational age was 12.96±1.89 and 12.88±2.06 weeks, and NIPT uptake was 71.3% and 69.7%, with no significant changes. Positivity rates were low in both periods and did not differ significantly. Conclusion: After relaxation of age restrictions, PGC clients became younger, whereas age among NIPT test takers changed only modestly. The uptake and positivity rates of NIPT did not change significantly. PGC may support informed decision-making, including the option not to undergo testing.
P3-01-03: [Introduction] Cleft lip and/or palate can cause feeding difficulty, delayed speech, and malocclusion. Because sibling recurrence burdens parents, prenatal diagnosis and counseling are important. We report two sibling cases diagnosed prenatally by three-dimensional ultrasonography (3D-US). [Case 1] A 26-year-old gravida 4, para 3 woman had no relevant history. Her third child had cleft lip. Cleft lip was suspected at 24 weeks, and 3D-US at 34 weeks showed a hard-palate defect, leading to diagnosis of cleft lip and palate. No other anomalies were detected. She delivered vaginally at 36 weeks. The male infant weighed 2,164 g, had Apgar scores of 8/9, and had cleft lip and palate. After Hotz plate placement on day 13, feeding improved, and he was discharged on day 26. [Case 2] A 26-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman used topical steroids for atopic dermatitis. Her first child had cleft lip. 3D-US at 21 weeks showed fetal cleft lip without cleft palate; the same finding was confirmed at 25 weeks. Labor was induced at 39 weeks, followed by vaginal delivery under epidural anesthesia. The female infant weighed 2,942 g, had Apgar scores of 9/9, and had cleft lip and alveolar cleft without cleft palate. Mother and infant were discharged on day 5. [Discussion and Conclusion] Cleft palate is harder to diagnose prenatally because it is difficult to visualize by ultrasonography. 3D-US may help diagnose fetal morphological abnormalities and explain treatment plans to families. In these cases, 3D-US enabled prenatal diagnosis, genetic counseling, and planning of postnatal management.
P3-01-04: Objectives: NIPT was introduced in Japan, including our center, in 2013. The launch of the new NIPT accreditation system in 2022 led to an increase in testing facilities. With the growing number of NIPT cases, amniocentesis has shown a downward trend. While most current cases have high-risk indications (e.g., ultrasound abnormalities, positive NIPT), some choose it solely for advanced maternal age (AMA). We aimed to clarify the backgrounds and psychological factors (K6 scores) of women who chose amniocentesis. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 68 women whose sole indication was AMA requesting amniocentesis (2020-2025), divided into pre- (2020-2022, n=53) and post-accreditation (2023-2025, n=15) groups to compare backgrounds and K6 scores. Results: Requests due to previous amniocentesis history decreased from 24.5% to 6.7%(p=0.17), while requesting tests beyond three major trisomies increased from 13.4% to 26.7%(p=0.24). Multiparous women decreased (56.6% to 26.7%, p=0.077). Conversely, pregnancies via fertility treatment (28.3% vs 53.3%,p=0.12), miscarriage history (17.0% vs 33.3%, p=0.28), and K6 scores >=5 (5.7% vs 13.3%,p=0.30) showed upward trends post-accreditation. Conclusions: Changes in patient backgrounds and reasons for testing have changed before and after 2022. Pregnant women currently requesting amniocentesis are considered a group with higher anxiety, who may be actively seeking information regarding congenital disorders and prenatal testing. Meticulous pre-test genetic counseling and careful post-test follow-up are necessary.
P3-01-05: Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is a prenatal screening method that evaluates the risk of fetal chromosomal abnormalities using fetal-derived cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in maternal blood. Expanded NIPT, which additionally screens for sex chromosome aneuploidies and microdeletion syndromes, has recently been introduced overseas. We report a case of a vanishing twin pregnancy in which expanded NIPT detected a 4.05-Mb deletion in the 11p15.4 region. She was a 44-year-old Japanese woman (gravida 2, para 1) who conceived by IVF-ET with her Chinese partner. NIPT performed in China revealed a 4.05- Mb microdeletion in 11p15.4, and she was referred to our hospital for amniocentesis at 17 weeks of gestation. Medical interview and ultrasonography revealed a vanishing twin pregnancy. G-banding demonstrated a maternal karyotype of 46, XX and a fetal one of 46, XY. Chromosomal analyses of maternal and amniotic fluid samples showed no 11p deletion or other pathogenic abnormalities, although loss of heterozygosity was observed on maternal chromosomes 2 and 3. Vanishing twin syndrome occurs in 10-39% of IVF pregnancies, and cfDNA from the demised twin may persist in maternal plasma for several weeks after fetal demise. In this case, the absence of abnormalities in the surviving fetus by G-banding, amniocentesis, and ultrasonography suggested that the NIPT finding reflected the genetic background of the demised twin. These findings indicate that NIPT results in vanishing twin pregnancies should be interpreted carefully because cfDNA from the demised fetus may cause false-positive results.
P3-01-06: [Background] Our hospital offers prenatal screening including amniocentesis (AC), chorionic villus sampling (CVS), combined screening, maternal serum marker testing, and non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT). In February 2022, the Japanese Association of Medical Science issued new guidelines on prenatal testing, introducing changes in information provision for pregnant women and eligibility criteria for NIPT. [Objective] This study aimed to investigate trends in prenatal screening utilisation at our hospital. [Methods] We analysed the numbers and demographic characteristics, including maternal age, of patients undergoing prenatal testing at our hospital between April 2018 and March 2026. Patients were included regardless of their planned delivery site. [Results] During the study period, 7,288 patients underwent prenatal testing. The number of NIPT tests increased from 658 in fiscal year (FY) 2018 to 760 in FY2025. The proportions of each test changed as follows: AC/CVS, 9.4% to 3.7%; maternal serum marker testing, 5.3% to 1.8%; combined screening, 17.2% to 5.4%; and NIPT, 68.1% to 89.1%. The proportion of NIPT recipients aged 34 years or younger increased from 4.1% to 45.8%, while the median maternal age decreased from 38 to 35 years. [Discussion] Prenatal tests other than NIPT showed a decreasing trend. The increasing proportion of younger NIPT recipients and decrease in median maternal age may indicate expansion of NIPT use across a broader maternal age range.
P3-01-07: Molecular diagnosis is essential for recurrence-risk counseling in fetal skeletal dysplasia. We report a family in which a maternally inherited COL1A1 variant segregated with severe fetal/infantile skeletal disease despite minimal maternal manifestations. The mother had short stature (138.5 cm) but no fractures, blue sclerae, dental abnormalities, hearing loss, or relevant family history. In the first affected pregnancy, ultrasonography showed severe short and bowed long bones, and postmortem radiography revealed a very thin skull and multiple fractures, consistent with severe osteogenesis imperfecta; genetic testing was not performed. In the second affected pregnancy, targeted gene panel testing of products of conception identified a heterozygous COL1A1 variant, NM_000088.4:c.2236G>A (p.Gly746Ser), classified as likely pathogenic. The variant was confirmed in the fetus and mother, but not in the father. After one early miscarriage, a subsequent child showed severe limb shortening from 18 weeks, carried the same variant after birth, and was diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta type III; she remains alive at over 1 year with bisphosphonate therapy. In contrast, the next child had normal prenatal skeletal findings, was appropriate for gestational age, and did not carry the variant. These findings support segregation of the maternal COL1A1 variant with the phenotype. This case highlights the importance of molecular and parental testing, as counseling may change from apparently sporadic disease to autosomal dominant inheritance with a 50% recurrence risk.
P3-01-09: Background: At our institution, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) is offered to pregnant women with fetal ultrasound abnormalities requesting further genetic evaluation. CMA is a useful test when rapid chromosomal testing indicates a low likelihood of trisomy 13, 18, 21, and sex chromosome aneuploidies. We reviewed cases that underwent CMA and examined the role of genetic counseling (GC). Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 13 cases that underwent CMA between 2023 and 2025: 5 with increased nuchal translucency, 5 with cystic hygroma, and 3 with other structural abnormalities. GC was evaluated according to test results and clinical circumstances. Results: No pathogenic copy number variants were detected in any case. During pre-test GC, information on additional testing options, including RASopathy panel testing and exome analysis, was provided. However, considering cost, turnaround time, and inconclusive findings, no additional testing beyond CMA was selected. Most cases underwent second-trimester ultrasound examinations. Discussion: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends CMA for invasive prenatal diagnosis when fetal structural abnormalities are identified. However, GC should include an explanation of CMA limitations, including the possibility that abnormalities may remain undetected. Information regarding disorders beyond CMA, such as single-gene disorders, may broaden testing options. Cost and turnaround time may burden patients. Individualized GC is essential to support informed decision-making based on patient circumstances and values.
P3-02-01: Pathogenic KIF11 variants cause microcephaly with or without chorioretinopathy, lymphedema, or intellectual disability (MCLMR), characterized by incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. The proband is a 5-year-old girl born to non-consanguineous healthy parents at 37weeks and 5days of gestation. She presented microcephaly and non-pitting edema from neonatal period. Follow-up revealed persistent microcephaly, developmental delay, and chorioretinopathy. Congenital infection screening was negative, and karyotyping was normal. Exome sequencing of the proband identified a heterozygous KIF11 variant (NM_004523.4:c.1604G>A p.(Gly535Asp)). Sanger sequencing confirmed paternal somatic mosaicism via a mutant allele peak in the asymptomatic father. The variant was classified as uncertain significance (PM2 + PP3 + PP4). The clinical presentation of the proband supports pathogenicity of the variant, aligning with documented KIF11 transmission from asymptomatic mosaic parents. The Sanger sequencing chromatogram of unaffected father's leukocyte DNA suggests a high mutant allele fraction. Incomplete penetrance or tissue-specific mosaicism may be responsible for his asymptomatic condition. Therefore, apparently de novo cases necessitate parental mosaicism screening. Paternal gonadal mosaicism cannot be ruled out, elevating recurrence risk. We recommended paternal ophthalmological evaluation to unmask subclinical retinal lesions. This strategy is vital for accurate recurrence risk assessment, carrier management, and genetic counseling.
P3-02-02: With the widespread use of multigene panel testing for hereditary cancer (MGPT), genetic testing has increasingly been recommended for diagnosing hereditary tumor predisposition syndromes. We report a case in which MGPT and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) helped clarify the genetic background of disease. A 14-year-old boy was found to have colorectal polyposis at 12 years of age. Because he also exhibited mild intellectual developmental delay, MGPT was performed and revealed deletions of APC promoter 1A and 1B regions, leading to a diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). However, his neurodevelopmental phenotype could not be fully explained by the APC promoter deletions alone. CMA subsequently identified a copy number loss at 5q21.3-q22.2 including APC (5q22.2) and an approximately 1-Mb copy number gain at 21q22.13. Loss of the 5q22 region containing APC has previously been reported in patients with FAP and intellectual developmental delay. In this case, the 5q21.3-q22.2 deletion may have contributed to the neurodevelopmental phenotype through haploinsufficiency of neighboring genes. In addition, the duplicated 21q22.13 region contains several genes associated with intellectual developmental delay in trisomy 21. These findings suggest that the developmental delay may result from the combined effects of the 5q deletion and 21q duplication. Comprehensive genomic analysis, including CMA, may be useful in patients with polyposis accompanied by atypical clinical features such as intellectual developmental delay.
P3-02-03: CTNNB1 encodes β-catenin, a multifunctional protein involved in cell adhesion and Wnt signaling, and has recently emerged as an important cause of neurodevelopmental disorders and cerebral palsy-like phenotypes. The phenotypic spectrum of CTNNB1 neurodevelopmental disorder (CTNNB1-NDD) is broad and includes developmental delay, intellectual disability, microcephaly, motor impairment, visual abnormalities, and various dysmorphic features. A 3-year-old Japanese boy was referred for evaluation of global developmental delay and microcephaly. He was unable to walk independently and had no meaningful speech. Physical examination revealed microcephaly (-2.5 SD), poor weight gain, large ears, downslanting palpebral fissures, bilateral fifth-finger clinodactyly, right fifth-toe macrodactyly, and truncal hypotonia. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and metabolic investigations were unremarkable. Chromosomal microarray analysis failed to identify a causative abnormality. Trio-based whole-exome sequencing performed through the Initiative on Rare and Undiagnosed Diseases (IRUD) identified a de novo variant in CTNNB1 (c.274C>T, p.Gln92Ter). This variant has been reported in ClinVar as pathogenic and was considered causative of the patient's phenotype. This case highlights the clinical utility of comprehensive genomic testing in children with unexplained neurodevelopmental disorders and expands awareness of the phenotypic spectrum of CTNNB1-NDD among physicians and geneticists.
P3-02-04: Background: ADAR (Adenosine Deaminase, RNA specific) variants usually cause autosomal recessive Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome (AGS) 6 and autosomal dominant (AD) dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH). The heterozygous c.3019G>A, p.(Gly1007Arg) variant is associated with AD AGS/hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), with or without DSH, and incomplete penetrance. Case: A 6-year-old girl developed frequent falls and spastic gait at age 2 years after normal walking acquisition. Brain MRI showed only nonspecific findings, and HSP was suspected. During a febrile infection at age 3 years, she transiently lost speech and ambulation. Whole-genome sequencing identified a heterozygous ADAR c.3019G>A, p.(Gly1007Arg) variant, also detected in her neurologically normal father. After the diagnosis, both were found to have brown macules on the dorsal hands, consistent with DSH. Brain CT revealed bilateral basal ganglia calcifications. Cerebrospinal fluid findings, including neopterin, were normal. Her 1-year-old brother is asymptomatic and has not undergone genetic testing. Discussion: In HSP with this variant, testing neurologically asymptomatic parents can clarify recurrence risk. Neurological deterioration may be triggered by inflammation, including infection or vaccination. Corticosteroids and Janus kinase inhibitors have been reported as treatment options. As no preventive therapy is established, carrier testing in asymptomatic minors may be deferred until they can decide for themselves. Conclusion: Genetic diagnosis for ADAR-related HSP facilitates family evaluation and management.
P3-02-05: [Background] Pathogenic PIEZO2 variants cause the distal arthrogryposis (DA) spectrum, including DA3, DA5, and Marden- Walker syndrome. Although spinal deformities are recognized, tethered cord has not been well characterized. We report two patients with PIEZO2-related DA who had sacral dimples and tethered cord. [Cases] Patient 1 was a 9-month-old girl of Japanese and Filipino ancestry. She had arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, deep-set eyes, and a hypomimic face. Spinal MRI performed for a sacral dimple showed a low-lying conus at L3 without lipoma. She underwent untethering at 9 months. Panel testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic PIEZO2 variant, NM_022068.4:c.8181_8183del, p. (Glu2727del). Patient 2 was a Japanese boy referred neonatally with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, deep-set eyes, and a hypomimic face. Spinal MRI showed a low-lying conus at L4 and a filum terminale cyst without lipoma. He underwent untethering at 5 months. Panel testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic PIEZO2 variant, NM_022068.4:c.8057G>A, p.(Arg2686His). In both patients, postoperative urodynamic abnormalities were observed. [Discussion] To our knowledge, tethered cord has not been described in detail in PIEZO2-related DA. Although causality remains unclear, the recurrent combination of sacral dimples, low-lying conus, and bladder dysfunction is noteworthy. Careful examination for lumbosacral cutaneous stigmata and consideration of spinal imaging may be useful in PIEZO2-related DA. Deep-set eyes and a hypomimic face may help recognize the DA spectrum in congenital arthrogryposis.
P3-02-06: Introduction Williams-Beuren syndrome (WS; OMIM #194050) is caused by a heterozygous deletion in 7q11.23. WS is characterized by supravalvular aortic stenosis (SVAS), peripheral pulmonary stenosis (PPS), intellectual disability, and elfin facies. Although FISH is commonly used for diagnosis, atypical deletions may yield false-negative results. Case report The proband was a female infant born at 40 weeks and 4 days of gestation, weighing 2,962 g. Right ventricular hypertrophy was noted prenatally. Postnatal echocardiography showed severe PPS, mild aortic stenosis, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Her mother and maternal grandfather had ventricular hypertrophy and had been diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Although the mother had mild cognitive impairment and anxiety disorder, typical facial features and neurodevelopmental abnormalities were absent in both relatives. FISH for WS was negative. Chromosomal microarray analysis and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification identified a 7q11.23 microdeletion involving the entire ELN and part of LIMK1 , in all three individuals. Discussion The ventricular hypertrophy in this family was likely caused by SVAS-related pressure overload due to ELN haploinsufficiency. This highlights the risk of delayed diagnosis when FISH is negative and typical WS features are absent. Partial LIMK1 deletion may confer risk for subtle visuospatial impairment. Conclusion7q11.23 microdeletion involving ELN and LIMK1 can present with atypical WS phenotype including cardiovascular and potential neurocognitive features.
P3-02-07: Background: 5p deletion syndrome is characterized by variable clinical features, including a cat-like cry, dysmorphic facial features, microcephaly, and developmental delay or intellectual disability. Although genotype-phenotype correlations have been investigated, prediction of individual phenotypes remains limited because deletion size and gene content vary among patients. Case: A five-month-old girl born to non-consanguineous Japanese parents as their first child. She was born at 39 weeks and 3 days via vacuum-assisted delivery. Her weight was 2,444 g (-1.4 SD), length was 49.3 (+0.4 SD), and head circumference was 30.5 cm (3-10th percentile). From birth, she had stridor, a round face, telecanthus, epicanthus and micrognathia. She was hospitalized at one month of age due to worsening respiratory conditions and poor feeding. She was diagnosed with bilateral vocal cord paralysis and laryngomalacia and underwent a tracheostomy at two months of age. G-banding karyotyping showed 46,XX. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) identified a 3.9-Mb deletion at 5p15.33: arr[GRCh37] 5p15.33(22149_3955850)x1. Discussion: The observed variability of phenotypes among individuals with 5p deletion is thought to be influenced by differences in breakpoints, deletion size, and gene content. Deletions in similar in size to that in the present case have been reported in apparently asymptomatic individuals. We compare this case with previous reports and discuss the relationship between the extent of the deletion and the clinical manifestations.
P3-02-08: With the widespread use of comprehensive genomic analysis such as whole exome sequencing (WES), dual molecular diagnoses are increasingly recognized. We report a case of a child with congenital hypothyroidism and neurodevelopmental symptoms in whom WES revealed variants in both the EBF3 and TG genes. The patient is a 3-year-old girl born small for gestational age. Congenital hypothyroidism was detected by newborn mass screening, and thyroid hormone replacement therapy was initiated during the neonatal period. Despite treatment, she had hypotonia, poor growth, epilepsy, limited facial expression, and severe developmental delay. Her developmental quotient was 53 on the Kyoto Scale of Psychological Development. At 18 months of age, G-banded karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis revealed no pathogenic abnormalities. WES was performed at 27 months of age because of the severe neurodevelopmental phenotype. WES revealed a de novo heterozygous variant in EBF3, NM_001375380.1:c.486-8_501delinsGCT. This novel variant involved the splice acceptor site, and SpliceAI predicted exon 6 skipping. Because congenital hypothyroidism could not be fully explained by EBF3 alone, additional evaluation identified compound heterozygous TG variants, NM_003235.5:c.[2131C>T];[6017G>A], inherited from each parent. In this case, a single molecular diagnosis could not fully explain the complex clinical phenotype. WES led to dual molecular diagnoses, highlighting the importance of reconsidering the phenotype in complex neurodevelopmental disorders.
P3-02-09: Background: Williams syndrome (WS) is caused by a microdeletion in the 7q11.23 region of chromosome 7, and is associated with developmental delay, growth failure, characteristic facial features, and cardiac complications. However, it may also be accompanied by skeletal abnormalities, requiring consideration of skeletal disorders. We report this case as a lesson in the differential diagnosis of WS, without cardiac complications and exhibiting primarily skeletal changes. Case: A 6-year-old boy, born at 40 weeks of gestation and weighing 2735 g, exhibited shortened femurs since the fetal period. His nose was upturned and small, and his auricles were slightly low-set. He had a developmental delay and remained small for his age, with a height of -2 SD and a weight of -1.5 SD. Chromosome analysis revealed a normal male karyotype (46XY), and growth hormone secretion was normal. A cardiac echocardiogram at birth and thereafter, following a diagnosis of Kawasaki disease at 18 months, showed no abnormalities. At the age of 4, he was unable to perform pronation and supination of the forearms effectively. X-ray and MRI examinations revealed bilateral radioulnar synostosis. Microarray chromosomal analysis revealed a 1.4 Mb deletion at 7q11.23, leading to a definitive diagnosis of WS. Discussion: This case was characterized by shortened femurs and radioulnar synostosis, without cardiac complications. Specifically, radioulnar synostosis is reported in 10% of WS cases, suggesting its importance in the differential diagnosis.
P3-02-10: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is characterized by congenital heart disease in approximately 80% of affected individuals, along with developmental delay, characteristic facial features, immunodeficiency due to thymic hypoplasia or aplasia, cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency, hypernasal speech, and hypocalcemia. The condition results from a microdeletion on chromosome 22 that encompasses approximately 30 genes, whose haploinsufficiency contributes to the clinical manifestations. In particular, deletion of TBX1 is strongly associated with conotruncal cardiac defects such as tetralogy of Fallot and interrupted aortic arch. We report a Vietnamese patient who did not exhibit typical features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome but presented with congenital hearing loss and a low TREC value on newborn screening. Genetic evaluation using a next-generation sequencing-based hearing loss gene panel and chromosomal microarray analysis identified congenital sensorineural hearing loss caused by a homozygous pathogenic GJB2 variant, as well as a 22q11.2 microdeletion. Assessment of characteristic facial features was challenging because the patient was of foreign nationality and clinicians were less familiar with dysmorphic features in this population. Moreover, the clinical presentation was atypical for 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, making a clinical diagnosis difficult prior to genetic testing. Through detailed investigation of the underlying etiology and pathophysiology, we were able to establish diagnoses of two distinct genetic disorders in this patient.
P3-02-11: Background: Noonan syndrome (NS), one of the RASopathies, is characterized by a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations. Although clinical diagnostic criteria have been proposed, the diagnosis of NS remains challenging because of its clinical heterogeneity. Prior studies have increasingly elucidated genotype-phenotype correlations in NS, suggesting that the age at diagnosis may differ according to the underlying molecular diagnosis. To further clarify genotype-phenotype correlations, we investigated the association between genotype and age at diagnosis in NS. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 49 patients with molecularly diagnosed NS between 2018 and 2025. Genotypes, diagnostic age, and reasons for referral and genetic testing were extracted. Results: The overall median age at diagnosis was 15 months, ranging from 0 months to 14 years. The gene-specific analysis revealed that patients with RAF1, RIT1 and SHOC2 variants were more likely to be diagnosed during infancy, with median ages at diagnosis of 3.5, 4.0 and 9.0 months, respectively. In contrast, NS patients with PTPN11, SOS1 and KRAS variants were generally diagnosed after infancy, with median ages at diagnosis of 20.0, 24.0 and 50.5 months, respectively. Discussion: The increased prevalence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy among patients with RAF1 or RIT1 variants may contribute to earlier recognition and diagnosis of NS. Furthermore, the early age at diagnosis in patients with SHOC2 variants may reflect their specific clinical features.
P3-02-12: Background: A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is an inborn error of immunity caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in TNFAIP3, presenting with overlapping autoinflammatory and autoimmune features. Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) has rarely been reported in HA20. Case : A 13-year-old boy had perianal abscesses in infancy and periodic fever in early childhood. At 7 years, he developed swelling and pain of the right lateral malleolus. Bone biopsy of the right distal tibial epiphysis showed aseptic osteomyelitis, followed by multifocal lesions in the left tibia and right navicular bone, consistent with CRMO. Genetic testing identified a TNFAIP3 variant, NM_006290.4:c.448C>T (p.Gln150Ter), confirming HA20. Anti-TNF-α therapy controlled the bone inflammation, however, Behcet-like manifestations, including oral aphthae, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and ileocecal aphthous ulcers, subsequently became apparent. His mother had genital/oral ulcers and chronic diarrhea at his diagnosis. She carried the same variant and was also diagnosed with HA20, leading to therapeutic intervention. Discussion: This familial case highlights HA20 as a monogenic cause of CRMO and underlines its intrafamilial phenotypic variability. A20 negatively regulates NF-κ signaling, and its dysfunction promotes inflammatory bone disease through dysregulated osteoclastogenesis and autoinflammation. When CRMO is accompanied by recurrent fever, mucosal ulcers, or gastrointestinal inflammation, HA20 should be considered, and family-based genetic evaluation is essential.
P3-02-13: Subgaleal hematoma (SH) is a neonatal hemorrhagic condition typically associated with instrument-assisted delivery. We report a rare case of SH following non-instrumental vaginal delivery in an infant subsequently diagnosed with Marfan syndrome (MFS). A female infant was born at 39 weeks of gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Her length and weight were average, but arachnodactyly was noted. Immediately after birth, progressive scalp swelling was observed, and SH was diagnosed. Progressive anemia developed, requiring packed red blood cell transfusion on day 2 of life. No coagulation abnormalities or intracranial hemorrhage were identified. At 9 months of age, ankle joint laxity, instability while standing, and marked postnatal growth acceleration raised suspicion of MFS. At 1 year of age, genetic testing identified a pathogenic de novo FBN1 variant, confirming the diagnosis of MFS. Fibrillin-1 abnormalities may increase connective tissue fragility and predispose neonates to SH in response to delivery-related mechanical stress. This case suggests that SH following non-instrumental delivery may represent an early clue to an underlying connective tissue disorder, including MFS.
P3-02-14: Background: Pathogenic variants in QRICH1 are associated with a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmental delay, growth deficiency, and skeletal abnormalities. Severe prenatal manifestations have rarely been reported. Case Presentation: A female infant was referred prenatally because of reduced fetal movements, micrognathia, bell-shaped thorax, and polyhydramnios. At birth, she showed multiple congenital contractures, micrognathia with limited mouth opening, and thoracic hypoplasia. Skeletal radiographs revealed mandibular hypoplasia, slender ribs, and vertebral abnormalities. Brain MRI, karyotyping, and chromosomal microarray analysis showed no significant abnormalities. She exhibited developmental delay with impaired motor and adaptive skills but relatively preserved language development. Trio-based exome sequencing identified a heterozygous de novo missense variant in QRICH1, c.1649A>G, p.(Tyr550Cys). Discussion and Conclusion: The clinical features were largely consistent with those previously reported in QRICH1-related disorder. Reduced fetal movements, congenital contractures, micrognathia with limited mouth opening, and polyhydramnios suggest a severe prenatal presentation of this condition. Micrognathia with limited mouth opening may represent a clinically important manifestation because of its potential impact on feeding and airway management. QRICH1-related disorder should be considered in the differential diagnosis of fetuses with reduced movements and congenital contractures when conventional neuromuscular etiologies are excluded.
P3-02-15: Background: The prime editing (PE) system allows the introduction of point mutations at specific genomic loci without creating double-strand breaks. However, the conventional PE is limited to its target sequences because of the PAM preference to the Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 protein. Here, we report the efficiency of engineered PE-mediated gene correction in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Purpose: To establish iPSCs carrying the BRAF p.V600E variant, which is a well-known driver mutation in various cancers. Methods: Wildtype- PE or engineered-PE plasmids were transfected into iPSCs derived from healthy man via electroporation. Transfected cells were selected using flow cytometry-based cell sorting. Single-cell clones were expanded and analyzed by Sanger sequencing. Results: Among the clones, engineered-PE improved prime editing activity (6-10%) compared with the activity of wildtype-PE (0%). After expansion, all corrected clones expressed pluripotent stem cell markers. Conclusion: The engineered-PE system represents a promising approach for precise gene correction.
P3-02-16: Introduction and case presentation: CNKSR2 is a crucial regulator of RAC1, which plays a significant role in the growth of neuronal dendrites. Heterozygous pathogenic variants of CNKSR2 are associated with intellectual disability with epilepsy, including Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep (DEE-SWAS). However, due to its X-linked recessive genetic disorder, girls are typically asymptomatic. In this study, we identified a pathogenic variant in CNKSR2 (c.2134C>T, p. (Arg712Ter) heterozygous variant (de novo, previously reported)) in a girl with intractable epilepsy and also demonstrate that there was a strong skewing of X chromosome-inactivation (XCI) (85:15). This made it possible to make a definitive diagnosis and provide appropriate treatment. We also present a case of a boy with a novel pathogenic variant in CNKSR2 (c.492C>A, p.(Cys164Ter) hemizygous variant (maternal, novel)). He had symptoms like Angelman syndrome, including a distinctive facial appearance and ataxic gait. Discussion: There have been reports of neurological symptoms caused by a skewing of XCI in females with heterozygous pathogenic variants in CNKSR2. However, this case was more severe than the previously reported female cases, and the skewing of XCI was more pronounced. There is a strong possibility that the severity of this condition in women is correlates with the skewing of XCI.
P3-03-01: Background: BRACAnalysis, a germline BRCA1/2 genetic test, became covered by the national health insurance system in Japan for pancreatic cancer as a companion diagnostic for Olaparib. We investigated the current status of BRACAnalysis in pancreatic cancer patients. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed pancreatic cancer patients who underwent BRACAnalysis at Tokushima University Hospital between March 2021 and April 2026. We evaluated the timing of BRACAnalysis, pathogenic variants, and clinical outcomes. This study was approved by the ethics committee of Tokushima University Hospital (No. 3095). Results: BRACAnalysis was performed in 25 patients. Testing was conducted during first-line chemotherapy in 21 patients, second-line chemotherapy in 2 patients, and third-line chemotherapy in 2 patients. Pathogenic BRCA variants were identified in 3 patients, all of whom harbored BRCA2 pathogenic variants. All patients had a family history of pancreatic cancer. Olaparib was administered in 2 patients. Two patients died 9 and 19 months after diagnosis, whereas 1 patient remains alive 42 months after diagnosis. In the surviving patient, mFOLFIRINOX achieved a partial response, followed by Olaparib treatment and conversion surgery, resulting in recurrence-free survival. Conclusions: BRACAnalysis identified pathogenic BRCA2 variants in 12% of pancreatic cancer patients. Early implementation of BRACAnalysis and appropriate use of Olaparib and platinum-based chemotherapy may improve outcomes in patients with BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants.
P3-03-02: Introduction: Lynch syndrome (LS) is caused by germline variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes and is associated with various malignancies. Gliomas are the most common brain tumors associated with LS, and recent reports suggest the efficacy of the immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) in tumors with a high tumor mutation burden (TMB). The majority of LS cases are attributed to germline variants in either MLH1 or MSH2; however, cases with concomitant germline variants in other DNA repair genes have also been reported. Case Presentation: A male patient with a family history of LS with germline MLH1 variant in his mother. At 26 years of age, he underwent surgery of brain tumor, which was pathologically diagnosed as anaplastic oligodendroglioma. At 49 years of age, surgery was performed for a newly developed brain tumor, which was pathologically diagnosed as high-grade glioma. In the same year, he was diagnosed with transverse colon cancer and subsequently underwent surgery for a cerebellar tumor, which was pathologically diagnosed as glioblastoma. A comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) using GenMineTOP performed on the cerebellar tumor specimen revealed TMB-high status (81.2 mut/Mb).
