Pembrolizumab treatment was administered; however, no therapeutic response was observed, and the patient died 6 weeks later. Secondary findings from the CGP identified germline variants in both MLH1 and ATM. Discussion: ATM is a well-known DNA repair gene. Further investigation is warranted regarding both the prevalence of such cases and their responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
P3-03-03: [Introduction] Lynch syndrome (LS) is an autosomal dominant hereditary disorder caused by pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, significantly increasing the risk for colorectal (CRC) and endometrial cancers (EC). We report a case of LS diagnosed via genetic testing after EC treatment in a patient with early-onset CRC, which subsequently led to detecting metachronous sigmoid colon cancer. [Case Report] A 50s female with a history of rectal cancer at age 29 had undergone regular colonoscopies and multiple endoscopic resections for polyps. Her father had CRC at age 34 and died of gastric cancer at 45. At age 48, she was diagnosed with EC and underwent hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and pelvic/para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Pathology showed Grade 2 endometrioid carcinoma, Stage IB (pT1bN0M0). Postoperatively, she received six cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. Given her clinical history, MMR protein immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed a loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression. Following genetic counseling, a pathogenic variant in the MLH1 gene was identified, confirming LS. One year later, surveillance colonoscopy identified early sigmoid colon cancer within a polyp, which was managed by laparoscopic total colectomy and ileo-lower proctostomy in our Hospital. [Conclusion] In gynecology, EC and ovarian cancer are key sentinel indicators for LS diagnosis. Clinicians must prioritize not only proband treatment and surveillance but also strategies for the early detection and prevention of cancer in at-risk relatives.
P3-03-04: <Background> GAPPS is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder predispose to development of proximal gastric polyposis, that is associated with a high risk dysplasia and gastric adenocarcinoma. Several pathogenic variants for GAPPS in the APC promoter 1B region have already been identified. <Patient> A 50 years old male patient who developed a proximal gastric polyposis at the age of 35, who has a family history of gastric cancer in his mother and maternal aunt, and gastric polyposis in his sister at 37 years old. Moreover, his cousin has diagnosed as clinically GAPPS(PP$). <Method> We conducted a panel sequencing of genes relative to the gastrointestinal cancer-polyposis syndromes. For functional analysis, we constructed luciferase reporter constructs driven by a 500 bp fragment of APC promoter 1B region harboring a wild type or variants and examined the promoter activities in DLD-1 cells. <Results> We identified a novel variant, APC(NM_001127511.2):c.-195A>T located within the APC promoter 1B region in the proband. This variant is not registered at gnomAD nor ToMMo jMorp 61KJPN datebases (PM2). A promoter activity was reduced to 63.5% compared to those of the WT variant and was comparable to the established pathogenic variant for GAPPS, c.-191T>C (PS1). Sanger sequencing demonstrated the proband's sister also possessed this novel variant, while his healthy brother did not (PP1). <Consideration> According to the ACMG/AMP guidelines, we classified this novel variant as likely pathogenic. The functional analysis was key evidence for a proper classification of the variant.
P3-03-05: Background: Japan's 2026 medical fee revision expanded insurance coverage for HBOC care, including BRCA1/2 testing for unaffected first-degree relatives and subsequent risk-management services such as RRSO, RRM, and breast MRI surveillance. Objective: To report the streamlined clinical system established at our institution to accept eligible relatives. Methods: We adopted a mainstreaming approach and developed a pathway linking the Department of Breast Oncology, the Risk Assessment Unit, and the Regional Medical Liaison Office. Breast oncologists provide dedicated outpatient slots, standardized pre-test information, and test ordering, while genetics professionals support complex counseling, interpretation of results, and post-test decision-making. Referrals are centralized through the liaison office, and eligibility checklists, referral forms, patient information sheets, and web-based guidance have been prepared. Results: An operational intake system was established. The pathway clarifies referral routes, initial explanation and testing, timing of genetics involvement, and access to result disclosure and risk management. This structure is expected to reduce confusion, distribute workload beyond genetics-only access points, and enable smooth acceptance of eligible relatives. Conclusion: The 2026 medical fee revision requires not only expanded coverage but also institutional redesign to transition HBOC care from special to standard. Our experience illustrates one practical approach to implementing HBOC care for unaffected relatives in routine oncology practice.
P3-03-06: Background: Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO) reduces ovarian and fallopian tube cancer risk in women with BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants, but factors influencing RRSO uptake and timing in Japan remain unclear. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 70 women with BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants who received genetic counseling at Nagasaki University Hospital from 2013 to 2025. Clinical factors associated with RRSO uptake and with RRSO within 365 days after genetic testing were evaluated using logistic regression. Time to RRSO was also assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression. Results: The mean age was 47.8 years; 55 patients had breast cancer. BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants were identified in 26 and 44 patients, respectively. Overall, 32 patients underwent RRSO, giving an uptake rate of 45.7%. RRSO was covered by public insurance in 29 patients. Multivariable analysis showed that age >45 years and breast cancer history were significantly associated with RRSO uptake. Among patients who underwent RRSO, BRCA1 carriers were more likely than BRCA2 carriers to undergo surgery within 365 days after genetic testing. Kaplan-Meier analysis also showed a shorter median time to RRSO in BRCA1 carriers. The main reasons for not undergoing RRSO were young age or no cancer onset, and ongoing breast cancer treatment. Conclusion: Older age and breast cancer history were associated with RRSO uptake, while BRCA1 status was associated with earlier surgery. Individualized counseling and longitudinal support are essential for informed and timely RRSO decision-making.
P3-03-07: Background) MEN1 is diagnosed either by identifying a pathogenic MEN1 variant or clinically by the presence of tumors in at least two of the parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreas. However, the interpretation of variant negative cases remains controversial. Case Presentation) A woman in her 60s with recurrent urolithiasis was referred for hypercalcemia and elevated iPTH levels. Ultrasonography suggested enlargement of the left inferior parathyroid gland, and 99Tc-MIBI scintigraphy showed abnormal uptake in both the left lower neck and right thyroid region, suggesting multiglandular parathyroid disease. Further endocrine evaluation at a referral center revealed a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma causing acromegaly. Based on the coexistence of PHPT and a pituitary adenoma, she fulfilled the clinical diagnostic criteria for MEN1. Genetic testing was performed, but no MEN1 variant was identified. Discussion) Approximately 5-10% of clinically diagnosed MEN1 patients have no detectable MEN1 variant. Possible explanations include phenocopies, pathogenic variants in other MEN1 related genes such as CDKN1B, or mosaic MEN1. Mutation negative patients are generally older at diagnosis and less likely to develop pancreatic NEN and multiple parathyroid tumors. Considering these characteristics, in this case makes a simple phenocopy difficult to conclude. This case highlights the limitations of current germline testing and emphasizes the importance of integrating clinical phenotypes with genetic findings when managing suspected hereditary endocrine tumor syndromes.
P3-03-08: Background Comprehensive genomic profiling may identify presumed germline pathogenic variants in addition to somatic alterations. However, the clinical handling of such findings can be challenging in patients with advanced cancer, particularly when the patient's condition, treatment course, and family circumstances must be considered. Case and Clinical Course A 35-year-old woman was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 32 and received multimodal therapy. She subsequently developed lymph node recurrence and continued systemic treatment. BRACAnalysisR identified a germline BRCA1 pathogenic variant, and olaparib was administered. During fourth-line therapy, FoundationOneR CDx detected a frameshift variant in STK11, which was reported as a presumed germline pathogenic variant. The patient had a minor child, and the result had potential implications for her relatives. The CGP result, including the presumed germline finding, was disclosed to the patient and her mother. However, as her disease progressed, she required repeated hospitalizations, and confirmatory germline testing could not be pursued. She died 3 years and 10 months after the initial diagnosis. Conclusion This case illustrates the complexity of managing presumed germline pathogenic variants identified by CGP in patients with advanced cancer. Even when disclosure is performed, confirmatory testing and subsequent genetic counseling may be limited by disease progression and family circumstances. Flexible and context-sensitive approaches are needed when addressing presumed germline findings in advanced cancer care.
P3-03-09: Background: Our hospital established a genetic counseling clinic in 2012 and began accepting external referrals in 2019. We evaluated referrals coordinated through the Community Liaison Office to clarify the role of our cancer genetic services. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed clients referred through the Community Liaison Office between April 2019 and March 2026. Reasons for referral, genetic testing, and subsequent management were analyzed. Results: During the study period, 197 clients were referred, accounting for 379 genetic counseling sessions and 118 genetic tests (16%, 15%, and 11% of total clinic activity, respectively). HBOC testing was the most common test (86 cases, 73%), followed by MGPT (14 cases, 12%) and other genetic tests (18 cases, 15%). Sixty clients (30%) had already received a genetic diagnosis elsewhere and were referred mainly for consultation regarding risk-reducing surgery and management of at-risk relatives. Conclusions: Although hereditary cancer testing has become widely available, comprehensive post-test management remains limited. Thirty percent of referrals involved clients already diagnosed elsewhere, indicating a regional need for specialized services, including risk-reducing interventions and management of at-risk relatives. Referrals are expected to increase as insurance coverage expands for testing of relatives. Continued demand for self-funded testing, surveillance, and risk-reducing interventions highlights the need to strengthen cancer genetic services.
P3-03-10: Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Syndrome (HBOC) treatment has rapidly spread nationwide since 2020. But significant institutional disparities remain. Two years ago, we started providing breast cancer (BC) treatment and genetic counseling (GC) at the emergency hospital with the highest number of ambulance arrivals in the prefecture, with no previous experience in GC. This paper outlines the development and status of a hereditary tumor care system in our hospital. Weekly hereditary tumor clinic has been established by a clinical geneticist specializing in BC. Ovarian cancer surveillance and risk-reducing salpingo oophorectomy were referred to another institution, and risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM) was started at our hospital. 70 BC patients received GC and 67 underwent BRCA genetic testing (GT) (62 for diagnosis, 5 as a CDX for olaparib). Of the 62 for diagnosis, 23 were ≤ 45 years old, 12 had TNBC ≤ 60, 14 had multiple breast cancers and 36 had a family history of HBOC-related cancers. Pathogenic variants (PV) of BRCA1 /2 were detected in 6. 2 of them decided to undergo a contralateral RRM during surgery for BC. One received olaparib. Even emergency hospitals without prior experience in GC were able to establish a system for treating HBOC rapidly by a clinical geneticist. The results of GT were used to reduce the mortality risk through surveillance, risk-reducing surgery, and olaparib administration. However, only 3 have utilized MGPT, and only 2 have received GC for cancers other than breast cancer. To further promote genetic medicine, awareness education is necessary.
P3-03-11: Background: Breast/ovarian cancer cluster regions (BCCRs/OCCRs), defined by Kuchenbaecker et al. (JAMA 2015), are BRCA1/2 genomic segments with differentially elevated organ-specific cancer risks. However, major guidelines including NCCN do not recommend cluster region-based management stratification. Methods: Among 301 individuals undergoing BRCA testing at our institution (September 2018-January 2025), 31 PV-positive carriers were identified (BRCA1: n=19, BRCA2: n=12). PVs were annotated by BCCR/OCCR framework. BCCRs: BRCA1 c.179-505 (BCCR1), c.4328-4945 (BCCR2); BRCA2 c.772-1806 (BCCR1'), c.7394-8904 (BCCR2). OCCRs: BRCA1 c.1380-4062; BRCA2 c.3249-5681 (OCCR1), c.6645-7471 (OCCR2). Surveillance and risk-reducing surgery (RRM/ RRSO) were reviewed. Results: 8 carriers (26%) had BCCR variants (5 types: BRCA1 BCCR1 c.188T-A [n=4], BRCA1 BCCR2 c.4485-2A-G [n=1], BRCA2 BCCR1' c.933G-T [n=1], c.1013del [n=1], BRCA2 BCCR2 c.7954dup [n=1]). 13 (42%) had OCCR variants (8 types: BRCA1 OCCR c.2800C-T [n=2], c.1931del [n=2], c.2269del [n=2], c.3038_3040delinsGAAG [n=1], c.2389_2390del [n=1], c.3397_3398del [n=1]; BRCA2 OCCR2 c.6952C-T [n=2], c.7187del [n=2]). 10 had non-cluster variants. RRSO was more frequent in OCCR carriers; however, cluster region-based counseling was not systematically differentiated. Conclusion: 68% of PV carriers harbored BCCR or OCCR variants. Mutation location-aware counseling - enhanced breast surveillance/RRM for BCCR carriers and proactive RRSO for OCCR carriers - may enable more individualized HBOC management beyond gene-level distinction.
P3-03-12: Background: Following the expansion of insurance coverage for BRCA genetic testing in Japan, the number of patients undergoing testing has increased, leading to a growing number of families diagnosed with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC). We reviewed the current status of BRCA genetic testing at our institution. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 233 patients with breast, ovarian, prostate, or pancreatic cancer who underwent BRCA genetic testing at our institution between October 2018 and April 2026. Results: Of the 233 patients, 155 had breast cancer, 9 ovarian cancer, 44 prostate cancer, and 25 pancreatic cancer. Pathogenic BRCA variants were identified in 27 patients. BRCA1 pathogenic variants were detected in 12 patients (9 breast cancers, 2 ovarian cancers, and 1 pancreatic cancer), and BRCA2 pathogenic variants in 15 patients (11 breast cancers, 2 ovarian cancers, 1 prostate cancer, and 1 pancreatic cancer). Three breast cancer patients had variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Genetic counseling was provided to 10 patients. Two families subsequently received genetic counseling, and genetic testing of relatives was confirmed in one family. Conclusions: Differences in testing practices and surveillance were observed among departments. Closer collaboration is needed to ensure appropriate access to BRCA genetic testing. Establishing follow-up systems for pathogenic variant carriers and their relatives remains an important challenge.
P3-03-13: Background: Few reports have described differences in clinical behavior among BRCA1/2 variants, and the efficacy of PARP inhibitors by genotype has rarely been studied. No reports exist on PARP inhibitor efficacy in carriers of the BRCA2 c.5576_5579del variant(KAKO variant), which is common in the Kansai region, particularly Hyogo Prefecture. Methods: In this retrospective study using our hospital's Genetic Counseling Department database, we compared PARP inhibitor efficacy between carriers of the KAKO variant and patients with other genotypes. Results: We analyzed 298 patients: 224 tested for BRCA1/2 at our hospital between 2013 and 2025 with confirmed pathogenic variants, and 74 referred after confirmation elsewhere. KAKO variant accounted for 44 cases (14.8%) and was the most common variant in both BRCA2 and BRCA1/2 overall. Excluding relatives, 218 associated cancers were diagnosed: 120 breast, 84 ovarian, 8 prostate, 5 pancreatic, and 1 of unknown primary. PARP inhibitors were prescribed to 91 patients (olaparib 80, niraparib 6, rucaparib 2, veliparib 3). By genotype, 42 had BRCA1 and 49 had BRCA2 (including 8 with KAKO variant). The median PARP inhibitor duration was 12 months (range 0-72): 12 for BRCA1 and 13 for BRCA2 (8 for KAKO variant vs 19 for other BRCA2 variants). Discussion: Treatment duration was longest for other BRCA2 variants, followed by BRCA1, and shortest for KAKO variant. Because PARP inhibitor duration is strongly influenced by cancer type and treatment setting, further investigation is warranted.
P3-03-14: Background: Breast cancer diagnosed before 30 years of age strongly suggests an inherited cancer predisposition. Although TP53 testing is often prioritized because of its association with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, multigene panel testing (MGPT) may identify pathogenic variants in other susceptibility genes. Case Presentation: A woman in her 20s presented with a right breast mass and was diagnosed with luminal HER2 type breast cancer. She was referred to our institution for treatment. Because of her young age at diagnosis, BRCA1/2 genetic testing was performed and was negative. She was subsequently referred for genetic counseling. Although no remarkable family history of hereditary cancer was identified, hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes were suspected because of the early onset of disease. While TP53 testing would generally be prioritized in a patient diagnosed before 30 years of age, MGPT was selected to evaluate a broader range of cancer susceptibility genes. A pathogenic PALB2 variant, c.3350+5G>A (NM_024675.3), was identified. Functional studies have demonstrated that this variant causes exon skipping (from 11 to 12) , resulting in loss of PALB2 function. Current NCCN Guidelines estimate the lifetime breast cancer risk for PALB2 pathogenic variant carriers from 32% to 53%. Conclusion: MGPT identified a germline PALB2 pathogenic variant in a young woman with breast cancer despite negative BRCA1/2 testing. This case highlights the clinical utility of MGPT in early-onset breast cancer and its value in detecting actionable pathogenic variants beyond TP53 and BRCA1/2.
P3-03-15: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly heterogeneous malignancy, and many aspects of hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related hepatocarcinogenesis remain poorly understood. In particular, the relationship between carcinogenesis and gene expression in HCC has not been fully elucidated. Comprehensive analysis of full-length transcripts may reveal novel gene expression patterns associated with HBV-related HCC. We performed long-read RNA-seq of 114 HCC and 72 nontumor liver tissues using the Oxford Nanopore. Analysis of the resulting data identified and quantified 52,997 transcripts, including 8,368 novel transcripts, providing a comprehensive view of the HCC transcriptome. HBV-derived transcripts were detected in 119 samples (64%), including fusion transcripts between HBV and host genes such as fibronectin and cyclin family genes. Differential expression analysis identified 7,956 upregulated and 3,513 downregulated genes. Notably, 1,036 differentially expressed genes were detected only at the transcript level, indicating that isoform-resolved analysis can uncover novel HCC-associated genes that are missed by conventional gene-level approaches. To identify novel genes involved in HCC pathogenesis, we conducted a knockdown screen of 18 differentially expressed genes in HepG2 and Huh-7. Knockdown of several candidates significantly inhibited cell proliferation, whereas overexpression enhanced proliferation. Further characterization of these candidates will provide insights into the biological functions and molecular mechanisms of novel driver genes involved in the HCC development.
P3-03-16: BACKGROUND: It has been suggested that the BRCA2 p.Ser2616Phe variant may be a likely pathogenic variant specific to the Japanese population. We report a case of breast cancer with this variant. CASE: A 57-year-old woman with no significant past medical history. Family history of gastric cancer (father, died at age 37). She visited our hospital following an abnormal screening result and was diagnosed with bilateral breast cancer after further evaluation. During preoperative chemotherapy, a BRACAnalysis was performed, which identified this variant in BRCA2; this was classified as a VUS. ClinVar lists this as a 'Conflicting classification of pathogenicity.' After discussion during genetic counseling, the management strategy was determined. Breasts: Among the options of (1)bilateral mastectomy or (2)partial resection followed by breast surveillance, option (1) was selected. Ovaries and fallopian tubes: If RRSO is desired, the plan is to consider performing it as self-pay treatment following ethical review. Genetic testing for relatives: Testing is available upon request. DISCUSSION: This variant has been reported in Japanese patients with breast or ovarian cancer, and in silico functional analyses suggest a high likelihood of pathogenicity. Furthermore, while the allele frequency is reported in the Japanese ToMMo38KJPN database, it is not reported in gnomAD, TopMed, HGVD, or other databases. Since ethnicity-specific variants are also found in genes associated with hereditary tumors, measures are needed to ensure that variants specific to the Japanese population are not overlooked.
P3-03-17: Objective: This study aimed to investigate the clinicopathological factors and outcomes of patients with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer who underwent risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy . Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 22 patients who underwent RRSO at our hospital between April 2021 and March 2026. Data extracted from medical records included age at HBOC diagnosis and surgery, pathogenic variants, history and family history of breast cancer, concurrent risk-reducing mastectomy, parity, surgical procedure, and histopathological findings. Results: The median age at HBOC diagnosis was 51 years (range: 32-68), and the median interval from diagnosis to RRSO was 19 months (range: 3-128). The median age at surgery was 52.5 years (range: 41-68). 8 patients carried BRCA1 pathogenic variants, and 14 carried BRCA2 pathogenic variants. A history of breast cancer was present in 21 patients. No concurrent RRM was performed, while concurrent total hysterectomy was performed in 6 patients (27.3%). In one case, ovarian cancer was suspected intraoperatively, leading to primary debulking surgery following frozen section examination. Histopathological evaluation using the SEE-FIM protocol revealed serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in one case (4.5%). Conclusion: Although no unaffected individuals underwent self-funded RRSO at our hospital due to financial barriers, the FY2026 medical fee revision has expanded insurance coverage for HBOC medical care to include first-degree relatives under specific criteria. This change is expected to broaden options for high-risk individuals.
P3-03-18: Introduction When individuals with HBOC develop cancer at a young age, it is not uncommon for this to coincide with their reproductive years. However, there are few case reports in Japan regarding HBOC patients who have undergone in vitro fertilisation. We report on our experience providing genetic counselling for a case of HBOC related breast cancer in which pregnancy was achieved. Case Report The patient developed breast cancer in her thirties. Preoperative chemotherapy was administered. During genetic counselling, the option of fertility preservation was also discussed. Subsequently, the AYA Support Team became involved, and it was decided that egg retrieval and freezing would be carried out at another hospital. Chemotherapy was administered following the egg retrieval. A pathogenic BRCA2 variant was subsequently detected. A total mastectomy was performed, and during post operative genetic counselling, the patient said through tears, While I was in hospital, the doctor told me, you can not possibly have children. I was so sad. I wondered if it had all been in vain. Following hormone therapy, she took a break from treatment and subsequently became pregnant. Conclusion Patients with hereditary tumours experience significant stress as they must simultaneously consider their cancer diagnosis, disclosure of the hereditary tumour, and concerns regarding fertility. The medical team must prioritise the patient`s life above all else and provide support that is sensitive to their personal outlook on life.
P3-03-19: It has been noted that hereditary retinoblastoma is associated with an increased risk of secondary malignancies, including breast cancer. Patients with hereditary retinoblastoma are highly sensitive to radiation, and it is recommended that they avoid radiation exposure. Because the diagnosis and treatment of malignant tumors carry a high risk of radiation exposure, special consideration is required when performing examinations and treatments. We report a case of breast cancer in an adult woman with a history of right retinoblastoma in childhood. Genetic testing of the Rb1 gene suggested a somatic mosaic with a mutation arising during the early embryonic two cell stage. We discuss breast cancer in hereditary retinoblastoma, including considerations for diagnosis and treatment. The patient is a woman in her 30s. She has a history of right retinal blastoma. There is a family history of pancreatic cancer on her maternal grandmother side. She was referred to our hospital due to a lump in her right breast and was diagnosed with right breast cancer, cT3N2bM0, Stage 3A, estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor negative, and HER2 negative. MRI was used for the systemic examination. She underwent preoperative chemotherapy, surgery, postoperative radiation therapy, and medical therapy.
P3-03-20: Background and Objectives Following the 2026 revision of medical fees in Japan, genetic testing and surveillance for asymptomatic relatives of HBOC patients became covered by national health insurance. This requires more efficient follow-up systems. We evaluated surveillance practices at our institution and identified future challenges. Methods We retrospectively reviewed asymptomatic relatives of individuals with confirmed HBOC who underwent genetic counseling between April 2019 and April 2026. Genetic test results and surveillance status were analyzed. Results Twenty-eight relatives were included (6 males, 22 females; median age 39.5 years). HBOC was identified at our hospital in 22 cases (4 of whom were participants in our department of surgery study) and at other institutions in 6 cases. Pathogenic variants were BRCA1 (n = 15) and BRCA2 (n = 13). Surveillance was initiated at our hospital and continued either locally or at other facilities. Genetic counseling was provided alongside surveillance. Of the 28 individuals, 23 (82.1%) continued surveillance, 3 (10.7%) did not initiate, and 2 (7.1%) transferred care. Reasons for non-initiation included younger age (n = 2) and patient preference (n = 1). Discussion High adherence may reflect centralized management and annual consultations. However, increasing numbers of identified carriers under insurance coverage may exceed the capacity of specialized centers. Collaboration with regional providers will be essential for sustainable surveillance.
P3-03-21: [Background and Objectives] In recent years, genomic cancer medicine has become increasingly widespread. While our hospital offers several testing panels, we currently use three main panels: Foundation One CDx (F1CDx), Foundation One Liquid (F1Liquid), and GenMineTop. This study focuses on GenMineTop - a test using paired tumor and normal tissue samples that became eligible for National Health Insurance coverage in August 2023- intending to retrospectively evaluate its current status at our hospital and contribute to the future advancement of genetic medicine. [Subjects and Methods] We analyzed 63 cases (41 men and 22 women) who underwent GenMineTop testing at our hospital between July 2024 and April 2026. We compared the GPV detection rate and gene distribution with C- CAT data reported by Habano et al. [Results] The median age was 57 years for both men and women (men: 25-83 years, women: 7-80 years). Central nervous system tumors, including glioblastoma and glioma, accounted for 37 cases (approximately 60%). The next most common were gallbladder and bile duct cancers, with 10 cases (approximately 16%). The GPV detection rate was 4 cases (6.3%), but none of these patients requested genetic counseling. [Discussion] One possible reason for the lack of referrals for genetic counseling was that patients with central nervous system tumors may have found it difficult to understand their own condition and test results.
P3-03-22: Clinical outcomes following androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in prostate cancer vary considerably. Because endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress mediates apoptosis and tumor adaptation, we investigated associations between ER stress‒related genetic variants and overall survival (OS) in patients receiving ADT. This multicenter study enrolled 630 prostate cancer patients undergoing ADT across three Taiwanese medical centers. We analyzed 89 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) across 12 ER stress–related genes, utilizing Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models to evaluate prognostic associations. Public databases were also integrated for expression, gene set enrichment, and immune infiltration analyses. Among the analyzed SNPs, BAX rs182509214 demonstrated the strongest association with OS; its minor G allele significantly correlated with poorer OS. Prostate tumors exhibited elevated BAX expression compared to normal tissues, predicting worse survival outcomes. Functionally, BAX-associated genes were predominantly enriched in ribosomal, oxidative phosphorylation, and proteasomal pathways. Additionally, BAX expression negatively correlated with CD8+ T-cell infiltration, indicating a regulatory impact on the tumor immune microenvironment. Ultimately, the ER stress–related variant BAX rs182509214 influences OS in prostate cancer patients undergoing ADT. BAX may drive disease progression by modulating mitochondrial metabolism and the immune microenvironment, emerging as a potential prognostic biomarker that warrants broader validation in larger cohorts.
P3-03-23: Structural variants (SVs) are frequently associated with adverse outcomes in hematologic malignancies. Detection remains challenging in clinical laboratories due to limitations of conventional cytogenetics and molecular methods. Reliable identification of these SVs is crucial for improving risk stratification and guiding treatment. Electronic genome mapping (EGM), a solid-state nanochannel-based platform, was used to detect SVs and copy number variants (CNVs) associated with leukemia in 11 cell lines. High molecular weight DNA was extracted, processed with a dual-enzyme workflow, and analyzed on the OhmX™ Platform. SVs were detected using Human Chromosome Explorer® de novo assembly, SV- Verify™, a targeted, alignment-based variant detection application, and CNV analysis pipeline. Variants were confirmed with orthogonal techniques such as sequencing, OGM, and CMA. EGM accurately detected TP53 deletions ranging from 3.8–87 kb, an inv(3) leading to a MECOM rearrangement, a 22.3 kb KMT2A-PTD, an 848 kb deletion forming FILIP1: PDGFRA, a microRNA cluster deletion of miR-15a/16-1, as well as gene fusions such as BCR::ABL1, PML::RARA, and RUNX1::RUNX1T1. These results were resolved with high concordance to published data and orthogonal techniques. We demonstrated EGM’s capability to detect various classes of SVs and CNVs associated with hematological malignancies, complementing traditional cytogenetic and molecular technologies. The cost-effectiveness, precision, and throughput of EGM using the OhmX Platform make it a strong candidate for integration into hematopathology workflows.
P3-03-24: Background: Quality control (QC) in cancer genomic profiling (CGP) testing is essential for identifying optimal therapeutic strategies; however, few studies have evaluated how QC outcomes affect CGP results in routine community hospital practice. We compared clinicopathological and genomic characteristics between QC status groups. Methods: Fifty-three patients who underwent FoundationOne CDx testing were analyzed. Differences between QC groups (Pass vs. Qualified) were evaluated by comparing tumor cell content, tumor purity estimated from CGP data, sequencing depth, number of short variants, variant allele frequency (VAF), and tumor mutational burden (TMB). The relationship between histological tumor cell content (% tumor nuclei, %TN) and tumor purity was also examined. Results: Of 53 cases, 44 were Pass and 9 Qualified. The Pass group showed significantly higher %TN (36.8% vs. 27.2%, p=0.008) and tumor purity (52.8% vs. 17.1%, p<0.001). Mean exon depth and median exon coverage did not differ significantly. The number of short variants (10.6 vs. 7.1, p=0.019) and TMB (4.44 vs. 0.81 mut/Mb, p<0.001) were significantly higher in the Pass group, whereas mean VAF showed no significant difference. Tumor purity predicted QC Pass status with an AUC of 0.962 and an optimal cutoff of 28.7%. %TN moderately correlated with tumor purity. Conclusions: Histological tumor cell content is important for achieving QC Pass status in FoundationOne CDx testing.
P3-04-01: Background and Objectives: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17) is a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG/CAA repeat expansion in TBP. Digenic TBP/STUB1-related SCA17 (SCA17-DI) has recently been proposed. However, their clinical spectrum in Japanese patients remains insufficiently characterized. We investigated clinical and genetic characteristics of patients with SCA17 and SCA17-DI. Methods: We reviewed clinical and genetic data of patients diagnosed with SCA17 or SCA17-DI registered in J-CAT. Results: Six patients were identified, including 3 with SCA17 and 3 with SCA17-DI. Among SCA17 patients, TBP repeat lengths ranged from 48 to 54 repeats. Age at onset ranged from 20 to 50 years. Clinical manifestations were heterogeneous and included cerebellar ataxia, cognitive impairment, dystonia, and parkinsonism. Among SCA17-DI patients, TBP repeat lengths ranged from 45 to 46 repeats and all harbored pathogenic STUB1 variants. Age at onset ranged from 36 to 43 years. Cerebellar ataxia, cognitive impairment, parkinsonism, tremor, and sensory disturbance were observed. Family history suggestive of autosomal dominant inheritance was present in 5 patients. Brain MRI demonstrated cerebellar atrophy in all 6 patients. Discussion and Conclusion: Japanese patients with SCA17 and SCA17-DI exhibited heterogeneous but overlapping clinical manifestations. These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive genetic evaluation, including both TBP repeat and STUB1 variant analyses, in patients with adult-onset cerebellar ataxia and SCA17-like phenotypes.
P3-04-02: A long-term follow up of a case with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease caused by a rare mutation is presented. The patient is a 75 years-old female subject with a long history of weakness in all extremities. She first noticed a gradual wasting at her lower legs when she was 40. When she became 50, she could only walk by using cane, and she also felt numbness on her feet and weaknesses in hand and fingers. Neurological examination at the age of 52 disclosed bilateral, distal dominant weakness in 4 extremities. Electrophysiological tests revealed severe sensory and motor axonal neuropathy. Sural nerve biopsy disclosed severe loss of myelinated fibers with thickening of myelin in remaining nerves. A diagnosis of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease was made. The patient also had bilateral sensory healing loss. After this diagnosis, she gradually became unable to move her extremities. She can still speak now, but cannot eat as normal, which made her to have gastrostomy and feeding. Respiratory muscles are also affected. She is also complicated with a pericardial effusion leading to low cardiac output. A panel genetic testing disclosed a homozygous 2-base pair deletion in a gene, SH3TC2, predicted to cause frameshift. The SH3TC2 protein is specifically expressed in Schwann cells where it is localized to the plasma membrane and to the perinuclear endocytic recycling compartment, suggesting a possible function in myelination and/or in regions of axo-glial interactions. Several mutations are reported from western countries. Report on longstanding course is very few.
P3-04-03: GNE myopathy is a rare autosomal recessive myopathy caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GNE, which encodes an essential enzyme for sialic acid biosynthesis. Most variants are located in exonic regions, whereas significance of intronic variants remains unclear, leaving many suspected cases genetically unresolved. We aimed to assess the pathogenicity of intronic GNE variants using targeted whole-genome and RNA sequencing. We performed Combined Long Amplicon Sequencing (CoLAS) in two siblings with GNE myopathy. DNA and RNA were extracted from muscle biopsy specimens and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Variants were validated using Sanger sequencing. Splicing effects were predicted using SpliceAI and SpliceRover and validated by RNA sequencing. Muscle sialylation was assessed using peanut agglutinin lectin staining. An uncharacterized intronic variant, NC_000009.12(NM_001128227): c.1163+5G>T, was identified in trans with a known missense variant (NM_001128227): c.1807C>G, p.V603L). RNA sequencing demonstrated aberrant splicing caused by intronic mutation, leading to a non-productive transcript in muscle and blood cells. Reduced sialic acid biosynthesis further supported the pathogenicity of the intronic mutation. These findings demonstrate that CoLAS can elucidate the genetic basis of GNE myopathy undetectable by exome sequencing. This approach provides a clinically applicable, less invasive diagnostic strategy and expands the spectrum of pathogenic GNE variants.
P3-04-04: Background/Objectives: DM1 is often diagnosed in mothers after the birth of a child with congenital DM1 (cDM) and is associated with perinatal complications. We investigated perinatal experiences among families affected by DM1 in Japan. Methods: We analyzed data from a nationwide questionnaire survey of parents of patients with congenital or childhood-onset DM1. Participants were recruited through the Remudy registry, patient groups, and medical institutions. Maternal diagnosis, perinatal experiences, and reproductive genetic testing were examined. Results: Of 483 questionnaires, 145 were returned. Fifty-eight mothers with DM1 were analyzed. Histories of infertility treatment, infertility, miscarriage, and stillbirth were reported by 36%, 48%, 18%, and 5%, respectively. DM1 symptoms worsened during pregnancy in 33%. Delivery occurred in general hospitals in 61% of cases, and 47% underwent cesarean section. Only 10% had been diagnosed before pregnancy and 10% during pregnancy, whereas 64% first became aware of possible DM1 after the birth of their affected child. These trends remained unchanged over four decades. Conclusion: Perinatal complications were common, while maternal diagnosis often remained unrecognized until after childbirth. Families may therefore first encounter disease- and genetics-related decisions during the perinatal period. Earlier access to genetic services and information is needed. Further analyses of reproductive genetic testing and its influence on subsequent reproductive decisions will be presented.
P3-04-05: Background: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is an autosomal dominant neuromuscular disorder. Undiagnosed childbearing women are at high risk of delivering neonates with severe congenital DM1, often preceded by non-specific perinatal complications. Case Presentation: A 34-year-old, Gravida 2, Para 1 woman without family history of neuromuscular disorders conceived spontaneously. At mid-trimester, she was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Despite insulin therapy, glycemic control remained poor. She was transferred to our hospital at 34 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound examination revealed that the estimated fetal weight was +2.2 SD and severe polyhydramnios (AFI: 48 cm). Maternal serum CK was elevated. 5 days later, she delivered following premature rupture of membranes and labor onset. The neonate presented with severe generalized hypotonia and respiratory depression, requiring immediate and extensive resuscitation by neonatal team. The postpartum course was complicated by uterine atony requiring intrauterine balloon tamponade. Due to retained products of conception (RPOC) and progressive hemorrhage, uterine artery embolization (UAE) was performed on postpartum day 20. Subsequent genetic testing revealed an abnormal CTG triplet repeat expansion in the DMPK gene in both the mother and the infant, confirming a definitive diagnosis of DM1. Conclusion: This case illustrates that refractory GDM, severe polyhydramnios, uterine atony, and RPOC can serve as critical diagnostic clues for maternal DM1, which carries profound implications for congenital neonatal outcomes.
P3-05-01: <Introduction> In the management of weight in adult patients with Down syndrome accompanied by obesity, there are cases where patients find it difficult to understand the necessity of self-weight management and to take action toward weight reduction. Therefore, this report presents cases of two adult patients with Down syndrome and mild diabetes mellitus who were treated with oral semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist. <Subjects> Two women in their 40s. Both were classified as severely obese. Despite undergoing dietary and exercise therapy for six months, there was no significant weight loss. Consequently, oral semaglutide (3mg daily) was initiated, resulting in approximately 10kg (about 13%) weight loss over one year. No adverse effects or rebound weight gain were observed during the course. Furthermore, the patients’ joy in weight loss led to increased motivation for health, expressed as “happy” and “I will work hard on dieting.” <Discussion> The use of GLP-1 receptor agonists not only contributed to weight reduction but also enhanced patients’ health awareness. For patients with Down syndrome exhibiting severe obesity, where consciously understanding and implementing weight management can be challenging, pharmacotherapy may serve as a viable treatment option.
P3-05-02: Background: Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) is an X-linked metabolic disorder characterized primarily by progressive demyelination within the central nervous system. Clinical presentations vary in age at onset and phenotype, making differentiation sometimes challenging. As hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in the initial stages is the only effective therapy, prompt diagnosis is critical. Case: A 17-year-old boy developed acute irritability and incoherence following pneumonia infection. There were no other abnormal neurological findings. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated hyperintense lesions extending from the lateral lemniscus to the medial geniculate body. Infectious or autoimmune encephalitis was initially suspected, but the treatment was ineffective. Detailed reassessment of the family history revealed that the maternal grandfather was previously diagnosed with ALD after manifesting gait disturbance. Additional investigations demonstrated elevated very-long-chain fatty acids levels, and genetic analysis identified a pathogenic ABCD1 variant (c.1772G>T, p.Arg591Leu), confirming the diagnosis of ALD. The patient was eligible for HSCT and subsequently underwent transplantation. Conclusion: Clinical manifestations of ALD vary even within families, highlighting the importance of detailed family history assessment. ALD should be considered in patients with an acute onset of isolated psychiatric symptoms for early diagnosis and favorable prognosis.
P3-05-03: Introduction OTC deficiency is an X linked urea cycle disorder. Although molecular diagnosis is usually established by genetic testing of the OTC gene, pathogenic variants may remain undetected by conventional sequencing approaches. We report a family in which a novel intronic variant affecting the splice acceptor site was identified approximately 40 years after the initial diagnosis, enabling definitive carrier diagnosis. Case The proband was a boy who died of hyperammonemia at three years of age. Reduced hepatic OTC enzyme activity confirmed the diagnosis of OTC deficiency. A male cousin in the maternal lineage also died of hyperammonemia in early childhood, and the proband's mother had been presumed to be a carrier. Approximately 40 years later, the proband's younger sister requested carrier testing prior to marriage. Genetic Analysis Commercial genetic testing using short read sequencing in the proband's mother failed to identify a pathogenic variant. Targeted long read sequencing did not detect any structural variants but identified a novel intronic splice altering variant, c.387-12G>A. In silico analysis predicted abnormal splicing. A minigene assay confirmed that the variant caused aberrant splicing, resulting in insertion of a 10bp sequence between exons and a consequent frameshift predicted to trigger nonsense mediated mRNA decay. Conclusion Our findings highlight the utility of minigene assays for evaluating suspected splice-altering variants and the importance of extended genetic analysis in genetically unresolved families with OTC deficiency.
P3-05-04: Background: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) can cause adrenal insufficiency and cerebral demyelination in boys. Presymptomatic detection enables endocrine surveillance and timely hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Kumamoto introduced ALD newborn screening (NBS) in October 2024. Methods: Male newborns were screened using dried blood spots collected at 4-6 days of age. LysoPC(26:0) was measured by LC- MS/MS, and infants above the cutoff underwent repeat testing. Screen-positive infants were referred to Kumamoto University Hospital for assessment, genetic counseling, plasma very-long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) analysis, and ABCD1 sequencing. Follow-up included adrenal testing from infancy and brain MRI from 2 years. Results: From October 2024 to March 2026, 8,072 boys were screened. Seven exceeded the initial LysoPC(26:0) cutoff, and two remained positive after repeat testing. Both had no known family history, were clinically normal at referral, and showed elevated VLCFA ratios. Genetic testing identified an ABCD1 variant of uncertain significance in one infant and a pathogenic ABCD1 variant with suspected somatic mosaicism in the other. Both remain asymptomatic with age-appropriate growth and development under regular endocrine follow-up. Conclusion: ALD NBS in Kumamoto identified boys requiring long-term surveillance, including cases with uncertain variant interpretation and somatic mosaicism. The program highlights the need for multidisciplinary follow-up, careful genetic interpretation, counseling, and psychosocial support.
P3-05-05: Background: Pathogenic variants in TWNK, encoding the mitochondrial DNA helicase Twinkle, cause mtDNA maintenance disorders with severe neurological involvement. Disease-relevant human neural cell models for testing mitochondrial rescue strategies remain limited. Methods: We generated iPSC-derived neural progenitor cells (NPCs) from a patient with compound heterozygous TWNK variants and control iPSC lines. NPC identity was confirmed by neural progenitor markers. Mitochondrial phenotypes were assessed by qPCR for mtDNA copy number, ROS levels, and ATP measurement. Mutant NPCs were treated with deoxynucleoside supplementation and compared with vehicle-treated cells. Results: TWNK-mutant iPSCs were successfully differentiated into NPCs. Compared with controls, patient-derived NPCs showed reduced mtDNA copy number, increased ROS, and decreased ATP production, indicating mitochondrial dysfunction. Deoxynucleoside supplementation partially restored mtDNA copy number, reduced ROS accumulation, and increased ATP production in mutant NPCs. Conclusion: Patient-derived iPSC-NPCs recapitulate mtDNA depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction associated with TWNK-related disease. These findings support deoxynucleoside supplementation as a potential mitochondrial rescue strategy and highlight the utility of this model for investigating neural vulnerability caused by mtDNA maintenance defects.
P3-06-01: Clinical and Genetic Analysis of Cleidocranial Dysplasia with RUNX2 MissenseVariants Cleidocranial dysplasia (CCD) is a rare autosomal dominant skeletal disordercharacterized by delayed closure of the cranial sutures, clavicular hypoplasia, delayedpermanent tooth eruption, and supernumerary teeth. Pathogenic variants in runt-relatedtranscription factor 2 (RUNX2), a key regulator of bone and tooth development, are themajor cause of CCD. In particular, missense variants in the runt domain may impair DNAbinding and transcriptional regulation, although their clinical significance can sometimes bedifficult to interpret because of phenotypic variability. Recent advances in clinical genetics have highlighted the importance of integrated variantinterpretation using clinical findings, in silico analyses, segregation data, and functionalstudies based on ACMG/AMP guidelines. However, the pathogenicity of rare or novelRUNX2 missense variants may remain uncertain. Here, we report 3 patients clinically diagnosed with CCD based on characteristic skeletaland dental findings. Genetic analyses identified heterozygous missense variants within theRUNX2 runt domain, including one novel variant. To evaluate its pathogenicity, in silicoanalyses and molecular functional studies were performed. We discuss the clinicalsignificance of RUNX2 runt domain variants and the utility of integrated variantinterpretation in CCD.
P3-06-02: Background: Cowden syndrome is autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) variant. NCCN Guideline 2023, Version 1, simplified the testing criteria of Cowden syndrome. Breast, endometrial or thyroid cancer female patients with head circumference greater than 58cm are eligible for PTEN genetic testing. We report a case meeting this criteria, disclosed two pathogenic PTEN variants. Case Report: A 35-year-old woman underwent bilateral partial mastectomies for breast cancers at age 34. On tamoxifen use, she was found to have endometrial atypical hyperplasia. She had a past history of hemithyroidectomy at 21. Her mother suffered from endometrial cancer at 61. BRCA1/2 testing was negative; head circumference of 61.6cm met Cowden testing criteria, prompted PTEN analysis. Results and Discussion: PCR/direct sequencing analysis from peripheral blood lymphocytes (PBL) identified two pathogenic variants (PTEN NM_000314.8 c.733C>T p.Gln245Ter and c.737C>T p.Pro246Leu), both ClinVar-Pathogenic. RT-PCR/direct sequencing analysis from puromycin treated PBLs resulted in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay for both variants, implying Cis-localization. PCR-SSCP analysis separated the mutant allele; sequencing of the excised band revealed two adjacent variants on the same allele. HGVS nomenclature was corrected to c.733_737delCAGCCinsTAGCT. This report emphasizes routine head circumference measurement in case with relevant cancers and demonstrates that careful RNA and allele-specific analyses may be required to define complex PTEN variants.
P3-06-03: Introduction: Usher syndrome is autosomal recessive disease with hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa, and is the most popular cause of deaf-blindness. USH2A is one of the genes which are known to cause Usher syndrome. We report a case in which retinitis pigmentosa was identified after USH2A variants were detected by genetic analysis of hearing loss, leading to the diagnosis of Usher syndrome. Case: The proband is a 21-years-old female with congenital hearing loss. The pure-tone audiometry bilaterally showed sloping sensorineural hearing loss. After filtering and selection of the candidate variants detected by targeted resequencing of 156 deafness genes, we identified two heterozygous nonsense variant NM_206933.2:c.13639G>T(p.E4547*) and NM_206933.2:c.7252C>T(p.Q2418*) of USH2A. In addition, each variant was identified in the normal-hearing parents as a heterozygous variant. These nonsense variants were interpreted as autosomal recessively pathogenic according to the ACMG2015/ClinGen HLEP criteria. A detailed medical interview after genetic testing results revealed symptoms of night blindness recently. Ophthalmological findings were consistent with retinitis pigmentosa, and the patient was diagnosed with Usher syndrome. Discussion: In this case, genetic analysis detected USH2A variants, and USH2A is known as the representative gene mutation for Usher syndrome. Thus, the identification of USH2A variants enabled the early detection of retinitis pigmentosa, leading to the diagnosis of Usher syndrome even though this patient had few noticeable eye symptoms.
P3-06-04: Background: NF1 causes learning disabilities. Individual variability requires personalized assessment beyond diagnostic labels. Objectives: Profile a child with a novel NF1 variant using KABC-II and CHC theory. Methods: A 13-year-old female with NF1 underwent KABC-II testing; cognitive results were interpreted via CHC theory, a framework mapping intelligence domains. Subsequent genetic testing was performed. Results: Sequencing identified a novel frameshift variant in the NF1 gene [NM_000267.3:c.1344_1350del p.(His448GlnfsTer23)], judged Likely Pathogenic. The CHC Composite was 76 (Gc:77, Gf:82, Gv:72, Glr:87, Gsm:85). Achievement scores were Vocabulary:77, Reading:77, Writing:90, and Mathematics:93. Unlike typical NF1 profiles with 20-50 point language-over-visuospatial (Gc-Gv) gaps, this case showed only a 5-point difference. Mathematics and writing approached population means despite below-average cognition. Discussion: While the variant's pathogenicity (loss-of-function) likely caused overall cognitive reduction, the unique profile with high mathematics/writing scores cannot be explained by genotype alone. This suggests phenotypic modification by environmental factors, such as education and compensatory strategies. This approach applies to other conditions, though single-case findings limit generalizability and necessitate verification through more cases. Conclusions: NF1 profiles are variable. Achievement exceeding cognitive predictions proves genetic vulnerability is compensable with support, highlighting the necessity of personalized assessment.
P3-06-05: Background: Synonymous substitutions and variants distal to exon-intron boundaries (more than 3 bp) may affect splicing, but established guidelines often categorize them as variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Functional validation of these variants is difficult due to inaccessibility of expressed tissues or low gene expression in blood. Therefore, a functional analysis system would be essential to evaluate their splicing aberrations. The aim of this study is to establish a minigene assay using the pSpliceExpress vector that allows for the rapid analysis (within two weeks) of large genomic fragments (from 5 kb to 15 kb). Material and Method : A previously reported and functionally characterized variant in FBN1 (NM_000138.4:c.6354C>T). We cloned the three-exon fragment (the variant-carrying exon and flanking exons) into pSpliceExpress, transfected it into HEK293 cells, and extracted total RNA 48 hours later. Splicing aberrations were evaluated using RT-PCR, electrophoresis, and Sanger sequencing. Result: The c.6354C>T variant in FBN1 was found to disrupt the splice site recognition, resulting in the complete skipping of the target exon, consistent with the previously reported findings of this variant. Conclusion: Minigene assay enables splicing evaluation in challenging cases: difficult tissue sampling or low gene expression in blood. We plan to evaluate multiple VUS in FBN1 using this system, and to validate whether "frozen blood mRNA analysis" could also be a useful method for low-expression genes in blood like FBN1.
P3-06-06: Introduction DYNC1H1 encodes the heavy chain of cytoplasmic dynein 1, a motor protein essential for retrograde axonal transport and other intracellular trafficking processes. Pathogenic heterozygous variants cause a broad, domain specific spectrum, ranging from CMT disease to neurodevelopmental brain disorders. Case presentation Case1 was a 4-year-old boy with global developmental delay (DD) and bilateral congenital vertical talus; examination showed lower-limb-predominant hypotonia, reduced reflexes, and electrophysiology confirmed axonal neuropathy. He developed febrile status epilepticus and had no meaningful words at age 4. Case 2 was a 15-year-old girl who developed focal epilepsy (FE) at the age of 5; her seizures have remained well controlled, and despite mild intellectual disability (ID) requiring special education, she is independent in daily life with good social skills. Whole-genome sequencing revealed de novo heterozygous variants in DYNC1H1 in both cases: a previously reported CMT type 2O allele in the N-terminal tail domain in Case 1 and a novel variant in the C-terminal AAA+ ATPase motor domain in Case 2. Case 1 additionally carried a de novo variant in ZMYND11, an ID-associated gene. Conclusion These cases highlight the broad phenotypic spectrum of DYNC1H1-related disorders. They also suggest that additional variants, such as ZMYND11, may act as modifiers, emphasizing the need for detailed phenotyping and comprehensive genomic analysis in DYNC1H1-associated disease.
P3-06-07: Background: Lynch syndrome is a hereditary cancer syndrome caused by germline pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair genes. We report a case in which an MSH2 variant was identified after discordant MLPA results. Case: A 49-year-old man was diagnosed with rectal cancer at age 39. His tumor showed MSI-H and loss of MSH2/MSH6 protein expression. His mother had early-onset colorectal and endometrial cancers, and his sister had ovarian and rectal cancers. Genetic testing: MSH2 sequencing detected no pathogenic variant in exons and exon-intron boundaries. MLPA analysis using probe set P003 for MLH1/MSH2 showed a significantly reduced signal in a single probe for MSH2 exon 10. We validated this using another probe set, P248, though no alterations were detected. We then conducted long-range PCR using primers set on exon 10 and 11 and identified a 2705-bp deletion in intron 10 (MSH2:c.1661+8_c.1662-1445del). RT- PCR analysis using total RNA from cultured T cells demonstrated aberrant transcripts: one lacking exon 10, whereas the other harbored a truncated exon 10 lacking 82 bp from its 3' region by activation of a splicing donor within exon 10; both resulted in a frameshift. Discussion: Detection of structural variants by MLPA depends on probe design, and pathogenic variants may be missed when only a single probe mix is used. When MLPA shows a single-probe or single-exon deletion/duplication, or when MMR deficiency is suggested despite negative sequencing and inconclusive MLPA findings, confirmation with another probe mix and structural/RNA analyses should be considered.
P3-06-08: USH2A, spanning ~800 kb with 72 exons, is a major cause of Usher syndrome type 2 (USH2). Short-read copy-number variant (CNV) analysis is limited in resolving structural variant (SV) boundaries, allelic phase, and copy-number gains, often leaving cases genetically unsolved. We applied Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing (PromethION P2 Solo, adaptive sampling) with haplotype phasing to five USH2A cases that were undiagnosed or incompletely diagnosed by short-read panel testing. Five distinct and diagnostically challenging SV configurations were resolved: two cases of compound heterozygous deletions that appeared as a single-copy loss or two spatially separated losses on CNV analysis; one homozygous deletion in which haplotype phasing failed to separate alleles, raising suspicion of consanguinity; one family with an apparently autosomal dominant pedigree that was re-interpreted as two independent compound heterozygotes, each carrying a different point variant in trans with the same inherited deletion allele; and one case of a heterozygous tandem duplication in compound heterozygosity with a point variant, identified by breakpoint-spanning split reads and allele-length discrepancy on phased reads. All five cases reached a definitive biallelic USH2A diagnosis. Long-read sequencing with haplotype phasing enables allele-resolved characterization of complex USH2A SVs - including dominant inheritance mimics and cryptic tandem duplications - and substantially complements short-read-based genetic diagnosis of USH2.
P3-06-09: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) is a potentially lethal inherited arrhythmia characterized by exercise- or emotion-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest. Heterozygous missense or in-frame deletion variants in RYR2 typically cause CPVT through a gain-of-function mechanism. Although RYR2 contains 105 exons, pathogenic variants cluster within four hotspot regions. Exome sequencing identified a novel synonymous RYR2 variant, c.11880G>A p.(Gln3960=), in a 49-year-old woman with CPVT. She had an unusually mild phenotype, only with premature ventricular contractions and no major arrhythmic events. The variant was absent from population databases and was inherited from her asymptomatic 74-year-old mother. This variant affects the last nucleotide of exon 88 within a hotspot region, and exon 88 skipping was predicted. Blood RNA analysis was uninformative, likely owing to low RYR2 expression. A minigene assay followed by repeated subcloning of transcripts from wild-type and mutant constructs also failed to detect a difference. Given the exceptionally mild phenotype, aberrant transcripts were suspected to be present at very low levels. Therefore, nanopore-based deep amplicon sequencing of minigene-derived transcripts was performed, revealing a low but significant increase in exon 88 skipping (1.2% in mutant vs. 0.3% in control transcripts), resulting in an in-frame deletion of 35 amino acids [p.(3925_3960del)] within a hotspot region. The low abundance of aberrant transcripts may explain the reduced penetrance in this family.
P3-06-10: Background: Transposable elements (TEs) are a type of mobile genetic element that play important roles in gene regulation and transcription. TE insertions into coding or regulatory regions can result in various genetic disorders. Although a molecular diagnosis can be confirmed in the vast majority of patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), 5% of cases remain genetically unresolved. Here, we report two cases of NF1 resulting from transposable element insertions in NF1. Case 1: A 11-month-old boy exhibiting multiple cafe-au-lait spots (CALS), suggesting NF1 in infancy. He had no family history of NF1 and no clinical manifestations other than CALS. Case 2: A 16-year-old girl clinically diagnosed with NF1 based on the presence of CALS and an optic pathway glioma. She had no family history and cutaneous or plexiform neurofibromas. Targeted analysis of NF1 and SPRED1 using next generation sequencing (NGS) and MLPA were performed for both cases. NGS analysis indicated soft-clipped alignments suggestive of transposable element insertions in exon 25 and exon 13, respectively. Discussion: To date, TE insertions have been reported to account for 0.4% of pathogenic variants in NF1 and may explain approximately 10% of NF1 cases unresolved by conventional molecular analysis. However, hybrid capture-based NGS approaches have limited sensitivity for soft-clipped reads, which restricts the detection of TE insertions. Conclusion: Analysis of TE insertions using soft-clipped reads contributes to early diagnosis of NF1, and further investigation is warranted to improve sensitivity.
P3-06-11: Background Inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs) are a major cause of blindness. Voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) and PrismGuide highlight recent advances in IRD care. The full field stimulus test (FST) was a primary endpoint in the RPE65 gene therapy trial (Fujinami et al., 2025), but genotype specific luminance threshold profiles remain unclear. We evaluated FST thresholds in IRD patients with night blindness. Methods Patients with night blindness were selected from 130 patients (234 eyes) who underwent FST. After 45 minutes of dark adaptation, colour FST used blue, red, and white stimuli (Diagnosys ColorDome) following the ISCEV/IPS guideline. Controls were 40 eyes from 20 healthy subjects. Results We analysed 123 eyes from 62 IRD patients; most had retinitis pigmentosa. Median age at onset was 10.0 years (0 to 70), median age at examination was 48.0 years (0 to 83), and median visual acuity was 0.80 logMAR. Median blue, red, and white FST thresholds were minus 3.7, minus 2.5, and minus 3.5 log10 cd s per square metre, respectively, compared with minus 7.7, minus 5.3, and minus 7.1 in controls. Eighteen causative genes were identified, most commonly EYS, RPE65, and RPGR. Thresholds were higher in disease associated with RPE65 and lower in disease associated with PRPH2. Conclusions FST provides a practical measure of visual sensitivity in IRDs. IRD patients showed markedly elevated luminance thresholds and genotype specific patterns. These findings support FST as a quantitative outcome measure for clinical assessment and therapeutic trials.
P3-06-12: Background and Objectives: Cascade testing (CT), based on the pathogenic variant identified in a proband, can guide health management among relatives. However, many relatives do not receive genetic information, genetic counseling, or genetic testing, limiting opportunities for cancer prevention and surveillance. This study investigated factors associated with genetic testing uptake among relatives. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of 48 probands with hereditary tumor syndromes who underwent genetic counseling at our institution. Clinical information, pedigrees, and CT implementation among relatives were collected. The primary outcome was uptake of genetic testing among relatives. Univariate analyses were performed to evaluate associations between testing uptake and characteristics of relatives. Results: A total of 387 relatives (first-, second-, and third-degree relatives) were included, and 33 (8.7%) underwent genetic testing. Testing uptake was significantly associated with female sex (11.7% vs. 5.5%), first-degree versus second-/third-degree relatives (17.8% vs. 2.7%), relationship to the proband (children 23.3%, siblings 14.1%, parents 17.8%), attendance at the proband's genetic counseling session (44.4% vs. 6.0%), and a personal history of cancer (24.1% vs. 6.2%) (all p<0.05). Conclusions: The CT uptake rate among first-degree relatives was 17.8%. Degree of kinship and characteristics of relatives were associated with CT uptake. Further multivariable analyses accounting for familial clustering are needed to identify independent factors.
P3-06-13: Background: The genetic etiology of many rare diseases remains unresolved due to the limitations of short-read sequencing in detecting complex genomic variants. Long-read technologies offer a promising path toward resolving complex genomic rearrangements at single-nucleotide resolution. Here we report a phased, haplotype-resolved de novo genome assembly for a female patient with an undiagnosed rare disease. Methods and results: The proband was sequenced using PacBio HiFi long-read technology (coverage 32.5×, read N50 17.4 kb), and parental Illumina short-read sequencing data were used to generate parental k-mer databases for trio-based assembly with Hifiasm. The resulting assembly represents a fully phased, diploid genome in which each haplotype is anchored to either the maternal or paternal origin. Assembly contiguity, completeness, and base-level accuracy were assessed using gfastats and yak. Contig N50 was 55 Mb, total assembly length was 3.03 Gb, the number of contigs was 707, and the QV score was 60, all consistent with published HiFi-based human genome assemblies of comparable quality. These assemblies constitute a high-quality genomic resource for downstream variant discovery. Comprehensive SV calling and identification of candidate de novo SVs underlying the proband's phenotype are ongoing and will be reported in a future study. Conclusion: This work demonstrates the utility of long-read, trio-based assembly as a foundation for unbiased variant discovery in rare disease genomics.
P3-06-14: Diphenylarsinic acid (DPAA), an organoarsenic compound associated with neurological abnormalities, has been reported to induce neurobehavioral dysfunction; however, the molecular basis of its neurotoxicity remains incompletely understood. In this study, we performed an integrated multi-omics analysis to characterize molecular responses to DPAA exposure in the primate brain. Brain tissues from 30 control and DPAA-exposed cynomolgus monkeys were collected from the medial temporal lobe (MTL), cerebellum (Cb), lateral temporal lobe, and occipital lobe, across multiple exposure durations (5, 29, 170, and 339 days). Whole-genome sequencing (WGS), RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), and DNA methylation (DNAm) profiling using the Infinium MethylationEPIC array were performed. WGS analysis revealed no substantial increase in genomic mutation burden following DPAA exposure. In contrast, RNA-seq and DNAm analyses identified region- and time-dependent molecular alterations. Transcriptional changes were particularly prominent in the MTL at early stages and in the Cb at later stages. Limited overlap between differentially expressed and methylated genes suggested partially independent regulatory responses. These findings suggest that DPAA-induced neurotoxicity is associated primarily with transcriptional and epigenetic alterations rather than direct genomic changes.
P3-07-01: [Background] SDHB, located on 1p36.13, encodes a subunit of succinate dehydrogenase and acts as a tumor suppressor gene. SDHB-related paragangliomas (PGLs) are associated with early onset and metastasis. [Case] A man in his 50s with metastatic PGL was referred for debulking surgery prior to 177Lu-DOTATATE therapy. He had no relevant medical or family history. He underwent resection of a retroperitoneal PGL in his 20s, and later developed metastases to the liver and bone. CVD chemotherapy was partially effective but discontinued due to neuropathy, and 131I-MIBG therapy was ineffective. Preoperative plasma normetanephrine was markedly elevated. After metyrosine pretreatment, the liver tumor was removed. SDHB immunostaining was negative. [Genetic analyses] Targeted sequencing of 28 PGL-related genes identified a novel germline SDHB variant, c.685_687dup, p.(Glu229dup). Variant allele frequency was higher in tumor than in blood DNA (76% vs 45%). Array-CGH revealed a somatic 1p deletion. [Discussion] Arg230, adjacent to Glu229, is a known mutation hotspot, where disruption of the ionic bond with Asp224 destabilizes SDHB. The p.(Glu229dup) variant may similarly impair protein function. Although in-frame indels are often difficult to interpret, somatic loss of the SDHB wild-type allele and loss of SDHB immunoreactivity supports pathogenicity in this case. [Conclusion] We identified a novel SDHB in-frame insertion in metastatic PGL. Integration of tumor immunohistochemistry and genomics is valuable for variant interpretation.
P3-07-02: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has 13 subtypes and is associated with severe complications during pregnancy. However, there have been no previous reports of pregnancy and perinatal outcomes of cases of periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS). The patient was 34 years old, para 0, and she had no family history suggestive of pEDS. Previously, symptoms such as tooth loss and slow-healing skin wounds were present. Three years previously, genetic testing (complement deficiency gene testing) was submitted, and a missense mutation (c.1013G>A) was detected in the C1R gene. Although this variant has not previously been reported, an amino acid substitution at the same position (p.Cys338Tyr) has been established as a cause of autosomal dominant pEDS. Since this position is essential for CCP1 domain formation in the C1R gene, it was considered likely to have pathogenic significance, leading to a diagnosis of pEDS. The patient and her partner wanted to have children and underwent genetic counseling. They understood that there were many unknown risks associated with pregnancy and childbirth but still wished to undergo infertility treatment. Pregnancy was achieved through assisted reproductive technology. She was hospitalized for preterm labor from 28 to 36 weeks of pregnancy. At 38 weeks, vacuum extraction was performed because of fetal distress. The postpartum course was uneventful, and there were no major problems with wound healing after delivery. This case provides clinically important information regarding pregnancy management and perinatal outcomes in women with pEDS who wish pregnancy.
P3-07-03: Musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mcEDS) is caused by dermatan sulfate (DS) deficiency due to pathogenic variants in CHST14 or DSE. Patients with mcEDS develop progressive skeletal deformities; however, the role of DS deficiency in skeletal pathophysiology remains unclear. Chst14-deficient mice (Chst14-/- ), an animal model of mcEDS, exhibit progressive spinal deformity and impaired bone architecture (Takahashi et al., Glycobiology, accepted). To investigate the role of DS deficiency in bone repair and regeneration, a 0.8-mm drill-hole defect was created in the femur of Chst14-/- and wild-type (WT) mice. Bone repair was evaluated on days 0, 3, 7, 10, 14, 21, and 28. Bone closure was longitudinally monitored by micro-CT, while harvested femurs were used for macroscopic analysis and assessment of cortical bone volume and mineral density. No apparent difference in drill-hole closure was observed between the groups. Reactive bone formation was observed in all groups; however, the reactive bulge disappeared by day 28 only in Chst14-/- with drill-hole defects. Micro-CT analyses of cortical bone volume and mineral density around the defect suggested that WT mice showed sustained reactive bone formation followed by remodeling, whereas Chst14-/-exhibited altered timing and reduced persistence of these responses. These findings suggest that DS deficiency impairs maintenance of reactive bone formation and alters the balance between bone formation and remodeling.
P3-07-04: Musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mcEDS) is a systemic dermatan sulfate (DS) deficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the CHST14 or DSE genes. It is characterized by multiple malformations and progressive fragility-related manifestations. Craniofacial features include large fontanelle, down slanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, microretrognathia, and brachycephaly in early childhood; and asymmetry and mandibular protrusion from adolescence. The aim of this study was to explore the development of craniofacial features of mcEDS e through a mouse model for the disorder. Chst14 gene-deleted mice (Chst14 -/- ) and wild-type mice (WT) were used; and craniofacial radiographs and photographs were obtained and analyzed at 8 and 52 weeks of age. Radiographs showed that the occipital-to-frontal length was significantly shorter in Chst14 -/- mice than WT mice at both ages, and that the mandibular body length was significantly shorter in Chst14 -/- mice than WT mice at 52 weeks. Photographs showed no significant difference in facial symmetricity, facial width ratio, or interpupillary distance to facial length ratio between Chst14 -/- mice and WT mice at both ages. Chst14 -/- exhibited congenital occipital hypoplasia and delayed mandibular growth, representing some overlaps with features in mcEDS. DS deficiency is suggested to affect craniofacial morphogenesis beginning in the fetal period and persisting after birth.
P3-07-05: Background: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a congenital disorder characterized by bone fragility, short stature, and scoliosis. We report a case of perforated descending colon diverticulitis treated with emergency surgery in a patient with osteogenesis imperfecta. Case Presentation: A 50-year-old man with osteogenesis imperfecta was referred to our hospital for suspected gastrointestinal perforation. He had a history of conservative treatment for descending colon diverticulitis. One week before admission, he developed left upper abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed abdominal tenderness with muscular guarding and rebound tenderness. Abdominal computed tomography showed fluid collection with free air around the descending colon. Perforated descending colon diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis was diagnosed, and emergency surgery was performed. Despite severe scoliosis and abdominal deformity, left hemicolectomy, transverse colostomy, and sigmoid mucous fistula creation were successfully performed. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 20. Conclusion: Severe scoliosis and truncal deformity associated with osteogenesis imperfecta may complicate abdominal surgery and perioperative management. As long-term survival of patients with congenital disorders improves, appropriate management of adult-onset gastrointestinal diseases will become increasingly important.
P3-07-06: Introduction: Analytical validation is essential when introducing clinical laboratory tests, including genetic testing. Following the introduction of a D006-4 reimbursed multi-gene panel test in 2024, we conducted analytical validation of an NGS-based genetic test and identified genomic regions that are difficult to analyze using short-read NGS(SR-NGS). Methods: Target regions comprised coding sequences of 187 genes associated with 43 diseases. Variant calling was performed using the DRAGEN pipeline. Analytical accuracy was evaluated using standard DNA samples purchased from NIST and simulation data with variants for all CDS.
