Results: Using both standard materials and simulation data, technically challenging regions were identified in SELENON, NEB, and COL6A1 in the muscle weakness group, and in TTN and GBA1 in the cardiomyopathy group. In SELENON, difficulty was due to lack of capture probes, whereas in the other genes, sequence-specific characteristics caused instability in variant detection. Discussion: Standard materials enabled platform benchmarking, whereas simulation data allowed comprehensive evaluation of variant detection when variants were present. The combined use of these approaches enabled multifaceted assessment of technically challenging SR-NGS regions. Conclusion: Rare disease genetic testing is primarily performed as laboratory-developed tests. Even with limited clinical specimens are unavailable, an analytical validation framework within individual laboratories is required. The approach presented here provides a practical method to meet this requirement.
P3-07-07: Background: Loss-of-function variants in KAT6B are associated with Say-Barber-Biesecker-Young-Simpson syndrome (SBBYSS) and Genitopatellar syndrome (GPS). Isolated sagittal craniosynostosis has been described in only two of more than 150 reported cases of KAT6B-related disorders, leaving the association with KAT6B unclear. Case: The patient was a boy who presented with iris hypopigmentation, micrognathia, laryngomalacia, cryptorchidism, micropenis and developmental delay. At 7 months of age, he was referred for further evaluation of his clinical features. Whole exome sequencing identified a pathogenic nonsense variant c.3718G>T (p.Glu1240Ter) in KAT6B, which is consistent with the diagnosis of GPS. At the age of 4 years, he exhibited marked bitemporal narrowing and ridging of the coronal sutures, suggesting the presence of craniosynostosis. Subsequently, cranial CT revealed complex craniosynostosis. Discussion: A recent study has demonstrated premature ossification and accelerated osteoblast differentiation in Kat6B null mice. The present case may provide further insight into the association between craniosynostosis and KAT6B, highlighting the importance of clinical evaluation for craniosynostosis in KAT6B-related disorders.
P3-07-08: Coatopathies are a heterogeneous group of congenital genetic disorders caused by mutations in coat proteins and their associated factors, which are involved in intracellular vesicle transport. Among them, coatomer protein complex I (COPI) is responsible for retrograde trafficking from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum. COPB2 encodes a component of COPI, and pathogenic variants in COPB2 have been reported to be associated with primary microcephaly in an autosomal recessive manner and childhood- or juvenile-onset osteoporosis with developmental delay in an autosomal dominant manner. In this study, we report three unrelated individuals with novel de novo COPB2 (NM_004766.3) variants identified by exome sequencing: c.893_894inv p.(Lys298Thr), c.1186T>A p.(Trp396Arg), and c.2318G>A p.(Trp773*). cDNA analysis using patient-derived lymphoblastoid cell lines confirmed that c.893_894inv caused skipping of exon 8, leading to a premature termination codon. Clinical features of the three individuals included dystonia, pyramidal signs, spasticity, abnormal muscle tone, developmental delay, dental malocclusion, and variable skeletal features. Our findings expand the phenotypic spectrum of COPB2-related disorder and emphasize the importance of COPI functions in neuronal and skeletal development.
P3-07-09: Introduction: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11.2DS) predisposes to autoimmunity, but type 1 diabetes (T1D) is rare despite islet autoantibody positivity. A previous study suggested that an autoimmunity locus within the standard 3-Mb 22q11.2 deletion may modify T1D susceptibility. We report a child with 22q11.2DS and T1D whose deleted range was examined by array CGH. Case report: A 2-year-9-month-old boy presented with polydipsia, polyuria, and decreased activity. Hyperglycemia, elevated HbA1c, urinary ketones, low fasting serum C-peptide, and positivity for anti-GAD, IA-2, and ZnT8 antibodies led to a diagnosis of acute-onset type 1A diabetes with diabetic ketoacidosis. Short stature, atrial septal defect, speech delay, and characteristic facial features suggested 22q11.2DS, and FISH confirmed a 22q11.2 deletion. Array CGH revealed an approximately 2.81-Mb heterozygous deletion at 22q11.21. This corresponded to the common standard 3-Mb deletion and included the autoimmunity locus suggested to modify T1D susceptibility. Discussion: Although deletion of this locus has been proposed to protect against T1D, this patient developed despite carrying the standard 3-Mb deletion. This suggests that loss of this locus does not fully prevent T1D, and that additional factors such as HLA-related background and multiple islet autoantibody positivity may contribute to diabetes development in 22q11.2DS. Conclusion: This case suggests that deletion of the T1D-related autoimmunity locus alone cannot fully explain T1D development and provides insight into autoimmune diabetes in 22q11.2DS.
P3-07-10: Introduction:AMN encodes amnionless, a protein involved in vitamin B12 absorption and proximal tubular protein reabsorption. Biallelic AMN variants cause Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome type 2, typically with megaloblastic anemia and low-molecular-weight proteinuria. Isolated asymptomatic proteinuria without megaloblastic anemia has been reported in only one prior case. AMN has not been routinely included among the analyzed genes in previous genetic studies of proteinuria. Case Description: We report two Japanese brothers, aged 12 and 8 years, with isolated asymptomatic proteinuria detected by urinary screening. Their urinary protein/creatinine ratios were 0.7 and 0.5 g/gCr. Neither had anemia, impaired kidney function, or extrarenal manifestations. Urinary α-1-microglobulin was mildly elevated only in the elder brother. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous AMN variant, c.750T>G, p.Cys250Trp, in both siblings; both parents were heterozygous. The variant was extremely rare and unreported. In silico tools predicted deleterious effects, and Missense3D structural analysis classified it as damaging. Serum vitamin B12 levels were low in both siblings, consistent with the expected phenotype. It was classified as Likely Pathogenic based on ACMG/AMP criteria with ClinGen recommendations. Discussion: This sibling pair suggests that AMN-associated disease can present as isolated asymptomatic proteinuria with subclinical vitamin B12 deficiency but without anemia. These findings support including AMN in genetic analysis with unexplained isolated asymptomatic proteinuria.
P3-08-01: Background: Chromosome testing is important for diagnosing hematologic malignancies. However, in addition to abnormalities originating from neoplastic clones, non-neoplastic chromosomal abnormalities, including constitutional chromosomal abnormalities, age-related changes, findings originating from transplant donors, and polymorphic findings, may also be detected. Materials and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 5099 lymph node and bone marrow chromosome tests performed for the diagnosis of hematologic malignancies between January 2016 and December 2025, including repeated examinations in the same patients. We investigated the frequency, distribution, clinical significance, and challenges associated with the interpretation of non-neoplastic chromosomal findings. Results: Non-neoplastic chromosomal findings were identified in 49 cases. These included sex chromosome abnormalities (n=1), chromosomal abnormalities suspected to be constitutional or representative of non-neoplastic mosaicism (n=1), age-related Y chromosome loss (n=15), chromosomal abnormalities thought to be donor-derived following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (n=2), inv(9)(p12q13) (n=29), and both inv(1)(p13q21) and inv(9) (p12q13) (n=1). Discussion: When interpreting these findings, it is necessary to distinguish them from neoplastic abnormalities and to comprehensively consider constitutional background, aging, transplantation history, and polymorphic findings. These findings demonstrate practical issues in the explanation of test results and information management.
P3-08-02: Background: Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), formerly persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV), is a congenital ocular disorder caused by failed regression of the fetal hyaloid vasculature. Most cases are sporadic, and familial PFV is rare. Case Presentation: Here, we report PFV-related findings across three generations. The proband was a 35-year-old man diagnosed with PFV of the left eye. He had bilateral microcornea, a mature cataract, and total retinal detachment. Vitreoretinal surgery failed to achieve retinal reattachment, resulting in left-eye loss of vision. G-banding revealed a balanced reciprocal translocation, 46,XY,t(4;7)(p15.3;q36), which was confirmed by FISH. His mother was also diagnosed with PFV. His sister had multiple congenital anomalies involving the heart, limbs, and proptosis, and died at 16 months of age. His daughter was diagnosed with PFV and was found to have microphthalmia, exotropia, and coloboma. Chromosomal microarray analysis revealed a terminal deletion of 4p16.1-p16.3 and a terminal duplication of 7q36.3, both confirmed by subtelomeric FISH. Discussion: Given that the proband carried a balanced translocation, a pathogenic mechanism other than simple gene dosage imbalance is suggested. A position effect associated with the chromosomal rearrangement may have altered the regulation of developmental genes within the 7q36 region, including SHH, a key regulator of ocular and systemic development. Conclusion: Familial PFV associated with t(4;7)(p15.3;q36) suggests a possible position effect involving 7q36 genes in disease pathogenesis.
P3-08-03: Background: Three-to-one segregation in balanced reciprocal translocation carriers may result in a supernumerary derivative chromosome and partial trisomy. We report a patient with a supernumerary der(15) derived from a familial balanced translocation t(11;15)(q23.3;q12). Case Presentation: The patient was a boy with severe developmental delay, congenital heart defects, pharyngeal stenosis, laryngomalacia, hearing loss, and cerebral white matter abnormalities on brain MRI. Chromosome analysis revealed 47,XY,+der(15)t(11;15)(q23.3;q12). His mother carried a balanced reciprocal translocation, 46,XX,t(11;15) (q23.3;q12). Chromosomal microarray analysis demonstrated a 17.7 Mb duplication of 11q23.3-qter and a 7.3 Mb duplication of 15q11.1-q12, consistent with a supernumerary der(15) generated through 3:1 segregation. Discussion: The maternal uncle was also a carrier of the same translocation, and his child reportedly had severe developmental delay with a similar chromosomal imbalance, suggesting recurrence of unbalanced segregation within the family. The proband exhibited severe neurodevelopmental impairment, feeding difficulties, airway abnormalities, epilepsy and white matter abnormalities, overlapping with features of Emanuel syndrome. However, the underlying chromosomal rearrangement differed from the recurrent der(22) associated with t(11;22). Familial supernumerary der(15) resulting from 3:1 segregation of t(11;15)(q23.3;q12) appears extremely rare. This family broadens the phenotypic spectrum associated with partial trisomy of distal 11q and proximal 15q.
P3-08-04: Exchange-type chromosomal aberrations (CAs) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) are useful for retrospective dosimetry and follow-up studies of over-exposed patients after radiation accidents. The dicentric chromosome frequency ranges from 0 to 0.001 in occupationally non-exposed healthy donors at any age, whereas the background translocation frequency increases with age or uncertain factors [1]. The objective of this pilot study was to investigate individual differences in CAs. To this end, chromosomal analysis was performed using the three-color FISH method with chromosomes 1, 2 and 4 paints, combined with the modified FPG staining [2] on a group of ten healthy donors aged 19 to 23 (non-smokers). The selection of this age group was done by the practical considerations of obtaining informed consent and minimizing the influence of acquired factors. More than 1000 metaphases per donor were analyzed to examine cell kinetics and CAs. As a result, the frequency of 2nd metaphase (M2) ranged from 2.9% to 17.0%. Notethat even M3 and M4 metaphases were observed in some donors. The dicentric frequency of M1 detected by DAPI-stain ranged from 0 to 0.001. The mean translocation frequency of M1 per 100 cell equivalent was 0.59 (95%CI, [0.80, 0.38]). The results give rise to a number of intriguing questions, including those concerning inter-individual differences in subpopulations of PBMCs and responses to reagent, and reconsideration of protocols for dosimetry. [1] IAEA: Cytogenetic Dosimetry, pp. 90-94, IAEA, Vienna, 2011. [2] Miho Akiyama et al., Cytologia 89: 1-8, 2024.
P3-09-01: [Background] X chromosome contains genes subject to X chromosome inactivation (XCI) (S), escape genes (E) and genes on pseudoautosomal region 1 (PAR1) expressed from both X chromosomes, and variable escape genes (VE). A DNA methylation index of CpGs in the promoter of genes (MI) is elevated in inactive X of S and inversely correlated with gene expression. Although XCI occurs independently of parental origin, comprehensive analysis of parent-of-origin allele-specific MI (ASM) analysis remains limited. [Objective] To clarify ASM profiles of X chromosomal genes. [Methods] We analyzed four individuals with a 46,XX karyotype, and two individuals each with 46,XY, 45,X, and 47,XXY karyotypes. Promoter regions were defined based on ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements, and the mean MI was evaluated using Long-read sequencing (LRS). Genes were classified as S, VE, and E and genes on PAR1. We evaluated MI differences (>=0.25) among cases with different karyotypes, and examined δMI (maternal allele - paternal allele) for S in four 46,XX cases. [Results] Most S showed karyotypes-dependent MI. For ASM, the median δMI (minimum, maximum) across S was -0.13 (-0.41, 0.07), -0.02 (-0.26, 0.22), -0.02 (-0.23, 0.19), and -0.68 (-0.85, 0.17) in four 46,XX cases, respectively. [Discussion]δMI varied among S in female individuals, suggesting gene-specific MI on inactive X. XCI effects may be gene-specific, although validation by expression analysis is needed. [Conclusion] We established an ASM analysis system for X chromosome using LRS. The effect of XCI on DNA methylation may be gene-specific.
P3-09-02: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is an imprinting disorder primarily caused by epigenetic alterations at chromosome 11p15.5. Conventional diagnostic approaches for imprinting disorders rely on locus-specific assays and have limited ability to evaluate haplotype-resolved methylation patterns. We applied long-read nanopore sequencing to profile genome-wide DNA methylation patterns in individuals with BWS (n = 10) and controls. Using 5-methylcytosine basecalling, haplotype phasing, and DSS (Dispersion Shrinkage for Sequencing data), we evaluated haplotype-resolved methylation patterns across 48 known imprinted differentially methylated regions (DMRs). At 11p15.5, methylation patterns consistent with established BWS subtypes were observed in all cases: loss of methylation at KCNQ1OT1:TSS-DMR (n = 6), gain of methylation at H19/IGF2:IG- DMR (n = 2), and mosaic paternal uniparental disomy (patUPD) (n = 2). In patUPD cases, phasing across KCNQ1OT1:TSS-DMR or H19/ IGF2:IG-DMR could not be achieved. However, Integrative Genomics Viewer visualization demonstrated skewed methylation read distributions consistent with mosaic patUPD. Among individuals with loss of methylation at KCNQ1OT1:TSS-DMR, additional hypomethylation affecting 2-13 imprinted DMRs per sample was identified, supporting multi-locus imprinting disturbance in a part of BWS patients. These findings suggest that epigenetic abnormalities in BWS extend beyond canonical imprinting regions and demonstrate the utility of haplotype-resolved long-read methylation analysis.
P3-09-03: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) regulates post-transcriptional gene expression via mRNA stability and translation. In human trophoblast stem cells (hTSCs), METTL3 is highly expressed and required for maintenance, while m6A profiles change upon differentiation. However, it remains unclear whether m6A modification mainly contributes to mRNA stabilization or degradation in hTSCs. In this study, we detected m6A modification signals in hTSCs at single-base resolution by Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) and calculated gene-level m6A density scores. We also estimated changes in mRNA stability under DOX-inducible METTL3 depletion using a public Actinomycin D chase RNA-seq dataset of hEPSC-derived TSCs (GSE280039), and integrated these data with DRS-derived m6A density scores. Representative candidate genes were validated using METTL3 inhibitor STM2457, GLORI, ActD chase qPCR, and RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP)-qPCR. Integrated analysis showed that m6A -rich genes tended to exhibit prolonged stability after METTL3 depletion, suggesting direct m6A -mediated decay. Genes destabilized after METTL3 depletion showed limited m6A signals, suggesting indirect regulation. In DLX3, a representative m6A -regulated candidate, GLORI confirmed STM2457-induced reduction of m6A modification on DLX3 mRNA, and ActD chase qPCR showed prolongation of mRNA half-life. RIP-qPCR further confirmed YTHDF1/2 binding to the 3'UTR m6A -enriched region of DLX3 mRNA. Although mRNA fate regulation by m6A is considered highly context-dependent, our findings suggest a bias toward mRNA decay in hTSCs.
P3-09-04: DNA methylation profiling has become an essential component of modern brain tumor diagnosis and is increasingly incorporated into integrated molecular classification schemes. Although array-based methylation classifiers are widely used in clinical practice, they require additional laboratory workflows and often involve prolonged turnaround times. Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing provides a unique opportunity to simultaneously generate genomic and methylation information from a single assay, potentially streamlining molecular diagnostics. In this study, we evaluated the performance of MethyLYZR for methylation-based classification of brain tumors using ONT sequencing data. A total of 19 brain specimens were analyzed, representing a diverse cohort of CNS tumors, including gliomas, medulloblastomas, ependymomas, meningiomas, germ cell tumors, craniopharyngiomas, and other brain lesions. Pathology diagnoses, DFKZ classifications, and NIH classifications were available for a subset of samples. All specimens underwent ONT sequencing with modified-base detection enabled and were analyzed using MethyLYZR. MethyLYZR predictions were compared with available pathology diagnoses, integrated diagnoses, DFKZ classifications, and NIH classifications. Classification confidence, concordance, and sequencing depth requirements were assessed. MethyLYZR successfully classified 10 samples from 19 samples with 53% concordance to pathological e diagnoses. Furthermore, the real-time nature of nanopore sequencing enabled rapid generation of diagnostic predictions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of performing brain tumor classification directly from ONT-derived methylation profiles and highlight the potential of MethyLYZR as a rapid and cost-effective approach for integrated molecular diagnostics in neuro-oncology.
P3-10-01: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a high-risk condition for dementia, and multidomain interventions may delay cognitive decline in older adults with MCI. However, responses vary substantially among individuals. We previously conducted the Japan-Multimodal Intervention Trial for the Prevention of Dementia (J-MINT), a multicenter randomized controlled trial evaluating a multidomain intervention in older adults with MCI. Results from the J-MINT suggested that greater cognitive benefits may be achieved in individuals with specific biological profiles. To identify individuals most likely to benefit from the multidomain intervention, we measured blood-based biomarkers (BBMs) in 269 J-MINT participants. Overall cognitive improvement did not differ significantly between the intervention and control groups. However, hierarchical clustering analysis identified a subgroup characterized by elevated glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) levels and multiple biomarker abnormalities, which showed a significant benefit from the intervention. This subgroup was characterized by four associated genetic variants. Furthermore, a predictive model integrating the four associated variants with clinical variables to identify intervention-responsive individuals achieved a mean area under the curve (AUC) of 0.887 (95% confidence interval, 0.866-0.904). These findings suggest that integrating BBMs and genomic information may help identify individuals with MCI who are responsive to interventions and support the development of personalized prevention strategies for dementia.
P3-10-02: Social isolation is increasingly recognized as a public health concern, yet its genetic basis remains poorly understood. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) to identify genetic variants associated with social isolation in Japanese adults. We analyzed 63,497 participants from the Tohoku Medical Megabank Community-Based Cohort Study. Social isolation was assessed using the 6-item Lubben Social Network Scale (LSNS-6) and dichotomized with established cutoffs for the total score and family and friend subscales (<12 and <6, respectively). GWASs were performed using generalized linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, 10 genetic principal components, and genotyping batch. Summary statistics stratified by study site and recruitment route were combined by sample-size-weighted meta-analysis. Social isolation was observed in 25.8%, 14.8%, and 34.1% for the total scale, family subscale, and friend subscale, respectively. Two loci reached genome-wide significance: rs10736933 near ACADSB/HMX3 for the total scale (P = 4.9 × 10-8) and rs1778366 near LINC02315/LRFN5 for the friend subscale (P = 1.1 × 10-8). The family subscale had no significant locus; the top variant was rs780848113 near LMOD1/TIMM17A (P = 4.6 × 10-7). Heritability estimates were 4.0%, 2.4%, and 3.8%, respectively. This GWAS of LSNS-6-defined binary social isolation identified loci associated with overall and friend-related social isolation in Japanese adults. The findings suggest that genetic associations with social isolation may differ by LSNS-6 domain.
P3-11-01: Aim Biological sex differences such as variations in serum oestrogen levels are well known. However, sex differences in gene expression at the cellular level remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether sex differences exist in gene-level and transcript-level expression. Methods We performed the analysis using RNA-seq data from lymphoblastoid cell lines derived from healthy individuals. Differential expression analysis at the gene and transcript levels was performed using the Subio Platform. Isoform switching analysis was performed using IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR. Results Gene-level analysis identified 186 genes with ≥ 2-fold sex-biased expression. These genes comprised 570 transcripts, among which 164 showed differential expression at both gene and transcript levels, whereas 406 showed no differential expression at either level. Transcript-level analysis identified 1,700 differentially expressed transcripts, including 1,536 detected exclusively at the transcript level. Isoform switching analysis identified 43 genes with significant changes in isoform usage. Conclusion Transcript-level analysis detected sex differences not identified by gene-level analysis. Isoform switching occurred independently of overall gene expression changes, suggesting additional regulatory mechanisms. These findings highlight the importance of transcript-level analysis for understanding sex-associated differences in gene regulation and potential disease susceptibility.
P3-11-02: Background: Eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis (ECRS) is a clinically heterogeneous disorder that is frequently severe and resistant to conventional treatment. We have previously demonstrated that nasal brushing, a minimally invasive technique, could elucidate the pathophysiology of ECRS. In this study, we aimed to validate these findings in an expanded cohort. Methods: Nasal brushing specimens were collected from the ethmoidal mucosa in the middle meatus. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on samples from 41 patients with ECRS and 11 controls to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Hierarchical clustering of the 41 patients with ECRS was performed using the top 100 DEGs. In addition, CIBERSORTx was used to infer cellular composition from bulk RNA-seq data. Results: RNA-seq analysis of nasal brushing samples identified 1,225 DEGs between ECRS patients and controls, including 1,019 upregulated and 206 downregulated genes. Hierarchical clustering based on the top 100 DEGs classified ECRS patients into three distinct transcriptomic clusters. Cluster 1 was associated with a significantly lower postoperative recurrence rate than clusters 2 and 3. Cell-type deconvolution analysis indicated that nasal brushing samples comprised epithelial cells as well as diverse immune cell populations, including NK cells, macrophages, and mast cells. Conclusion: Minimally invasive nasal brushing combined with transcriptomic profiling provides a useful approach for molecular endotyping of ECRS and may help predict clinical outcomes, including postoperative recurrence.
P3-12-01: Blood type systems, determined by antigen variation on red blood cells, are widely used genetic markers, including the ABO, RHCE and MNS systems. However, blood group variation in the Jomon, a Neolithic population representing a basal lineage of East Asians, remains poorly characterized beyond limited data from Hokkaido and a small number of systems. In this study, we analyzed blood group-associated variants and inferred genotypes using previously published whole-genome sequencing data from 18 ancient Jomon individuals sampled across the Japanese archipelago (Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu). While ABO variation showed little differentiation from present-day East Asians, Jomon individuals exhibited distinctive allele patterns in several systems, including RHCE*E, GYPB*S, and FUT1*01.02. These findings highlight the distinct red blood cell antigen variation in the Jomon and underscore the value of inferring blood group genotypes from ancient genomes for understanding human population history, as well as the evolutionary dynamics of immune-related genetic variation.
P3-12-02: Taste and olfactory preferences represent complex polygenic traits influenced by sensory, metabolic, and neurobiological determinants. Although associations between specific SNPs and diseases via sensory traits are reported in some studies, their molecular basis requires further elucidation for clinical application. This study examines correlations between SNPs and sensory-cognitive phenotypes to establish a foundation for future studies on personalized healthcare. A total of 108 completed questionnaires were collected from participants aged 20 years or older. Phenotypic data including aroma discrimination, taste perception, and overall preference were collected using two contrasting wine styles to emphasize distinct sensory characteristics as evaluation metrics. Salivary genetic data regarding taste, olfaction, and alcohol metabolism were statistically analyzed against questionnaire-based phenotypic responses. This study was approved by the ethics committees of the Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo and A. D. A. M. Innovations Co. Associations between SNPs and wine-related phenotypes, such as aroma discrimination and taste perception, were analyzed. This pilot study was conducted to identify candidate SNPs and estimate sample sizes for future validation studies. Despite limitations such as a small sample size and subjective questionnaire bias, we plan to expand targeted SNPs and cases. We aim to contribute to improve quality of life through preventive personalized healthcare.
P3-12-03: More than 800 GLA mutations causing Fabry disease are known, but founder effects due to single gene variant have been reported in Taiwan (IVS4+919G>A). The first report of this variant in Japan was by Ishii S et al (2002). Inoue T et al. (2013) identified Fabry disease patients with pathogenic variants, including this variant, in a pilot study of newborn screening in Fukuoka City and its vicinity in Japan. Based on these reports, we hypothesized that the presence of the variant in Japan (especially Kyushu) is related to historical population mobility. The terms "Minato" (Port) and "Tojin-machi" (Chinese settlements) provide evidence of inflows into Japan through trade across the East China Sea (such as Japanese pirates and Japan-Ming trade). "To" in "Tojin-machi" is a place name that has existed in the inner part of Kyushu, and it suggests that a group with the same variant expanded inland via the "Highways". Liang KH et al. (2020) analyzed the haplotype and reported that the variant originated from a single ancestor and occurred in China more than 800 years ago. It may also imply that Japanese patients share the same haplotype. Yoshida S et al. (2020) reported patients with this variant in Fabry high-risk screening in Japan, demonstrating a geographical distribution that extends beyond Kyushu. This study analyzed trade connections and the geographic distribution of the variant using place names as indicators, examining the historical movements of population and considering the role of "Ports" as hubs for maritime transportation and "Highways" as routes for land transport.
P3-12-04: Balancing selection is an evolutionary process that maintains multiple allelic variants in a population over long periods of time. Such long-term maintenance of variation can contribute to adaptation and may be particularly important in genomic regions related to immune response and host-pathogen interactions. This study aimed to identify candidate regions in the human genome that may have been shaped by balancing selection. To detect such regions, we focused on trans-species polymorphisms (TSPs), which are genetic variants shared between humans and closely related primates. Because humans and other great apes diverged millions of years ago, shared polymorphisms may reflect ancient variation that has persisted across species. We compared human population genomic data with genomic data from non-human primates to search for TSP candidates. The analysis identified regions consistent with long-term balancing selection. Some candidates were located near genes related to immune function, including pathways potentially involved in pathogen recognition, inflammation, and host defense. Others were found near genes associated with neurological function, sensory perception, and other physiological traits. These results suggest that balancing selection may affect functions beyond immune response alone. By combining evidence from shared polymorphisms and patterns of variation within human populations, this study narrows down candidate regions for balancing selection and provides a basis for understanding how ancient genetic variation contributed to present-day human diversity.
P3-12-05: Population-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) resources are essential for understanding the impact of rare functional variants on human phenotypes. The Tohoku Medical Megabank (TMM) Project has performed WGS on ~100,000 Japanese individuals and constructed a reference panel of ~61,000 unrelated individuals. Here, we characterized predicted loss-of-function (pLoF) variants and examined their population-level features in the Japanese population. Variant annotation was performed using Variant Effect Predictor and LOFTEE to identify high-confidence pLoF variants, including stop-gained, frameshift, and essential splice-site variants. In the ~61K reference panel, we identified ~157,000 autosomal pLoF variants, >99% of which were rare (minor allele frequency <1%). Comparison with gnomAD showed fewer observed pLoF variants than in global populations but similar numbers to East Asian datasets, reflecting population-specific variation patterns. The per-individual pLoF burden was consistent with previous large-scale sequencing studies, averaging ~220 pLoF variants per individual. Gene-level pLoF counts were generally concordant with gnomAD, although several genes, including MUC family genes and clonal hematopoiesis-associated genes such as DNMT3A and TET2, showed notable deviations. Most identified pLoF variants were absent from ClinVar, indicating substantial unexplored functional variation in the Japanese population. These results provide a large-scale reference for pLoF variation in the Japanese population and support future disease genetics studies.
P3-13-01: Lynch syndrome (LS) is a hereditary cancer syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, and endometrial cancer is a major LS-associated tumor. Although insurance coverage for MMR immunohistochemistry (MMR-IHC) has recently expanded in Japan, uptake of subsequent germline testing remains low. This study evaluated germline testing uptake after MMR- IHC in endometrial cancer patients at our institution. We retrospectively reviewed endometrial cancer patients who underwent MMR-IHC after February 2025. At our institution, MMR-IHC is recommended for surgical cases with advanced disease, high-risk histology, or a family history of LS-related cancers. We assessed MMR abnormality patterns, germline testing uptake, and results. Among 41 surgical cases, seven underwent MMR-IHC. Five showed deficient MMR, but only two proceeded to germline testing. Three declined testing because it was not covered by insurance. Patients who accepted testing were influenced by family history of aggressive LS-related tumors or concern for their adult children. Among patients with MSH2 loss, one had a pathogenic germline variant and one declined testing. Among those with MLH1/PMS2 loss, one tested negative and two declined testing. In conclusion, germline testing uptake was low. Financial burden and the absence of a strong family history may reduce acceptance. Because LS-related endometrial cancer may not show the classic family history seen in colorectal cancer, greater awareness and broader screening strategies may be needed in Japan.
P3-13-02: Background: The detection of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC) has increased with companion diagnostics and comprehensive genomic profiling. Although surveillance of the probands for HBOC-associated cancers and genetic testing of at risk-relatives are recommended after the genetic confirmation of the probands, they are not always performed. We evaluated factors affecting their implementations. Methods: Fifteen patients diagnosed as HBOC at our institution between January 2024 and December 2025 (BRACAnalysis, MyChoice, or CGP) were analyzed. We assessed the impact of the probands' disease status at the genetic confirmation of HBOC and the genetic counseling on the surveillance rates for HBOC-associated cancers and the genetic testing rates of at-risk relatives with chi square test. Results: The surveillance of the probands for HBOC-associated cancers was performed in 5/8 patients with stable disease and 0/7 with unstable disease, that was statistically significant. The genetic testing of HBOC for at-risk relatives was performed in 1/8 stable cases and 4/7 unstable cases with a trend toward higher testing when the proband's disease was unstable. However, the genetic counseling of the probands did not influence the surveillance rates of the probands for HBOC-associated cancers and the genetic testing rates of HBOC for at-risk relatives. Conclusion: At HBOC diagnosis, the probands' disease status rather than the genetic counseling was associated with implementation of the surveillance for HBOC-associated cancers and the genetic testing of at-risk relatives.
P3-13-03: [Background] Risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM) and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO) for BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant carriers became insurance-covered in Japan in 2020. Factors associated with risk-reducing surgery selection in HBOC patients with prior breast cancer remain unclear. [Methods] Among 59 HBOC patients with prior breast cancer diagnosed since April 2020, 38 who underwent risk-reducing surgery were analyzed. Patients were classified into RRM alone (n=6), RRM+RRSO (n=16), and RRSO alone (n=16). Primary analysis compared patients undergoing RRM (n=22) with those undergoing RRSO alone (n=16). Factors included age at HBOC diagnosis, timing of BRCA testing, BRCA1/2 status, breast cancer subtype, family history, reproductive history, neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), and contralateral RRM (CRRM). [Results] Median age at HBOC diagnosis was 41.2, 43.8, and 55.5 years across the three groups. Preoperative BRCA testing rates were 100%, 68.8%, and 43.8%, respectively, and were significantly higher in the RRM group than in the RRSO-alone group (77.3% vs. 43.8%; p=0.047). Non-luminal subtype and NAC use were more frequent in the RRM group. CRRM was concurrently performed in 68.2% of RRM cases. No significant differences were observed in BRCA1/2 status, family history, or reproductive history. [Conclusion] Preoperative BRCA testing was significantly associated with RRM selection. Earlier genetic diagnosis during breast cancer treatment may facilitate consideration of prophylactic breast surgery and contribute to individualized risk-reduction strategies.
P3-13-04: Background: Barth syndrome(BS) is an X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic TAFAZZIN variants, characterized by multisystem manifestations requiring medical care from infancy. We report two genetic counseling(GC) sessions for a female carrier and her mother, conducted five years apart, which facilitated disease understanding tailored to life-stage and family context. Case: A woman in her twenties was identified as a carrier following her brothers' diagnoses of BS, leading to referral of her and her mother to our GC clinic. At the initial GC, she struggled to comprehend the implications of her carrier status, and ongoing GC opportunities were assured. Five years later, as she entered a relationship with a prospective marriage partner, she requested a second GC with her mother to better understand and explain the condition to her partner. GC addressed disease course, inheritance, and the importance of early intervention. Her mother had initially expressed negative feelings toward genetic testing and family disclosure, but following the second GC, both adopted a positive perspective, recognizing its value for the next generation. Discussion: The client's awareness of her carrier status was initially limited, but her informational needs evolved with life-stage transitions. These GC appeared most effective when aligned with psychosocial circumstances and stages of acceptance, offering support for mother and daughter. For female carriers of X-linked disorders, GC should be regarded as a continuing process that reframes genetic information and supports adaptation across life stages.
P3-13-05: Introduction: We report two couples who, following positive maternal serum screening (MSS) or NIPT results, had a diagnosis of fetal trisomy 21 (T21) by amniocentesis and decided to continue their pregnancies. We discuss their conflicts in decision-making and the role of continuous genetic counseling (GC). Case 1: A 43-year-old woman (G2P1) had a positive MSS. Amniocentesis confirmed T21, and the couple was referred for GC. She had thought of continuation of pregnancy but had hesitation considering social trends in Japan that most decided termination after definitive diagnosis. We provided information on expected welfare support for the baby and discussed possible psychological burden of termination. She decided to continue the pregnancy, realizing the reality of raising the child and the psychological burden of termination unbearable for her. Case 2: A 38-year-old woman (G3P0, 2 miscarriages) underwent NIPT. Despite her pre-test intention to continue the pregnancy regardless of the result, her anxiety escalated hearing the positive result. Through GC, we provided information and discussed. After confirmation of the diagnosis by amniocentesis, she decided to continue the pregnancy. Discussion: : Prior to screening, both couples agreed that they would unlikely consider termination. However, the definitive diagnosis triggered their hesitation, driven by anxieties about rearing the baby with T21 and confronting negative social trends. These experiences highlight the critical role in GC of information on welfare support for the baby and realization of termination process.
P3-13-06: Background: Familial genetic counseling has increased as hereditary tumor syndromes are increasingly identified in pediatric cancer patients through paired tumor panel sequencing. While genetic counseling (GC) highlights medical benefits such as surveillance and risk-reducing surgery, Certified Genetic Counselors (CGCs) must also address concerns, stress, and conflicts related to familial cancer predisposition as well as the cancer treatment of the proband. We evaluated the roles of CGCs and optimal support models. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed two families with pediatric cancer patients diagnosed with hereditary tumor syndromes in whom pathogenic variants in BRCA2 and TP53 were identified through paired tumor panel sequencing. CGCs supported these families, who experienced difficulties in decision-making, psychosocial distress, and complex family dynamics. We analyzed their clinical courses, psychological responses, and multidisciplinary interventions. Results: Decision-making support helped families understand genetic issues, including testing of at-risk relatives such as siblings of the proband and management of unaffected variant carriers. This support facilitated decisions consistent with family values. However, conflicts and anxiety persisted after standard GC sessions, indicating the need for ongoing support and interdisciplinary collaboration with pediatric oncologists and geneticists. Conclusion: CGCs should establish a seamless multidisciplinary framework between clinical genetics and oncology departments to address persistent psychosocial vulnerabilities.
P3-13-07: Background: Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (WSS) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized by short stature, developmental delay, hypertrichosis, and distinctive facial features, caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in KMT2A. Objective: To report the clinical and genetic features of three patients with WSS and discuss important findings for clinical diagnosis and genetic counseling. Patients: We report three female patients with WSS (age at diagnosis: Cases 1 and 2, 6 years; Case 3, 15 years). Common findings included developmental delay, short stature, hypertrichosis, growth hormone deficiency, and characteristic facial features with down-slanting and narrow palpebral fissures. In addition, Case 2 had avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, and Case 3 had cervical vertebral fusion anomalies. Trio whole-exome sequencing identified heterozygous pathogenic KMT2A variants in all patients (Case 1: c.676delC, p.Thr225fs; Case 2: c.8806_8809del, p.Val2936* ; Case 3: c.5251A>T, p.Lys1751*). The variants in Cases 1 and 3 occurred de novo, whereas the mother of Case 2 showed mosaicism for the variant. Discussion/ Conclusion: In addition to short stature and developmental delay, hypertrichosis, and characteristic facial features are important clues for the clinical diagnosis of WSS; however, diagnosis based on clinical findings may be difficult because of the nonspecific manifestations. Trio whole-exome sequencing is therefore useful for establishing the diagnosis. The parental mosaicism in Case 2 highlights an important consideration for genetic counseling.
P3-13-08: Background Our department launched a preconception care clinic in February 2024 for women with medical or hereditary conditions who have concerns regarding future pregnancy and childbirth. However, utilization of preconception care among patients with hereditary diseases remains unclear. Methods We retrospectively reviewed patients managed and delivered at our institution between February 2024 and February 2025. We evaluated the implementation of preconception care and genetic counseling among patients with hereditary diseases or hereditary risk pregnancies. Results During the study period, 33 patients attended the preconception care clinic. Only two sought counseling because of hereditary diseases: one with familial adenomatous polyposis and one with Marfan syndrome. During the same period, eight pregnancies complicated by hereditary diseases and five with hereditary fetal risk were managed. Among these 13 cases, six underwent genetic counseling, but none had received preconception care before pregnancy. In six cases, genetic counseling was initiated only after hereditary risks became apparent during pregnancy. Discussion Despite the presence of hereditary diseases and hereditary risk pregnancies, preconception care utilization was limited. Genetic counseling was frequently initiated after conception, reducing opportunities for reproductive decision-making and maternal risk assessment before pregnancy. These findings highlight the need to improve awareness of preconception care and its role in genetic medicine among both healthcare providers and the public.
P3-13-09: At our center, prenatal genetic counseling is provided by a multidisciplinary team, including clinical geneticists, through two outpatient clinics per week. Referral indications include advanced maternal age, suspected fetal abnormalities on ultrasound, a previous child with congenital anomalies, and concerns regarding medication exposure during pregnancy. Between 2021 and 2025, a total of 1,570 prenatal genetic counseling sessions were conducted. Following counseling, prenatal testing included 1,103 non-invasive prenatal tests (NIPT), 110 maternal serum screening tests, and 67 amniocenteses (overlapping cases included). Approximately 70% of patients chose NIPT. Among NIPTs performed at our center, 14 were positive and 4 were inconclusive. Of the 14 positive cases, 3 resulted in miscarriage or stillbirth and 11 underwent termination of pregnancy after confirmatory testing. Among the 4 inconclusive cases, 3 were negative on repeat testing, while 1 was diagnosed with a chromosomal abnormality by amniocentesis and subsequently miscarried. Our center is a certified core facility within the national NIPT program and a regional perinatal medical center. Referrals of NIPT-positive patients from affiliated institutions have increased in recent years. We provide comprehensive counseling and decision-making support for patients with positive NIPT results, fetal abnormalities, or suspected genetic disorders. As NIPT use expands, demand for specialized prenatal genetic counseling continues to increase, highlighting the important role of certified NIPT centers in regional prenatal care.
P3-13-10: Background: The mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variant m.8363G>A in MT-TK, encoding mitochondrial tRNA-Lys, is associated with Leigh syndrome, MERRF-like features, cardiomyopathy, and hearing loss. Although higher mutant loads have been linked to disease, a reliable heteroplasmy level (HL) threshold for predicting severity has not been established. We report a family with m.8363G>A who sought genetic counseling (GC) regarding preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M). Case presentation: The proband developed recurrent vomiting and developmental delay at 5 months. At 8 months, dysphagia and lactic acidosis emerged, followed by death from heart failure. Brain MRI showed bilateral basal ganglia abnormalities, and homoplasmic m.8363G>A in blood confirmed Leigh syndrome. The proband's mother had a blood HL of 64% and remained asymptomatic. She and her partner, residing in the United States, visited our university hospital for GC regarding PGT-M in Japanese. We discussed uncertainty in genotype-phenotype correlation and limitations of PGT-M. The mother preferred male embryos to avoid passing on a similar emotional burden. The couple ultimately chose to pursue PGT-M in the United States. Discussion: PGT-M for mtDNA disorders aims to reduce severe disease risk by selecting embryos with low HL; however, phenotype prediction remains difficult because of the mitochondrial bottleneck and tissue-specific heteroplasmy. This case highlights the complexity of reproductive decision-making for mtDNA disorders and the importance of GC under prognostic uncertainty.
P3-13-11: Introduction: Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) is increasingly used for hematologic malignancies and may reveal hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes as secondary findings, requiring appropriate genetic counseling (GC). Case: The proband was a 47-year-old woman who received a HemeSight genetic panel test to investigate the genetic background of the breast diffuse large B-cell lymphoma . She had been diagnosed with colorectal cancer in their forties., and her mother had died of breast cancer in her 30s. The analysis identified a pathogenic variant in the BRCA2 gene (c.8504C>A, p.Ser2835Ter; variant allele frequency, 44%) as a secondary finding, raising suspicion of HBOC syndrome. Using peripheral blood, we performed BRACAnalysis and confirmed the result. Discussion: Primary breast lymphoma is extremely rare, accounting for less than 0.5% of all malignant breast tumors. To our knowledge, no primary breast lymphoma directly linked to a germline BRCA2 (gBRCA2) pathogenic variant has been reported before. However, the report from overseas have demonstrated an association between gBRCA2 pathogenic variants and non-Hodgkin lymphoma in CAYA generation. This is an atypical case of HBOC, and the proband has two young daughters. Although evidence regarding risks of the future tumor event is limited, ongoing genetic counseling with careful consideration of the timing and approach to sharing genetic information with children, together with longitudinal support through a multidisciplinary team, may be useful for at-risk relatives.
P3-13-12: [Background] Microsatellite instability (MSI) testing is an important biomarker for determining eligibility for immune checkpoint inhibitors. MSI-H may also indicate Lynch syndrome and prompt consideration of genetic counseling (GC) and genetic testing. However, referral of MSI-H cases to genetic services varies among institutions. [Objective] To evaluate GC implementation for MSI-H cases at our institution and identify operational challenges through a physician questionnaire survey. [Methods] We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent MSI testing at our institution between January 2020 and December 2025. Clinical characteristics, GC, and additional testing were assessed. A questionnaire was administered to physicians who had ordered MSI testing regarding GC referral, awareness of GC, and collaboration with the genetics department. [Results] Among 879 patients who underwent MSI testing, 97 were MSI-H. GC was performed in 13 cases, and genetic testing for Lynch syndrome in 4. Awareness of genetics department notifications was reported by 37.5% of physicians; all had experience offering GC. Reasons for not offering GC included patient age and poor general condition. Reasons patients declined GC included low interest in hereditary cancer, cost concerns, and poor health. [Discussion] Despite widespread use of MSI testing, referral of MSI-H cases to genetic services remained limited at our institution. Both physician-and patient-related factors appeared to contribute. More effective strategies are needed to facilitate referral of MSI-H cases to genetic services.
LS1: The treatment of genetic disorders has made remarkable advances in recent years. In particular, in inborn errors of metabolism, direct therapeutic intervention at the protein level has become possible through replacement of deficient or dysfunctional enzymes. In lysosomal storage disorders, enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) was developed relatively early because of the therapeutic advantage provided by the cross-correction mechanism, whereby lysosomal enzymes secreted from normal cells are taken up by deficient cells through receptors on the cell surface and subsequently delivered to the lysosomes, thereby correcting the underlying metabolic defect. ERT, through the exogenous administration of recombinant enzymes, enables these enzymes to reach patient cells via receptor-mediated uptake and has been shown to reduce substrate accumulation in the liver, spleen, heart, skeleton, and skeletal muscle, leading to improvements or stabilization of clinical manifestations and substantial benefits to patients’ quality of life (QOL) . More recently, novel therapeutic strategies have been introduced, including the development of modified enzymes capable of crossing the blood–brain barrier, optimization of administration routes, and combination therapies with pharmacological chaperones. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has also demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in certain lysosomal storage disorders, including effects on the central nervous system when performed at an early stage of disease, and approaches to conditioning regimens continue to evolve. Furthermore, accumulating evidence indicates that early intervention with enzyme replacement, particularly during infancy or early childhood, can prevent or delay irreversible organ damage involving the central nervous system, skeletal muscle, and respiratory muscles, thereby providing substantial benefits in terms of long-term functional outcomes. In this context, mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I; Hurler syndrome), mucopolysaccharidosis type II (MPS II; Hunter syndrome), and glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease) have been included in Tokyo’s publicly funded expanded newborn screening program since 2024, reflecting the growing recognition of the importance of early diagnosis and treatment. In this review, we discuss the clinical benefits of early treatment in these disorders, the current status and limitations of established therapies, and the prospects for emerging therapeutic approaches, including gene therapy and nucleic acid–based therapeutics.
LS2: Long-read sequencing is transforming human genetics by enabling analysis of genomic regions that remain difficult to resolve with short-read DNA sequencing. Using Oxford Nanopore (ONT) ultra-long reads with some PacBio HiFi reads, we constructed diploid telomere-to-telomere genomes of 12 Macaca fascicularis, generating 24 haplotype-resolved DNA sequences. These genomes revealed extensive repetitive and structural variation and enabled complete resolution of 24 MHC haplotypes, including haplotype-specific differences in gene content, copy number, segmental duplications, and genomic organization. Similar approaches should transform human immunogenomics by resolving highly polymorphic HLA, TCR, and BCR loci, that are likely to be associated with immune-related diseases. Long reads also permit accurate analysis of VNTRs reported in Science in 1987 and other tandem repeats, defining repeat number, internal sequence structure, and parental haplotype. Native-DNA ONT sequencing further enables simultaneous detection of sequence variation and DNA methylation. These capabilities are particularly important for rare diseases that remain unexplained after exome or short-read whole-genome sequencing, where causal alterations may include structural variants, repeat expansions, complex rearrangements, or epigenetic abnormalities. Integration of accurate ultra-long sequencing can therefore move human genetics from variant-centric analysis toward complete personal genomes encompassing haplotypes, repetitive sequences, immune-genomic diversity, structural variation, and epigenetic states.
LS3: Human genome analysis relies on reference genomes such as GRCh38. Because GRCh38 was assembled from genomic clones derived from multiple volunteers, it does not represent the genome of any single individual. Advances in long-read sequencing have enabled Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) genome assembly, allowing the reconstruction of continuous end-to-end chromosome assemblies. The Human Pangenome Reference Consortium has generated T2T genomes from 231 individuals representing populations worldwide. We have also released a pangenome graph from 10 Japanese and 9 Saudi Arabian individuals. These resources are emerging as alternatives to conventional linear reference genomes. Long-read sequencing and genome assembly are increasingly used in clinical genome analysis. By combining long-read sequencing with trio analysis or Hi-C, chromosome-scale assemblies can be generated with maternal and paternal haplotypes resolved separately. Although conventional reference-based analyses accurately detect structural variants, they remain limited in regions containing segmental duplications, multicopy genes, and complex structural polymorphisms. T2T genome analysis reconstructs patient-specific diploid genomes at chromosome scale, enabling direct characterization of copy number, gene organization, repetitive structures, and structural variants within individual haplotypes. This approach can reveal complex pathogenic variants and sequences absent from existing references, providing new opportunities to identify disease-causing variants in undiagnosed disorders and advance genomic medicine.
LS4-1: Illumina offers a full range of sequencers—from compact to large-scale models—equipped with the latest technologies, such as XLEAP-SBSTM reagents and DRAGENTM. A wide range of multi-omics applications are being developed for these state-of-the-art sequencers. Already on the market and receiving positive feedback are Illumina Single Cell Prep, a single-cell solution with low upfront costs; the Illumina 5-base solution, which enables simultaneous genome and methylation analysis using a new enzyme that converts methylated cytosine to thymine; SomaSeqTM Discovery, which enables highly reproducible protein analysis using aptamers; and TruPathTM Genome, which enables long-range WGS analysis without the hassle of library preparation—a product that Dr. Miya will introduce. StrataMapTM Spatial, a new spatial expression analysis technology, was added to this product lineup in September. We will introduce Illumina’s latest multiomics platform, which goes beyond sequencing, including the integrated analysis software Illumina Connected Multiomics (ICM).
LS4-2: Short-read sequencing (SRS) has transformed human genome analysis, yet tandem repeats, low-uniqueness regions, and complex structural variants (SVs) remain difficult to resolve. In these areas, long-read sequencing (LRS) has traditionally held the advantage. Illumina has long dominated SRS, but long-range genomic analysis has remained a major challenge. In 2026, Illumina (re)entered this arena with TruPath, a new approach that uses existing NovaSeq instruments while reconstructing short-read data into long-range haplotype information. In other words, Illumina is now taking the fight to LRS on its own territory. TruPath aims to combine long-range phasing and improved access to difficult genomic regions with Illumina’s strengths in throughput and cost efficiency. In this luncheon seminar, I will present our early hands-on experience with TruPath and direct comparisons with multiple sequencing platforms, focusing on difficult genomic regions, SV detection, genome-wide phasing, and clinically relevant disease-causing variants. So, does Illumina dream of long reads? If Illumina can match the genome-variant detection sensitivity of existing LRS technologies while delivering it at substantially lower cost, it may not simply enter the long-read race—it may rewrite the rules.
LS5-1: Electronic Genome Mapping (EGM) is a single-molecule genome mapping technique that analyzes long, labeled DNA molecules using electronic detection. By providing long-range genomic analysis, EGM enables the detection and characterization of structural variants (SVs), copy number variations (CNVs), repeat expansions and contractions, and other complex genomic alterations that can be challenging to resolve using conventional genomic technologies. Structural variants (SVs) — including deletions, duplications, insertions, inversions, and translocations — underlie a substantial share of genomic variation associated with human disease and are frequently missed or incompletely resolved by conventional sequencing and cytogenetic methods. Accurate SV detection is therefore important for rare disease and hematologic malignancy research and for investigating genomic complexity across a wide range of clinical and translational research applications. EGM has the ability to combine genome-wide SV analysis with targeted analysis using either CRISPR/Cas9-mediated approaches or through targeted pipelines. One example of such a pipeline is the RepX pipeline, which supports sizing and analysis of repeat expansions at several disease-associated loci, including C9orf72, DMPK, FMR1 and FXN. This capability is of particular interest in rare disease research, where EGM can provide comprehensive characterization of the wide spectrum of “unstable alleles” at the single-molecule level. I will present recent results from Nabsys researchers and collaborators that demonstrate EGM’s performance and high resolution for detecting disease-associated SVs and CNVs in rare disease and hematologic malignancy research. This highlights EGM’s potential to provide complementary structural genomic information across applications currently investigated using tiered approaches involving multiple genomic technologies.
LS5-2: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is rapidly accelerating the identification of causal variants in rare disease research. National projects worldwide perform whole-exome sequencing (WES) analysis or whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analysis using short-read NGS. WES analysis identifies the cause in approximately 40–50% of undiagnosed cases, whilst WGS analysis finds new causes in around 10% of cases unresolved after WES analysis. Pathogenic variants are nonetheless highly diverse, SNVs, indels, copy number variants (CNVs), indels exceeding 500 bp, structural variants (SVs) such as large, band-level insertions, deletions and inversions, chromosomal translocations, and epigenetic modifications (e.g., methylation), and some escape detection by both WES and WGS. Although long-read NGS detects a wider range of variant types, it too has limits, and detecting large-scale SVs and segmental duplications remains particularly difficult. Plus, some variants may be missed computationally in whole-genome analyses. Detecting all potentially causative variant types is therefore the essential first step, and the analytical method must be selected accordingly. Genome Mapping (GM) analysis like Optical Genome Mapping (OGM) and Electronic Genome Mapping (EGM), which enables comprehensive detection of relatively large SVs including translocations, is increasingly used to complement the limitations of NGS analyses. In this talk, I will present practical examples and best practices for selecting variant types, analytical methods and analytical strategies.
LS6-1: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by pathogenic variants in PAH, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 70,000 births in Japan and requires lifelong control of blood phenylalanine (Phe). Nationwide newborn screening has enabled early diagnosis since 1977, and medical nutrition therapy (MNT) has long been the cornerstone of treatment. However, adherence to dietary restriction and regular Phe monitoring becomes increasingly difficult from adolescence into adulthood. The Assessment of the Treatment and Management LAndScape of phenylketonuria (ATLAS) survey, the first study to characterize PKU management in Japan, evaluated 176 active patients from eight medical institutions before the introduction of pegvaliase. Overall, 76.7% were managed with MNT alone, while sapropterin use was more common in younger patients. Visit and Phe-monitoring frequencies decreased with age, and metabolic control deteriorated markedly after adolescence; except during pregnancy, the proportion of patients achieving target Phe levels declined in older age groups. Persistent hyperphenylalaninemia in adults is associated with impaired attention, working memory, executive function, processing speed, and neuropsychiatric symptoms, which may further complicate self-management. With the recent introduction of pegvaliase and sepiapterin, treatment options in Japan are expanding. Nevertheless, achieving sustained metabolic control while reducing treatment burden remains a major unmet need, particularly for adolescents and adults.
LS6-2: Since pegvaliase (Palynziq) became available in Japan in 2023, treatment of classical phenylketonuria (PKU) has changed markedly. Pegvaliase lowers blood phenylalanine (Phe) independently of phenylalanine hydroxylase and its cofactor BH4. Although PEGylated to reduce immunogenicity, adverse reactions are very common, and both immune responses and the onset of benefit vary widely among patients. Many responders achieve a physiological Phe level of ≤120 µmol/L, and restrictions on natural protein intake may be lifted. Sustained Phe reduction in adults with PKU has highlighted the reversibility of the effects of hyperphenylalaninemia on the brain. Deep white matter lesions on brain MRI have shown improvements, and patients report less irritability and depression, fewer forgotten tasks, less procrastination, and better planning. Clinical benefit may take months or years to emerge, during which patients must cope with hypersensitivity reactions and injection pain. This seminar will discuss practical approaches to ease treatment burden and support patients through the early phases. Adjusting dietary Phe intake and reducing pegvaliase dosage after response will also be focused.
LS7: Homo sapiens reached the Japanese Archipelago 38,000 years ago. The formation of Japanese populations has been studied through archaeology, physical anthropology, and genetics. Ancient DNA (aDNA) provides direct evidence of past human movement and population relationships. Advances in next-generation sequencing have enabled genome-wide analysis of ancient remains, beyond earlier studies focused mainly on mitochondrial DNA. Ancient DNA is fragmented, scarce, and vulnerable to modern DNA contamination. Target capture selectively enriches specific DNA sequences, enabling recovery of genetic information from limited aDNA. Methods targeting many SNPs have improved analysis of poorly preserved remains. Ancient genomic studies show that Jomon people had a distinctive genetic composition, while migration from continental Asia after the Yayoi period strongly influenced Japanese population formation. Studies of ancient genomes have also shown regional differences in admixture between Jomon-related and migrant-related groups during the Yayoi period, followed by increasing homogenization across the archipelago during the Kofun period. Kinship analysis of Kofun individuals provides new insights into burial practices, family relationships, and social structure. This presentation will introduce ancient genomic analysis, focusing on target capture, and review findings on Japanese population formation. It will also discuss integrating genomics with archaeology, physical anthropology, and isotope analysis to reconstruct ancient mobility and social organization.
LS8: Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) is an ultra-rare premature aging disorder caused by LMNA variants that lead to the production of progerin or other abnormal prelamin A species. HGPS has traditionally been regarded as a childhood-onset disorder, meanwhile a broad clinical spectrum has been recognized. Disease severity appears to be determined by the molecular structure of progerin, the extent of aberrant splicing, the amount of the abnormal Lamin A. Notably, a Japanese patient with LMNA c.1868C>G (p.Thr623Ser), which produces prelamin AΔ35, exhibited milder phenotype, whereas other variants with remarkable increase of progerin caused neonatal progeria. Further support comes from somatic rescue, in which a secondary mutation reduces pathogenic splicing, demonstrating that even partial correction of abnormal Lamin A production can modify disease severity. The naturally occurring mild phenotypes therefore provide biological proof of concept for therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing the burden of pathogenic Lamin A. Lonafarnib reduces progerin toxicity by inhibition of farnesylation and is expected to delay vascular disease and prolong survival.
LS9-1: In hereditary neuromuscular diseases, disease-modifying therapies are being developed. With these therapeutic advances, presymptomatic genetic testing has become increasingly important for early intervention. In our previous nationwide survey in Japan, hereditary ATTR amyloidosis was the disorder for which presymptomatic genetic testing was most frequently performed following the introduction of disease-modifying therapies, with a testing rate of 75.2%. Clinical research targeting the presymptomatic stage is also underway. In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, an ongoing study is evaluating the efficacy of presymptomatic administration of the antisense oligonucleotide in individuals carrying SOD1 variants. Along with these developments, in 2025, the Japanese society of neurology published the “Guidelines for presymptomatic genetic testing for adult-onset hereditary neuromuscular diseases in Japan.” The guidelines are intended for use not only in clinical practice but also in clinical research settings. They provide 45 recommended items organized into three phases: pre-testing, test performing, and describing the results and post-testing. However, the guidelines emphasize that the need for each recommended item may vary among clients and should therefore be determined based on an assessment of each client’s individual situation, with care taken to ensure that the guidance itself does not disadvantage clients. This presentation will provide an overview of presymptomatic genetic testing and genetic counseling for hereditary neuromuscular diseases.
LS9-2: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurological disease characterized by generalized muscle weakness caused by motor neuron degeneration. Although several treatments are available, their efficacy remains limited, emphasizing the need for therapies targeting the underlying cause. Familial ALS accounts for 5–10% of all cases, and mutations of superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) gene are identified in approximately one-third of familial cases in Japan. Most SOD1-associated ALS (SOD1-ALS) shows autosomal dominant inheritance and is thought to result from a toxic gain of function of mutant SOD1 rather than loss of its normal activity. Reducing mutant SOD1 expression may therefore offer a disease-modifying treatment. Tofersen (Qalsody®) is an antisense oligonucleotide that binds to SOD1 mRNA, promotes its degradation, and decreases SOD1 protein production. Its efficacy and safety have been evaluated in the international Phase III VALOR trial since 2019, with participation from Japan. Tofersen was approved in Japan in December 2024 and is now available under health insurance. This seminar will review the clinical features of SOD1-ALS and present patients treated with tofersen at our institution. We will also discuss its clinical efficacy, safety, and practical considerations based on our experience and published evidence.
LS10: Long-read sequencing has long held promise for rare disease diagnosis, but clinical implementation has been constrained by cost, turnaround time, sequencing accuracy, and the complexity of interpretation. Recent advances, particularly major improvements in sequencing accuracy, are progressively changing this landscape and making practical clinical use increasingly feasible. As accuracy improves, long-read sequencing can reveal diagnostic information that remains difficult to resolve with conventional short-read approaches. This presentation reviews how historical technical limitations restricted the clinical value of long-read sequencing and how cumulative advances are enabling a transition from research use toward clinical implementation. Using an exceptionally rare case, we demonstrate the value of integrated long-read analysis, with particular focus on repeat contraction, structural variation, phasing, and DNA methylation abnormalities. We do not propose long-read whole-genome sequencing as a universal first-line test. Rather, we consider it an advanced complementary approach for unresolved cases in which conventional testing fails to yield a diagnosis. Through this experience, we aim to illustrate how technologies once difficult to implement clinically are becoming practical diagnostic tools, expanding the possibilities for rare disease diagnosis.
LS11-1: The introduction of disease-modifying therapies and newborn screening has dramatically changed the motor developmental trajectory of patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). In particular, diagnosis and treatment before or shortly after symptom onset have enabled many affected children to achieve motor milestones that were rarely observed in the natural history of the disease. However, as survival and motor outcomes improve, new challenges are emerging, including long-term motor management, musculoskeletal complications, and the need to establish optimal rehabilitation strategies. Our experience in caring for patients with SMA, whether identified through newborn screening or diagnosed after symptom onset, has highlighted the importance of multidisciplinary follow-up, including early attention to scoliosis and other musculoskeletal problems. At Kobe University, pediatricians, rehabilitation physicians, and physical therapists hold regular multidisciplinary meetings to discuss the long-term management of children with neuromuscular disorders, including SMA, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy, as well as other neuromuscular diseases and inherited metabolic disorders. We are also exploring how best to collaborate with rehabilitation professionals in the community. In this presentation, I will discuss the remaining challenges in long-term SMA care, the importance of multidisciplinary and regional collaboration, and the clinical questions for which further evidence is still needed.
LS11-2: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severe, progressive hereditary neuromuscular disease caused by variants in the DMD gene. Delandistrogen moxeparvovec (Elevidys®), a non-replicating recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) vector-based gene therapy expressing a functional micro-dystrophin, was approved in Japan in 2025 and entered clinical practice in 2026. In Japan, eligibility is restricted to ambulatory patients aged 3 to under 8 years who test negative for anti-AAVrh74 antibodies, excluding specific genetic variants. While representing a promising therapeutic option, efficacy data from clinical trials remain limited. Furthermore, severe adverse events, including hepatotoxicity, immune-mediated myositis, and myocarditis, as well as fatal acute liver failure, have been reported. In real-world clinical practice, determining treatment eligibility requires a holistic evaluation that incorporates medical indications, predictable safety risks, and patient/family values, alongside multidisciplinary collaboration across cardiology, hepatology, and intensive care. In addition, informed decision-making with patients/families is paramount. To ensure appropriate candidate evaluation, rigorous safety management, long-term follow-up, and systematic collection of real-world effectiveness and safety data, administration of Elevidys® in Japan is restricted to 13 designated facilities accredited by the Japanese Society of Child Neurology. Here, we report the practical experiences and challenges of DMD gene therapy at our center alongside current evidence and clinical data.
LS12-1: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an inherited neuromuscular disorder primarily caused by deletion or mutation of the SMN1 gene and is characterized by progressive muscle weakness and atrophy. In recent years, newborn screening (NBS) for SMA has been implemented in many regions of Japan, enabling presymptomatic diagnosis and earlier initiation of treatment. In parallel, the development and approval of multiple disease-modifying therapies over the past decade have dramatically transformed the management of pediatric SMA. While these advances have substantially improved patient outcomes, new challenges have emerged, highlighting the growing importance of comprehensive long-term care, including the maintenance of motor function and the management of scoliosis, respiratory complications, and nutritional issues. In this lecture, we will review the pathophysiology of SMA and trace the evolution of pediatric SMA treatment from the past to the present, focusing on how novel therapies and the expansion of NBS have reshaped the clinical landscape. We will then look toward the future of SMA treatment, drawing on accumulated evidence and clinical experience with systemic onasemnogene abeparvovec to explore the evolving potential of gene replacement therapy, including novel routes of administration, in pediatric SMA.
LS12-2: In recent years, several disease-modifying therapies have been developed for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), expanding treatment options across pediatric and adult populations. Advances in early diagnosis and early intervention improve patient outcomes, whereas treatment goals in patients with SMA are diverse, depending on patient backgrounds such as individual’s disease severity and life stage. Consequently, long-term treatment strategies and appropriate methods for treatment assessment have become increasingly important in SMA care. In this lecture, I will review the evolution of SMA treatment and share insights into the clinical challenges and unmet medical needs that emerge with the advent of therapy. I will also present the characteristics and evidence of efficacy of intrathecal onasemnogene abeparvovec, which was launched this year, and discuss treatment strategies and perspectives for adult with SMA.
LS13-1: Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (MPS II) is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the IDS gene, resulting in iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency and accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfates. In severe MPS II, developmental stagnation and neurological regression emerge in early childhood, when CNS disease may already be progressing. In Japan, expanded newborn screening (eNBS) provides an opportunity to identify MPS II before symptoms appear.
