Biochemical and genetic testing can establish the diagnosis, while genotype, family history, and clinical findings help guide follow-up and treatment timing. This shift toward earlier diagnosis is particularly important in severe MPS II, where intervention before neurological regression may offer the greatest opportunity to preserve neurodevelopment. Intravenous enzyme replacement therapy improves systemic manifestations but has limited effects on CNS disease because the enzyme does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Intracerebroventricular enzyme replacement therapy enables direct delivery of enzyme to the CNS. At our center, we combine this approach with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation to address both CNS and systemic disease, including in patients with severe MPS II identified through eNBS. Our experience highlights the importance of linking early genetic diagnosis to CNS-directed treatment. MPS II care is shifting from treatment after symptom onset toward earlier diagnosis and intervention before neurological regression becomes established.
LS13-2: Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (MPS II) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase, resulting in accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. In addition to systemic manifestations such as joint contractures, skeletal deformities, hepatosplenomegaly, and valvular heart disease, approximately 70% of patients develop central nervous system (CNS) manifestations, including developmental delay and neuronal regression. Intravenous enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) can improve systemic manifestations; however, it has limited effects on CNS manifestations. To address this limitation, we developed intra-cerebroventricular enzyme replacement therapy (ICV-ERT). Six patients with neuronopathic MPS II joined in the investor-initiated clinical trial. They received 30 mg (2 mL) of idursulfase beta every 4 weeks using a cerebrospinal fluid reservoir. The three patients who initiated ICV treatment at ≤3 years of age showed sustained increases in developmental age. Idursulfase beta for ICV administration was approved in January 2020 and is currently administered to more than 40 patients. Four patients who started the combination therapy of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and ICV-idursulfase beta at ≤1 years of age, showed continuous increase of developmental age. All four patients showed age-appropriate development until 60,48,39,20 months old, respectively. This is the first demonstration in the world showing treatment of CNS manifestation is achievable by ICV-ERT using idursulfase beta in neuronopathic MPSII.
SW1-1: Chromosomal microarray testing (CMT) is a powerful tool to detect copy number variations (CNVs); however, we sometimes experience complex findings that cannot be explained by simple deletions or duplications. Since CMT can only detect the existence of CNVs, actual genomic structures of them cannot be detected. Cytogenetic techniques—specifically FISH—can be used to verify structural details in cases involving, for instance, subtelomeric translocations. However, confirmation via FISH is difficult when the regions involved are not amenable to commercial FISH testing or when the CNVs affect very small genomic segments. In such cases, nanopore long-read DNA sequencing has advantages. CMT results initially interpreted as three independent deletions or as a duplication superimposed on another duplication were actually complex structural abnormalities resulting from processes such as chromothripsis or chromoanasynthesis. Conversely, nanopore long-read DNA sequencing also can be used to detect cryptic structural changes in the non-coding regions. In cases where possible candidate genes were narrowed down based on characteristic clinical symptoms but no single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) were found through whole exome sequencing, nanopore long-read DNA sequencing may detect genomic alterations in the deep intronic regions. Here, we present cases in which nanopore long-read DNA sequencing successfully identified the structural abnormalities responsible for the disease.
SW1-2: Short-read RNA-seq is well suited to gene-level quantification, but its limited read length cannot directly determine which exons are joined on the same molecule. As a result, reconstruction of complex alternative splicing, novel isoforms, fusion transcripts, and allele-specific isoform usage relies on inference, complicating the interpretation of splicing defects relevant to rare disease. Oxford Nanopore long reads can sequence nearly full-length cDNA or native RNA and thereby resolve transcript structure at the single-molecule level. We will present recent advances in Nanopore transcriptome sequencing that enable isoform identification and quantification as well as fusion-gene detection, and compare the results with those of an alternative long-read platform. This approach enables direct assessment of how complex genomic structural variants affect RNA transcripts.
SS-C1: Under the Program for the Integrated Use of Health and Medical Research Data, AMED promotes the use of data generated through AMED-funded research in accordance with government policy. Since FY2024, the program has provided a pre-research service for genomic and omics data, enabling researchers to review data overviews and explore potential research opportunities. Beginning in FY2027, the program plans to expand data use to clinical research data, including imaging data related to dementia. Three projects have been selected through an open call, and MRI, PET, and SPECT imaging data from more than 2,500 cases will be made available, covering a broad spectrum from preclinical stages and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia and dementia with behavioral and psychological symptoms. The pre-research service will also provide access to more than 350 clinical and related data items, including imaging acquisition parameters, blood and other laboratory test results, and cognitive assessment scores for each case. In collaboration with the selected research projects, we are also deriving features such as brain volume and cortical thickness from brain imaging data and preparing them for use in pre-research. We expect these dementia imaging data to be used not only by dementia researchers but also by experts in data science fields such as artificial intelligence (AI), thereby advancing research and development in drug discovery and medical devices and contributing to the creation of new healthcare services.
SS-C2: This program was conducted over a five-year period from FY2021 to FY2025 under a strategic policy that prioritized the analysis of biological samples to address the needs of both academia and industry. Eight projects were selected, and through the analysis of samples collected and stored in a variety of cohorts and biobanks, the program generated datasets that are readily available for research use. The program focused on common multifactorial diseases, including COPD, atrial fibrillation, chronic heart failure, and diabetes. Using biological samples obtained from the same individuals, researchers performed comprehensive multi-omics analyses, including WGS. These analytical results were subsequently integrated with health and clinical information to establish comprehensive “three-layer datasets.” The resulting datasets have been deposited in AGD, the public database operated by AMED. In addition, the associated metadata have been registered in CANNDs, AMED’s data utilization platform, enabling integrated searches across all projects supported by the program. Because the diseases targeted by this program are common conditions influenced by a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors, the datasets are expected to provide valuable resources for advancing biomedical research. By making these “three-layer datasets” broadly accessible, the program aims to foster participation from researchers across diverse disciplines, promote new scientific insights, and expand the overall research community working toward the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of these conditions.
SS-1: Cardiovascular diseases arise from complex interactions between genetic susceptibility and environmental factors, yet how these influences converge to shape disease development and progression remains incompletely understood. Recent advances in genomics and multi-omics technologies provide an opportunity to move beyond the identification of disease-associated genes toward a comprehensive understanding of disease mechanisms at cellular and tissue levels. We have integrated large-scale human genomic data with transcriptomic, epigenomic, single-cell, and spatial omics analyses to investigate the molecular basis of cardiovascular diseases, including atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, and heart failure. These approaches reveal that cellular mechanisms underlying genetic susceptibility may differ from those driving pathological tissue remodeling and disease progression. By resolving cell-type-specific regulatory programs and interactions among diverse cardiac cell populations, integrated multi-omics analyses provide new insights into how genetic and acquired factors contribute to disease heterogeneity. This framework enables a shift from disease classification based primarily on clinical phenotypes toward molecularly defined disease endotypes, providing a foundation for patient stratification and the development of mechanism-based precision cardiovascular medicine.
SS-2: The National Center Biobank Network (NCBN) is a collaborative framework connecting six National Centers in Japan, each operating a disease-oriented biobank. NCBN collects and manages high-quality biospecimens and associated clinical information across a wide range of diseases, providing valuable resources for biomedical research and genomic medicine. To establish a large-scale genomic reference dataset for the Japanese population, NCBN conducted whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of 9,850 individuals from five participating biobanks. The resulting dataset provides comprehensive information on genetic variation in the Japanese population and serves as an important control resource for studies of rare diseases and cancer. The data have been utilized in collaborative research projects, including investigations of population genetic diversity and disease-associated variants. To further promote the utilization of these genomic resources, the AMED Genome group sharing Database (AGD), operated by the DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ), provides a platform for controlled access to individual-level genomic data. Sharing NCBN genomic data through AGD is expected to facilitate broader research access while ensuring appropriate data governance and protection of participant privacy. In this presentation, I will introduce the activities of NCBN, highlight the current utilization of its WGS dataset, and discuss ongoing efforts and challenges in establishing a sustainable framework for genomic data sharing.
SS-3: BioBank Japan (BBJ) supports research on common diseases through biospecimens and clinical and genomic data from approximately 270,000 patients. For CANNDS, BBJ selected 6000 participants to serve as controls for cancer/rare diseases, aiming for balanced representation across Japan's 47 prefectures. Their genomic data have been used by many researchers and are being analyzed as a reference resource for the Japanese population such as imputation panel. To ensure sustainable access, BBJ revised its data management framework in 2026. Whole-genome sequencing data are stored on the supercomputer, SHIROKANE, at the University of Tokyo, and access applications are reviewed by the BBJ Sample and Data Access Committee. This framework supports continued use of the CANNDS resource. BBJ is also preparing to introduce a Trusted Research Environment to enable secure data analysis and research collaboration while respecting consent restrictions and protecting personal information. BBJ also contributes to the Japan Mega Biobank and Cohort Consortium (JAMBO), launched in 2026. JAMBO brings together approximately 30 biobanks and cohorts, covering around 1.5 million participants. Its activities include harmonizing clinical and genomic data and developing pilot studies on the allergic march and age-dependent genetic effects on height, weight, and BMI. These efforts will connect disease biobanks with population and birth cohorts to advance life-course research. This presentation reviews CANNDS data use and outlines these ongoing activities.
